### [1] [Didactic knowledge or Clinical Cases? How Data Types Shape Medical Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22161)
*Yuzheng Fan,Haochun Wang,Sendong Zhao,Xiao Han,Ming Ma,Bing Qin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Medical LLMs trained on different data types (didactic vs clinical) show asymmetric performance: clinical data improves clinic-oriented tasks while remaining good on knowledge tasks, while didactic data mainly boosts knowledge tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Medical LLMs are typically trained on mixtures of didactic data (textbooks) and clinical data (patient records), but it's unclear how these different data types differentially shape model capabilities and performance.

Method: Used token-matched experiments varying the didactic-to-clinical ratio to analyze how data composition affects performance, capability profiles, and error patterns across knowledge-intensive and clinic-oriented tasks.

Result: Found asymmetric transfer: clinical data improves clinic-oriented tasks while remaining competitive on knowledge-intensive ones, whereas didactic data mainly improves knowledge-intensive tasks. Modest clinical data yields most gains on EHR-grounded tasks. Optimal mixture ratio varies with knowledge and clinical reasoning demands of downstream tasks.

Conclusion: Medical LLM data curation should be application-driven, with higher proportions of clinical data preferred for reasoning-intensive use cases. The knowing-doing gap suggests improvements in knowledge recall don't reliably generalize to clinical reasoning.

Abstract: Medical large language models are commonly trained on mixtures of didactic data (e.g., textbooks) and clinical data (e.g., patient records), yet how these data types differentially shape model capabilities remains unclear. We address this issue with token-matched experiments that vary the didactic-to-clinical ratio and analyze how data composition affects performance, capability profiles, and error patterns across knowledge-intensive and clinic-oriented tasks. We uncover an asymmetric transfer across task types: clinical data improves clinic-oriented tasks while remaining competitive on knowledge-intensive ones, whereas didactic data mainly improves knowledge-intensive tasks. Error analysis suggests a knowing-doing gap, where improvements in knowledge recall do not reliably generalize to clinical reasoning. We further observe that modest amounts of clinical data yield most of the gains on EHR-grounded tasks, while the optimal mixture ratio varies with the knowledge and clinical reasoning demands of downstream tasks. These findings suggest that medical LLM data curation should be application-driven, with higher proportions of clinical data preferred for reasoning-intensive use cases.

</details>


### [2] [An Affordable AI-Integrated Smart Cane for Multimodal Mobility Assistance of Visually Impaired Users](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22277)
*Ali Akarma,Adeel Ahmad,Toqeer Ali Syed*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: An $88 offline AI smart cane using Raspberry Pi Zero 2W with RGB vision and ToF sensors provides mobility assistance with vibrotactile feedback and audio alerts, achieving 0.82 F1-score with 330ms latency and 2.8W power consumption.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Over 2.2 billion people have visual impairment, but existing white canes cannot detect elevated hazards or provide environmental context. Current AI-assisted navigation systems are expensive, rely on cloud connectivity, and are inaccessible in resource-constrained settings.

Method: The system uses an ultra-low-power Raspberry Pi Zero 2W with RGB vision and Time-of-Flight distance estimation. It employs an INT8-quantized SSD MobileNet V1 model with distance-aware vibrotactile feedback and real-time audio alerts. A multiprocessing architecture isolates sensor acquisition, neural inference, and haptic feedback into independent processes for robustness.

Result: The system achieved macro-averaged F1-score of 0.82 (precision: 0.85, recall: 0.81) in indoor mobility scenarios, with mean end-to-end latency of 330ms and peak power draw of 2.8W. Usability study with 12 participants showed SUS score of 78.5 and positive user perception with enhanced obstacle awareness.

Conclusion: The prototype validates the feasibility of deploying privacy-preserving, edge-native assistive intelligence for cost-sensitive mobility assistance, providing an affordable solution that doesn't rely on cloud connectivity.

Abstract: Visual impairment affects over 2.2 billion people worldwide, yet conventional white canes cannot detect elevated hazards or provide semantic environmental context. Existing AI-assisted navigation systems typically rely on expensive hardware or cloud connectivity, limiting accessibility in resource-constrained settings. This paper presents an affordable (\$88 USD), fully offline AI-integrated smart cane designed for multimodal mobility assistance on an ultra-low-power Raspberry Pi Zero 2W. The system fuses RGB vision sensing with Time-of-Flight (ToF) distance estimation, pairing an INT8-quantized SSD MobileNet V1 model with distance-aware vibrotactile feedback and real-time audio alerts. To ensure operational robustness on constrained hardware, a multiprocessing architecture isolates sensor acquisition, neural inference, and haptic feedback into independent processes with fail-safe sensing support. Experimental evaluation across indoor mobility scenarios demonstrates a macro-averaged F1-score of 0.82 (precision: 0.85, recall: 0.81), a mean end-to-end latency of 330\,ms, and a peak power draw of 2.8\,W. A preliminary usability study with 12 participants (SUS: 78.5, NASA-TLX) demonstrated positive user perception and enhanced obstacle awareness. The proposed prototype validates the feasibility of deploying privacy-preserving, edge-native assistive intelligence for cost-sensitive mobility assistance.

</details>


### [3] [PAANI : On Device Visual Evidence Fusion and Explainable Guidance for River Robot Simulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22353)
*Savio Cardoz,Santhiya Rajan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PAANI: On-device perception-to-guidance architecture for mobile river robots combining YOLO11n detection and MobileNetV3 segmentation with evidence fusion on Arduino UNO Q, providing inspectable guidance for obstacle and water boundary interpretation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mobile river monitoring robots need to interpret obstacles and water boundaries beyond geographic waypoints. On resource-constrained platforms, converting imperfect visual predictions into timely, inspectable guidance is challenging - simple object labels or steering commands don't explain evidence supporting decisions or reliability of that evidence.

Method: PAANI combines YOLO11n detector (trained on 10k WaterScenes images) and custom MobileNetV3 Small semantic segmenter (trained on 1,127 MaSTr1325 images) with timestamp-aligned evidence fusion on Arduino UNO Q. Uses bounded tracking for object persistence and explicit corridor policy combining surface labels, accepted detections, urgency, and mask uncertainty. ROS 2 interfaces connect to Gazebo vessel testbed.

Result: Models occupy 14.817 MB FP32 ONNX. Detector achieves 0.7388 test mAP, segmentation achieves 0.9750 validation mIoU. Pipeline latency: median 467.8 ms, 95th percentile 580.3 ms at 0.5 Hz cadence. System supports inspectable guidance with exposed evidence and policy reasons, though evaluation identified black input misclassification and sampling rate mismatch issues.

Conclusion: PAANI provides an inspectable and reusable edge robotics foundation, clearly distinguishing model accuracy from on-board execution and validated collision avoidance. The architecture enables evidence-based, explainable guidance for river robots despite resource constraints.

Abstract: Mobile river monitoring robots must interpret obstacles and water boundaries that geographic waypoints alone cannot describe. On resource constrained platforms, converting imperfect visual predictions into timely and inspectable guidance is a distinct challenge. An object label or steering command does not explain which evidence supports a decision or when that evidence is unreliable. We present PAANI, an on-device perception to guidance architecture that combines a project trained YOLO11n detector and a custom MobileNetV3 Small semantic segmenter with timestamp aligned evidence fusion on Arduino UNO Q. Bounded tracking supplies object persistence, while an explicit corridor policy combines surface labels, accepted detections, urgency and mask uncertainty. Each final advisory exposes its contributing evidence and policy reasons. ROS 2 interfaces connect the local AI pipeline to a separate Gazebo vessel, localization and control testbed. Training uses 10,000 WaterScenes images for four-class detection and 1,127 MaSTr1325 images for segmentation, including 198 segmentation validation images. The selected FP32 ONNX models occupy 14.817 MB. Detector checkpoint test mAP at 0.5 IoU is 0.7388, while the separately evaluated rectangular ONNX export achieves validation mAP at 0.5 IoU of 0.7367. Segmentation ONNX validation mIoU is 0.9750. A five-minute UNO Q recording produced median and 95th percentile pipeline latencies of 467.8 ms and 580.3 ms at a configured 0.5 Hz cadence. The evaluation also identifies black input misclassification and a sampling rate mismatch that prevents the diagnostic apparent motion estimator from collecting sufficient evidence. These results support an inspectable and reusable edge robotics foundation while clearly distinguishing model accuracy and on-board execution from validated on-water collision avoidance.

</details>


### [4] [Social Influence and the Allocation of Scientific Attention in AI Populations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22408)
*Maxim Chupilkin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AI agents' paper selection patterns change dramatically with social influence, showing decreased volume, increased concentration, and high sensitivity to initial selections in scientific attention markets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI systems increasingly engage with scientific research, there's uncertainty about how human-designed metrics (citations, downloads, popularity lists) affect artificial readers, and how social information shapes AI attention patterns in academic markets.

Method: Adapted Music Lab design to academic attention markets. First experiment: 1,000 AI agents chose from 114 AER 2025 papers, with five independent-choice communities and five social-influence communities. Second experiment: 200 agents across twenty social communities tested how random initial selections affect subsequent choices.

Result: Social-information communities selected 17.2% fewer papers, showed greater concentration of choices, covered only 73 papers (vs 90 independently), and exhibited greater between-community variation. Initial selections raised subsequent selection rates by 45.55 percentage points. Choices correlated modestly with citations and minimally with downloads.

Conclusion: Simple information rules significantly shape AI attention in scientific markets - affecting volume, breadth, and distribution patterns, demonstrating that social influence mechanisms designed for humans have different, sometimes amplified, effects on artificial readers.

Abstract: AI systems are becoming participants in the evaluation and use of scientific research. They encounter citation counts, download statistics and lists of popular articles developed around human readers, but the collective consequences of these signals for artificial readers remain uncertain. This paper adapts the Music Lab design to a market for academic attention. In the first experiment, 1,000 AI agents choose papers from the titles and abstracts of all 114 regular research articles published in the American Economic Review in 2025. The experiment has five independent-choice communities and five social-influence communities, each with 100 sequential agents. Only agents in the social-influence condition observe earlier selections within their community. Agents may select any number of papers. Social-information communities select 17.2 percent fewer papers per agent, concentrate their choices more heavily, and collectively cover 73 papers, compared with 90 independently. Between-community variation is greater under social information. In a second experiment with 200 agents across twenty social communities, randomly assigning papers five initial selections raises their subsequent selection rate by 45.55 percentage points (95% CI: 41.20 to 49.90). Choices have modest correspondence with external citations and little correspondence with download counts. The results show how a simple information rule shapes the volume, breadth and distribution of scientific attention in an artificial population.

</details>


### [5] [Learning 3D biophysical cell properties from 2D images and cell-population statistics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22410)
*Santiago Hernández-Orozco,Hector Zenil*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A framework for inferring 3D cellular properties from 2D microscopy images using only population-level reference measurements, achieving high correlation with ground truth instruments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Inferring 3D cellular properties from 2D microscopy is challenging when reference instruments only provide population statistics rather than individual cell labels. Traditional methods require paired single-cell measurements, which aren't available when only population aggregate data exists.

Method: Population-supervised framework with shared local inference, biophysically structured decoder for volume and hemoglobin, learned instance weighting, device-specific calibration, and formal theoretical analysis of identifiability conditions for aggregate observations.

Result: Achieved Pearson correlations of 0.86-0.98 against Sysmex analyser using dataset of 390 specimens and 1,105 acquisitions across six devices, demonstrating reliable inference of cellular biophysics from 2D images.

Conclusion: Provides a testable framework for inferring 3D cellular biophysics from 2D images using population supervision without claiming explicit 3D reconstruction, addressing the fundamental challenge of mapping individual 2D observations to 3D properties using only aggregate references.

Abstract: Inferring 3D cellular properties from 2D microscopy is difficult when a reference instrument reports only population statistics rather than labels for individual cells. Here we develop a population-supervised framework that maps single 2D red-cell images to latent biophysical quantities and aggregates them to mean corpuscular volume, red-cell distribution width and mean corpuscular haemoglobin. The model combines shared local inference, a biophysically structured decoder for volume and haemoglobin, learned instance weighting and device-specific calibration. We formalise conditions under which aggregate observations identify restricted instance predictors, show why population agreement does not by itself identify single-cell properties or 3D geometry, and derive the dispersion penalty induced by subset mean matching. The development dataset comprises 390 specimens and 1,105 acquisitions across six devices, with reported Pearson correlations of 0.86--0.98 against a Sysmex analyser. The framework provides a testable route from 2D images and population supervision to 3D cellular biophysics without claiming explicit 3D reconstruction.

</details>


### [6] [AutoGym: Blueprint-First Generation of Verifiable Agent Gyms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22592)
*Aarati Andrea Noronha,Kavya Ravikumar,Carly Xiaoyu Lin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AutoGym is an automated framework that generates complete reinforcement learning environments (gyms) with tasks, executable environments, and verifiers from minimal domain seeds or prior trajectories, using blueprint-first generation, explicit difficulty controls, and active curriculum synthesis to create challenging benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current RL gym construction is manual, expensive, and static. Existing task sets saturate as models improve and suffer from contamination issues. Synthetic generation methods produce tasks with only cosmetic difficulty that strong models can solve despite convoluted phrasing, and verification relies on unreliable LLM judges.

Method: AutoGym introduces three key mechanisms: (1) Blueprint-first generation that specifies solution space, environment requirements, and verification criteria before environment materialization, ensuring solvability; (2) Explicit generation parameters to control task topology, interaction depth, capability axes, obfuscation, and distractors; (3) Active curriculum synthesis that adjusts parameter distributions based on model performance evolution.

Result: AutoGym successfully generates gyms across productivity and temporal-reasoning settings that span the capability spectrum, including instances that challenge frontier models. The framework can create benchmarks that evolve with model capabilities.

Conclusion: AutoGym addresses the limitations of current RL gym construction by providing an automated, scalable approach to generate challenging and evolving benchmarks. The blueprint-first approach ensures meaningful difficulty, explicit parameters enable fine-grained control, and active curriculum synthesis allows the benchmarks to adapt as models improve.

Abstract: Training agents with reinforcement learning requires a gym, comprising a task, an executable environment in which the task can be attempted, and a verifier that reliably distinguishes success from failure. Constructing such gyms remains manual, expensive, and static. Task sets saturate as models improve and are increasingly exposed to contamination. Synthetic generation offers scale, but single-pass synthesis produces tasks whose difficulty is largely cosmetic. Models comparable in capability solve them despite convoluted phrasing, and correctness must be adjudicated post-hoc by unreliable LLM judges. We present AutoGym, a framework that generates complete gyms (tasks, executable environments, and verifiers) from a minimal domain seed or prior model trajectories. AutoGym introduces three mechanisms. (1) Blueprint-first generation specifies the valid solution space, environment requirements, and verification criteria before the environment is materialized, making solvability a construction prerequisite rather than a property verified after the fact. (2) Explicit generation parameters control task topology, interaction depth, capability axes, question obfuscation, and distractor composition, enabling fine-grained difficulty steering. (3) Active curriculum synthesis uses performance-informed calibration to adjust the distribution over these parameters as model capabilities evolve. Across productivity and temporal-reasoning settings, AutoGym generates gyms spanning the capability spectrum, including instances that challenge frontier models.

</details>


### [7] [Goal-driven Variant Categorization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22475)
*Daniel Calegari,Daniel Amyot*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes a goal-driven approach for process variant categorization using LLMs, where variants are interpreted in the context of predefined organizational goal models instead of relying on structural clustering.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional process discovery yields multiple variants that are typically clustered based on structural similarity, requiring manual interpretation and consolidation into business-meaningful categories, which becomes increasingly difficult as variants grow in number and complexity.

Method: First author an organization's goal model that predefines categorization axis. Transform each variant into textual narrative describing its behavior, then use LLM to interpret the narrative in context of goal model and assign variant to most appropriate category.

Result: Evaluated on three public logs with differing scale and behavioral diversity. Goal-model guidance yields partitions different from unguided induction and responds to controlled edits to declared alternatives, demonstrating LLM-based semantic reasoning effectively connects low-level process behavior with analyst-defined business goals.

Conclusion: Goal-driven approach using LLMs successfully reverses traditional workflow by starting with business goals rather than structural analysis, enabling more meaningful categorization of process variants at the cost of requiring goal model authoring.

Abstract: Process discovery rarely yields a single coherent process structure. For analysis, a common step is to cluster process variants based on structural similarity and then assign business meaning to the resulting groups. Since these partitions are not derived from the organization's goals, analysts must manually interpret and consolidate variants into business-meaningful categories. This judgment-intensive step becomes increasingly difficult as the number and complexity of variants grow. In this paper, we propose a goal-driven approach to variant categorization that reverses this workflow. We first author an organization's goal model that predefines the categorization axis. Each variant is transformed into a textual narrative describing its behavior, and a Large Language Model (LLM) interprets it in the context of the goal model and assigns the variant to the most appropriate category. LLM-based semantic reasoning connects low-level process behavior with analyst-defined business goals. We instantiate this approach end-to-end and evaluate it on three public logs differing substantially in scale and behavioral diversity. Goal-model guidance yields partitions that differ from those produced by unguided induction and respond to controlled edits to the declared alternatives, at the cost of authoring a goal model.

</details>


### [8] [Self-Organizing Agent Teams Learn to Reason Together](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22682)
*Aneesh Pappu,Mirac Suzgun,Yongchan Kwon,Federico Bianchi,Batu El,Mykel J. Kochenderfer,Hancheng Cao,James Zou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AI agent teams can learn self-organizing collaboration strategies from experience, enabling them to solve complex problems that individual agents cannot solve alone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI agent teams rely on fixed protocols, explicit task decomposition, or routing, but human teams adaptively organize their work when solution structures are unknown. The researchers aim to develop AI agent teams that can learn how to organize reasoning and collaboration from experience.

Method: Self-Organizing Agent Teams (SAT): fixed teams of AI agents that learn reusable strategies from prior collaborations to organize roles, conversational phases, participation, and information flow. They enable collaborative computation where agents exchange, challenge, repair, and synthesize partial reasoning.

Result: Across five mathematics and physics benchmarks, self-organizing teams achieved 66.7% accuracy vs. 48.8% for their strongest member. On AIME 2026, they exceeded perfect routing by 13.4 points. Gains strongly correlate with demonstrability (Spearman ρ=0.90, p=0.005), showing teams benefit most when correct reasoning can be recognized.

Conclusion: Organization can become an agent capability: agent teams can learn how to reason together and produce solutions their members could not reach independently. Demonstrability strongly predicts when self-organizing collaboration is beneficial.

Abstract: Collective intelligence depends not only on what team members know, but also on how they organize their work. When the structure of a solution is unknown, useful roles and divisions of labor cannot be specified in advance; teams must learn from experience how to organize reasoning as it unfolds. Human teams routinely adapt this way, while existing AI agent teams rely on fixed protocols, explicit task decomposition, or routing. We introduce Self-Organizing Agent Teams (SAT), fixed teams of AI agents that learn reusable strategies from prior collaborations to organize roles, conversational phases, participation, and information flow. These strategies enable what we call collaborative computation: agents exchange, challenge, repair, and synthesize partial reasoning into solutions no member produced independently. In two independent settings, we learn teamwork strategies that transfer unchanged to unseen benchmarks, using only 15 mathematics and 25 graduate-level knowledge problems. Across five mathematics and physics benchmarks, self-organizing teams average 66.7% accuracy, versus 48.8% for their strongest member, 58.7% for compute-matched inference by that agent, and 59.0% for a perfect router over members' independent answers; on AIME 2026, they exceed this router by 13.4 points. Because gains vary across benchmarks, we ask when self-organizing collaboration helps. Across eight benchmarks, demonstrability (the organizational-psychology construct of whether a team can distinguish correct from incorrect reasoning) strongly tracks improvement over the strongest member (Spearman $ρ=0.90$, $p=0.005$): teams benefit most when correct reasoning can be recognized once it appears. More broadly, these results suggest that organization itself can become an agent capability: agent teams can learn how to reason together and produce solutions their members could not reach independently.

</details>


### [9] [Replication Without Persistence in Hosted LLMs: Measurement Sensitivity in Action-Time Belief Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22478)
*Bhushan Kashinath Joshi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper examines three distinct validation questions for hosted language model evaluations: replication, measurement sensitivity, and persistence, using Regent Chess as a test environment where model performance can be objectively measured against ground truth.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Behavioral evaluations of hosted language models can yield inconsistent results due to variations in the evaluated service, measurement instruments, or both. The authors aim to separate and study three validation questions to understand when and why evaluations might differ.

Method: The study uses Regent Chess, a sequential environment with hidden, mutable state that allows exact recording and scoring of stated beliefs against ground truth. Positive endpoint values indicate worse performance than a matched-uniform comparator. The authors conduct multiple comparisons: replication tests on fresh data, measurement sensitivity tests by rebuilding configurations, and persistence tests across different model identifiers.

Result: The Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite deficit replicates on fresh games (+0.0530, 95% CI [+0.0329,+0.0714]). Measurement sensitivity is demonstrated with a 0.0429 lower endpoint under rebuilt configurations (95% CI [+0.0182,+0.0667]). Persistence tests show reversed performance signs between Gemini 3.1 and Gemini 3.7, with additional serving-period contribution unresolved (-0.0166, [-0.0483,+0.0157]).

Conclusion: Replication, measurement sensitivity, and persistence can yield different conclusions within a single evaluation. This motivates explicit indexing of hosted-model behavioral claims by tested identifier, serving period, measurement instrument, and inference configuration to ensure proper interpretation and comparison of results.

Abstract: Behavioural evaluations of hosted language models can vary because the evaluated service, the measurement instrument, or both differ across runs. We separate three validation questions: whether a prior finding recurs on fresh data under its historical configuration (replication), whether the endpoint changes when the evaluation-and-inference configuration is rebuilt under the same identifier (measurement sensitivity), and whether the finding persists across subsequently tested identifiers under one common instrument (persistence). We study these questions in Regent Chess, a sequential environment in which a hidden, mutable state is recorded exactly, allowing stated beliefs to be scored against ground truth at action time; positive endpoint values mean worse performance than a matched-uniform comparator. The previously reported Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite deficit recurs on fresh games under its historical configuration (+0.0530, 95% CI [+0.0329,+0.0714]). In a back-to-back same-day H/R comparison under the same public identifier, the model-minus-uniform endpoint is 0.0429 lower under the rebuilt configuration (95% CI for the H-minus-R contrast [+0.0182,+0.0667]); all six configuration components vary jointly, so no component is isolated. Under rebuilt R, the prospectively frozen, interleaved same-window 4K comparison reverses sign between Gemini 3.1 and Gemini 3.7, identifiers that differ in release and product tier; additional descriptive and exploratory cells show the same directional pattern. Any additional serving-period contribution remains unresolved (-0.0166, [-0.0483,+0.0157]). Replication, measurement sensitivity, and persistence can therefore yield different conclusions within one evaluation, motivating explicit indexing of hosted-model behavioural claims by tested identifier, serving period, measurement instrument, and inference configuration.

</details>


### [10] [The Wisdom of Artificial Deliberative Crowds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22497)
*Federico Barrera-Lemarchand,Mariano Sigman,Joaquin Navajas*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Large language models can improve collective judgment through deliberation similar to human groups, but only when models are diverse rather than clones of the same model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The wisdom of crowds works well for humans, especially with deliberation, but it's unknown whether large language models can achieve similar benefits through deliberation among themselves.

Method: Adapted a three-stage human deliberation paradigm for use with LLMs from three families. Tested across four domains: visual numerical estimation, peer review of ML papers, detection of malicious AI behavior, and sports forecasting against real prediction markets.

Result: Deliberation reduced collective error beyond passive aggregation of independent responses. Post-deliberation individual judgments retained collective gains. Critically, benefits only occurred with model diversity - homogeneous groups of cloned models didn't improve.

Conclusion: Machine deliberation serves as an effective aggregation mechanism, and model diversity is essential for realizing deliberation benefits in LLMs, similar to human group wisdom effects.

Abstract: The aggregation of many lay estimates often outperforms individual expert judgment, a phenomenon known as the wisdom of crowds. While this is usually attributed to the independence of estimates, an even stronger effect arises through deliberation: averaging the consensus estimates of small deliberating groups outperforms the classical wisdom of crowds, with individual judgments themselves also becoming more accurate after deliberation. Whether these improvements transfer to large language models deliberating amongst themselves is unknown. Here we adapt a three-stage deliberation paradigm previously used with human participants for use with large language models from three different families, and test it across four domains of increasing real-world stakes: visual numerical estimation (Study 1), peer review of machine-learning papers (Study 2), detection of hidden malicious behavior by an artificial intelligence agent (Study 3), and sports forecasting against a real prediction market (Study 4). Across domains, deliberation reduced collective error beyond passive aggregation of independent responses, and post-deliberation individual judgments retained this collective gain. Notably, the advantage required model diversity: groups composed of clones of a single model did not benefit from deliberating. These results establish machine deliberation as a general-purpose aggregation mechanism, and point to diversity as an active ingredient.

</details>


### [11] [AgentRouter: Heterogeneous Model Routing for Cost-Optimal Multi-Step Agentic Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22951)
*Rudrendu Kumar Paul,Sourav Nandy*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AgentRouter is a lightweight classifier for step-level model routing in enterprise agentic systems that reduces inference costs by 72% while maintaining 97.3% of frontier-model quality by dynamically assigning each trajectory step to appropriate model tiers based on subtask complexity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current enterprise agentic systems waste 60-80% of their inference budget by using frontier models for all trajectory steps, even when smaller models could handle many subtasks equally well. Existing routing solutions fail to account for the unique property of agentic workflows where subtask complexity varies widely within a single trajectory, requiring different levels of model capability for different steps.

Method: The authors formalize step-level model routing as a sequential assignment problem over agent trajectories and propose AgentRouter - a lightweight classifier (12M parameters, <5ms overhead per step on A100 GPU) that maps each trajectory step to one of four model tiers using five features extractable at routing time. The system was trained on 50,000 annotated agent trajectory steps spanning planning, coding, research, and data analysis tasks.

Result: AgentRouter achieves 72% cost reduction relative to frontier-only baselines while retaining 97.3% of frontier-only quality (less than 3% degradation in end-to-end task completion). Per-step routing accuracy reaches 91% on minimal-complexity steps and 85% on efficient-tier steps, with 76-82% on harder mid-range and frontier tiers. Significantly outperforms RouteLLM (31% cost reduction) and FrugalGPT (44% cost reduction) by addressing trajectory-level quality dependencies.

Conclusion: Step-level model routing using trajectory-aware classifiers like AgentRouter offers substantial cost savings for enterprise agentic systems while maintaining high quality, addressing the key limitation of existing single-turn routing approaches that ignore the varying complexity within agent trajectories.

Abstract: Enterprise agentic systems that route every trajectory step to a frontier model waste 60-80% of their inference budget on subtasks that smaller models handle equally well. Existing routing solutions optimize single-turn query assignment but ignore a property unique to agentic workflows: subtask complexity varies widely within a single trajectory. A planning step may require frontier-class reasoning while a subsequent formatting step needs only a 7B model. We formalize step-level model routing as a sequential assignment problem over agent trajectories and propose AgentRouter, a lightweight classifier (12M parameters, <5ms overhead per step on an A100 GPU) that maps each trajectory step to one of four model tiers using five features extractable at routing time. Trained on 50,000 annotated agent trajectory steps spanning planning, coding, research, and data analysis tasks, AgentRouter achieves 72% cost reduction relative to frontier-only baselines, retaining 97.3% of frontier-only quality (less than 3% degradation in end-to-end task completion); per-step routing accuracy reaches 91% on minimal-complexity steps and 85% on efficient-tier steps, with 76-82% on the harder mid-range and frontier tiers. On the same benchmarks, RouteLLM and FrugalGPT (applied per-step) achieve only 31% and 44% cost reduction respectively, because their single-turn training signal misses trajectory-level quality dependencies.

</details>


### [12] [Agreement Overstates Evidence: Error Dependence in LLM Judge Consensus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22512)
*Elias Hossain,Niloofar Yousefi,Ser-Nam Lim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM judges exhibit substantial error correlation that significantly reduces the statistical power of consensus, requiring methods to account for shared errors when evaluating AI systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper challenges the common assumption that consensus among LLM judges indicates correctness, noting that LLMs are trained and evaluated similarly and thus can make correlated errors rather than independent ones.

Method: Researchers study error correlation across both open-weight and frontier LLM judges, measure pairwise correlation between judge errors, analyze how dependency affects statistical information, examine different voting methods, and propose using trusted examples to estimate accuracy and identify shared mistakes.

Result: Found substantial error correlation (average pairwise correlation of 0.21) that reduces statistical information from 10 judges to roughly equivalent to 3.5 independent judges. In 28% of comparisons, ignoring shared errors leads to incorrect conclusions about system superiority. Different error patterns affect different voting methods.

Conclusion: Researchers should account for LLM judge error correlation by using trusted examples to estimate accuracy and identify shared mistakes before applying voting methods to new data, as measuring correlation alone is insufficient due to varying error patterns.

Abstract: Consensus among LLM judges is often taken as strong evidence that a decision is correct. This assumes that judges make their errors independently. In practice, LLM judges are often trained and evaluated in similar ways, so they can make the same mistakes. We study how this dependency affects the reliability of consensus. We find substantial error correlation across both open-weight and frontier LLM judges. In our main bank of ten judges, the average pairwise correlation between judge errors is 0.21. As a result, the ten judges only provide roughly as much statistical information as 3.5 independent judges. The dependency is even stronger among the high-accuracy frontier judges we evaluate, including judges from different providers. In up to 28% of our comparisons, ignoring shared errors leads to the conclusion that one system is significantly better, while accounting for them does not. We also find that the pattern of errors matters. Errors shared by most judges and errors concentrated among a smaller group affect consensus differently and favor different voting methods. Measuring the overall amount of correlation alone is therefore insufficient. Our results suggest a simple approach: use a small set of trusted examples to estimate judge accuracy and identify shared mistakes. These shared errors should then be considered when analyzing the results, and the voting method should be chosen using trusted examples before it is applied to new data.

</details>


### [13] [Total Cost of Agency: Exact Attribution of Memory Injection Cost in Multi-Agent LLM Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23790)
*Vivek Kumar Singh,Preeti Priyam,Gautam Bhowmick*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TCA (Total Cost of Agency) decomposes multi-agent LLM workflow costs, revealing memory injection accounts for significant variable costs (up to 27.6% at depth 6), growing linearly with workflow depth and being controllable through retrieval window capacity reduction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current production observability tools obscure memory injection costs in multi-agent LLM workflows - they lump together generated tokens and injected tokens, making this significant cost component invisible to teams. There's a need for accurate attribution and understanding of where costs actually accrue in complex multi-agent systems.

Method: Introduces Total Cost of Agency (TCA) decomposition with five components (base prompt, inference, memory injection, miss penalty, context-accumulation). Uses two-pass, non-billable token counting method that directly measures injected tokens rather than estimating via word-count proxies. Evaluates on 200-task enterprise benchmark against real model APIs, with controlled experiments on retrieval window capacity (32 to 2 entries).

Result: Memory injection accounts for 13.6% of variable cost for compile-time optimization, ~12% of full billed cost, rising from 0% at depth 1 to 27.6% at depth 6. Injected tokens grow linearly with depth (R²=0.9974). Reducing retrieval capacity from 32 to 2 entries lowers injected tokens by 28.7% with negligible accuracy impact. Graph-rewriting transforms are cost-neutral, and workflow cost is dominated by model tier assignment.

Conclusion: Memory injection represents a significant and controllable cost component in multi-agent LLM workflows that grows with system depth. The TCA framework enables better cost visibility and optimization opportunities, though overall workflow cost remains primarily determined by model tier selection.

Abstract: Every node in a multi-agent large language model (LLM) workflow retrieves context from memory and injects it into its prompt, where those injected tokens are billed as input tokens at the same per-token price as the system prompt and the user query. Production observability tools report total token cost but do not separate the tokens a node generates from the tokens it is handed, so this component of the bill is invisible to the teams paying it. We introduce the Total Cost of Agency (TCA), a decomposition of multi-agent workflow cost into base prompt, inference, memory injection, miss penalty and context-accumulation components, and an exact attribution method: a two-pass, non-billable token count that measures injected tokens directly rather than estimating them from word-count proxies. On a 200-task enterprise benchmark executed against real model APIs, memory injection accounts for 13.6 percent of the variable cost a compile-time optimizer can act on, about 12 percent of the full billed cost, and its share rises from a structural zero at workflow depth one to 27.6 percent at depth six. Injected tokens grow linearly with depth over the measured range (R^2 = 0.9974, depths two through six); a quadratic fit yields a negative leading coefficient, so the data do not exhibit convex growth at these depths. We show the component is controllable at fixed model tier: reducing the retrieval window capacity from 32 to 2 entries lowers injected tokens by 28.7 percent with an accuracy change within seed-level variation. We report in full that our graph-rewriting transforms are approximately cost-neutral in isolation, that two of the five decomposition terms are zero by construction in this harness, and that total workflow cost is dominated by model tier assignment, which we hold fixed and treat as prior work. Prompt caching is not evaluated; all figures are for the uncached case.

</details>


### [14] [IntLawNER: A Named Entity Recognition Dataset and Benchmark in International Law](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22529)
*Genis Skura,Roland Bouffanais,Didier Wernli*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: IntLawNER introduces the first NER dataset for international law with 2,987 sentences annotated with 7 entity types, created via a hybrid pipeline combining algorithmic filtering, LLM vetting, and human review, achieving 89.6% silver-to-gold retention and revealing limitations of existing NER models on domain-specific legal texts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: International law texts lack token-level NER resources despite being crucial for state coordination, armed conflict regulation, and human rights protection, creating a gap in computational legal analysis tools.

Method: A cost-effective hybrid algorithmic-agentic pipeline: candidate retrieval from 468k sentences, LLM-based vetting, human review to create 2,987 gold-annotated sentences with 7 institution-specific entity types. Used multiple benchmark models including zero-shot GLiNER, fine-tuned transformers, and few-shot LLMs.

Result: Zero-shot GLiNER performed poorly (0.243 micro-F1) on institution-dependent entities, fine-tuned transformers struggled with rare labels, while carefully selected few-shot examples improved all LLMs, with Claude Opus 4.6 achieving 0.873 micro-F1. Human-machine agreement metrics were misleading: high Cohen's kappa (0.964) masked lower macro-F1 (0.753) when considering missing entities and boundary errors.

Conclusion: IntLawNER fills a critical resource gap for international law NER, demonstrating that domain-specific legal entities require careful annotation and evaluation, with few-shot prompting on carefully curated examples proving most effective for institutional entity extraction.

Abstract: International law provides the normative framework through which states coordinate action, regulate armed conflict, and protect human rights, yet its texts remain without token-level named entity recognition (NER) resources. We introduce IntLawNER, a NER dataset and benchmark for codified sources of international law, covering 2,987 gold-annotated sentences and 8,094 entity spans from International Court of Justice (ICJ) decisions, UN Security Council resolutions, and European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) judgments, annotated with seven institution-specific entity types. We construct IntLawNER with a cost-effective hybrid algorithmic-agentic pipeline that reduces 468k source sentences to a compact annotation set through candidate retrieval, LLM-based vetting, and human review, with 89.6% of gold spans accepted unchanged from the silver layer. However, the silver-to-gold analysis reveals that human-machine aggregate agreement metrics can be misleading in domain-specific NER: Cohen's kappa=0.964 on boundary-matched spans masks a macro-F1 of 0.753 when missing entities, boundary errors, and label corrections are included. The benchmark shows that zero-shot span-based GLiNER collapses on entity types dependent on institutional function rather than surface form (0.243 micro-F1), while fine-tuned transformers struggle on rare labels. Carefully selected few-shot examples that demonstrate label contrasts improve every LLM over zero-shot prompting, with Claude Opus 4.6 reaching the best score of 0.873 micro-F1. We release IntLawNER as a benchmark and reusable resource for extracting references in international legal texts.

</details>


### [15] [EvidenT: Building Trustworthy Enterprise Assistants through Evidence Groundedness and Traceability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22537)
*Anubha Kabra,Katie Jooyoung Kim,Colin Zhiwei Kou,Helene Sajer,Yimei Fan,Radomir Cisar,Heather Greenhalgh,Gabriel Martinez Vidiri*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EvidenT is a lightweight RAG pipeline that verifies extracted evidence against retrieved documents before answer generation to improve citation accuracy and source traceability without model retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprise AI assistants need verifiable responses with traceable source evidence, but current RAG approaches suffer from citation drift (citations pointing to wrong sources), unsupported content, and weak source traceability.

Method: Combines structured passage extraction with deterministic lexical alignment to filter unsupported content, correct citation drift, and preserve source-span traceability. Verifies extracted evidence against retrieved documents before answer generation, without requiring model retraining.

Result: On ~500 real enterprise queries: improves gold-source hit rate by avg 29% over prompting baselines, produces no citations to non-retrieved URLs, achieves near-saturated answer-to-source lexical coverage.

Conclusion: EvidenT effectively addresses citation quality issues in enterprise RAG systems by providing a lightweight, training-free approach that ensures verifiable, traceable responses with improved citation accuracy.

Abstract: Enterprise AI assistants must produce responses that are verifiable and traceable to source evidence. However, retrieval augmented generation (RAG) over heterogeneous enterprise data can suffer from citation drift, unsupported content, and weak source traceability. We present EvidenT (T = Trust + Transparency + Traceability), a lightweight pipeline that verifies extracted evidence against retrieved documents before answer generation, without model retraining. EvidenT combines structured passage extraction with deterministic lexical alignment to filter unsupported content, correct citation drift, and preserve source-span traceability. On approximately 500 real enterprise queries, EvidenT improves gold-source hit rate by an average of 29% over prompting baselines, produces no citations to nonretrieved urls, and achieves near-saturated answer-to-source lexical coverage.

</details>


### [16] [Testing, not presuming, adequacy: calibrating generative social simulators against emergent network structure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24012)
*Tengfei Shao,Chao Li,Xu Wang,Masayuki Goto*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Authors develop a comprehensive protocol for validating generative social simulators that includes identifiability assessment, adequacy checks, diagnosis-guided repair, and held-out audit, demonstrating it on a luxury resale market case.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current validation of generative social simulators often stops at face validity without quantified parameter uncertainty or adequacy checks, limiting scientific rigor.

Method: Proposed adequacy-aware calibration protocol with amortized posterior estimation, synthetic identifiability assessment, matched-sample-size adequacy check (prior-predictive reachability + per-statistic posterior-predictive localization), diagnosis-guided repair, and statistic-held-out audit.

Result: Behavioral parameters recoverable in all four market cells; calibration approximate/overconfident for one parameter; observed data falls outside simulator's reachability in all cells (mean purchased tier as main discrepancy); repair only partially successful; held-out audit revealed new buyer-breadth-dispersion miss; language-model profiles beat flat baseline.

Conclusion: An independent-aggregation account without agent interaction or buyer-breadth mechanism cannot jointly reproduce the market's purchased-tier level, head-brand concentration, community structure, and buyer-breadth heterogeneity.

Abstract: Validation of generative social simulators often stops at face validity: emergent network structure is compared descriptively, without quantified parameter uncertainty or an adequacy check. We present an adequacy-aware calibration protocol that couples amortized posterior estimation with a synthetic identifiability assessment, a matched-sample-size adequacy check (prior-predictive reachability plus per-statistic posterior-predictive localization), a diagnosis-guided repair, and a statistic-held-out audit. We demonstrate it on a real second-hand luxury resale market with four channel-by-residency cells, each a bipartite buyer-brand network, using a forward model built from persona profiles elicited once, offline, by a language model. The behavioural parameters are recoverable in all four cells, though calibration is approximate and overconfident for one parameter. The observed summary falls outside the simulator's reachability reference in every cell, with the mean purchased tier as the pervasive discrepancy. The repair meets the value-block criterion in two of four cells but does not restore adequacy, and the held-out audit surfaces a buyer-breadth-dispersion miss no earlier diagnostic detected. A profile-source ablation finds the language-model profiles beat a flat rule baseline in all four cells, yet within-category brand relabelling causes no consistent degradation, so the profiles are a partially validated input whose value rests on structure, not brand identity. Making no causal claim, we conclude that an independent-aggregation account, without agent interaction or a buyer-breadth mechanism, cannot jointly reproduce the market's purchased-tier level, head-brand concentration, community structure and buyer-breadth heterogeneity.

</details>


### [17] [MAWILE: Multi-Axis Workbench for Inspecting LLM Evaluators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22599)
*Jackson Hassell,Farima Fatahi Bayat,Pouya Pezeshkpour,Estevam Hruschka*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MAWILE is a developer workbench tool for auditing LLM judge sensitivity across four surfaces: judge prompt, rubric, input, and output, measuring both robustness to irrelevant variations and sensitivity to meaningful changes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM judges provide flexible and scalable evaluation but their verdicts are sensitive to incidental changes in evaluated responses, judge instructions, and scoring rubrics. Existing systems only examine subsets of these failure modes, and auditing a configured judge requires testing both the judge instrument and the items it evaluates.

Method: MAWILE constructs and validates controlled perturbations across four surfaces (judge prompt, judge rubric, target-system input, and target-system output), re-executes the judge, and localizes resulting sensitivity. Each perturbation declares whether verdicts should remain invariant or change in specific directions.

Result: MAWILE enables auditing of binary, ordinal, and pairwise judges without requiring gold labels, allowing measurement of both robustness to irrelevant variations and sensitivity to meaningful changes. The tool is publicly available on GitHub.

Conclusion: MAWILE provides a comprehensive workbench for developers to systematically audit LLM judge sensitivity across multiple critical surfaces, addressing limitations of existing evaluation systems by enabling controlled perturbation testing of both judge instruments and evaluation items.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) judges provide a flexible and scalable method for evaluating model and agent outputs, but their verdicts can be sensitive to incidental changes in the evaluated response, judge instructions, and scoring rubric. Existing systems examine important subsets of these failure modes, but auditing a configured judge requires testing both the judge instrument and the items it evaluates. We introduce MAWILE, a developer-facing workbench for auditing judge sensitivity across four surfaces: the judge prompt, judge rubric, target-system input, and target-system output. Given a user-supplied judge and representative evaluation items, MAWILE constructs and validates controlled perturbations, re-executes the judge, and localizes the resulting sensitivity. Each perturbation declares whether the verdict should remain invariant or change in a specified direction, allowing the same system to measure both robustness to irrelevant variations and sensitivity to meaningful changes. MAWILE audits binary, ordinal, and pairwise judges without requiring gold labels. The code for this tool is available at: github.com/megagonlabs/mawile-judge.

</details>


### [18] [GaitVista: Reliability-Aware AI Measurement toward Accessible Longitudinal Gait Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22619)
*Nethmi Jayasinghe,Mihir Parashar,Amit Ranjan Trivedi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GaitVista is a reliability-aware measurement system that intelligently fuses visual (camera) and inertial (IMU) sensor data for gait analysis, using quality-aware gating to improve accuracy by exposing and weighting reliable sensor contributions, reducing errors by 27%+ compared to baseline methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional 3D motion capture for gait analysis is confined to specialized labs, while accessible alternatives using small camera sets and wearable sensors have reliability issues where sensing failures can be misinterpreted as patient progress, limiting clinical adoption of objective gait measurement outside controlled environments.

Method: GaitVista uses a lightweight gating mechanism that assigns joint- and frame-specific contributions based on multiple reliability criteria: camera coverage, local visual quality, cross-modal disagreement between visual and inertial data, and root-motion continuity, exposing these contributions for human inspection and validation.

Result: On TotalCapture dataset with seven sensing conditions, GaitVista reduced average full-body and lower-body error by 27.7% and 27.8%, achieved lowest worst-condition error among fusion methods, and reduced the gap to an oracle from 2.76-5.33 cm to 1.11 cm. On MoVi dataset, it was the only deployable method improving over both unimodal streams, reducing error by 6.4% over strongest baseline.

Conclusion: GaitVista represents significant progress toward accessible gait assessment by addressing reliability issues in multi-modal sensing, though current benchmarks use healthy participants in controlled settings and are not yet validated for clinical deployment, demonstrating a promising approach for objective gait tracking outside specialized labs.

Abstract: Tracking recovery of walking function requires detecting meaningful gait change across rehabilitation sessions, yet objective 3D measurement remains confined to specialized motion-capture laboratories. Small camera sets and body-worn inertial sensors broaden access, but reliability varies across joints and time, allowing sensing failures to masquerade as patient change. We present \textsc{GaitVista}, a reliability-aware measurement layer whose lightweight gate assigns joint- and frame-specific visual contributions using camera coverage, local visual quality, cross-modal disagreement, and root-motion continuity, and exposes them for inspection. Across seven clean and degraded sensing conditions on TotalCapture, \textsc{GaitVista} reduces average full-body and lower-body error by \textbf{27.7\%} and \textbf{27.8\%}, attains the lowest worst-condition error among fusion methods, and reduces the gap to a joint-frame oracle from $2.76$--$5.33$~cm for condition-blind baselines to $1.11$~cm. On MoVi with image-derived keypoints, it is the only deployable fusion method to improve over both unimodal streams, reducing marker-supported error by \textbf{6.4\%} relative to the strongest learned fusion baseline. On TotalCapture, it improves bilateral knee-flexion waveform accuracy by \textbf{18.9\%}. Raw inertial measurements from five TotalCapture participants show location- and time-varying magnetic disturbance, supporting the design's reliability premise. Both benchmarks contain neurologically healthy participants in controlled settings and retain participant-specific IMU calibration; we therefore report progress toward accessible gait assessment, not validated clinical deployment.

</details>


### [19] [Splitting Documents at Lower Cost: Multi-Split Boundary Decisions for LLM-Based Page Stream Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22620)
*Nikhil Reddy Pottanigari,Sepideh Kharaghani,Saverio Vadacchino,Alejandro Posada,Ying Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Multi-Split Boundary Decision (MSBD) enables zero-shot document boundary detection by predicting multiple boundaries per inference call, improving efficiency while maintaining accuracy within optimal window sizes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scanned mail, PDFs, and attachments often come as continuous page streams that need to be split into individual documents for downstream processing. Current zero-shot LLM approaches for boundary detection are inefficient because they require separate inference calls for each potential boundary decision.

Method: Introduces Multi-Split Boundary Decision (MSBD), which predicts multiple document boundaries within a page window in a single LLM call, reducing inference requests. Evaluated across multiple language models, document collections, input modalities (text vs. image), and window sizes.

Result: MSBD reveals a model- and corpus-dependent operating range where it preserves strong segmentation accuracy while substantially improving inference efficiency. There's a sharp decline at larger window sizes. MSBD provides the best overall accuracy-efficiency trade-off, with large windows showing distinct over- and under-segmentation patterns across models.

Conclusion: Multi-boundary prediction can make zero-shot page stream segmentation more efficient when window size is appropriately selected for the target corpus, achieving a strong balance between accuracy and computational efficiency.

Abstract: Scanned mail, uploaded PDFs, and consolidated attachments often arrive as page streams that must be split into individual documents before downstream classification, extraction, or routing. Zero-shot large language models can detect document boundaries without task-specific training, but standard Page Classification (PC) and Boundary Decision (BD) formulations resolve only one boundary per model call. We introduce Multi-Split Boundary Decision (MSBD), which predicts multiple boundaries within a page window in a single call, reducing the number of inference requests. We evaluate MSBD across multiple language models, document collections, input modalities, and window sizes. The results reveal a model- and corpus-dependent operating range in which MSBD preserves strong segmentation accuracy while substantially improving inference efficiency, followed by a sharp decline at larger windows. MSBD provided the strongest overall accuracy--efficiency trade-off, while large windows expose distinct over- and under-segmentation behavior across models. These findings show that multi-boundary prediction can make zero-shot page stream segmentation more efficient when the window size is selected for the target corpus.

</details>


### [20] [Text, Pixels, or Both? Evaluating Input Representations for Multimodal Document QA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22628)
*Nikhil Reddy Pottanigari,Sepideh Kharaghani,Saverio Vadacchino,Alejandro Posada,Ying Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Page images outperform text for document QA when images fit budget, but text is faster/cheaper. A lightweight router using both achieves better accuracy than text alone while reducing latency vs. vision-only.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate the fundamental choice in document QA systems between using page images, extracted text, or both representations, which is rarely studied independently despite being a critical design decision.

Method: Systematically isolates the representation choice while keeping other factors constant (prompt, judge, scoring pipeline). Tests across 4 commercial model endpoints, 2 corpora, and 2 context regimes (gold evidence pages and full documents). Develops a lightweight TF-IDF router that reads only question text to choose between text and image representations.

Result: Page images achieve higher accuracy than text for documents fitting the image budget, but with increasing latency/cost premiums. Text latency stays flat while image latency rises with document length. Representations fail on different questions (19-25% items only one correct). TF-IDF router improves accuracy by 2.6 points over text-only while cutting median latency 30% vs. vision-only.

Conclusion: Neither representation subsumes the other; they show complementary strengths. Lightweight routing can effectively exploit this complementarity to balance accuracy and latency/cost in document QA systems.

Abstract: Every document QA system begins with a choice that is rarely studied on its own: whether to feed the model page images, extracted text, or both. We isolate this choice, holding the prompt, judge, and scoring pipeline fixed, across four commercial model endpoints, two corpora, and two context regimes (gold evidence pages and the full document). On documents that fit the image budget, page images lead on accuracy at every document length on both corpora, but this advantage carries a growing latency and cost premium: text latency stays roughly flat as documents lengthen while image latency rises steadily. Text and images also fail on different questions, with exactly one representation correct on 19--25% of items across the reported cells, so neither subsumes the other. Exploiting this complementarity, a lightweight TF-IDF router that reads only the question text gains 2.6 points over always-text while cutting median latency 30% relative to always-vision, on a document-disjoint held-out split.

</details>


### [21] [Generative Embodied Multiple Behavior Control Systems for Human-like Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22691)
*Chongyu Bao,Haokai Yang,Yuhan Wang,Zhaochong An,Kunpeng Liu,Xiaolan Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A framework combining goal-directed and habitual controllers with an arbiter for balanced human-like behavior, enhanced by keyframe-guided 3D motion generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing human-like agent frameworks primarily focus on modeling goal-directed behavior while overlooking habitual behavior, which plays a crucial role in human daily life. There is a gap in jointly modeling both behavior control systems.

Method: Proposes a human behavior control mechanism-inspired framework with: 1) Habitual Controller that retrieves cue-triggered behaviors from personalized habit memory, 2) Goal-directed Controller using a context-aware world model to predict action consequences and estimate values, 3) Arbiter that dynamically balances both systems based on individual differences and momentary internal states, and 4) Keyframe-guided 3D motion generation module to reconstruct diverse human-level behavior instructions in 3D environments.

Result: Experimental results through extensive evaluation methods, human studies, and ablation studies demonstrate that human-likeness performance is significantly improved by their approach compared to existing methods.

Conclusion: The efficacy of the approach indicates the benefits of leveraging habitual behavior and multiple behavior control system coordination for creating believable embodied human-like agents, addressing the crucial but overlooked aspect of habitual behavior in human-like agent frameworks.

Abstract: An enduring and richly elaborated dichotomy in cognitive neuroscience is that of human behavior control mechanisms, divided into habitual versus goal-directed. While existing human-like agent frameworks primarily focus on modeling goal- directed behavior, habitual behavior has been largely overlooked, though it plays a crucial role in human daily life. In this paper, we address this gap by studying multiple behavior control systems that jointly model goal-directed and habitual behaviors. We propose a human behavior control mechanism-inspired framework which the Habitual Controller retrieves cue-triggered behaviors from personal- ized habit memory, while the Goal-directed Controller employs a context-aware world model to predict action consequences and estimate their values. The Arbiter dynamically balances the influence of both systems according to individual differ- ences and momentary internal states. To reconstruct diverse human-level behavior instructions in 3D environments, we further develop a keyframe-guided 3D mo- tion generation module. Through extensive evaluation methods, human studies, and ablations studies, experimental results demonstrate that human-likeness per- formance is significantly improved by our approach. The efficacy of our approach indicates the benefits of leveraging habitual behavior and multiple behavior con- trol system coordination for believable embodied human-like agents.

</details>


### [22] [Toward Auditable and Calibrated AI for Dementia-Related Crash Severity Prediction: A Selective Deferral Framework to Support Human Review](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22694)
*Gaurab Chhetri,Anika Baitullah,Subasish Das*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents a decision-aware triage framework for dementia-related crash severity prediction that focuses on practical deployment considerations like outcome leakage control, calibration, and selective deferral rather than just classification accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Crash severity prediction models are difficult to translate into public-sector decision workflows when evaluated primarily as ordinary classifiers. There's a need for practical systems that address real-world concerns like outcome leakage, uncertainty calibration, and auditability.

Method: Framed crash severity modeling as decision-aware triage problem with three severity classes (O, BC, KA). Used 4,781 Texas crash records with structured fields and police narratives. Evaluated structured, narrative, fusion, calibrated fusion, BERT-family, and local large-language-model baselines under stratified 70/15/15 split. Implemented selective deferral for uncertain cases.

Result: Leakage-controlled Gemma achieved highest macro-F1 (0.545). Best calibrated fusion model got macro-F1 0.522 with expected calibration error 0.033. Selective deferral improved performance: at 70% coverage, macro-F1 rose to 0.573 and severity cost fell to 0.577.

Conclusion: The study contributes a reproducible, leakage-controlled, and uncertainty-aware evaluation framework for crash AI systems that emphasizes auditability and selective deferral over accuracy alone, making such systems more practical for public-sector decision workflows.

Abstract: Public crash databases increasingly support automated safety analysis, but crash severity prediction remains difficult to translate into public-sector decision workflows when models are evaluated primarily as ordinary classifiers. This study reframes dementia-related crash severity modeling as a decision-aware triage problem in which a system must classify crashes into no-injury/property-damage-only (O), minor or moderate injury (BC), and fatal or severe injury (KA), while also controlling outcome leakage, reporting severe under-triage, calibrating confidence, and preserving every raw prediction for audit. Using 4,781 Texas crash records with structured fields and police narratives, we evaluate structured, narrative, fusion, calibrated fusion, BERT-family, and local large-language-model baselines under a stratified 70/15/15 split. In the reported split, leakage-controlled Gemma obtains the highest observed macro-F1 (0.545; 95% bootstrap CI [0.507, 0.583]). The best calibrated fusion model obtains macro-F1 of 0.522 and expected calibration error of 0.033. Selective deferral improves performance among cases retained for automatic classification. At 70% coverage, macro-F1 rises to 0.573 and severity cost falls to 0.577, while deferred cases are treated as candidates for a proposed human-review process and are not further evaluated in the present experiment. The study contributes a reproducible, leakage-controlled, and uncertainty-aware evaluation framework for crash AI systems, emphasizing auditability and selective deferral rather than accuracy alone.

</details>


### [23] [A Survey on the Linear Representation Hypothesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22695)
*Sewoong Lee,Marc E. Canby,Ikhyun Cho,Julia Hockenmaier*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper critically examines the "linear representation hypothesis" (LRH) across AI, neuroscience, and cognitive science, proposing a more rigorous formalization that makes the hypothesis falsifiable and identifies open problems for future research.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous works have inconsistently treated the linear representation hypothesis as a falsifiable scientific hypothesis, leading to ambiguities in interpreting theoretical and methodological results across AI, neuroscience, and cognitive science fields.

Method: The authors analyze inconsistencies in how LRH has been treated across different fields, propose a more rigorous formalization that makes dependencies explicit (model, representation location, feature definition, evaluation dataset), and establish criteria for evaluating LRH as a falsifiable scientific claim.

Result: The paper demonstrates that claims about linear representations are only well-defined through careful examination of four key dependencies, provides a formalization framework for testing LRH, and identifies non-trivial open problems requiring community attention.

Conclusion: A more rigorous, falsifiable formalization of the linear representation hypothesis is needed that explicitly addresses model, representation location, feature definition, and evaluation dataset dependencies to advance scientific understanding across AI, neuroscience, and cognitive science fields.

Abstract: The term "linear representation hypothesis" (LRH) has appeared across diverse subfields of artificial intelligence, neuroscience, and cognitive science. But previous works have not consistently treated the LRH as a falsifiable scientific hypothesis; we analyze these inconsistencies and examine their implications for how prior theoretical and methodological results should be interpreted. Based on this analysis, we argue that claims regarding linear representations become well-defined only through careful examination of the model, representation location, feature definition, and evaluation dataset. We therefore propose a more rigorous formalization of the LRH that makes these dependencies explicit and allows the hypothesis to be evaluated as a falsifiable scientific claim. Finally, we identify some non-trivial open problems that warrant further attention from the research community.

</details>


### [24] [Building Trustworthy Mental Health Benchmarks on Bluesky: A Validation-Aware Weak-Supervision Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22696)
*Gaurab Chhetri,Anandi Dutta,Subasish Das*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Researchers develop a validation-aware weak-supervision system for constructing suicidal ideation and mental health disclosure benchmarks on Bluesky (a decentralized social media platform), showing performance depends on task definition and validation protocols.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Decentralized social media platforms create new opportunities and challenges for computational mental health research due to distributed responsibilities across technical and governance layers, requiring new approaches for reproducible benchmarking.

Method: A validation-aware weak-supervision system integrating public firehose collection, lexicon filtering, Llama-3-8B-assisted binary annotation, human-adjudicated validation subsets, and transformer-based model benchmarking on Bluesky's AT Protocol.

Result: Constructed two corpora with 8,346 SI-labeled and 9,988 MH-labeled posts; found model performance varies by task and validation protocol, with different weak-label failure modes: SI dominated by false negatives, MH by false positives.

Conclusion: Decentralized social media can support reproducible mental health benchmarking, but only when system design, label provenance, validation strategy, and deployment constraints are evaluated together.

Abstract: Decentralized social media platforms create new opportunities and challenges for computational mental health research because data access, moderation, labeling, and deployment responsibilities are distributed across multiple technical and governance layers. This paper presents a validation-aware weak-supervision system for constructing and evaluating suicidal ideation (SI) and broader mental health (MH) disclosure benchmarks on Bluesky, a decentralized social media platform built on the AT Protocol. The system integrates public firehose collection, task-specific lexicon filtering, Llama-3-8B-assisted binary annotation, human-adjudicated validation subsets, and transformer-based model benchmarking. Using this pipeline, we construct two task-specific corpora containing 8,346 SI-labeled posts and 9,988 MH-labeled posts. The evaluation shows that model performance depends strongly on both task definition and validation protocol. BERT+LSTM achieves the highest SI stratified cross-validation F1-score, RoBERTa achieves the strongest SI holdout F1-score, and DistilRoBERTa achieves the best MH cross-validation F1-score. Human validation reveals different weak-label failure modes across tasks, with SI labels dominated by false negatives and MH labels dominated by false positives. These findings show that decentralized social media can support reproducible mental health benchmarking, but only when system design, label provenance, validation strategy, and deployment constraints are evaluated together.

</details>


### [25] [Hapi: A Multivariable Land-Surface Transformer for Medium-Range Hydrological Forecasting at Continental Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22702)
*Hong Zhang,John K. Hutchison,Rao Kotamarthi,Jeremy Feinstein,Haiwen Guan,Romit Maulik,Vijay P. Ramalingam,Jason Stock,Tom Wall*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Hapi: A U-Net Swin Transformer model for high-resolution (0.05°) 24-72 hour flood forecasts across the contiguous US, outperforming physics-based and AI models in flood detection and discharge prediction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Accurate multi-day flood forecasts at high resolution across continental domains are essential for flood control, water-resource management, and emergency response. This requires capturing both local hydrological details and broader spatial patterns from river basins to synoptic weather systems.

Method: Developed Hapi, a U-Net Swin Transformer architecture using fine 3D patches and hierarchical shifted-window attention. The model forecasts discharge, surface runoff, snow water equivalent, and soil wetness using learned Laplacian task weights to balance variable contributions during training.

Result: Hapi outperformed operational physics-based and state-of-the-art AI models in flood detection using 2024 test data with ERA5-Land inputs. Independent validation at 3,881 USGS gauges and Hurricane Helene case study showed better discharge prediction than physics-based models. Conclusion: Hapi demonstrates superior flood forecasting capabilities through its hybrid U-Net Swin Transformer architecture with learned task weighting, providing fast, high-resolution predictions that could enhance flood management and emergency response systems.

Abstract: Accurate flood forecasts several days in advance are essential for flood control, water-resource management, and emergency response. Producing them at high resolution over a continental domain calls for local hydrological detail together with spatial context extending from river basins to synoptic weather systems. We developed Hapi, a U-Net Swin Transformer that uses fine three-dimensional patches and hierarchical shifted-window attention to forecast discharge, surface runoff, snow water equivalent, and soil wetness across the contiguous United States. The model produces 24--72-hour forecasts at $0.05^{\circ}$ resolution, with learned Laplacian task weights adjusting each variable's contribution to training. On 2024 test data using reconstructed weather and land-surface inputs from ERA5-Land, Hapi outperformed an operational physics-based model and a state-of-the-art AI model in flood detection. Independent validation against 3,881 U.S. Geological Survey gauges and a Hurricane Helene case study supported its advantage over the physics-based model in reproducing daily discharge.
