*Pawan K. Tripathi,Hemant Sharma,Andrew Chuang,Mathew J. Cherukara*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: APEXA is a deployed multi-agent framework that automates synchrotron data reduction (calibration and integration) from natural language at major light sources, featuring execution-integrity enforcement to prevent fabricated results and APEXA-Bench evaluation harness with physical-consequence taxonomy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Synchrotron data reduction (detector calibration + azimuthal integration) is a multi-step, expert-bound bottleneck that limits science rates at user facilities. Current LLM agents can produce fabricated results that appear correct in transcripts but weren't actually executed, creating a critical failure mode not captured by chat benchmarks.

Method: APEXA is a multi-agent framework with 61 tools over heterogeneous compute, run as a single reasoning loop. Key innovation: execution-integrity enforcement with a deterministic tool-layer guard that refuses to surface any result not backed by an executed tool call. Also created APEXA-Bench with 58 facility tasks organized by four-class physical-consequence taxonomy.

Result: The execution-integrity guard prevented fabricated results in deployment (frontier model fabricated calibration reports for commands that never ran, which guard converted to explicit non-result). APEXA-Bench surfaced two latent pipeline bugs through cross-detector grading. APEXA successfully recovered detector geometry and integrated full attenuation/exposure sweep from single natural-language prompt on real beamline data.

Conclusion: APEXA demonstrates practical automation of synchrotron data reduction through execution-integrity enforcement that addresses critical LLM failure modes, with APEXA-Bench providing meaningful evaluation of physical consequences. The framework enables natural-language-driven pipeline automation while maintaining correctness guarantees essential for scientific facilities.

Abstract: Synchrotron data reduction, detector calibration followed by azimuthal integration of terabyte-scale diffraction series, is a multi-step, expert-bound bottleneck that increasingly limits the science rate of user facilities. LLM agents promise to collapse it, but driving a real pipeline with a stochastic model creates a failure mode chat benchmarks cannot see: an agent can report a calibration that was never computed. Correctness here is a property of what executed, not of the transcript. We present APEXA, a deployed multi-agent framework (61 tools over heterogeneous compute, run as a single reasoning loop) automating calibration and integration from natural language at a major light source. We make three contributions. First, execution-integrity enforcement: a deterministic tool-layer guard that refuses to surface any result not backed by an executed tool call, with a parser tolerant of cross-model tool-call format drift: in deployment, a frontier model fabricated a complete calibration-comparison report for commands that never ran, which the guard converts to an explicit non-result; the same code gates an optional motor-control surface at 0/200 adversarial violations against a simulated IOC, versus 15/200 for an equivalent safety prompt. Second, we release APEXA-Bench, an evaluation harness of 58 facility tasks (50 base plus an 8-task cross-detector slice) organized by a four-class physical-consequence taxonomy, the first benchmark axis we know of separating a wasted compute cycle from a damaged instrument; its cross-detector grading against NIST-traceable lattice constants surfaced two latent pipeline bugs. Large-scale agent scoring is left to a full-length study. Third, we validate APEXA on real beamline data: from one natural-language prompt it recovers detector geometry and integrates a full attenuation/exposure sweep. We release the framework, harness and traces.

</details>


### [77] [CREDO: Variance-Guided Rubric Evolution for Replay-Corrected Credit Assignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24174)
*Xuchun Hu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Credo is a framework for language agent training that combines semantic rubrics with selective execution-based credit correction to efficiently handle sparse terminal feedback and improve credit assignment in long-horizon tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon language agents face sparse terminal feedback problems, and while intermediate rubrics provide structured assessments, they can be misspecified. Traditional counterfactual rollouts for credit assignment are computationally expensive.

Method: Credo couples evolving semantic rubrics with selective execution-based credit correction using a frozen judge that maps transitions to rubric features, a credit head predicting terminal reward changes, and two-sided replays with recorded inclusion probabilities to correct prediction residuals.

Result: The framework provides theoretical guarantees (conditional unbiasedness, variance decomposition) and practical implementation guidelines (PPO-based). It includes design criteria weighting prediction errors by policy-score sensitivity and replay coverage, plus cost-aware budget allocation.

Conclusion: This is a preliminary report presenting the method, proofs, audit framework, and evaluation protocol without claiming empirical superiority on benchmarks. It focuses on theoretical foundations and controlled evaluation rather than large-scale empirical validation.

Abstract: Long-horizon language agents receive sparse terminal feedback, while intermediate rubrics provide structured but potentially misspecified assessments of progress. In resettable training environments, counterfactual continuation rollouts can measure local credit, but exhaustive replay is costly. We propose Credo, a framework that couples evolving semantic rubrics with selective, execution-based credit correction. A frozen judge maps visible transitions to rubric features, and a credit head predicts the change in expected terminal reward associated with the realized transition. Independently sampled two-sided replays correct prediction residuals using their recorded inclusion probabilities. We derive conditional unbiasedness and a variance decomposition that connects two design choices: which rubric features to retain, and where to allocate a fixed expected replay budget. The resulting criterion weights prediction errors by policy-score sensitivity and missing replay coverage; its allocation rule additionally accounts for continuation cost. We also describe a practical mixture with terminal leave-one-out advantages and distinguish its clipped, token-normalized PPO implementation from the ideal policy-gradient estimator. This preliminary report provides the method, proofs, an exact finite-model audit, and a controlled evaluation protocol. It makes no claim of empirical superiority on language-agent benchmarks.

</details>


### [78] [LIMIT: Less Is More for Instruction Tuning in Text-to-SQL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24186)
*Haoyuan Ma,Hengwei Liu,Linjuan Wu,Yongliang Shen,Weiming Lu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LIMIT framework achieves state-of-the-art Text-to-SQL performance with less than 1,000 carefully selected samples, challenging the conventional belief that massive instruction data is necessary for effective fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current Text-to-SQL approaches rely heavily on massive instruction corpora, assuming scale drives performance. The paper challenges this paradigm by investigating the fundamental question: what is the minimal data requirement for effective Text-to-SQL instruction tuning?

Method: Proposes LIMIT (Less Is More for Instruction Tuning in Text-to-SQL), a data-centric framework with four stages: 1) difficulty-aware filtering to identify samples within the model's learning frontier, 2) chain-of-thought synthesis with consistency-based selection, 3) multi-dimensional quality scoring via LLM-as-judge, and 4) genetic algorithm optimization that jointly maximizes schema coverage and sample quality.

Result: On BIRD and Spider benchmarks, LIMIT selects only 796 and 863 samples respectively while achieving 100% table coverage, enabling Qwen3-8B to reach 69.1% and 88.9% execution accuracy. This surpasses methods trained on 20 times more data and establishes a new state-of-the-art among open-source approaches.

Conclusion: Careful data curation, rather than scale, is the key to efficient Text-to-SQL learning. The approach demonstrates that strong database reasoning can emerge from an extremely compact training set when examples are strategically selected.

Abstract: Large language models have achieved remarkable progress on Text-to-SQL through reasoning-enhanced fine-tuning, yet existing approaches predominantly rely on massive instruction corpora under the assumption that scale drives performance. We challenge this paradigm by investigating a fundamental question: what is the minimal data requirement for effective Text-to-SQL instruction tuning? We propose LIMIT(Less Is More for Instruction Tuning in Text-to-SQL), a data-centric framework that demonstrates strong database reasoning can emerge from an extremely compact training set when examples are strategically selected. LIMIT operates through four stages: difficulty-aware filtering that identifies samples within the model's learning frontier, chain-of-thought synthesis with consistency-based selection, multi-dimensional quality scoring via LLM-as-judge, and genetic algorithm optimization that jointly maximizes schema coverage and sample quality. On the BIRD and Spider benchmark, LIMIT selects only 796 and 863 samples while achieving 100% table coverage, enabling Qwen3-8B to reach 69.1% and 88.9% execution accuracy.This result surpasses methods trained on 20 times more data and establishes a new state-of-the-art among open-source approaches. Our findings suggest that careful data curation, rather than scale, is the key to efficient Text-to-SQL learning.

</details>


### [79] [SKstars at SHROOM: Visions Agreement-Guided Ensembling of Zero-Shot and LoRA-Adapted Vision--Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24198)
*Ali Athar,Imran Ahsan,Joon-Yong Jung*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A team combined a large zero-shot vision-language model with a smaller fine-tuned model using ensemble methods for fine-grained hallucination detection in multimodal outputs, achieving moderate performance in the SHROOM-Visions 2026 competition.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To develop an effective system for the SHROOM-Visions 2026 shared task, which requires fine-grained hallucination detection in vision-language model outputs, including identifying hallucinated spans, categorizing hallucination types, and providing confidence scores.

Method: Combined zero-shot predictions from Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct with predictions from a LoRA-adapted Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct model. Used lightweight ensemble integration followed by span refinement and confidence adjustment. Evaluated components on internal development subset.

Result: Achieved Cor+Lbl score of 0.2902 (15th/29 teams), Cor score of 0.3642 (18th), and IoU score of 0.3151 (18th) on the official English test set. Showed combination of large zero-shot model with smaller adapted model is practical for fine-grained hallucination localization.

Conclusion: The ensemble approach combining large zero-shot and smaller fine-tuned models provides a practical framework for multilingual fine-grained hallucination detection, though results highlight challenges in transferring development-set improvements to hidden test data.

Abstract: This paper describes the SKstars submission to SHROOM-Visions 2026, a shared task on fine-grained hallucination detection in large vision-language model outputs. The task requires systems to identify hallucinated character spans, assign hallucination categories, and provide confidence estimates for their predictions. Our approach combines zero-shot predictions from Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct with those of a LoRA-adapted Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct model. The outputs of the two models are integrated through a lightweight ensemble procedure, followed by span refinement and confidence adjustment. We evaluate the main system components on a small internal development subset and report the performance of the submitted system on the official English test set. SKstars achieved a Cor+Lbl score of 0.2902, ranking 15th among 29 teams, and obtained Cor and IoU scores of 0.3642 and 0.3151, respectively, ranking 18th on both metrics. The results show that combining a large zero-shot model with a smaller adapted model provides a practical framework for multilingual and fine-grained hallucination localization, while also highlighting the difficulty of transferring development-set improvements to hidden test data. Code and predictions: https://github.com/aliathar1401/SK-Stars-shroom-visions-2026

</details>


### [80] [Recovering Lost Details: Multi-Scale Frequency Compensation for Long-Term Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24229)
*Runmin Zou,Siyi Xie,Yaohui Huang,Yun Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MWMixer is a novel model for long-term time series forecasting that uses wavelet-based multi-scale analysis with bidirectional frequency mixing and dynamic scale fusion to better preserve temporal details while capturing hierarchical patterns.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multi-scale time series forecasting methods lose important temporal details due to downsampling and over-emphasis on dominant trends, resulting in insufficiently expressive representations.

Method: Proposes Multi-Scale Wavelet Mixing (MWMixer) model with: 1) Bidirectional Frequency-Bands Mixing to recover lost temporal details across scales, 2) Dynamic Scale-Adaptive Fusion module with time-varying weights for each scale, and 3) Cross-scale consistency loss and multi-scale supervision loss for consistent learning.

Result: Extensive experiments on seven real-world datasets demonstrate that MWMixer achieves competitive performance in long-term forecasting compared to existing methods.

Conclusion: MWMixer effectively addresses the information loss problem in multi-scale time series forecasting by preserving temporal details through wavelet-based mixing and adaptive fusion, leading to improved forecasting performance.

Abstract: Long-term time series forecasting has made significant progress by leveraging multi-scale information to capture hierarchical temporal patterns and model long-range dependencies. However, temporal downsampling in existing multi-scale methods inevitably smooths detailed temporal fluctuations, and this information loss is further aggravated by their emphasis on dominant trends across scales, resulting in insufficiently expressive representations. To address this, we propose a Multi-Scale Wavelet Mixing (MWMixer) model, which incorporates a Bidirectional Frequency-Bands Mixing strategy to recover lost temporal details across scales, enabling complementary cross-scale information interactions. Then, a Dynamic Scale-Adaptive Fusion module learns time-varying weights for each scale to fuse multi-scale forecasts into the final prediction, enhancing the flexibility of multi-scale aggregation. In addition, a cross-scale consistency loss aligns each coarse-scale prediction with the interval-averaged fine-scale outputs, while a multi-scale supervision loss enforces prediction accuracy at each scale, promoting consistent learning across scales. Extensive experiments on seven real-world datasets demonstrate that MWMixer achieves competitive performance in long-term forecasting.

</details>


### [81] [Taming CoT Obfuscation in VLMs: From Mechanistic Evidence to Activation Enforcement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24243)
*Xutao Mao,Jianing Zhu,Jinman Zhao,Tongliang Liu,Xiaowen Chu,Cong Wang,Bo Han*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RL improves VLMs but can cause CoT obfuscation where reasoning becomes less monitorable; TAME combines SAEs with targeted suppression of template activations to maintain monitorability while preserving accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RL improves reasoning in VLMs but causes CoT obfuscation - where accuracy increases but reasoning traces become less grounded and monitorable. Prior work only documented this behaviorally, leaving representation-level mechanisms and controls unclear.

Method: Found that template- and ground-associated activations become less separable during RL. Proposed TAME: uses Sparse Autoencoders to combine behavioral feedback with targeted suppression of template-associated activations. Asymmetrically penalizes template activations only above pre-RL baseline to anchor localized features while behavioral feedback promotes grounded refinements.

Result: TAME improves CoT monitorability by up to 30.9 and 16.7 percentage points over GRPO on VIRL-39k and SPA-VL datasets. Blinded human evaluation shows higher human monitorability, and held-out monitor families reproduce gains. Task accuracy changes are small/mixed, with task-specific trade-offs on general-capability benchmarks.

Conclusion: Provides a path from behavioral monitoring to representation-level oversight for more auditable RL-trained multimodal systems, demonstrating actionable controls against CoT obfuscation while maintaining task performance.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) improves reasoning in vision-language models (VLMs) but can induce chain-of-thought (CoT) obfuscation: an operational, non-intentional outcome where task reward or accuracy rises while traces become less grounded and monitorable. Prior work largely documents this decay behaviorally, leaving its representation-level correlates and actionable controls unclear. We find that template- and ground-associated activations become less separable during RL; matched interventions support the contribution of selected features to monitorability degradation. Guided by this evidence, we propose Targeted Anti-obfuscation with Mechanistic Enforcement (TAME), which uses Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to combine behavioral feedback with targeted suppression of template-associated activations during RL. Its asymmetric constraint penalizes template activations only above their pre-RL baseline, anchoring the localized features while behavioral feedback promotes grounded refinements. Across VIRL-39k, SPA-VL, and two model families, TAME improves CoT monitorability by up to 30.9 and 16.7 percentage points over Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), respectively. Blinded human evaluation finds higher human monitorability on both datasets, and two held-out monitor families reproduce the monitorability gains. Task accuracy changes are small and mixed, and general-capability benchmarks show task-specific trade-offs. These results provide a path from behavioral monitoring to representation-level oversight for more auditable RL-trained multimodal systems.

</details>


### [82] [Unsupervised Brain Anomaly Detection as a Bayesian Inverse Problem with Diffusion Prior](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24265)
*Hugues Roy,Reuben Dorent,Ninon Burgos*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: UAD-DAPS: A Bayesian inverse problem approach to unsupervised anomaly detection in medical scans using diffusion priors with joint inference of pseudo-healthy images and anomaly masks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current diffusion-based unsupervised anomaly detection methods rely on heuristic noise schedules or synthetic corruptions to balance subject-specificity and anomaly removal, which is suboptimal.

Method: Formulates UAD as a Bayesian inverse problem under a diffusion prior: introduces a latent spatial anomaly mask to model pixel-wise consistency, approximates the unknown generation process linking healthy anatomy and anomalies, and uses annealed posterior sampling to jointly infer pseudo-healthy images and anomaly masks.

Result: Improved anomaly localization performance on FDG PET (ADNI) and FLAIR MRI (BraTS 2021) compared to other diffusion-based approaches, with validation of the proposed model's effectiveness.

Conclusion: The Bayesian formulation provides a principled alternative to heuristic approaches for unsupervised anomaly detection in medical imaging, offering better performance through joint inference of healthy anatomy and anomaly masks.

Abstract: Unsupervised anomaly detection (UAD) aims to localize abnormal regions in medical scans without pixel-level annotations. A typical strategy seeks to reconstruct a pseudo-healthy image that preserves subject-specific anatomy. Recently, diffusion models have been proposed to perform UAD. However, these methods rely on heuristic noise schedules or synthetic corruptions to balance subject-specificity and anomaly removal. In this work, we propose an alternative formulation of UAD as a Bayesian inverse problem under a diffusion prior. First, we introduce a latent spatial anomaly mask that models pixel-wise consistency between a test image and its latent corresponding pseudo-healthy image. Then, we propose an approximation of the unknown generation process that links healthy anatomy, anomalies, and the observed image, enabling a well-defined likelihood within the Bayesian framework. Building on recent advances in diffusion-based inverse problem methods, we jointly infer the pseudo-healthy image and the anomaly mask via annealed posterior sampling. We evaluate our approach on FDG PET (ADNI) and FLAIR MRI (BraTS 2021), demonstrating improved anomaly localization performance compared to other diffusion-based approaches and validating the contribution of our introduced model. Our code is available at https://github.com/HuguesRoy/UAD_DAPS.

</details>


### [83] [How Many Pixels Is a Digit Worth? Place-Aware Coordinate Entropy for GUI Agent Confidence Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24277)
*Yunxiang Li,Xixin Wu,Helen Meng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GUI agents use PACE (Place-Aware Coordinate Entropy) to better estimate confidence in click predictions by weighting digit entropy by place value, outperforming existing methods at lower cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current GUI agents predict click coordinates as digit sequences, but standard text-LLM confidence estimation methods poorly distinguish correct from incorrect clicks. Existing GUI-specific alternatives using K samples or additional supervision still have room for improvement.

Method: Addresses place-value asymmetry in coordinate predictions by weighting each digit's Shannon entropy by its place value, creating Place-Aware Coordinate Entropy (PACE). This captures that higher-place digits in bounding-box coordinates are often more important for correctness than lower-place digits.

Result: PACE outperforms existing methods across fixed-scale agents on ScreenSpot-Pro and ScreenSpot-v2 datasets, achieving better AUROC and selective accuracy on all primary comparisons with a single forward pass. It matches or beats K-sample baselines at a fraction of the computational cost.

Conclusion: PACE provides an effective per-click confidence estimation method that transforms coordinate-token internals into practical confidence signals for GUI agent deployment, offering improved performance with reduced computational overhead.

Abstract: GUI agents predict click coordinates as digit-token sequences, but standard text-LLM confidence estimation methods rank correct clicks from wrong ones only weakly. GUI-specific alternatives use K samples or new supervision, but still leave room for improvement. We trace part of this to place-value asymmetry: bounding-box correctness often makes higher-place digits more important than lower-place digits, so uniform aggregation weakens the signal that determines correctness. The fix is to weight each digit's Shannon entropy by its place value. We call this Place-Aware Coordinate Entropy (PACE). Across fixed-scale agents on ScreenSpot-Pro and ScreenSpot-v2, PACE wins both AUROC and selective accuracy on all primary comparisons in a single forward pass, matching or outperforming K-sample baselines at a fraction of the cost. PACE provides a per-click confidence estimate that turns coordinate-token internals into a practical confidence signal for GUI agent deployment.

</details>


### [84] [When and How Should an Agent Clarify? CIGAsk: Teaching LLMs to Clarify via Counterfactual Information Gain](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24290)
*Yunxiang Li,Xixin Wu,Helen Meng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CIGAsk: An RL approach that teaches LLMs when and how to ask clarifying questions for underspecified queries, using two complementary reward signals without requiring a separately trained critic.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Instruction-tuned LLMs often commit to single interpretations of underspecified queries instead of asking for clarification, producing confidently wrong answers. Prompting alone is insufficient as models either ask clarification on every query or ask vague questions that fail to recover missing information.

Method: Proposes CIGAsk, an RL recipe that teaches two coupled skills within a multi-turn GRPO loop: 1) When to ask rather than answer via Asymmetric Ambiguity Bonus (signed reward at terminal token based on gold ambiguity label), and 2) How to ask clarifying questions that recover disambiguating information via Counterfactual Information Gain (compares gold-answer log-likelihood with and without user response, providing per-turn credit).

Result: CIGAsk-7B outperforms strongest external baselines across three clarification benchmarks spanning table, passage, and open-domain QA, despite using a smaller backbone. It transfers across datasets without per-dataset tuning while preserving single-turn QA performance on out-of-distribution benchmarks.

Conclusion: CIGAsk successfully teaches LLMs to handle underspecified queries through learned clarification skills, addressing limitations of existing methods that either address only one skill or require separately trained critics, achieving effective performance across diverse benchmarks with good transferability.

Abstract: Instruction-tuned LLMs faced with underspecified queries often commit to a single interpretation rather than ask for clarification, producing confidently wrong answers. In our experiments, prompting alone is insufficient: models either ask for clarification on every query or ask vague questions that fail to recover the missing information. Addressing this failure requires learning two coupled skills: when to ask rather than answer and how to ask a question that recovers the disambiguating information. Existing recipes either address only one of these skills or require a separately trained critic. We propose CIGAsk, an RL recipe that teaches both skills through two complementary reward signals within a multi-turn GRPO loop. Counterfactual Information Gain (CIG) compares the gold-answer log-likelihood under a frozen reference model with and without the user response, providing per-turn credit that guides how to ask. The Asymmetric Ambiguity Bonus assigns a signed reward at the terminal token based on the gold ambiguity label, guiding when to ask. Across three clarification benchmarks spanning table, passage, and open-domain QA, CIGAsk-7B outperforms the strongest external baseline despite using a smaller backbone. It also transfers across datasets without per-dataset tuning while preserving single-turn QA performance on out-of-distribution benchmarks.

</details>


### [85] [Brain-Token Learning: Microstate-Based Tokenization and Multi-Scale Interaction for Long-Horizon EEG Sequence Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24324)
*Weishan Ye,Yue Pan,Li Zhang,Gan Huang,Zhen Liang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Brain-Token Learning is a neuroscience-inspired framework that represents EEG sequences as recurrent microstate-derived brain tokens rather than fixed temporal segments, enabling more biologically meaningful long-horizon EEG sequence modeling through multi-scale token interaction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current EEG tokenization methods use artificial temporal boundaries (fixed-window or patch-based representations) that disrupt intrinsic brain-state dynamics. There's a need for biologically meaningful sequence representations that account for high temporal complexity and substantial cross-subject variability in EEG data.

Method: Proposed Brain Tokenization represents EEG as sequences of recurrent microstate-derived brain tokens, where each token corresponds to a quasi-stable large-scale brain state with variable duration. Also developed a multi-scale token interaction module with Latent State Aggregation and State Transition Modeling to capture global brain-state context and local microstate transitions.

Result: Evaluated on five heterogeneous EEG datasets (including NeuroLong, SEED, DEAP, MDD, NSSI). Brain-Token consistently outperformed conventional CNN/LSTM architectures, Transformer-based models, and domain adaptation methods across diverse EEG scenarios. Verified effectiveness of microstate-based tokenization and multi-scale interaction for learning robust and interpretable EEG representations.

Conclusion: Brain-Token establishes a biologically grounded tokenization paradigm for long-horizon EEG sequence modeling, providing more interpretable and effective representations compared to existing artificial temporal segmentation approaches.

Abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) provides a non-invasive window into dynamic brain activity, yet modeling long-horizon EEG sequences remains challenging due to their high temporal complexity, substantial variability across subjects, and the lack of biologically meaningful sequence representations. Existing tokenization strategies, such as fixed-window and patch-based representations, discretize EEG signals according to artificial temporal boundaries, which may disrupt intrinsic brain-state dynamics. In this work, we propose Brain-Token Learning, a neuroscience-inspired framework that introduces Brain Tokenization for long-horizon EEG sequence modeling. Instead of partitioning EEG signals into predefined temporal segments, Brain Tokenization represents EEG as sequences of recurrent microstate-derived brain tokens, where each token corresponds to a quasi-stable large-scale brain state with variable temporal duration. Based on these biologically grounded tokens, we further develop a multi-scale token interaction module consisting of Latent State Aggregation and State Transition Modeling to jointly capture global brain-state context and local microstate transitions. We evaluate Brain-Token on five heterogeneous EEG datasets, including the newly collected long-horizon NeuroLong dataset and four affective or clinical EEG datasets (SEED, DEAP, MDD, and NSSI). Extensive experiments demonstrate that Brain-Token consistently outperforms conventional CNN/LSTM architectures, Transformer-based models, and domain adaptation methods across diverse EEG scenarios. Further analysis verifies the effectiveness of microstate-based tokenization and multi-scale interaction for learning robust and interpretable EEG representations. These results establish Brain-Token as a biologically grounded tokenization paradigm for long-horizon EEG sequence modeling.

</details>


### [86] [LADDER: Graph-Guided Diffusion Language Models for Efficient Multi-Hop Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24346)
*Senlei Zhang,Linhao Luo,Qian-Wen Zhang,Siyu An,Junnan Dong,Shuhao Zhang,Xing Sun*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LADDER accelerates GraphRAG by combining diffusion language models with graph-guided parallel decoding, achieving both higher accuracy and faster inference than autoregressive methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing GraphRAG frameworks rely on standard autoregressive language models with sequential generation, which severely hinders inference efficiency. The authors want to leverage diffusion language models' parallel decoding capabilities to accelerate GraphRAG while handling the challenges of dynamic graph grounding and noisy denoising states.

Method: 1) Event-driven self-clocking retrieval that triggers graph retrieval only when graph-linkable entities expand, based on insight that 88% of target entities emerge early. 2) Incomplete-query graph propagation module that processes emerging entity queries using a specialized graph foundation model to aggregate multi-hop evidence and sharpen parallel predictions.

Result: On three challenging multi-hop QA benchmarks, LADDER raises average exact match from 39.6% to 45.2% while achieving a 4.1x latency reduction compared to existing methods.

Conclusion: LADDER successfully bridges diffusion language modeling with GraphRAG through graph-guided parallel decoding, addressing the key challenges of dynamic graph grounding and noisy denoising states to achieve both improved accuracy and significant inference speedup.

Abstract: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) has remarkably enhanced large language models on complex reasoning by leveraging structured entity topologies. However, existing frameworks heavily rely on standard autoregressive language models where the nature of inherent sequential generation severely hinders overall inference efficiency. Inspired by Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) that offer massive parallelism via continuous refine-in-parallel decoding, we aim to accelerate GraphRAG in the discrete space. However, it remains non-trivial for two challenges. First, partially denoised drafts are highly dynamic and uncertain, making dynamic graph grounding non-trivial. Second, raw denoising states are inherently noisy and unstable, making synchronous graph retrieval and multi-hop aggregation computationally prohibitive. To this end, we present LADDER, a novel framework that bridges diffusion language modeling with GraphRAG through graph-guided parallel decoding. Specifically, (i) we propose an event-driven self-clocking retrieval, inspired by our key insight that 88% of target entities emerge early in the partially denoised state, leading final commitment by an average of 5.7-9.6 steps. This mechanism dynamically triggers graph retrieval only when the set of graph-linkable entities expands, yielding an asynchronous self-clocking policy that bypasses learned gates or heuristic thresholds. (ii) An incomplete-query graph propagation module is designed to process the newly emerging entity queries using a specialized graph foundation model, continuously aggregating multi-hop evidence to sharpen parallel predictions and accelerate overall decoding convergence. Extensive experiments on three challenging multi-hop QA benchmarks show that LADDER raises average exact match from 39.6% to 45.2% while achieving a 4.1x latency reduction.

</details>


### [87] [Few-Shot Demonstrations Elicit the Use of In-Context World Representations in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24352)
*Kohsei Matsutani,Gouki Minegishi,Core Francisco Park,Takeshi Kojima,Yusuke Iwasawa,Yutaka Matsuo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Few-shot demonstrations with different world observations improve LLMs' ability to construct and use internal world representations for downstream prediction tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs acting as agents need to infer latent state spaces from observed data, but prior work shows they struggle with constructing representations of graph structures from in-context demonstrations for subsequent predictions.

Method: Extend the graph tracking task to few-shot settings where each demonstration comes from different worlds with varying graph topologies. Use linear probing to analyze low-dimensional world representations in hidden states that encode graph information.

Result: Few-shot demonstrations improve prediction performance across 6 models from 4 families. They cause world representations to shift in nearly orthogonal directions to original subspaces, and interventions on these representations selectively impair performance more than other interventions.

Conclusion: Few-shot demonstrations enhance in-context world modeling by relocating and increasing the predictive use of world representations. This insight generalizes to ARC-AGI, web agent tasks, and Othello games, advancing understanding of how LLM agents learn from in-context observations.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs), when acting as agents, are expected to take observed data in context, infer the latent state space underlying the world, and leverage it for downstream prediction. However, prior work demonstrated that LLMs struggle to use representations learned in context on a graph tracking task, where the model needs to construct a representation of the graph governing data generation process and use it for subsequent predictions. In this paper, we show that extending this to few-shot settings, where each demonstration is generated from a different world with either the same or different graph topologies, enhances its prediction on 6 models from 4 model families. To understand this improvement, we linearly probe a low-dimensional world representation that encodes graph information in the hidden states. Notably, we find that few-shot demonstrations relocate the world representation and increase its predictive use. Specifically, for each model, these world representations shift in directions nearly orthogonal to their original subspace, and interventions on these representations selectively impair performance more than interventions on other subspaces. Consistent with this insight, we show that few-shot demonstrations with observations from different worlds improve performance on ARC-AGI-1&2, web agent tasks, and Othello. Our findings elucidate the role and internal mechanisms of few-shot demonstrations in in-context world modeling. More broadly, our work advances our understanding of how LLM agents learn from in-context observations and provides implications for their further improvement.

</details>


### [88] [VLM-in-Sandbox: Visual Workspaces for Agentic Visual Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24362)
*Hexiong Yang,Mingrui Chen,Jie Cao,Ran He*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: VLM-in-Sandbox is a training-free framework for vision-language models that separates visual evidence generation from management using a Visual Workspace with image ledger and bounded active context, enabling efficient multimodal reasoning in sandboxed computer environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Extending sandboxed environments from language models to vision-language models creates a state-management problem where visual reasoning produces intermediate image-valued evidence (crops, masks, overlays, etc.) that must remain addressable without accumulating unboundedly in multimodal context.

Method: Introduces VLM-in-Sandbox framework with a Visual Workspace that registers generated artifacts in an image ledger, maintains bounded active visual context, and allows models to explicitly promote selected evidence for subsequent inspection. This separates visual evidence generation (by sandbox tools) from visual evidence management.

Result: Achieves highest sample-weighted average accuracy across 7 benchmarks and 4 base VLMs compared to Vanilla VLM and Append-only Sandbox. In a 2×2 study on 1,260 examples: 66.27% accuracy with 18.6% fewer total tokens than retain-all control. Over 6,350 GPT-4.1-mini examples: 302 rescues and 142 regressions relative to Original Append-only. Also reduces uncached tokens, time to first token, and end-to-end latency in vLLM study.

Conclusion: Identifies explicit visual evidence state as a central abstraction for sandboxed VLM agents, showing that separating evidence generation from management with bounded context improves both accuracy and computational efficiency.

Abstract: Sandboxed computer environments support multi-step reasoning with tools, executable programs, and persistent files, yet their extension from language models to vision-language models (VLMs) introduces a distinct state-management problem. Visual reasoning produces intermediate image-valued evidence---crops, masks, overlays, zoomed regions, and analytic renderings---that must remain addressable without accumulating unboundedly in multimodal context. We introduce VLM-in-Sandbox, a training-free framework for agentic multimodal reasoning in controlled computer environments. Its Visual Workspace registers generated artifacts in an image ledger, maintains a bounded active visual context, and lets the model explicitly promote selected evidence for subsequent inspection. This separates visual evidence generation, performed by sandbox tools, from visual evidence management. Across seven benchmarks and four base VLMs, VLM-in-Sandbox achieves the highest sample-weighted average accuracy among Vanilla VLM, Append-only Sandbox, and the proposed method. A compiler-matched $2\times2$ study on 1,260 examples further separates model-directed visibility from bounded retention: VLM-in-Sandbox reaches 66.27% accuracy with 18.6% fewer total tokens than the automatic, retain-all control. Over all 6,350 submitted GPT-4.1-mini examples, it produces 302 rescues and 142 regressions relative to Original Append-only. A local vLLM study with prefix caching confirms that the smaller request workload also reduces uncached tokens, time to first token, and end-to-end latency. These results identify explicit visual evidence state as a central abstraction for sandboxed VLM agents.

</details>


### [89] [Predicting Postprandial Glycemic Response from Meal Images, Clinical Variables, and Gut Microbiome Information](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24453)
*Varvara Kondratyeva,Kamilia Zaripova,Nassir Navab,Azade Farshad*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A multimodal framework that replaces manual dietary logging with image-derived macronutrient estimates, integrated with clinical variables and gut microbiome data, for personalized postprandial glycemic response prediction, achieving comparable performance to manual reporting methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing approaches for predicting postprandial glycemic response (PPGR) rely on manually reported dietary intake, which limits scalability in free-living settings. There's a need for more practical and scalable methods for personalized nutrition and type 2 diabetes management.

Method: A multimodal framework that jointly performs image-based macronutrient estimation and glucose prediction. Uses meal images to derive macronutrient estimates instead of manual dietary logging, integrates these with clinical variables and gut microbiome profiles, and employs an attention-based prediction module to model interactions between dietary and host-specific information.

Result: The proposed model outperforms existing PPGR baselines that use image-derived nutritional inputs and approaches the performance of methods that rely on manually reported macronutrients, despite using automatically estimated nutritional information. This was validated on a real-world dataset containing meal images, continuous glucose monitoring, clinical variables, and gut microbiome profiles.

Conclusion: Combining image-derived nutrition with complementary clinical and gut microbiome information provides a practical foundation for scalable personalized PPGR prediction, enabling more practical applications in free-living settings without the burden of manual dietary logging.

Abstract: Predicting postprandial glycemic response (PPGR) is fundamental to personalized nutrition and type 2 diabetes management, yet existing approaches typically rely on manually reported dietary intake, limiting their scalability in free-living settings. We propose a multimodal framework that replaces manual dietary logging with image-derived macronutrient estimates and integrates them with clinical variables and gut microbiome information for personalized PPGR prediction. The framework jointly performs image-based macronutrient estimation and glucose prediction, while an attention-based prediction module models interactions between dietary and host-specific information. We evaluate the proposed approach on a real-world dataset comprising meal images, continuous glucose monitoring, clinical variables, and gut microbiome profiles. The proposed model outperforms existing PPGR baselines using image-derived nutritional inputs and approaches the performance of methods that rely on manually reported macronutrients despite using automatically estimated nutritional information. These results demonstrate that combining image-derived nutrition with complementary clinical and gut microbiome information provides a practical foundation for scalable personalized PPGR prediction.

</details>


### [90] [Fathom-Vaidya: Advancing Medical Reasoning with Rubric-Based Rewards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24480)
*Kalash Shah,Kunal Singh,Snehan J,Shreyas Singh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A sequential training framework using synthetic data and rubric-based reinforcement learning improves both diagnostic and clinical healthcare reasoning in medical LLMs, achieving state-of-the-art performance on benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current medical LLMs show persistent weaknesses in two complementary dimensions: diagnostic reasoning (inferring conditions from clinical data) and clinical healthcare reasoning (broader navigational judgment for multi-turn interactions). Benchmarks like HealthBench and MedXpertQA reveal failures in complex diagnostic scenarios and limitations in contextual, patient-centered dialogue.

Method: A sequential training framework that: 1) improves diagnostic reasoning using MedBullets-derived questions with rule- and rubric-guided reinforcement learning, and 2) enhances clinical reasoning by generating 5.3k synthetic multi-turn scenarios paired with multi-dimensional rubrics for comprehensive assessment.

Result: Achieves over 10% improvement on MedXpertQA, with the 30B model reaching 50.1% accuracy on HealthBench-Hard, surpassing proprietary baselines including GPT-5 (thinking).

Conclusion: Targeted synthetic datasets and rubric-based training can systematically improve both diagnostic and interactive clinical reasoning in medical LLMs, addressing the dual challenges of medical AI deployment.

Abstract: Deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) in healthcare requires robust performance across two complementary dimensions - diagnostic reasoning: the convergent, evidence-driven task of inferring a patient's condition from clinical data to produce a diagnosis, and clinical healthcare reasoning: the broader, navigational judgment required to communicate, plan, and adapt across multi-turn clinical interactions where a single correct answer may not exist. Recent benchmarks such as HealthBench and MedXpertQA reveal persistent weaknesses in both areas, exposing failures in complex diagnostic scenarios and limitations in contextual, patient-centered dialogue. We introduce a sequential training framework that targets these facets using synthetic data and rubric-based reinforcement learning. First, we improve diagnostic reasoning using MedBullets-derived questions with rule- and rubric-guided Reinforcement Learning (RL). We then shift to clinical reasoning by generating 5.3k synthetic multi-turn scenarios, each paired with multi-dimensional rubrics to comprehensively assess the response. This approach yields over 10% improvement on MedXpertQA, and our 30B model achieves 50.1% accuracy on HealthBench-Hard, surpassing proprietary baselines including GPT-5 (thinking). Our results show that targeted synthetic datasets and rubric-based training can systematically improve both diagnostic and interactive clinical reasoning in medical LLMs.

</details>


### [91] [Not All Task Vectors Need Equal Rank: Energy-Proportional Allocation for Model Merging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24517)
*Hyunjoong Cho,Jinhyeok Jang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SERA is a task-adaptive model merging method that allocates ranks proportionally to each task's spectral energy instead of using uniform rank allocation, improving multi-task performance within the same rank budget.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing spectral merging methods use uniform rank capacity for all tasks, which is suboptimal because task vectors have heterogeneous spectral complexity. Uniform allocation wastes capacity on simple tasks while limiting capacity for complex ones.

Method: Spectral Energy-proportional Rank Allocation (SERA) allocates ranks according to the singular-value energy structure of each task vector. It examines the spectral complexity of tasks and assigns more capacity to complex/isolated tasks and less to compact tasks, using the same total rank budget as existing methods.

Result: Experiments under standard vision model merging protocols show SERA improves multi-task merging performance compared to existing spectral methods while preserving the same total rank budget. Analysis reveals task-level spectral concentration correlates with the benefits of adaptive rank allocation.

Conclusion: SERA effectively addresses the limitation of uniform rank allocation in model merging by adapting to task spectral complexity, providing insight into when adaptive rank allocation is most beneficial and extending SVD-based merging to task-dependent capacity allocation.

Abstract: Model merging aims to combine multiple fine-tuned models derived from a common pretrained model into a single multi-task model without additional joint training. Recent spectral merging methods improve over simple weight averaging by exploiting low-rank structures of task-specific updates, but they commonly assign the same rank capacity to every task. This uniform allocation ignores that task vectors can have heterogeneous spectral complexity, causing the shared merging space to be used suboptimally. In this paper, we propose Spectral Energy-proportional Rank Allocation (SERA), a simple task-adaptive strategy that allocates ranks according to the singular-value energy structure of each task vector. By assigning richer spectral capacity to complex or isolated tasks and fewer directions to compact tasks, SERA extends SVD-based model merging from uniform-capacity merging to task-dependent capacity allocation. Experiments under standard vision model merging protocols show that SERA improves multi-task merging performance while preserving the same total rank budget as existing spectral merging methods. Further analysis demonstrates that task-level spectral concentration is closely related to the per-task effect of adaptive rank allocation, providing insight into when and why SERA is effective.

</details>


### [92] [The Endless Exam: Mathematical Constructions from Today's Models toward Superintelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24555)
*Muhan Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The Endless Exam is a benchmark for measuring progress toward artificial superintelligence using parameterized mathematical construction problems that generate increasingly larger instances, with automatic verification and quality scoring against published frontiers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current benchmarks often cap improvements at human-level performance. The paper aims to create a benchmark that can measure progress from today's models toward artificial superintelligence by using mathematical construction problems that can scale beyond human capabilities.

Method: Developed fourteen parameterized construction families based on open mathematical problems that generate new instances at larger parameters. Each submitted construction is automatically checked for validity and assigned a relative quality score against published frontiers or construction baselines. Compact certificates keep large constructions verifiable.

Result: Evaluated eight models on 69 distinct instances. Continuous quality scores successfully distinguish performance between models, though no evaluated system surpasses published frontiers. Size-quality curves show how construction quality changes as problem size increases.

Conclusion: The Endless Exam provides a framework for continuous measurement of mathematical AI progress before and beyond human frontiers. The released generators, verifiers, references, and analysis support ongoing benchmarking toward artificial superintelligence.

Abstract: We introduce the Endless Exam, a benchmark for measuring mathematical progress from today's models toward artificial superintelligence through fourteen parameterised construction families. Each submitted object is checked automatically for validity and assigned a relative quality score against a published frontier or construction baseline, without capping improvements at $1$. The families draw on open mathematical problems for long-term targets and generate new instances at larger parameters, where compact certificates keep large constructions verifiable. Across eight models evaluated on 69 distinct instances, continuous quality scores distinguish performance even though no evaluated system surpasses a published frontier. Size-quality curves show how construction quality changes as problem size increases. We release the generators, verifiers, references, model responses and analysis to support continued measurement before and beyond human frontiers.

</details>


### [93] [Ascent: An Agentic System over the Model Context Protocol for Real-World Clinical Data Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24620)
*Angelo Ziletti,Leonardo D'Ambrosi,Melanie Tuchardt,Tim Kondziella*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Ascent is an agentic system for epidemiological analysis that improves accuracy by 20-27% over fixed pipelines but requires more computation, evaluated with the EpiTrap dataset for testing pharmacoepidemiological error avoidance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Answering epidemiological questions from real-world clinical data is challenging due to requirements for medical coding, SQL expertise, schema awareness, and validation of implicit choices about populations, denominators, and time. Current approaches lack standardized methods for these complex analyses.

Method: Ascent is an agentic system that exposes medical coding, question answering, and cohort analysis through a shared Model Context Protocol tool surface for both standardized and native schemas. The researchers introduce EpiTrap, a dataset specifically designed to test whether systems avoid recognized pharmacoepidemiological errors. They compare a fixed pipeline approach with agentic approaches across different models and orchestrators.

Result: With capable models, agents improve accuracy over the fixed pipeline by an average of 27 percentage points on native schemas and 20 percentage points on standardized schemas. However, these gains come with trade-offs: agents require more tool calls and longer runtimes. Experience from real projects demonstrates the system's value for feasibility assessment, diagnostic iteration, and expert-guided analysis.

Conclusion: Agentic systems like Ascent represent a significant advancement for epidemiological analysis, offering substantial accuracy improvements over traditional fixed pipelines, though at the cost of increased computational requirements. The EpiTrap dataset provides a valuable benchmark for evaluating such systems, and real-world applications show practical utility for complex medical research tasks.

Abstract: Answering epidemiological questions from real-world clinical data requires medical coding, schema-aware SQL, and validation of implicit choices about populations, denominators, and time. We present Ascent, an agentic system that exposes medical coding, question answering, and cohort analysis through a shared Model Context Protocol tool surface for standardized and native schemas. We introduce EpiTrap, a dataset testing whether systems avoid recognized pharmacoepidemiological errors, and compare a fixed pipeline with agents across models and orchestrators. With capable models, agents improve accuracy over the fixed pipeline by an average of 27 and 20 percentage points on native and standardized schemas, respectively. These gains require more tool calls and longer runtimes. Experience from real projects highlights the system's value for feasibility assessment, diagnostic iteration, and expert-guided analysis.

</details>


### [94] [Custom Named Entity Recognition and Topic Classification for Global Health Publications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24625)
*Genis Skura,Antoine Geissbühler,Jean-Luc Falcone*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This thesis explores NLP model selection for global health literature in resource-limited settings, comparing different approaches for semantic tag discovery, named entity recognition, and multi-label topic classification, finding trade-offs between accuracy and computational efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses the challenge of selecting and adapting NLP models for global health literature in environments with limited annotated data and computational resources, where practical solutions must balance accuracy with efficiency.

Method: 1) Compares skip-gram word2vec models trained on specialized corpora vs. BioWordVec for semantic tag discovery. 2) Compares convolutional spaCy models with RoBERTa-based transformers for named entity recognition on annotated sentences. 3) Evaluates MiniLM-based few-shot classification vs. BART-MNLI zero-shot inference for multi-label topic classification across 50 topics. 4) Integrates disease recognizer, PDF preprocessing, entity filtering, and MeSH enrichment into a pipeline.

Result: 1) Broader vocabulary coverage doesn't guarantee better domain-specific associations. 2) Transformer achieves 0.80 micro-F1 for NER vs. 0.65-0.69 for convolutional models but is 16x slower. 3) Disease recognizer achieves 81.33% test F1 on NCBI Disease Corpus. 4) BART-MNLI achieves 95.2% single-label accuracy vs. 59% for MiniLM, and 88% vs. 32% for multi-label classification.

Conclusion: The study provides empirical guidance for building knowledge systems under resource constraints: domain specialization and lightweight adaptation offer practical value where efficiency matters, while transformer accuracy may justify higher inference costs in specific applications, helping practitioners make informed model selection decisions.

Abstract: How should natural language processing models be selected and adapted for global health literature in environments where annotated data and computational resources are limited? This thesis investigates these challenges through experiments on semantic tag discovery, named entity recognition (NER), and multi-label topic classification. First, skip-gram word2vec models trained on progressively larger specialized corpora are compared with BioWordVec to assess how corpus size and domain context influence tag discovery. Vocabulary coverage and qualitative evaluation indicate that broader coverage does not necessarily yield more useful domain-specific associations. The analysis then turns to entity extraction, comparing convolutional spaCy models with a RoBERTa-based transformer on 1,000 annotated sentences. Under a lenient scoring protocol, the transformer achieves 0.80 micro-F1 versus 0.65-0.69 for convolutional models, but takes 82 seconds rather than 5-6 seconds. This trade-off motivates fine-tuning convolutional models and integrating a disease recognizer that achieves 81.33% test F1 on the NCBI Disease Corpus. Combined with PDF preprocessing, entity filtering, and MeSH enrichment, the resulting pipeline supports document-level indexing. To complement entity extraction with thematic annotation, MiniLM-based few-shot classification is compared with BART-MNLI zero-shot inference across 50 topics and 1,000 handcrafted test sentences. BART-MNLI achieves 95.2% single-label accuracy versus 59%; reported multi-label accuracies are 88% and 32% under partly manual assessment. However, its higher inference cost limits practical integration. The results show where domain specialization and lightweight adaptation offer practical value, and where transformer accuracy justifies higher inference costs, providing an empirical basis for building knowledge systems under resource constraints.

</details>


### [95] [DUMA-Bench: A Dual-Control Multi-Agent Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Agent Security](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24662)
*Ivan Aleksandrov,German Kochnev,Sabrina Sadiekh,Yaroslav Rogoza*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DUMA-Bench is a new benchmark that evaluates LLM agent security under interactive dual-control scenarios, showing that adversarial user interaction increases attack success rates from 26.9% to 41.1% across 14 models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current security evaluations for LLM-based agents are inadequate because they assume passive users and static control, ignoring the interactive dynamics of real-world deployments where both agents and users can influence the environment.

Method: DUMA-Bench extends τ²-bench with adversarial environments covering eight vulnerability classes (including RAG poisoning, cross-agent manipulation, unsafe output handling). It evaluates 14 models from five families (OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek, Qwen, Z.ai) across eight domains with multiple user-behavior regimes in dual-control scenarios.

Result: Introducing dual-control interaction increases attack success rate from 26.9% to 41.1% across experiments. The benchmark reveals significant security vulnerabilities that emerge from interactive dynamics rather than just model properties alone.

Conclusion: Agent security is not solely a property of the model but emerges from the interaction between model, user, and environment. DUMA-Bench provides a crucial evaluation layer for studying security in realistic agent deployments, highlighting the need for security evaluations that account for interactive dynamics.

Abstract: LLM-based agents increasingly operate in environments where they interact with users, tools, and external systems. Yet most security evaluations assume passive users and static control, ignoring the interactive dynamics that shape real agent behavior. We introduce \textbf{DUMA-Bench}, a benchmark and evaluation protocol for measuring agent security under \emph{dual-control} interaction, where both the agent and the user can influence the shared environment state. DUMA-Bench extends $τ^2$-bench ~\cite{barres2025tau} with adversarial environments covering eight vulnerability classes, including RAG poisoning, cross-agent manipulation, and unsafe output handling. We evaluate \textbf{14 models from five model families} (OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek, Qwen, and Z.ai) across eight domains and multiple user-behavior regimes. Across our experiments, introducing dual-control interaction increases the attack success rate from \textbf{26.9\%} to \textbf{41.1\%}. These results show that agent security is not solely a property of the model but emerges from the interaction between the model, the user, and the environment. DUMA-Bench provides a missing evaluation layer for studying security in realistic agent deployments.

</details>


### [96] [Beyond Endpoint Performance: Process-Level Evaluation of Self-Evolving Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24663)
*Hongqiang Lin,Chao Liu,Xiaofan Bai,Xuan Jin,Yuhong Li,Nenggan Zheng,Xipeng Cao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EvoPathBench is a benchmark for evaluating self-evolving agents' capabilities during artifact-level evolution, tracking individual capabilities as artifacts are updated over time rather than just measuring endpoint performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional endpoint performance evaluation is incomplete for self-evolving agents because capabilities evolve as artifacts (memories/skills) are iteratively updated. Process-level evaluation is needed to track when capabilities emerge and whether updates strengthen, preserve, or weaken them.

Method: EvoPathBench fixes the base model and tools, freezes evolving artifacts at successive checkpoints, and evaluates target capabilities on held-out episodes. It uses public trading data and calibrated trajectories to test three capabilities: generalization to unseen tasks, retention after unrelated learning, and rule adaptation to new evidence.

Result: Experimental results show: 1) gains on similar unseen tasks often weaken under distribution shift, 2) retention losses are concentrated in a minority of evolution paths, and 3) no method achieves reliable rule adaptation. Also, while agents can generate candidate artifacts with substantial potential gains, the selected updates consistently fail to realize this potential.

Conclusion: Capability-level process evaluation is essential for analyzing self-evolution, with candidate evaluation and selection identified as key targets for improvement. The benchmark establishes a foundation for tracking how individual capabilities evolve during artifact updates.

Abstract: Self-evolving agents convert interaction feedback into persistent artifacts, such as memories or skills, which in turn guide subsequent decisions. As these artifacts are iteratively updated throughout an experience stream, the capabilities they support may evolve. Consequently, endpoint performance alone offers an incomplete view of self-evolution. Process-level evaluation is therefore essential to identify when a target capability emerges and whether later updates strengthen, preserve, or weaken it. Motivated by this, we propose \textsc{EvoPathBench}, a benchmark that tracks individual capabilities during artifact-level self-evolution. EvoPathBench fixes the base model, tools, freezes evolving artifacts at successive checkpoints, and evaluates the target capability on held-out episodes. This benchmark evaluates agent self-evolution using public trading data and calibrated trajectories. It tests three capabilities: generalization to unseen tasks, retention after unrelated learning, and rule adaptation to new evidence. Experimental results show that gains on similar unseen tasks often weaken under distribution shift, retention losses are concentrated in a minority of evolution paths, and no method achieves reliable rule adaptation. Moreover, while self-evolution enables agents to generate candidate artifacts with substantial held-out gains, the selected updates consistently fall short of realizing this potential. Together, these findings establish capability-level process evaluation as a foundation for analyzing self-evolution, identifying candidate evaluation and selection as key targets for improvement.

</details>


### [97] [TimeLitmus: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Cross-Modal Understanding and Explanation Faithfulness in Event-Conditioned Time-Series Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24677)
*Jie Gong,Maowei Jiang,Zhiwei Liu,Yankai Chen,Guojun Xiong,Xue Liu,Min Peng,Qianqian Xie,Sophia Ananiadou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TimeLitmus is a diagnostic benchmark for evaluating LLMs' cross-modal understanding and explanation faithfulness in event-conditioned time-series prediction, revealing significant gaps between standard accuracy and reliable understanding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard prediction accuracy doesn't reveal whether LLMs truly integrate numerical time-series and textual event inputs effectively, or if they rely on shortcuts like event polarity, unimodal priors, or superficial cues. Explanations may rationalize predictions without faithfully reflecting the evidence driving model behavior.

Method: Created TimeLitmus benchmark with 4,856 evaluation records across Finance and Traffic domains, combining natural prediction with controlled counterfactual and contrastive interventions, explanation-targeted faithfulness tests, and systematic shortcut controls. Evaluated ten representative LLMs and compared with human annotators.

Result: Standard prediction accuracy substantially overstates reliable cross-modal understanding: Hard Paired Contrast correctness peaks at only 19.2% (Finance) and 11.7% (Traffic). Models often recognize scenario relations explicitly but fail to apply them during prediction. Explanation faithfulness shows similar gaps - models cite manipulated factors but behavioral support remains low (below 22%). Humans outperform LLMs on controlled diagnostics.

Conclusion: Current LLMs have significant limitations in cross-modal understanding and explanation faithfulness for event-conditioned time-series prediction. Natural-only adaptation yields selective gains but not consistent improvements in controlled understanding. The benchmark enables systematic evaluation and improvement of LLMs in this domain.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to make predictions from numerical time-series histories and textual events. Yet accuracy alone cannot reveal whether correct answers reflect effective integration of the two inputs or instead arise from event polarity, unimodal priors, or superficial cues. Likewise, plausible explanations may rationalize predictions without faithfully reflecting the evidence that drives model behavior. We introduce TimeLitmus, a diagnostic benchmark for cross-modal understanding and explanation faithfulness in event-conditioned time-series prediction. TimeLitmus contains 4,856 evaluation records across Finance and Traffic, combining natural prediction with controlled counterfactual and contrastive interventions, explanation-targeted faithfulness tests, and systematic shortcut controls. Across ten representative LLMs, standard prediction accuracy substantially overstates reliable cross-modal understanding: Hard Paired Contrast (HPC) pair correctness peaks at only 19.2% in Finance and 11.7% in Traffic, and all ten models show lower-than-expected consistency on Finance series-side controls. Models often recognize scenario relations explicitly yet fail to apply them during independent prediction. Explanation faithfulness shows a similar gap: in Traffic, most models cite the manipulated temporal factor in over 90% of cases, while behavioral support remains below 22%. Human annotators outperform LLMs on matched controlled and hard-pair diagnostics, confirming that these distinctions are recoverable from the inputs. Natural-only adaptation yields selective gains in evidence selection and input sensitivity, but not consistent gains in controlled or hard-pair behavior. The benchmark, evaluation suite, and supervised adaptation data will be released publicly.

</details>


### [98] [World State Generator](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24744)
*Sungheon Jeong,Sanggeon Yun,Ryozo Masukawa,Haleh Alimohamadi,Mahdi Imani,Mohsen Imani*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WSG trains on verified world trajectories to generate checkable world states, enabling plans to adapt to real-world constraints and recover from refusals, significantly boosting performance over prompted planning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Language-based planning fails when plans encounter real-world constraints that aren't explicitly stated in the plan. Prompted planners get stuck rewriting refused steps without adapting to the world's actual rules, leading to wasted attempts and task failure.

Method: Build synthetic worlds across 7 domains with rule-enforcing programs, extract 226K verified trajectories (failures paired with repairs), train World State Generator to write plans as checkable world states that can adapt to encountered constraints.

Result: WSG raises end-to-end success rates for two ~30B parameter open models over prompting and brings performance to proprietary model levels across 7 public benchmarks.

Conclusion: Aligning plans with real-world constraints through state-based representation enables effective adaptation to failures, overcoming limitations of language-only planning and achieving robust performance comparable to proprietary models.

Abstract: Language agents solve complex tasks through plans and actions. A single step the world refuses puts the goal out of reach, and what the agent does next decides the task. Prompted planners fail at exactly this point, rewriting the refused step in new words, meeting the same refusal, and burning the attempt budget without moving. They fail because the plan was never tied to the world, so a refusal has nothing in the plan to attach to. A world is where a task runs, and it has its own rules, its own admissible actions, and its own constraints. We build synthetic worlds across 7 domains and extract training data from them. A program enforces each world's rules and grades its goal, and every world is admitted only if its goal is reachable from its initial state. Agents run inside and leave verified failures paired with repairs that carried the run to a state the world certified, a record of about 226K trajectories. On this record we train the World State Generator, a model that writes a plan as checkable states of the world and keeps that plan aligned with the world it runs in. That alignment is what a plan written in language lacks, since the world it runs in has physical limits, logical dependencies, and required orders the language never states, and the plan encounters these rules only when a state fails. WSG takes that failure as the rule the world has stated and rewrites the remaining states to obey it, so the plan bends to the world as the run goes on. Across 7 public benchmarks, WSG raises end-to-end success for two open models near 30B parameters over prompting and brings to the level of proprietary model.

</details>


### [99] [Epi-Logic: A Conceptual Framework for Epistemic Runtime Control, Schema Validity Checking, and Controlled Accommodation in Autonomous AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24755)
*Boris Wetzk*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A framework called Epi-Logic for detecting when AI agents operate with outdated mental models (schema mismatch) and gradually reducing their autonomy while switching to validated schemas, using epistemic dissonance scoring.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI agents deployed in high-stakes environments where wrong decisions are irreversible often suffer from "schema mismatch" - operating with interpretive frames that no longer match current context. Current quality metrics fail to capture this underlying loss of validity since outputs can still appear plausible and internally consistent.

Method: Introduces Epi-Logic framework for epistemic runtime control. Defines schema as tuple (variable space, expectation model, validity conditions, axioms, metadata). Uses Epi-Score with 7 graded dimensions of epistemic dissonance plus separate categorical paths for temporal validity violations (D8), validity condition violations (G), and axiom violations. Employs checking asymmetry where validity conditions can be checked at runtime while action correctness is often only established ex post.

Result: Presents 8 falsifiable propositions with named baselines describing transition to empirical validation. These are testable hypotheses, not established results. The framework separates conditional results from sequential changepoint detection and an empirical remainder.

Conclusion: Epi-Logic provides a systematic approach to detect schema mismatch in autonomous AI agents, enabling graduated reduction of autonomy and auditable switching to validated schemas when operating conditions change, addressing the problem of plausible but invalid outputs in high-stakes environments.

Abstract: Autonomous AI agents are increasingly deployed in areas where wrong decisions are hard to reverse. This paper examines schema mismatch: the condition in which an agent operates within an interpretive frame that no longer applies to the current context. Outputs produced under such a mismatch can appear internally consistent, linguistically plausible, and largely factually correct; output-quality metrics alone therefore capture the underlying loss of validity only partially.
  The paper introduces Epi-Logic, a conceptual framework for epistemic runtime control. It couples the detection of schema dissonance, a graduated reduction of autonomy, and the auditable switch to a validated schema. A schema is formalised as a tuple of variable space, expectation model, validity conditions, axioms, and metadata. The Epi-Score aggregates seven graded dimensions of epistemic dissonance; the temporal validity dimension D8, violations of the validity conditions G, and axiom violations are carried as separate categorical paths that are not offset against the aggregate.
  The architecture rests on a checking asymmetry: formalised validity conditions can be checked at runtime, whereas the correctness of many actions is established only ex post. The paper separates two architectural properties, a conditional result from sequential changepoint detection, and an empirical remainder. Eight falsifiable propositions with named baselines describe the transition to empirical validation. All propositions are empirically testable hypotheses, not established results.

</details>


### [100] [Construting Reverse Thinking: Developing Large Language Models' Reverse Thingking Ability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24760)
*Xin Liu,Yunhai Li,Chunfu Jia,Ziliang Chen,Jisen Song*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a backward reasoning pattern construction method to enhance models' reverse thinking and dynamic adaptability, addressing five common error reasons in mathematical problem-solving by training on a specialized math dataset with forward/backward reasoning paths.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current models like GPT-o1, GPT-o3, and DeepSeek-R1 use forward reasoning by default when addressing complex problems, but statistical analysis revealed five key error sources: insufficient solution-space coverage, computational mistakes, unverified assumptions, ignoring constraint conditions, and maximum response length limitations. These limitations in current reasoning approaches motivate the need for more flexible reasoning patterns.

Method: 1) Constructed an easy-hard two-stage math dataset with both forward and backward reasoning paths; 2) Applied two-stage supervised fine-tuning to progressively train backward reasoning capability; 3) Developed a fine-grained reward mechanism with smoothed reward signals to avoid reward hacking; 4) Designed a linear-decay balanced sampling strategy to maintain balance between forward and backward reasoning samples during training.

Result: Experimental results show the method significantly improves reasoning efficiency and accuracy in mathematical proof tasks, providing a flexible and efficient reasoning paradigm for solving complex problems.

Conclusion: The backward reasoning pattern construction method successfully enhances models' reverse thinking ability and dynamic adaptability, offering an effective approach to overcome limitations of purely forward reasoning models and improve performance on complex mathematical problem-solving tasks.

Abstract: When facing complex problems, humans tend to try various ideas for different issues. Human thinking patterns exhibit remarkable flexibility in adapting to diverse scenarios.
