We conceptualise activity pattern mining as an integrated process of representation, clustering, and interpretation, and propose the Activity Chain Encoder (ACE) for the representation stage. ACE is a self-supervised model that combines pre-trained urban embeddings with visit timing and duration and uses a Transformer to model the sequential organisation of stays. It is trained using masked activity modelling and identity-guided contrastive learning without requiring deterministic activity purpose labels. Learned daily representations are aggregated into user-level profiles, clustered, and interpreted through temporal-functional patterns and Census-derived demographic context. Applied to mobile phone app location data from London and compared with three representative methods, ACE supports the identification of six differentiated weekday activity-pattern groups characterised by distinct daily rhythms, urban functional contexts, and demographic associations. These complementary forms of evidence further support the development of empirically grounded activity-pattern personas, establishing a holistic route for deriving behaviourally meaningful population patterns from unlabelled mobile phone location data. The source code for the entire analytical pipeline developed in this study is publicly available at https://github.com/xlwang233/ACE.

</details>


### [125] [Rank Portability Does Not Imply Feasibility Portability: Target-Specific Evaluation of Joint Hardware Constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22122)
*Wesley Shu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Cross-device hardware evaluation shows that even when architecture rankings transfer well between devices, proxy-based model selection often fails to guarantee feasibility under joint latency-energy constraints, requiring explicit reporting of target-specific operating points.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current cross-device hardware evaluation assumes that if architecture rankings transfer across devices, a proxy device can support target-side model selection. The paper aims to stress-test this assumption specifically for joint latency-energy feasibility assessment.

Method: The researchers conducted experiments across two public architecture families: NAS-Bench-201 and 10,000 GPT architectures across 13 HW-GPT-Bench devices. They measured rank correlations (SRCC) between devices, evaluated feasible-set overlap under joint constraints, used AdaProxy diagnostic for latency ranking improvement, and applied exact finite-sample split-conformal analysis to determine minimum calibration requirements.

Result: On NAS-Bench-201, cross-device rank correlations were moderate but target-comparable feasible-set overlap remained incomplete. Even with high latency SRCC (0.951-0.996) across GPT architectures, proxy-reuse violation risk ranged from 33.3% to 100% under joint constraints. The analysis revealed that at least nine calibration observations are needed for a finite one-sided 90% threshold.

Conclusion: Rank portability, feasibility portability, and target-specific decision support are distinct evaluation objectives. Cross-device evaluations should explicitly report which target environments actually support the claimed operating points, rather than assuming proxy-based selection guarantees feasibility under joint constraints.

Abstract: Cross-device hardware evaluation often assumes that if architecture rankings transfer across devices, a proxy device can support target-side model selection. We stress-test this assumption for joint latency-energy feasibility across two public architecture families. On NAS-Bench-201, cross-device rank correlations are moderate, while target-comparable feasible-set overlap remains incomplete. A faithful AdaProxy diagnostic substantially improves latency ranking, showing that the observed boundary failures are not simply due to weak adaptation. Exact finite-sample split-conformal analysis also exposes an evidence bottleneck: a finite one-sided 90% threshold requires at least nine calibration observations. We then replicate the phenomenon on 10,000 GPT architectures across 13 HW-GPT-Bench devices. Relative to an RTX3080 proxy, target latency SRCC ranges from 0.951 to 0.996, yet proxy-reuse violation risk ranges from 33.3% to 100% under matched joint constraints. These results show that rank portability, feasibility portability, and target-specific decision support are distinct evaluation objects. Cross-device evaluations should therefore report which target environments actually support the operating point being claimed.

</details>


### [126] [VISTA: An Attention-Based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Architecture for Space Situational Awareness Sensor Tasking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23875)
*Miguel Leiva-Vélez,Adalberto Claudio Quiros,Nicolas Gaston Rozado,Hodei Urrutxua,Víctor Rodríguez-Fernández*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: VISTA introduces a scalable deep reinforcement learning architecture for space situational awareness sensor tasking that handles variable object populations and sensor configurations through entity-centric attention and pointer-based decoding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rapid growth of resident space objects is increasing complexity for sensor tasking, challenging classical optimization methods as they allocate finite, heterogeneous sensing resources across ever-larger catalogues. Existing deep RL approaches are limited by fixed-dimensional state/action representations that can't scale to large, dynamic catalogues and distributed networks.

Method: VISTA combines physics- and mission-informed top-K retrieval with entity-centric attention, recurrent memory, and pointer-based action decoding to keep each agent's observation and action spaces independent of catalogue size. This enables scalable RL for variable object populations and sensor configurations.

Result: With 30 orbiting targets, VISTA recovers catalogue 31.2% faster than fixed-dimensional recurrent baseline. In large-scale regime, reduces five-hour uncertainty by 97.5% vs classical reference and 99.3% vs recurrent learner. Zero-shot tests up to 20,000 objects show near-linear relations between sensing capacity, catalogue size, and recovery horizon. Policies also exhibit sensor modality adaptation and generalization.

Conclusion: VISTA provides a scalable framework for adaptive space situational awareness sensor tasking across large, distributed networks of heterogeneous ground- and space-based sensors, overcoming limitations of both classical optimization and existing deep RL approaches.

Abstract: The rapid growth of resident space objects is increasing the complexity of space situational awareness sensor tasking, challenging classical optimization methods as they allocate finite, heterogeneous, and distributed sensing resources across ever-larger catalogues. Existing deep reinforcement learning approaches show promise in reduced settings, but fixed-dimensional state and action representations limit their ability to scale to large, dynamic catalogues and distributed sensing networks. We introduce VISTA (Variable-Entity Intelligent Sensor Tasking Architecture), a scalable deep reinforcement learning architecture for persistent uncertainty-driven catalogue maintenance across variable object populations and sensor configurations. VISTA combines physics- and mission-informed top-K retrieval with entity-centric attention, recurrent memory, and pointer-based action decoding, thereby keeping each agent's observation and action spaces independent of catalogue size. We evaluate VISTA across different scenarios, from fixed-size single-sensor benchmarks to large-scale space-based tasking and heterogeneous cooperative sensing. With 30 orbiting targets, VISTA recovers the catalogue 31.2% faster than the fixed-dimensional recurrent baseline. In the large-scale regime, VISTA reduces five-hour uncertainty by 97.5% relative to the strongest classical reference and by 99.3% relative to the recurrent learner. Zero-shot tests up to 20,000 objects reveal near-linear relations between sensing capacity, catalogue size, and recovery horizon. Learned policies also exhibit sensor modality adaptation and generalization to population and initial-uncertainty shifts. Together, these results demonstrate that VISTA provides a scalable framework for adaptive space situational awareness sensor tasking across large, distributed networks of heterogeneous ground- and space-based sensors.

</details>


### [127] [StationPDE: Station-Oriented Surface PDE Learning for Multi-Station Multivariate Weather Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22123)
*Xiao Wang,Changjian Chen,Rongwen Li,Hongwu Liu,Kun Fang,Zhuo Tang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: StationPDE bridges traditional station forecasting and PDE-based models by creating terrain-aware continuous surface fields from discrete station data, decomposing physical evolution into wind transport and upper-air inference, achieving state-of-the-art weather forecasting performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing station forecasting models learn statistical dependencies but lack explicit physical evolution, while PDE-based weather models require continuous fields and upper-air variables unavailable in surface station data. There's a gap between discrete station-based approaches and continuous physics-based models.

Method: StationPDE constructs terrain-aware continuous surface fields from discrete station observations, decomposing physical evolution into: 1) surface wind transport for explicit evolution of observable variables, 2) upper-air inference using learnable horizontal diffusion to approximate missing upper-air influences, 3) parallel data-driven diffusion branch for complementary patterns, and 4) adaptive router to integrate forecasts for station-level multivariate prediction.

Result: Experiments on Weather2K and MeteoNet datasets show StationPDE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, reducing MSE by about 9.6% on average compared to the strongest baseline.

Conclusion: StationPDE successfully bridges the gap between discrete station forecasting and continuous PDE-based models by incorporating physical dynamics into station-level forecasting while handling missing upper-air data through intelligent approximations, resulting in superior forecasting performance.

Abstract: Multi-station multivariate weather forecasting aims to forecast future weather variables at multiple weather stations from historical surface observations. Existing station forecasting models learn statistical dependencies among discrete stations, but lack explicit physical evolution. Meanwhile, PDE-based weather models provide interpretable physical dynamics, yet require continuous fields and upper-air variables unavailable in surface station data. To bridge this gap, we propose StationPDE, a station-oriented surface PDE learning model. StationPDE constructs a terrain-aware continuous surface field from discrete station observations and decomposes its physical evolution into surface wind transport and upper-air inference. Surface wind transport explicitly evolves observable weather variables, while upper-air inference uses learnable horizontal diffusion to approximate the missing influence of unavailable upper-air variables. A parallel data-driven diffusion branch captures complementary motion patterns, and an adaptive router integrates the two forecasts for station-level multivariate forecasting. Experiments on Weather2K and MeteoNet show that StationPDE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, reducing MSE by about $9.6\%$ on average compared with the strongest baseline. Code and implementation details are available at https://github.com/hnu-vis/StationPDE.

</details>


### [128] [SolarFlowRefiner: Refinement-Aware Flow Matching for Surface Solar Radiation Downscaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22126)
*Udbhav Srivastava,Antonita Racheal,Yiheng Chen,Runlong Yu,Xinyue Ye*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A flow-matching framework called SolarFlowRefiner improves solar radiation downscaling by jointly optimizing generation and refinement stages to handle sharp spatial variations between sunlit and cloud-shadowed regions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: High-resolution surface solar radiation (SSR) is crucial for solar forecasting and grid operations, but existing physically consistent reanalysis products like ERA5 are too coarse to capture localized cloud-driven variability, particularly the sharp boundaries between sunlit and cloud-shadowed regions within single grid cells.

Method: SolarFlowRefiner uses a refinement-aware flow-matching framework with two components: (1) a conditional FlowMatch generator that predicts normalized corrections to upsampled ERA5 baselines, and (2) a refiner trained on prediction-conditioned states between current FlowMatch outputs and target residuals, with refinement objectives backpropagated through the FlowMatch sampler for joint optimization.

Result: Experiments on a day-blocked ERA5-SolarCube benchmark show consistent improvements over both standalone generation approaches and post-hoc refinement methods that treat generation and refinement as separate stages.

Conclusion: SolarFlowRefiner effectively addresses the challenge of downscaling solar radiation by coupling generative predictors with iterative correctors in a joint optimization framework, providing a general strategy for multisource downscaling tasks with ambiguous high-resolution corrections.

Abstract: High-resolution surface solar radiation (SSR) is important for solar forecasting and grid operation. However, physically consistent reanalysis products are too coarse to resolve localized cloud-driven variability. In this paper, we study a multisource downscaling task that reconstructs high-resolution SolarCube SSR fields from coarse ERA5 radiative variables and co-registered satellite channels. The task is challenging because a single ERA5 grid cell may contain both sunlit and cloud-shadowed regions. As a result, the missing high-resolution correction can be spatially sharp and inherently ambiguous. One-stage predictors often oversmooth these structures. Post-hoc refinement also introduces a stage-wise mismatch: the generator is optimized independently, even though its output determines the refiner's initial state. We introduce SolarFlowRefiner, a refinement-aware flow-matching framework for SSR downscaling. A conditional FlowMatch generator first predicts a normalized correction to an upsampled ERA5 baseline. The refiner is then trained on prediction-conditioned states between the current FlowMatch output and the target residual. This exposes the refiner to the structured errors produced by the generator. The refinement objective is also backpropagated through the FlowMatch sampler, allowing generation and correction to be jointly optimized for the final reconstruction. Experiments on a day-blocked ERA5--SolarCube benchmark show consistent improvements over standalone generation and post-hoc refinement. More broadly, SolarFlowRefiner provides a general strategy for coupling generative predictors with iterative correctors.

</details>


### [129] [Helix-FNO: Spectral-Domain Operator Learning Coupled with a High-Fidelity Mechanistic Model for Fast Surrogate Simulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22129)
*Jiabao Zhao,Chuwei Wang,Jinxi Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Helix-FNO is a teacher-student architecture combining a mechanistic simulator with Fourier Neural Operators to create fast, generalizable surrogate models for wastewater treatment optimization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mechanistic simulation models for full-scale treatment processes are accurate but too slow for real-time decision support requiring thousands of forward evaluations at 5-minute intervals. Traditional surrogate models often fail to generalize to new conditions.

Method: Helix-FNO uses a teacher-student architecture: a 32-state mechanistic teacher generates high-fidelity training data using Latin-hypercube and uncertainty-based active learning, while a Fourier Neural Operator student learns the solution operator in the spectral domain, enabling generalization across parameter spaces.

Result: Helix-FNO achieves three orders of magnitude speedup over mechanistic simulations (millisecond inference), outperforms physics-informed and data-driven recurrent surrogates in accuracy and dataset efficiency, and enables massive candidate screening for online decision support.

Conclusion: Helix-FNO successfully bridges the gap between mechanistic accuracy and computational efficiency by learning entire solution families rather than single instances, providing a practical framework for real-time decision support in complex engineering systems.

Abstract: Mechanistic simulation models of full-scale treatment processes remain the only trustworthy, extrapolative description of the underlying physico-chemical dynamics, yet their runtime is far too slow to support the thousands of forward evaluations that a modern decision engine requires at a 5-minute decision cadence. The standard remedy-surrogate modelling-often produces a network that learns a single solution for a single configuration, so it generalises poorly to new influent profiles, control settings or plant layouts. This paper presents Helix-FNO, a teacher-student architecture that couples a thirty-two-state mechanistic teacher with a Fourier neural operator (FNO) student. The teacher supplies a high-fidelity dataset of input-field-to-solution pairs, curated by Latin-hypercube and uncertainty-based active learning to cover the boundary and overload regimes that matter in practice; the student learns, in the spectral domain, the solution operator itself rather than any single solution, thereby moving from learning one instance to learning an entire family of equations. We give the operator formulation, the spectral convolution definition, the weighted distillation loss and the active-learning criterion, and we analyse the approximation error of a truncated Fourier expansion with respect to the smoothness of the parametric solution manifold. An illustrative study compares Helix-FNO against a physics-informed network and a data-driven recurrent surrogate on accuracy, dataset efficiency and inference latency, and places the methods on a speed-accuracy Pareto front. The resulting operator is three orders of magnitude faster than the mechanistic teacher at millisecond inference, which is precisely the capability required for massive candidate screening and online decision support.

</details>


### [130] [Weak Ties, Strong Signals: Efficient Training Data Detection in Diffusion LLMs via Independent Token Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22145)
*Hongyao Yu,Tianqu Zhuang,Ziyuan Xu,Hao Fang,Jiaxin Hong,Bin Chen,Shu-Tao Xia*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ITS: A query-efficient framework for detecting memorization in diffusion LLMs by sampling weakly dependent tokens to reduce structural estimation error from random masking approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Detecting training data usage in diffusion LLMs is challenging due to their architecture lacking efficient probability decomposition of autoregressive models. Existing random masking methods fail to control dependencies among masked tokens, introducing structural estimation error that obscures memorization signals.

Method: Proposed Independent Token Sampling (ITS) framework: uses attention-derived pairwise dependency proxy to approximate CMI-aware selection criterion for sampling weakly dependent token sets, incorporates diversity-promoting strategy for better token coverage across sampling rounds, yielding aggregated token-wise signals with reduced dependency-induced error.

Result: ITS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across multiple datasets and models, achieving 0.18 AUC improvement on ArXiv dataset while maintaining strong performance under limited query budgets.

Conclusion: By addressing the token dependency problem in existing detection methods for diffusion LLMs, ITS provides more reliable memorization detection through query-efficient independent token sampling, making it practical for real-world privacy auditing applications.

Abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) offer a compelling alternative to autoregressive models, yet they may expose sensitive training data during denoising. Detecting such usage is challenging because dLLMs lack the efficient one-pass probability decomposition of causal architectures. Existing methods rely on random masking to obtain tractable token-wise detection signals under limited query budgets, but fail to control dependencies among masked tokens. We demonstrate that this token-wise approximation introduces a non-negative structural estimation error, which is theoretically characterized by the cumulative conditional mutual information (CMI) among masked tokens and can obscure subtle memorization signals. This insight suggests that reliable detection requires masked token sets with weak internal dependency. To avoid the prohibitive cost of directly estimating CMI over token combinations, we propose \textit{Independent Token Sampling} (ITS), a query-efficient framework that uses an attention-derived pairwise dependency proxy to approximate the CMI-aware selection criterion. ITS further incorporates a diversity-promoting strategy to improve token coverage across sampling rounds, yielding aggregated token-wise signals that are less affected by dependency-induced approximation error. Experiments on multiple datasets show that ITS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across different models and datasets, achieving an AUC improvement of 0.18 on the ArXiv dataset while maintaining strong performance under limited query budgets. The code is available at https://github.com/Chrisqcwx/DLLM-MIA .

</details>


### [131] [GRRR: The Geometry of Reshaping, Rotation, and Routing in Decoder LLM post-training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22146)
*Jianing Qi,Hao Tang,Zhigang Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Post-training primarily reconfigures pretrained pathways rather than substantially changing singular values; diagonal weight changes are less important for performance gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how post-training (SFT and RL) changes LLM weights relative to pretrained weights, specifically analyzing the geometric nature of these changes through SVD decomposition.

Method: Analyzed 12 post-training chains, expressing weight updates in pretrained matrix's SVD frame to decompose changes into three components: diagonal (singular value changes), off-diagonal (rotation of coupling), and null-space (routes outside original nonzero SVD core).

Result: Removing the diagonal component usually preserves most post-training gains on math evaluation, suggesting gains come primarily from reconfiguring/extending pretrained pathways rather than changing singular values.

Conclusion: Post-training gains in LLMs are carried mainly by reconfiguring and extending existing pretrained pathways rather than substantially altering the singular values, highlighting the importance of weight rotation and null-space routing.

Abstract: We study how post-training changes the weights of Large Language Models (LLMs) relative to their pretrained weights. Across 12 post-training chains with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL), we express each weight update in the pretrained matrix's singular value decomposition (SVD) frame. This decomposition separates the changes of three geometrically distinct components: diagonal values, which reshapes singular values; off-diagonal values, which rotates the coupling between pretrained input and output directions; and null-space values, which routes outside the matrix's original nonzero SVD core. On a math evaluation suite, we find that removing the diagonal component usually preserves most of the gains from post-training. These results suggest that post-training gains are carried primarily by reconfiguring and extending pretrained pathways rather than by substantially changing singular values of pre-trained models.

</details>


### [132] [SafeTune: A Unified Faithful Library for Auditing and Repairing Safety Drift in Fine-Tuned LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22153)
*Pratinav Seth,Saisab Sadhu,Anshul Kaushal,Vinay Kumar Sankarapu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SafeTune is a unified library that standardizes safety drift mitigation methods for fine-tuned LLMs across four intervention paradigms with shared utilities, enabling easier comparison and deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current methods for addressing safety drift in fine-tuned LLMs are scattered across incompatible implementations, different lifecycle stages, and varied evaluation protocols, making them difficult to adopt, compare, and integrate into practical workflows.

Method: SafeTune provides a source-available library that unifies four intervention paradigms: post-hoc weight recovery, safety-constrained fine-tuning, gradient-based unlearning, and inference-time steering. It offers a consistent configuration-driven workflow with shared interpretability, evaluation, and deployment utilities, while maintaining the distinct requirements of each paradigm. The system uses a modular registry to support new methods, benchmarks, judges, models, and domains without pipeline redesign.

Result: The library demonstrates effectiveness through controlled comparisons and real-world deployment case studies in finance and medical domains. It successfully characterizes safety drift, evaluates feasible interventions using common refusal-behavior and capability evaluations, and supports calibrated or layered mitigation strategies.

Conclusion: SafeTune addresses the fragmentation in safety drift mitigation by providing a unified, extensible framework that enables systematic comparison and deployment of safety interventions for fine-tuned LLMs, making safety improvements more accessible and practical across different domains.

Abstract: Methods for addressing safety drift in fine-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) are scattered across incompatible implementations, lifecycle stages, and evaluation protocols, making them difficult to adopt and compare. We introduce SafeTune, a source-available library that unifies four intervention paradigms: post-hoc weight recovery, safety-constrained fine-tuning, gradient-based unlearning, and inference-time steering, alongside shared interpretability, evaluation, and deployment utilities. SafeTune provides a consistent configuration-driven workflow while preserving the distinct inputs and intervention points each paradigm requires. Its modular registry supports new methods, benchmarks, judges, models, and fine-tuning domains without redesigning the surrounding pipeline. We demonstrate SafeTune through controlled comparisons and finance and medical deployment case studies, showing how it characterizes safety drift, evaluates feasible interventions on common refusal-behavior and capability evaluations, and supports calibrated or layered mitigation.

</details>


### [133] [A Comparative Framework for Evaluating Foundation Models on Tabular Data: A Case Study in Healthcare](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22154)
*Majid Lotfian Delouee,Sjors G. J. G. In 't Veld,Martijn C. Schut*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A framework for evaluating and ranking tabular foundation models across six clinically meaningful dimensions to help clinicians and data scientists choose appropriate models for healthcare applications.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: With the proliferation of tabular foundation models for healthcare data, there's a practical need to provide clinicians and data scientists with a structured way to compare models against real-world clinical requirements. Existing surveys catalogue models but lack systematic evaluation frameworks for real applications.

Method: Introduces a comparative evaluation framework that scores and ranks tabular foundation models across six dimensions: generalization to new datasets, patient privacy protection, data efficiency, scalability, interpretability, and fairness across patient subgroups. Each dimension has measurable sub-components, and super-metrics combine multiple dimensions for diagnostic analysis. The framework is demonstrated on two healthcare use cases (iron deficiency screening and heart failure prediction).

Result: The framework shows how the same metrics can lead to different model rankings depending on clinical context priorities. Also provides a taxonomy of 45 TFMs organized by architecture to help researchers and practitioners navigate the field.

Conclusion: A comprehensive evaluation framework is needed for practical model selection in healthcare, and the proposed system provides structured, clinically meaningful criteria that can adapt to different clinical priorities and contexts.

Abstract: Tabular data is the most common format in clinical practice, encompassing laboratory results, medication records, diagnostic codes, and patient demographics. As foundation models for tabular data have grown in number and variety, a practical question has become harder to answer: which model should a clinician or data scientist actually choose for a given task, and why? Existing surveys catalogue what these models can do, but they stop short of providing a structured way to compare them against the specific demands of a real application. We introduce \system{}, a comparative evaluation framework that scores and ranks tabular foundation models (TFMs) across six clinically meaningful dimensions: how well a model generalizes to new datasets, how effectively it protects patient privacy, how much data it needs to perform well, how it scales with growing datasets and feature spaces, how interpretable its predictions are to clinicians, and how fairly it performs across patient subgroups. Each dimension is broken down into measurable sub-components, and groups of sub-components can optionally be combined into supplementary compound scores, called super-metrics, that provide a diagnostic view of how a model performs across several dimensions simultaneously. To show how the framework works in practice, we apply it to two healthcare use cases, screening for iron deficiency and predicting heart failure, demonstrating how the same set of metrics leads to different model rankings depending on what matters most in each clinical context. We also provide a taxonomy of 45 TFMs organized by their underlying architecture, which serves as a reference for researchers and practitioners looking to navigate this rapidly expanding field.

</details>


### [134] [From Latent Biomarkers to Clinical Rules: Embedding-Guided Rule Mining and Attribution-Based Translation for Interpretable Tabular Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22155)
*Majid Lotfian Delouee,Hamed Ayoobi,Sjors G. J. G. In 't Veld,Martijn C. Schut*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Pipeline mines decision rules in latent space of FT-Transformer and translates them back to clinical features, outperforming raw-feature rules on most datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clinical decision tools need accurate predictions with understandable explanations. Rule-based models are transparent but may miss complex patterns from variable interactions.

Method: Four-step pipeline: 1) use FT-Transformer to create latent space, 2) identify embedding dimensions separating patient groups as latent biomarkers, 3) mine rules using small decision trees, 4) translate rules back to clinical features using gradient-input saliency and CLS attention attribution.

Result: Translated rules outperformed raw-feature rules in 5 out of 6 datasets, with mean AUROC gains from 0.04 to 0.23. On heart disease dataset, embedding-space rules achieved 0.98 AUROC but translation reduced to 0.72, showing some latent patterns can't be simply translated.

Conclusion: Latent-space rule discovery can uncover predictive patterns while providing clinically interpretable explanations, though some high-performing latent rules cannot be fully captured by simple raw-feature conditions.

Abstract: Clinical decision support tools are most useful when accurate predictions are accompanied by understandable explanations. Rule-based models provide transparency, but rules derived directly from raw clinical measurements may miss patterns arising from interactions between multiple variables. We present a four-step pipeline that mines decision rules in the latent space of an FT-Transformer and translates them back into measurable clinical features. Embedding dimensions that consistently separate patient groups are treated as latent biomarkers, rules are mined using small decision trees, and selected rules are translated using gradient-input saliency and CLS attention attribution. We evaluate the framework on six public clinical and population health datasets at four embedding dimensions. Translated rules outperformed raw-feature rules in five of six datasets, with mean AUROC gains ranging from 0.04 to 0.23. On the heart disease dataset, embedding-space rules reached 0.98 AUROC, but translation reduced this to 0.72, showing that high-performing latent rules cannot always be represented by simple raw-feature conditions. These results show that latent-space rule discovery can uncover predictive patterns while translating them into clinically measurable features that can be evaluated by clinicians.

</details>


### [135] [The Limits of Speculation: Bounding Speculative Decoding in Mixture-of-Experts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22156)
*Aidar Amankulov,Denis Mamatin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Speculative decoding in MoE models faces unstable verification costs due to input-dependent expert loading. The paper formulates speculation-budget selection as a stochastic shortest path problem and uses an Oracle to analyze the physics of verification cost decisions, revealing a linear boundary in delta space.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address the problem of unstable verification costs in speculative decoding for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, which arises from input-dependent expert loading patterns that make cost prediction and optimization challenging.

Method: The authors formulate speculation-budget selection as an offline Stochastic Shortest Path (SSP) problem over reference sequences. They build a diagnostic Oracle that uses counterfactual simulation to account for MoE verification cost. They analyze the Oracle's decisions on Qwen3-Coder and EAGLE-3 pairing in marginal deltas (Delta Space).

Result: Analysis shows that rejected candidates form a strict linear boundary in Delta Space. This demonstrates that complex global optimization is locally governed by a necessary condition balancing marginal cost against expected progress ($\frac{Δ\mathbb{E}[Cost]}{Δ\mathbb{E}[a]}$).

Conclusion: The linear boundary finding provides a rigorous mathematical reference point for designing future adaptive online heuristics for speculative decoding in MoE models, offering insights into the underlying physics of verification cost optimization.

Abstract: Speculative decoding in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models faces the problem of unstable verification cost caused by input-dependent expert loading. To study the physics of this process, we formulate speculation-budget selection as an offline Stochastic Shortest Path (SSP) problem over reference sequences and build a diagnostic Oracle that uses counterfactual simulation to account for MoE verification cost. A detailed analysis of the Oracle's decisions on the Qwen3-Coder and EAGLE-3 pairing, in the space of marginal deltas (Delta Space), shows that rejected candidates form a strict linear boundary. This result demonstrates that a complex global optimization is locally governed by a necessary condition balancing marginal cost against expected progress ($\frac{Δ\mathbb{E}[Cost]}{Δ\mathbb{E}[a]}$), providing a rigorous mathematical reference point for designing future adaptive online heuristics.

</details>


### [136] [PAGE: Partition-Aware Gated KV-Cache Eviction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22157)
*Pankaj Kumar,Subhankar Mishra*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PAGE is a per-input admission safeguard for KV-cache eviction that predicts when eviction is safe vs. catastrophic using prefill attention patterns, preventing accuracy collapse on capacity-bound inputs without training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing KV-cache eviction methods focus on which tokens to keep but not whether to evict at all, and benchmark averages can hide catastrophic accuracy drops (from 99% to 0%) on certain inputs where eviction is harmful.

Method: PAGE uses a label-free scalar computed from prefill attention patterns - the early-to-late drop in pairwise top-k head agreement - to predict whether inputs belong to capacity-bound (eviction catastrophic) or dilution-prone (eviction safe/beneficial) classes. It thresholds this drop and applies base evictors only when safe, otherwise retaining full cache. No training or accuracy labels needed.

Result: PAGE reduces harm rate on capacity-bound inputs from 0.75 to 0.026 (29× reduction) across 4 evictors, 4 models, and 2 benchmarks, turning catastrophic 99%→0% collapses into flat 89% accuracy. Achieves 1.8-3.4× compression (mean 2.9×) vs nominal 16× budget.

Conclusion: PAGE provides targeted safety for a small minority of capacity-bound inputs where eviction is catastrophic, serving as a per-input safeguard rather than a compressor. It enables safe KV-cache eviction without retraining evictors.

Abstract: KV-cache eviction methods decide which tokens to keep but not whether to evict at all, so a benchmark mean can hide a class of inputs on which compression drives accuracy from 99\% to 0\%. We reframe eviction as a per-input admission decision and show that inputs separate into a capacity-bound class, where eviction is catastrophic at every budget, and a dilution-prone class, where eviction is safe or beneficial. A single label-free scalar computed from prefill attention, the early-to-late drop in pairwise top-$k$ head agreement, predicts this class before any decoding. PAGE thresholds this drop: it applies any base evictor when the drop is large and retains the full cache otherwise, with no training and no accuracy labels. The drop orders inputs by eviction safety consistently across four architecture families, and a per-model unlabeled pilot of about 100 inputs recalibrates the threshold for a new family. Used as a safeguard, PAGE cuts the harm rate on the capacity-bound regime from 0.75 to 0.026, a 29 $\times$ reduction, across four evictors, four models, and two benchmarks, turning a 99\% to 0\% collapse into a flat 89\% without retraining the evictor. The gate is inert wherever eviction is already safe, and the capacity-bound class it protects is a small, identifiable minority of inputs, so the benefit is a targeted safety gain rather than an average one. PAGE is a per-input safeguard, not a compressor: realized compression is $1.8 - 3.4 \times$ (mean 2.9$\times$) against a nominal 16$\times$ budget and decays toward unity by batch 16 under static provisioning, and a trained evictor wins at matched memory.

</details>


### [137] [StepKV: Step-Aware KV Cache Compression for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22158)
*Boyu Feng,Jiahong Liu,Yifan Li,Wenhao Yu,Zexuan Qiu,Yuliang Sun,Ming Shen,Xiang Li,Quanyu Dai,Irwin King*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: StepKV proposes a novel KV cache compression method that retains reasoning steps as units rather than individual tokens, addressing reasoning continuity disruption in multi-step LLM agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current KV cache compression methods treat cache as flat token streams and prune based on recency or attention saliency, which disrupts reasoning continuity in multi-step agents where early observations/intermediate decisions remain essential for later evidence synthesis.

Method: StepKV treats reasoning steps as first-class retention units, associates cache entries with generating steps, estimates step utility from trajectory-derived signals, combines this with token-level saliency, and globally ranks prunable tokens to retain top-scoring entries under budget.

Result: StepKV sustains accuracy under low KV budgets where token-level baselines degrade sharply across multi-hop QA and long-horizon web reasoning tasks, offering more robust efficiency-accuracy trade-off.

Conclusion: StepKV provides a step-centric perspective for agent KV cache compression that better preserves reasoning continuity, enabling more efficient multi-step agent inference while maintaining accuracy.

Abstract: Key-value (KV) caching is essential for efficient autoregressive large language model (LLM) inference, but the cache grows linearly with context length, increasing storage and decoding costs. KV cache compression mitigates this cost by retaining only a subset of cached tokens. This challenge is particularly important for multi-step LLM agents, where a query expands into trajectories of reasoning, tool interactions, and retrieved observations. Existing pruning methods typically treat the cache as a flat token stream and rank tokens by recency or attention saliency. This creates a mismatch between the unit of compression and the unit of reasoning: token-level pruning removes individual entries, whereas useful information in multi-step agents is often organized into reasoning steps with uneven and delayed importance. Consequently, an early observation or intermediate decision may receive little recent attention yet remain essential for later evidence synthesis. We term this failure mode Reasoning Continuity Disruption.These observations motivate KV cache compression that jointly considers token- and reasoning-step-level information. StepKV addresses this goal by treating reasoning steps as first-class retention units. It associates cache entries with their generating steps, estimates step utility from trajectory-derived signals, and combines this utility with token-level saliency. The resulting scores globally rank prunable tokens, from which StepKV retains the top-scoring entries under a target budget. StepKV thus provides a step-centric perspective for agent KV cache compression. Across multi-hop QA and long-horizon web reasoning tasks, StepKV sustains accuracy under low KV budgets where token-level baselines degrade sharply, offering a more robust efficiency-accuracy trade-off for multi-step agent inference.

</details>


### [138] [Uncertainty and Business-Aware Remaining Useful Life Estimation for Semiconductor Manufacturing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22160)
*Davide Frizzo,Francesco Borsatti,Gian Antonio Susto*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A predictive maintenance framework using deep learning and simultaneous quantile regression for uncertainty-aware remaining useful life estimation in semiconductor manufacturing, with S4D models achieving the best results in reducing business costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Semiconductor manufacturing has tightly interconnected components where a single failure can disrupt the entire production pipeline. Maintenance planning needs to balance unexpected failures against prematurely interrupted operating life, requiring accurate remaining useful life estimation with uncertainty awareness.

Method: Combines Deep Learning sequence models with Simultaneous Quantile Regression for uncertainty-aware Remaining Useful Life estimation. Compares several architectures including State Space Models on ion-milling data from 2018 PHM Data Challenge. Uses prediction metrics and business metrics like Unexpected Breaks, Unexploited Lifetime, and cost-weighted objective.

Result: Diagonal State Spaces (S4D) delivers the best RUL estimates across quantiles. Compared to Preventive Maintenance baselines, it substantially lowers business cost by avoiding systematically early interventions. The framework supports uncertainty-aware, cost-sensitive maintenance planning.

Conclusion: The proposed Predictive Maintenance framework with uncertainty-aware RUL estimation using DL and SQR effectively supports risk-aware maintenance decisions in semiconductor production, with S4D models showing superior performance in both prediction accuracy and business cost reduction.

Abstract: Semiconductor manufacturing relies on tightly interconnected components, so early identification of the assets most likely to fail is essential to prevent a single breakdown from disrupting the entire production pipeline. Maintenance planning must therefore balance unexpected failures against prematurely interrupted operating life. We present a Predictive Maintenance (PdM) framework combining Deep Learning (DL) sequence models and Simoultaneous Quantile Regression (SQR)
  for uncertainty-aware Remaining Useful Life (RUL) estimation and risk-aware maintenance decisions. Several architectures are compared on ion-milling data from the 2018 PHM Data Challenge (PHM18), including architectures based on State Space Models (SSM), using prediction and business metrics: Unexpected Breaks (UB), Unexploited Lifetime (UL), and a cost-weighted objective. Diagonal State Spaces (S4D) delivers the best Remaining Useful Life (RUL) estimates across quantiles and, relative to Preventive Maintenance (PvM) baselines, substantially lowers business cost by avoiding systematically early interventions. The results support uncertainty-aware, cost-sensitive maintenance planning in semiconductor production.

</details>


### [139] [TARGet: Topology-Aware Fusion-based Radio Frequency Circuit Functional Modeling using Graph Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22165)
*Soroosh Noorzad,Sebastian Bodero,Morteza Fayazi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TARGet: A topology-aware RF circuit modeling method using graph neural networks and sub-circuit S-parameter representations for efficient multi-topology learning with significantly reduced training data requirements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing ML approaches for RF circuit synthesis require separate training for each topology, ignore circuit topology information, and rely on fully connected neural networks that need large training datasets, limiting their efficiency and transferability across circuit designs.

Method: TARGet uses a two-level hierarchical approach: 1) Sub-circuit level with S-parameter representations for reusable behavioral abstractions, 2) Circuit topology level with explicit topology incorporation. The model combines Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) with sub-circuit connectivity-aware neural networks in a novel fusion-based architecture.

Result: TARGet achieves sub-1% prediction error, reduces required training data by up to 35.5x compared to SOTA, achieves 9.7x higher accuracy under 1% error threshold, and demonstrates zero-shot transfer to unseen topologies with up to 45% NMAE reduction.

Conclusion: TARGet provides an effective open-source topology-aware RF circuit modeling solution that significantly improves data efficiency, prediction accuracy, and transfer learning capabilities across multiple circuit topologies compared to existing approaches.

Abstract: Automatic synthesis of analog and Radio Frequency (RF) circuits is an emerging area that requires an efficient circuit modeling method. In recent years, Machine Learning (ML) solutions have played a promising role in this regard. However, many existing ML approaches require separate training data for each circuit topology, even when a single circuit component is added or removed. In addition, they overlook circuit topology information, which limits their ability to capture complex component interactions. Furthermore, they rely on fully connected neural networks with flat feature representations, which require substantial amounts of training data. In this work, we propose an open-source topology-aware RF circuit modeling method, TARGet. Our model considers the circuit at two levels: sub-circuits and the overall circuit topology. At the sub-circuit level, TARGet leverages S-parameter representations to capture sub-circuit behavior rather than relying on individual circuit components, providing a reusable behavioral abstraction for RF building blocks. Moreover, TARGet explicitly incorporates circuit topology information into the model, enabling it to learn across multiple topologies. TARGet introduces a novel fusion-based architecture that integrates Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and sub-circuit connectivity-aware neural networks to improve data efficiency. Experimental evaluation across multiple RF circuit topologies demonstrates that TARGet achieves sub-1% prediction error while reducing the required training data by up to 35.5x compared to state-of-the-art (SOTA) approaches. Furthermore, TARGet achieves 9.7x higher prediction accuracy under a strict 1% error threshold relative to SOTA models. A held-out matching-network evaluation further demonstrates zero-shot transfer to an unseen sub-circuit topology, where TARGet reduces NMAE by up to 45%.

</details>


### [140] [Clustering-Based Collective Anomaly Detection in IoT Systems: A Graph Neural Network Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22166)
*Dalila Khettaf,Djamel Djenouri,Zeinab Rezaeifar,Youcef Djenouri*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A novel unsupervised framework called UGCAD for detecting collective anomalies in IoT network traffic using graph-structured data and variational graph autoencoders.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rapid expansion of IoT devices has increased network traffic and vulnerability to cyberattacks, creating a need for effective anomaly detection. However, existing research has predominantly focused on point anomalies while collective anomaly detection remains under-explored.

Method: UGCAD uses variational graph autoencoder (VGAE) to learn graph representations without prior knowledge of group labels, then enhances clustering algorithms for node grouping. It aggregates normal clusters, refines them, and applies anomaly scores to detect collective anomalies.

Result: Extensive experiments on CICIoT2023 and ToN-IoT datasets show UGCAD's effectiveness in both clustering and collective anomaly detection. Comparative evaluations demonstrate superiority over traditional and state-of-the-art clustering-based CAD approaches.

Conclusion: UGCAD provides an effective solution for collective anomaly detection in IoT networks, addressing a gap in existing literature and showing superior performance compared to existing methods.

Abstract: The rapid advancement of Internet of Things (IoT) technology has led to the widespread deployment of smart, interconnected devices across a range of domains. However, this expansion has also resulted in a substantial increase in network traffic, creating more opportunities for malicious actors to launch cyberattacks and compromise sensitive information, thereby increasing the need for effective anomaly detection. The state-of-the-art in anomaly detection has predominantly focused on point anomalies. In contrast, the detection of collective anomalies remains relatively under-explored in the literature. In this paper, we introduce Unsupervised Graph Collective Anomaly Detection (UGCAD), a novel frame- work designed to identify collective anomalies in IoT network traffic. Unlike many existing methods, UGCAD operates on graph-structured data without any prior knowledge of group labels or membership. It leverages a variational graph autoencoder (VGAE) to learn the graph representation, which is subsequently used to enhance a clustering algorithm for effective grouping of nodes. To detect collective anomalies, clusters identified as normal are first aggregated and refined, after which anomaly scores are applied to detect collective anomalies. Extensive experiments conducted on the CICIoT2023 and ToN-IoT network datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of UGCAD in both clustering and collective anomaly detection (CAD). Furthermore, comparative evaluations against several traditional and state-of-the-art clustering-based CAD approaches confirm the superiority of UGCAD in accurately detecting collective anomalies.

</details>


### [141] [Role-Aware Morgan Fingerprints for Reaction Yield Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22167)
*Chinmay Mirji,Prashant Shekhar,Foram Madiyar,Hao Peng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MFP is a reaction yield prediction method using role-aware Morgan fingerprints that outperforms state-of-the-art Transformers and graph neural networks while training much faster.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current reaction yield prediction methods using graph neural networks or Transformers have heavy preprocessing overhead and can break with inconsistent input formatting, creating a need for more robust and efficient approaches.

Method: Uses role-aware Morgan fingerprints where circular fingerprints are computed for each reaction component, aggregated by chemical role, combined with transformation-sensitive difference features, and fed to a feed-forward neural regressor.

Result: Achieves R2 = 0.878 on Suzuki-Miyaura and R2 = 0.969 on Buchwald-Hartwig benchmarks, training an order of magnitude faster than Transformer- or graph-based methods.

Conclusion: MFP establishes an effective, reproducible, and efficient baseline for reaction yield prediction with radius-2 representations at nBits=2048 providing the best balance of accuracy, speed, and stability.

Abstract: Predicting reaction yield from molecular structure and reaction context can cut experimental trial-and-error and speed up condition screening in synthetic chemistry. Recent methods for this task use learned representations such as graph neural networks or Transformer encoders over reaction SMILES (Simplified Molecular Input Line Entry System), but these approaches carry heavy preprocessing overhead and can break when input formatting is inconsistent. We propose MFP, a reaction yield prediction method built on role-aware Morgan fingerprints where count-based circular fingerprints are computed for each reaction component, aggregated by chemical role (reactant, reagent, product), and combined with transformation-sensitive difference features into a fixed-length reaction descriptor fed to a feed-forward neural regressor. We test MFP against state of the art methods such as YieldBERT (with and without data augmentation) and GNAN (graph neural network) on the Suzuki-Miyaura and Buchwald-Hartwig benchmarks using a shared preprocessing and evaluation protocol. MFP reaches R2 = 0.878 on Suzuki-Miyaura and R2 = 0.969 on Buchwald-Hartwig while training an order of magnitude faster than graph- or Transformer-based alternatives. A formal complexity analysis confirms that MFP folds all representation cost into a one-time preprocessing step, removing the per-epoch message-passing overhead that graph methods carry. An ablation over fingerprint radius and folded vector length shows that radius-2 representations at nBits =2048 give the best balance of accuracy, speed, and cross-split stability on both datasets. These results establish MFP as an effective, reproducible, and efficient baseline for reaction yield prediction.

</details>


### [142] [Multiple latent orderings better predict language model preferences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22170)
*Aviral Chawla,William H. W. Thompson,Jean-Gabriel Young*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LLM preferences often show intransitive patterns that can't be explained by single latent ordering, but reflect aggregation of multiple coherent preference components.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Language models are used for value judgments where observed preferences often show intransitivity (A>B, B>C, but C>A). Existing work treats inconsistencies as noise around single ordering, but the authors propose these reflect multiple latent coherent orderings.

Method: Introduced noise-augmented mixture Bradley-Terry (MBT) model that infers latent preference components from repeated pairwise comparisons. First proved observed inconsistencies can't be explained by single ordering under any monotone link function, then applied mixture model across seven models and four tasks.

Result: Mixture of orderings explains structural inconsistencies better than single-utility models. Aggregate preferences often hide underlying preference heterogeneity. Moral Machine case study shows models disagreeing on aggregate orderings can still share latent components.

Conclusion: LLMs reflect plural preferences rather than single ordering. Alignment and evaluation pipelines treating LLM preferences as single function risk averaging over coherent orderings that different users may endorse differently.

Abstract: Language models are frequently employed in settings where they are asked to make value judgments and choices. These observed choices often exhibit intransitivity: A model may prefer item $A$ to $B$ and $B$ to $C$, while also preferring $C$ to $A$. Existing work that models LLM preferences treats such inconsistencies as sampling noise around a single latent ordering. We instead propose that intransitivity reflects the aggregation of multiple latent, internally consistent orderings. We first show that observed inconsistencies cannot be explained by a single ordering under any monotone link function. We then introduce a noise-augmented mixture Bradley-Terry (MBT) model that infers latent preference components from repeated pairwise comparisons. Across seven models and four tasks, a mixture of orderings often explains structural inconsistencies better than single-utility models. We find that aggregate preferences often hide underlying preference heterogeneity. A case study on Moral Machine dilemmas shows that models which disagree on aggregate orderings can still share latent components. Together, these results suggest that LLMs reflect plural preferences. Alignment and evaluation pipelines that treat LLM preferences as a single function, therefore, risk averaging over coherent orderings that different users may endorse differently.

</details>


### [143] [Industrial Kinematic Trajectory Model (IKTM): Coordinate-Free Autoregressive Generator](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22173)
*Max Amiri,David Eyers*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: IKTM is a coordinate-free industrial vehicle trajectory generator using kinematic sequences (speed/heading changes) with autoregressive transformer that generalizes across sites without absolute spatial references.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing trajectory models rely on absolute coordinates or site-specific representations that don't work well for unstructured industrial terrain, requiring site-specific adaptation.

Method: Industrial Kinematic Trajectory Model (IKTM) uses autoregressive causal transformer with probabilistic mixture heads and explicit duration-conditioning signal, representing motion through kinematic sequences without absolute spatial reference.

Result: Zero-shot evaluation on 3 unseen sites shows matching turn-rate distributions with Jensen-Shannon divergence 0.032-0.050 bits; outperforms prior Markovian model by 5.3-6.0x; achieves perfect duration tracking with zero error.

Conclusion: IKTM enables site-generalizable trajectory generation for industrial environments without absolute coordinates, providing robust zero-shot performance across diverse sites with precise duration control.

Abstract: Mobility simulation supports logistics, safety, and communications planning in industrial environments such as ports, mines, and airports. Existing trajectory models, however, rely on absolute coordinates, road-network tokens, or semantic zones: representations that are site-specific and not well suited to unstructured industrial terrain. We introduce the Industrial Kinematic Trajectory Model (IKTM), a coordinate-free trajectory generator that represents industrial vehicle motion through kinematic sequences (speed and heading change) with no absolute spatial reference. IKTM uses an autoregressive causal transformer with probabilistic mixture heads and extends our prior coordinate-free Markovian model with deep sequence modelling and an explicit duration-conditioning signal. Trained on one site and evaluated zero-shot on three unseen sites, it matches the small-turn shape of the empirical turn-rate distributions of held-out telematics; across all four sites, the per-site mean Jensen-Shannon divergence over 100 sampling seeds spans approximately 0.035-0.050 bits under an oracle-length duration-target protocol and approximately 0.032-0.042 bits under a fully zero-shot prior-length protocol, with similar ranges whether out-of-distribution (OOD) duration targets are drawn from each held-out site's empirical length distribution or from the Site A prior. Both protocols stay above the metric's sampling-noise floor (<=0.0049 bits). Paired by site, the oracle-length values are 5.3-6.0x lower than those of a re-implementation of our prior Markovian model under the same 1 Hz protocol. Termination is duration-conditioned rather than spatial: rollouts stop on 100% of trials with a length-tracking error of +0.0 +/- 0.0 s against the sampled target (100 of 100 exactly on target; N=100, T=0.2, untouched in-distribution test split).

</details>


### [144] [Contrastive World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22175)
*Bonnie Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CWM replaces pixel reconstruction in world models with contrastive learning to maximize mutual information between state-action sequences and future observation features, improving performance in visually complex environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pixel reconstruction in world models struggles in visually complex environments because irrelevant visual information dominates the objective and distracts the model from information relevant to planning and control.

Method: Builds on Dreamer architecture but replaces observation reconstruction with a Deep InfoMax-like lower bound that maximizes mutual information between state-action sequences and local patch features of future observations, removing the pixel decoder entirely.

Result: Matches Dreamer and momentum prediction baseline in default settings, substantially outperforms both when distractors or natural video backgrounds are introduced, while training more efficiently by removing pixel decoder.

Conclusion: Contrastive, infomax-based objectives are a principled and promising direction for building world models robust to visual nuisance factors, which is particularly relevant for transferring model-based RL agents to the real world.

Abstract: World models trained via pixel reconstruction can struggle in visually complex environments, where irrelevant information dominates the objective and distract the model from information relevant to planning and control. We present Contrastive World Models, an approach for learning latent dynamics models without pixel reconstruction. Building on Dreamer, we replace observation reconstruction in the standard world model objective with a Deep InfoMax-like lower bound that maximizes the mutual information between state-action sequences and local patch features of future observations, encouraging state representations to retain information that is predictive of the future without requiring the model to reconstruct visually irrelevant details. We evaluate our approach in small-scale experiments across three settings of increasing visual complexity. Our method matches Dreamer and a momentum prediction baseline in the default setting, and substantially outperforms both once distractors or natural video backgrounds are introduced, while also training more efficiently by removing the pixel decoder entirely. Our approach is general and makes minimal assumptions beyond access to state-action sequences and future observations. These results suggest that contrastive, infomax-based objectives are a principled and promising direction for building world models that are robust to visual nuisance factors, a property particularly relevant for transferring model-based RL agents to the real world.

</details>


### [145] [OpenBlock: Constructive and Verified Content Generation for Adaptive Tile-Matching Games](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22177)
*Jiang Jun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Developed adaptive tile-matching platform with dual-track content generation: rule-based + learned generator, verified for piece placeability. RL agent identified long-bar pieces as dominant failure mode, with neural track improving player retention.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tile-matching puzzle games lack open platforms for studying adaptive difficulty, and proprietary algorithms limit research on how to improve player experience through intelligent content generation.

Method: Dual-track architecture: deterministic rule-based generator + optional learned generator, with exhaustive verification gate ensuring all piece sets are placeable. Self-play RL placement agent with auxiliary tasks exposing per-shape placeability to diagnose failure modes.

Result: RL agent achieved 35.6% win rate, identified long-bar pieces lose most legal placements at high board fill (70-75%). Neural track increased day-1 retention by 1.8 percentage points and session duration by 7% over rule track alone.

Conclusion: Board-state degeneration (not content difficulty) drives late-game failure. Per-shape placeability supervision is key for representation learning. Neural track provides asymmetric upside in live play while maintaining constructive feasibility guarantees.

Abstract: Tile-matching puzzle games serve hundreds of millions of players, yet the content-generation algorithms that decide which pieces to present at each turn remain proprietary, and no open platform exists for studying adaptive difficulty in this genre. We present an adaptive tile-matching platform whose central algorithmic contribution is a dual-track content-generation architecture: a deterministic rule-based generator that is always available, and an optional learned generator, both subject to a common verification gate that establishes, by exhaustive sequential-placement search, that every delivered piece set is fully placeable so the learned track can never degrade the constructive-feasibility guarantee of the rule track. A self-play reinforcement-learning placement agent, supervised by auxiliary tasks that expose per-shape placeability to shared representations, is used to diagnose the game's dominant failure mode: at high board fill, long-bar pieces lose the majority of their legal placements. Across 234,000+ self-play episodes the agent reaches a 35.6\% win rate (median score 4,200), and controlled simulation shows that at board fill rates of 70--75\%, 33--56\% of long-bar pieces have no legal placement, while spawn difficulty distributions are statistically indistinguishable between won and lost games---evidence that board-state degeneration, not content difficulty, drives late-game failure. Head-to-head ablations show that per-shape placeability supervision---not aggregate difficulty features---drives the representation gain, and a 14-day online gray rollout (48,000 players; sample-ratio verified, CUPED-adjusted) lifts day-1 retention by 1.8 percentage points and session duration by 7\% over the rule track alone, quantifying the neural track's asymmetric upside in live play.

</details>


### [146] [Beyond Task Completion: Training Capable and Safe Computer-Use Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22178)
*Zeyu Kang,Zhenyun Yin,Yang Zhang,Shan He,Shanzhe Lei,Yanjiu Zhong,Xinquan Chen,Yuhong Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SCOPE is a framework for joint post-training of computer-use agents to improve both task execution capability and safety-aware decision making through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current computer-use agents trained solely for task success lack reliable safety behavior. They need to condition execution on risk: complete benign tasks, avoid hazards, continue when safe paths exist, and refuse harmful goals or unsafe situations.

Method: Developed SCOPE framework with SCOPE-Gen pipeline to synthesize verifiable capability tasks and convert them into environment-risk variants. Created SATraj-OS dataset with capability demonstrations, safe continuations, and explicit refusals. Used supervised fine-tuning on all trajectory types followed by online reinforcement learning for further improvement.

Result: SCOPE-RL (based on Qwen3.5-9B) achieved 54.17% task success rate on OSWorld and 64.30% attack-avoidance rate on OS-BLIND, yielding best aggregate capability-safety score of 58.80% among evaluated agents.

Conclusion: The SCOPE framework effectively balances capability and safety in computer-use agents through joint training. Safety supervision has asymmetric complementary roles: refusal trajectories improve attack avoidance, while risk-handling trajectories preserve task utility at comparable safety levels.

Abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) have made rapid progress in completing complex tasks through graphical user interfaces, yet post-training centered on task success alone does not induce reliable safety behavior. A reliable CUA must condition its execution on risk: it should complete ordinary benign tasks, avoid environmental hazards and continue when a safe completion path remains, and refuse when the goal is harmful or no safe path exists. To learn this conditional policy, we develop Safety and Capability Optimization for Policy Execution (SCOPE), which jointly post-trains a CUA for task-execution capability and safety-aware decision making. To provide aligned training data for this joint objective, we further introduce SCOPE-Gen, an automated pipeline that synthesizes verifiable capability tasks and converts them into paired environment-risk variants while preserving their original goals. Using the resulting tasks, we construct SATraj-OS, a trajectory dataset comprising capability demonstrations, safe continuations, and explicit refusals. SCOPE first learns from all three trajectory types through supervised fine-tuning and then further improves task completion through online reinforcement learning. Starting from Qwen3.5-9B, SCOPE-RL achieves a 54.17% task success rate on OSWorld and a 64.30% attack-avoidance rate on OS-BLIND, yielding the best aggregate capability--safety score of 58.80% among the evaluated agents. Ablations reveal asymmetric but complementary roles for the two forms of safety supervision: refusal trajectories account for most of the attack-avoidance gain, whereas risk-handling trajectories preserve greater task utility at comparable attack-avoidance levels.

</details>


### [147] [Gaussian Process Decorrelation for Spatiotemporal Deep Learning-Based Snow Water Equivalent Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22182)
*Colin Fenster,Adrienne Marshall,Soutir Bandyopadhyay,Daniel McKenzie*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A novel approach combining Gaussian Process decorrelation with LSTM networks for improved snow water equivalent forecasting, enhanced by conformal prediction for uncertainty quantification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Accurate snowpack forecasting is critical for water policy and management in the Western US, where snowmelt is essential for agriculture and drinking water. SNOTEL stations provide accurate SWE measurements with strong spatiotemporal correlations that need better prediction methods.

Method: First uses Gaussian Process-based linear transformation to remove spatial correlations from SWE data, then trains LSTM neural networks on the decorrelated data to learn clean temporal signals at each station. Incorporates conformal prediction for uncertainty quantification.

Result: The separation of spatial and temporal components yields better predictive success than multiple baseline models. The approach provides accurate point forecasts and distribution-free uncertainty quantification for SWE predictions.

Conclusion: The framework enables improved SWE accumulation forecasting on subseasonal scales and supports future work in predicting large-scale, spatiotemporally complete SWE maps for better water resource management.

Abstract: In the Western United States, snowmelt is essential to the agricultural industry in addition to being a key source of municipal drinking water. Consequently, accurate snowpack forecasting is critical for water policy and management. Automated Snow Telemetry (SNOTEL) stations provide accurate daily measurements of snow water equivalent (SWE) that exhibit strong correlations in space and in time. We tackle the problem of predicting future SWE values across the SNOTEL network.
  Specifically, we use a Gaussian Process-based linear transformation to remove spatial correlations before training a long short-term memory (LSTM) neural network on the decorrelated SWE data. This approach allows the LSTM to learn a clean temporal signal at each station. We show that this separation of spatial and temporal components yields better predictive success than multiple baseline models.
  Furthermore, we incorporate conformal prediction to quantify uncertainty in the resulting SWE forecasts, providing a distribution-free approach to illustrate a potential framework for establishing predictive intervals for spatiotemporal data. Together, accurate point forecasts and distribution-free uncertainty quantification provide a framework for SWE accumulation forecasting on subseasonal scales or projecting SWE with future data while motivating and supporting future work in predicting a large-scale, spatiotemporally complete SWE map.

</details>


### [148] [CleanScore: Black-Box Benchmark Audits with Negative Controls and Sensitivity Bounds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22183)
*Jeffery Opoku,David Banahene*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CleanScore is a black-box audit method that detects benchmark exposure by creating fresh paraphrased versions of test questions, bounding surface-form inflation without needing training data access.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Public benchmark scores are unreliable because they may reflect either genuine skill or prior exposure to questions in training data. Since most models' training data are unknown, there's no way to distinguish between actual capability and exposure advantage.

Method: CleanScore creates three versions of each benchmark question: one public form and two independently written fresh forms that preserve numbers, facts, and answers. It uses a private negative-control bank with explicit transport radius to separate exposure from ordinary form mismatch, plus registered controlled-exposure experiments to detect planted exposure.

Result: The audit of five open models on 200 GSM8K and 200 ARC-Challenge items found no exposure-consistent advantage, bounding surface-form inflation below five points. Leaking an item raises accuracy on paraphrases almost as much as on leaked wording (52-110% invisible to paraphrase audits). On ARC, a planted 49-point advantage shows minimal observable gap (-0.020), and about 20 points survive rewriting stem and options across four training seeds.

Conclusion: Surface-form null bounds far less than phrase contamination audits imply. CleanScore provides a rigorous black-box method to audit benchmark exposure, revealing that current paraphrase-based audits significantly underestimate the extent of training data contamination effects.

Abstract: Public benchmark scores may reflect skill, prior exposure to the questions, or both, and for most models the training data are unknown. We present CleanScore, a black-box audit using scored outputs only. Each benchmark question becomes a parent item with one public form and two independently written fresh forms preserving its numbers, facts and answer. The audit reports an interval for the public-form advantage rather than a verdict, and a private negative-control bank with an explicit transport radius separates exposure from ordinary form mismatch. A registered controlled-exposure experiment detects planted exposure and stays quiet under fresh-form exposure. A registered audit of five open models on 200 GSM8K and 200 ARC-Challenge items finds no exposure-consistent advantage, bounding surface-form inflation below five points. Registered positive controls then bound what such a null can mean. Leaking an item raises accuracy on paraphrases the model never saw almost as much as on the leaked wording, leaving 52% to 110% of the effect invisible to a paraphrase audit. On ARC a planted 49-point advantage shows an observable gap of -0.020, and about 20 points survive rewriting stem and options, across four training seeds. A surface-form null bounds far less than the phrase contamination audit implies.

</details>


### [149] [DPTM-DT: Dual-Pretrained Transformer Multitask Representation Learning for Drug-Target Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22184)
*Ge Kong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DPTM-DT is a dual-pretrained Transformer framework that combines multiple drug and protein representations with cross-modal attention for multitask drug-target prediction (affinity regression, binary classification, and six-level classification).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing drug-target prediction models have limitations: 1) use incomplete drug/protein representations, 2) model cross-modal interactions shallowly, and 3) train affinity regression and interaction classification separately despite these tasks being closely related views of the same drug-target pair.

Method: DPTM-DT combines GROVER molecular graph embeddings, ESM protein language-model embeddings, and CTD physicochemical descriptors. It exchanges drug-target information through bidirectional cross-modal attention and uses a shared pair representation for three tasks: continuous affinity regression, high-affinity binary classification, and six-level affinity classification.

Result: On Davis dataset (80/20 split): MSE 0.193, CI 0.917; binary AUPR 0.727, MCC 0.654; six-class Macro-F1 0.800, Top-2 0.932. On KIBA (80/20 split): MSE 0.120, CI 0.918; binary AUPR 0.798, MCC 0.689; six-class Macro-F1 0.815, Top-2 0.962. DPTM-DT achieves best overall performance across all regression, binary, and multiclass classification settings compared to other methods.

Conclusion: DPTM-DT demonstrates superior drug-target prediction by effectively combining multiple representations, leveraging cross-modal attention, and using multitask learning. Ablation studies show dual target representation, gated fusion, and cross-modal attention all contribute to performance improvements.

Abstract: Drug-target relation prediction supports candidate screening, drug repositioning, and mechanism analysis. Existing models often use incomplete drug or protein representations, model cross-modal interactions shallowly, or train affinity regression and interaction classification separately, although these tasks describe closely related views of the same drug-target pair. This paper presents DPTM-DT, a dual-pretrained Transformer framework for multitask drug-target prediction.
