However, teacher supervision can be unreliable when conditioned on incomplete or low-quality student prefixes. We identify Teacher Uncertainty Contraction (TUC), a systematic phenomenon whereby the teacher's predictive uncertainty decreases as it continues from a student-generated prefix. We theoretically characterize this trade-off through a variance-bias decomposition of teacher-branch gradients, showing that uncertainty contraction reduces variance while teacher-student path divergence increases bias, thereby favoring a finite continuation. Guided by this insight, we propose Adaptive-Continuations On-Policy Distillation (AC-OPD), which augments informative states along student rollouts with teacher continuations and adaptively selects their effective supervision horizons. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation across model scales demonstrate that AC-OPD consistently improves over standard OPD. Controlled-continuations and matched-budget analyses further validate the adaptive-continuations design, highlighting adaptive teacher continuations as an effective principle for reliable on-policy distillation.The code will be made publicly available upon publication.

</details>


### [175] [Strategy Accumulation and Guided Execution for Automated LLM Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22257)
*Haoran Zhao,Wei Du,Dingwen Yang,Jixuan Huang,Junlin Shang,Lingyong Fang,Ya Guo,Tao Gui,Qi Zhang,Xuanjing Huang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SAGE is a two-stage framework that accumulates and reuses fine-tuning strategies across tasks, improving automated LLM tuning by 12.4 percentage points over stateless systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current automated fine-tuning systems are stateless - they discard discovered strategies, dataset insights, and hyperparameter findings after each search, requiring costly repetition for every new task. This wastes valuable experience and computational resources.

Method: A two-stage framework: 1) Multi-agent pipeline with Monte Carlo Tree Search-based exploration and a parallel Distillation Agent that extracts task-specific exploration records and confidence-scored cross-task insights into a structured experience repository. 2) Retrieves relevant experience from this repository and selects applicable strategies to guide training on new tasks.

Result: Evaluation on nine unseen tasks shows SAGE raises average relative improvement over baseline from 3.2% to 15.6% - a 12.4 percentage point gain over the same pipeline without accumulated experience. Works effectively in both single- and cross-category settings.

Conclusion: Persistent strategy experience provides effective guidance for automated fine-tuning on unseen tasks. Accumulating and reusing fine-tuning strategies across tasks significantly improves performance compared to stateless approaches that must start from scratch for each new task.

Abstract: Producing task-specific large language models requires discovering effective training strategies through experimentation. Automated fine-tuning systems have made this experimentation feasible with far less manual effort. However, these systems are stateless: each search discards its discovered strategies, dataset insights, and hyperparameter findings once it ends. Every new task must then repeat this costly search from a cold start. To address this, we propose Strategy Accumulation and Guided Execution (SAGE), a two-stage framework that makes automated fine-tuning search cumulative. In the first stage, a multi-agent pipeline performs Monte Carlo Tree Search-based exploration. A parallel Distillation Agent extracts task-specific exploration records and confidence-scored cross-task insights, which together constitute a structured experience repository. In the second stage, SAGE retrieves relevant experience from this repository and selects what applies to guide training on the new task. We evaluate SAGE on nine unseen tasks spanning both single- and cross-category settings. In single-round execution, SAGE's accumulated experience raises the average relative improvement over baseline from 3.2% to 15.6%, a 12.4-percentage-point gain over the same pipeline without it. These results show that persistent strategy experience provides effective guidance for automated fine-tuning on unseen tasks.

</details>


### [176] [RS-Claw-Evolution: Environment-Feedback-Driven Evolution for Lightweight Remote Sensing Agents in Long-Horizon Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22258)
*Kai Ouyang,Dongyang Hou,Liangtian Liu,Zeyuan Wang,Ziyu Li,Chengfu Liu,Zichao Tang,Xuezhi Cui,Shengwu Ouyang,Wentao Yang,Hanwen Yu,Haifeng Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RS-Claw-Evolution: A three-stage environment-feedback-driven framework that progressively improves lightweight remote sensing agents through interaction, experience, and decision evolution to handle long-horizon geospatial tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Lightweight remote sensing agents based on compact language models struggle with multi-step interactive tasks due to loss of long-horizon states, inefficient environmental feedback utilization, and sparse optimization signals.

Method: Three-stage evolution framework: 1) Interaction evolution uses executable code to control observations and maintain intermediate states; 2) Experience evolution combines failure-aware trajectory generation with error-turn masking to learn from failure-recovery experiences; 3) Decision evolution uses reinforcement learning with multi-dimensional environment rewards and turn-level advantage protection.

Result: Optimized Qwen3-4B-based agent achieves 65.9% accuracy in Autonomous Planning mode on Earth-Bench, outperforming untrained Qwen3-32B baseline (43.8%) and DeepSeek-V3.1 (60.8%), while approaching GPT-5 performance (71.6%).

Conclusion: Learning from environmental feedback can significantly improve lightweight agents and narrow their performance gap with larger models in long-horizon remote sensing tasks, demonstrating the effectiveness of the RS-Claw-Evolution framework.

Abstract: Large language model-driven remote sensing (RS) agents offer a promising approach to automating geospatial analysis. However, lightweight RS agents based on compact language models struggle with multi-step interactive tasks due to loss of long-horizon states, inefficient environmental feedback utilization, and sparse optimization signals. We propose RS-Claw-Evolution, an environment-feedback-driven framework that progressively improves lightweight agents through three stages. Interaction evolution uses executable code to control observations, maintain intermediate states, and reduce context redundancy. Experience evolution combines failure-aware trajectory generation with error-turn masking to learn from informative failure-recovery experiences without imitating faulty actions. Decision evolution uses reinforcement learning with multi-dimensional environment rewards and turn-level advantage protection to optimize tool-use behaviors and improve credit assignment in long sequences. On Earth-Bench, the optimized Qwen3-4B-based agent achieves 65.9% accuracy in Autonomous Planning mode, outperforming the untrained Qwen3-32B baseline (43.8%) and DeepSeek-V3.1 (60.8%), while approaching GPT-5 (71.6%). These results demonstrate that learning from environmental feedback can improve lightweight agents and narrow their performance gap with larger models in long-horizon RS tasks.

</details>


### [177] [Resist, Update, Reject: Preference Optimization Installs a Prior-Dependent Reliability Switch](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22359)
*Sen Yang,Yuen-Hei Yeung*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper shows that current anti-sycophancy training objectives fail to distinguish between source reliability, creating a fixation↔gullibility trade-off. By making reliability identifiable through preference optimization with reliability-labeled data, models can learn to use stated reliability as a prior-dependent switch for belief updating.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current anti-sycophancy approaches treat resistance to manipulation, updating on reliable sources, and rejecting unreliable sources as three separate behaviors. However, the standard training objective makes source reliability non-identifiable - models can't distinguish between same claims from reliable vs unreliable sources, forcing a trade-off between being overly fixated or overly gullible.

Method: Introduces a threshold benchmark where a source gives opposite information while stating its reliability r. The correct action is to flip belief iff r exceeds the model's prior strength p. Uses preference optimization (DPO and IPO) over balanced coverage of reliability-labeled data to make reliability identifiable, with controls to isolate the cause.

Result: The method successfully installs a prior-dependent reliability switch: threshold r* rises monotonically with prior strength p, achieving 0.84 accuracy with monotone flip curves (Spearman 0.56). The policy generalizes to unseen reliability values and notation, follows stated reliability over role prestige, and transfers to other models (Llama-3.1-8B).

Conclusion: The fixation↔gullibility frontier is an empirical property of training objectives, not a theorem. Preference optimization over reliability-labeled coverage (not pairing, loss function, or imitation learning) enables models to learn to use stated reliability as a calibrated belief switch, showing that source reliability can be made identifiable through proper data design.

Abstract: An aligned model asked to hold its answer against a manipulative source must still update on a reliable one and reject an unreliable one: resistance, reliable-update, and unreliable-source rejection are one three-way contract, not three independent behaviors. We show the objective most anti-sycophancy work optimizes is non-identifying with respect to source reliability: because no preference label depends on whether a source is actually reliable, any scalar mixture of the arms traces a single deference dial, and no point separates two same-template testimonies differing only in stated reliability. This fixation$\leftrightarrow$gullibility frontier is a property of the objective, not any model. We make reliability identifiable through data: a threshold benchmark where a source asserts the opposite answer while stating its reliability $r$, and the correct action is to flip iff $r$ exceeds the model's prior strength $p$. Preference optimization over balanced coverage installs a prior-dependent reliability switch: across three seeds on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct the threshold $r^\star$ rises monotonically with the prior, decision accuracy reaches $0.84$ with a monotone flip curve (Spearman $0.56$), and the policy generalizes to unseen reliability values and a held-out notation, following stated reliability over role prestige. Three controls localize the cause: an unmatched variant installs the switch equally ($0.80$), a second preference optimizer (IPO) installs it just as well ($0.86$), whereas supervised imitation does not ($0.50$), so the cause is preference optimization over reliability-labeled coverage, not pairing, loss, or imitation. A confirmatory battery replicates the switch on a fresh test draw, bounds it honestly (it keys on reliability stated in the testimony, not a separately audited record), and transfers it to Llama-3.1-8B. The frontier is empirical, not a theorem.

</details>


### [178] [Contrastive Siamese Representation Learning for Predictive Maintenance of Electrical Submersible Pumps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22360)
*Seshu K. Damarla,Xiuli Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A fault diagnosis framework for electrical submersible pumps that uses Siamese contrastive learning and prior-corrected KNN to handle class imbalance and improve generalization to unseen pump units.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ESPs are critical in offshore oil production, but unexpected failures cause significant losses. Current predictive maintenance is challenging due to nonlinear operating conditions, class imbalance, and variability between different pump units.

Method: 1) Extract features from vibration-domain indicators and engineered harmonic relationships; 2) Use Siamese neural network with class-balanced contrastive pairs to create an embedding space that clusters similar faults; 3) Apply prior-corrected distance-weighted KNN for classification to mitigate class imbalance.

Result: The framework was validated using Leave-One-ESP-Out (LOEO) strategy and demonstrated robust and consistent fault classification performance under realistic industrial conditions.

Conclusion: The proposed framework shows potential for reliable predictive maintenance and intelligent ESP system monitoring by effectively handling class imbalance and generalizing to unseen pump units.

Abstract: Electrical submersible pumps (ESPs) are essential in offshore oil production, where unexpected failures can result in significant operational and financial losses. Accurate predictive maintenance for ESP systems remains challenging due to nonlinear operating conditions, class imbalance, and variability among pump units. To address these issues, this study presents a fault diagnosis framework that incorporates class imbalance awareness by employing Siamese contrastive representation learning and prior-corrected k-nearest neighbor (KNN) classification. The method first extracts discriminative features relevant to fault detection from vibration-domain indicators and engineered harmonic relationships. A Siamese neural network is trained with class-balanced contrastive pairs to construct an embedding space that clusters samples of the same fault type and separates different fault classes. To further mitigate class imbalance during classification, a prior-corrected distance-weighted KNN is applied. The framework is validated using a Leave-One-ESP-Out (LOEO) strategy to evaluate generalization to previously unseen ESP units. Experimental results indicate that the proposed framework delivers robust and consistent fault classification performance under realistic industrial conditions, supporting its potential for reliable predictive maintenance and intelligent ESP system monitoring.

</details>


### [179] [Common Cause, Not Cross-Attention: Blocking Visual Shortcuts in Audio-Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22361)
*Jian Xu,Delu Zeng,John Paisley,Qibin Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Joint audio-video generators learn spurious visual shortcuts and fail when appearance-event correlations break, requiring causal interventions rather than shared latent spaces.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Joint audio-video generators trained on correlated data learn to predict sound from visual appearance rather than causal events, leading to failures when spurious correlations break at test time.

Method: Builds an audio-video structural causal model where audio is independent of visual appearance, tests various architectures (cross-attention, shared latents), proposes counterfactual invariance as solution, and validates across multiple domains.

Result: Models learn visual shortcuts (predict sound from appearance), fail when appearance-event correlation breaks; shared latent approaches don't fix the issue; pretrained video-to-audio generators are not invariant to sound-irrelevant edits.

Conclusion: Counterfactual invariance is necessary and sufficient for causal audio-video prediction; blocking spurious shortcuts requires interventions on nuisance variables rather than just shared latent representations.

Abstract: Joint audio--video generators are trained on data in which what an event looks like and what it sounds like are strongly, often spuriously, correlated: a particular material, texture, or object appearance co-occurs with a particular sound. This paper is a controlled causal study of the resulting failure mode. Building an AV structural causal model in which the audio is, by construction, independent of the video's nuisance appearance, we show that models which let audio read video directly-through cross-attention or a shared latent-learn a visual shortcut: they predict sound from appearance rather than from the causal event, and collapse when the appearance-event correlation is broken at test time, literally synthesizing the wrong event's sound. Crucially, the popular remedy of routing both modalities through a shared common-cause latent does not fix this: a bottleneck, an unsupervised shared/private factorization, and a faithful shared-prior model all grab the appearance proxy and fail like the direct model. Blocking the shortcut instead requires an intervention on the nuisance. Under the stated SCM and intervention assumptions we prove that counterfactual invariance is necessary and sufficient to identify the causal predictor, and we verify the mechanism across a feature-vector SCM, procedural pixel video, real images with spectrogram audio and a pretrained backbone, moving real digits, and a conditional generator. On a \emph{real, pretrained} video-to-audio generator, an input-intervention test shows the model is far from invariant to sound-irrelevant edits (recolouring or graying a video substantially changes the sound it generates).

</details>


### [180] [Complex-valued Phase-Coherent Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22415)
*Leona Hioki*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Complex Transformers need scaled cosine attention (L2-normalized queries/keys) to work properly - without this they perform poorly, with it they achieve state-of-the-art results on various complex-valued tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard complex-valued Transformers use softmax attention over raw complex inner products, but outside natively complex domains they perform near chance level. The authors aim to fix this fundamental issue in complex attention mechanisms.

Method: Propose phase-coherent Transformers (PCT) with scaled cosine attention: L2-normalize queries and keys to get cosine similarity (ignoring magnitudes), then scale the score to order-one magnitude. Also introduce complex screening with phase-coherent recurrence as a specific family member.

Result: PCT achieves strong results across long-range memory, positional retrieval, hierarchical reasoning, frequency-domain classification, and physical complex signals. It shows no degradation up to depth 20 and demonstrates log-linear loss decrease over wide parameter range. Specifically solves Path-X with 91.6% complex parameters vs 38.2% for S4.

Conclusion: Scaled cosine attention is essential for complex Transformers to work effectively. The PCT family shows generalization capabilities not previously seen in complex-valued neural networks, representing a significant advancement in complex neural architecture design.

Abstract: Complex-valued Transformers have inherited softmax attention over the raw complex inner product. Outside natively complex domains this standard form stays near chance, and no complex attention had been shown to correct it. We show that the match must be a scaled cosine score: L2-normalise queries and keys, so the score reads their cosine similarity and ignores their magnitudes, and hold that score at order-one scale. With this the same models train on four diagnostic tasks under two different gates; without the normalisation they stay at chance on ListOps and Needle under both gates and fall far below on the other two, and a normalised score placed at too small a scale fails as well. The resulting family of phase-coherent Transformers (\PCT) matches or exceeds the strongest real-valued baseline across long-range memory, positional retrieval, hierarchical reasoning, frequency-domain classification and physical complex signals; it shows no degradation up to depth 20; and its loss decreases log-linearly over a 61-fold range of parameters. A member of the family, complex screening combined with a phase-coherent recurrence, is the first genuinely complex-valued neural network to solve Path-X, with 91.6% of its trainable parameters complex-valued against 38.2% for S4. We record these as signs of generalisation not previously seen in complex-valued neural networks.

</details>


### [181] [Connected Content Retriever: Dense Graph Edge Features Powering Pre-Ranking at LinkedIn](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22441)
*Akhilesh Gupta,Sudarshan Srinivasa Ramanujam,Chirag Bhanuprasad Mehta,Reshma Asharaf Beena,Dhritiman Das,Birjodh Singh Tiwana,Bhargavkumar Kanubhai Patel,Mack Lee,Renyi Tang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LinkedIn developed CC Retriever, a GPU-based pre-ranking system that efficiently selects content from a billion-item candidate pool using graph affinity features, achieving 2.5% lift in content time spent.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In LinkedIn's recommendation systems, network-generated content drives over 70% of engagement, but the candidate pool from first and second-degree connections exceeds one billion items. Current systems must select and score tens of thousands of candidates within 120ms latency constraints, creating a scalability challenge for pre-ranking layers.

Method: Developed Connected Content Retriever (CC Retriever) with a core sorted-search GPU primitive that joins dense graph affinity features (viewer-author relationships) with document features stored on GPU. Uses full deep ranking models on GPUs with 50x more parameters than CPU-based approaches, achieving 5-10 ms runtime performance.

Result: Achieved 50x scale-up in ranking model parameters while maintaining low latency. Delivered +2.5% lift in content time spent on LinkedIn Feed in online experiments, significantly higher than typical gains observed in LinkedIn Feed experiments.

Conclusion: GPU-based scoring enables efficient pre-ranking at scale for large recommendation systems, leveraging graph affinity features from LinkedIn's professional knowledge graph to significantly improve content engagement metrics while meeting strict latency requirements.

Abstract: In large-scale recommendation systems like the LinkedIn Feed, content generated by a member's network (connections and follows) makes up over 70% of impressions and engagement. It is therefore essential that the pre-ranking layer forwards the best possible few hundred candidates to the ranking layer. LinkedIn's professional knowledge graph carries engagement signals across both the first degree network (connections and follows) and the second-degree network: posts that a 1st-degree connection reacted to, commented on or reshared but did not author (a.k.a. stranger viral). Due to this fan out, the resulting candidate index exceeds one billion; selection of activities from the viewer's network narrows it down to roughly tens of thousands of activities that must be scored within a 120 ms p99 latency budget. We present Connected Content Retriever (CC Retriever), a pre-ranking system that scores these candidates with a full deep ranking model on GPUs at low latency. At its core is a sorted-search GPU primitive that joins dense graph affinity features (viewer to author) with document level features stored on the GPU at runtime in 5-10 ms. The shift to GPU served scoring enabled a 50x scale up of the ranking model's parameters and delivered a +2.5% lift in content time spent on the LinkedIn Feed in online experiments, significantly higher than the typical gains observed in LinkedIn Feed experiments. In this work, we describe the feature set we leverage from LinkedIn's economic graph and the model architecture used for scoring, with a particular emphasis on the online system that scales the stack.

</details>


### [182] [Efficient Mixture-of-Experts with Speculative Decoding via Expert Coactivation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22471)
*Kumari Nishu,Han-Byul Kim,Santosh Chilkunda,Maxwell Horton,Arnav Kundu,Mohammad Samragh,Lauren Hannah,Mohammad Sekhavat,Nikhil Bhendawade,Manuel Ciosici,Iman Mirzadeh,Keivan Alizadeh Vahid,David Harrison,Irina Belousova,Mehrdad Farajtabar,Minsik Cho*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Optimizing Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) router design to enhance expert coactivation for faster speculative decoding inference while maintaining accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Combining Mixture-of-Experts models with Speculative Decoding for inference acceleration is challenging because the speedup depends heavily on the number of tokens being verified. More verification tokens require transferring more experts from DRAM to NPU, increasing memory transfer costs which bottleneck inference performance.

Method: Investigated the impact of MoE router design during training on inference speed with SD. Assessed various router design choices including global load-balancing loss, shared experts, consistency loss, and autoregressive expert selection mechanism on expert coactivation and runtime using billion-parameter transformer models.

Result: Found that routers with high degrees of expert coactivation result in much faster runtimes. The combination of global load-balancing loss, shared experts, consistency loss, and autoregressive expert selection during training yields significantly stronger expert coactivation, leading to 21% throughput improvement over MoE baselines while maintaining on-par accuracy.

Conclusion: Strategic router design during MoE training can substantially improve expert coactivation, which mitigates the memory transfer bottleneck in speculative decoding and enables faster inference without sacrificing model accuracy.

Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are increasingly deployed alongside Speculative Decoding (SD) to accelerate inference, but combining the two is challenging. SD improves the inference speed of dense models by verifying groups of tokens in parallel. However, the inference speedup for SD with MoEs depends heavily on the number of tokens being verified. Using more verification tokens results in more experts being transferred from DRAM to the Neural Processing Unit (NPU), which increases the memory transfer cost. This negatively impacts model runtime, as memory transfer is typically the bottleneck in inference. In this work, we investigate the impact of MoE router design during training on the speed of MoEs with SD. We find that routers with high degrees of expert coactivation result in much faster runtimes, mitigating the impact of using more verification tokens. Motivated by this observation, we assess the impact of various router design choices on expert coactivation and runtime using billion-parameter transformer models. We find that combining a global load-balancing loss, shared experts, a consistency loss, and an autoregressive expert selection mechanism during training results in significantly stronger expert coactivation. This increased coactivation translates into higher overall runtime throughput: our exploration yields a model that improves throughput by 21% over MoE baselines, while maintaining on-par accuracy with the baseline MoE.

</details>


### [183] [COREM: Cosine-Relation Momentum Reshaping with Stateful Writeback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22487)
*Yan Wang,Xiaochuan Wang,Yuxiang Sun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: COREM introduces a momentum reshaping method using cosine relations between matrix update units, which improves mid-to-late stage training performance while reducing computational overhead compared to baseline methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current optimizer states treat matrix entries independently, ignoring relational structure. The authors want to exploit these relations within matrix-valued optimizer states to improve optimization performance.

Method: COREM (Cosine-Relation Momentum Reshaping) partitions momentum state into update units, computes cosine relations among them, and uses these relations to reshape momentum before writing back to optimizer. This stateful mechanism affects both current updates and future optimization dynamics.

Result: On CIFAR-10 with MLP: COREM shows lower early-stage step efficiency but stronger mid-to-late stage improvement, achieving better final validation performance. On enwik8 with Transformer: Comparable final performance. COREM increases entropy effective rank, reduces concentration of singular energy in dominant modes while preserving anisotropic spectrum. Requires ~13.3% of transformation FLOPs of Muon with five Newton-Schulz iterations.

Conclusion: Exploiting relational structure in matrix-valued optimizer states via COREM's cosine-relation momentum reshaping improves optimization performance, particularly in mid-to-late training stages, with significantly lower computational cost than alternative approaches.

Abstract: Matrix-valued optimizer states may contain relational structure that is not captured by treating their entries independently. We study whether relations within matrix-valued optimizer states can be exploited to improve optimization. To this end, we introduce a unit-relation-transform abstraction and instantiate it as COREM, a Cosine-Relation Momentum Reshaping method with stateful writeback. COREM partitions the momentum state into update units, computes cosine relations among them, and uses these relations to reshape the momentum before writing the transformed state back to the optimizer. This stateful mechanism allows the reshaped momentum to affect not only the current update but also future optimization dynamics. We evaluate COREM on CIFAR-10 with an MLP and on enwik8 with a Transformer. Compared with Muon, COREM shows lower early-stage step efficiency but stronger improvement in the mid-to-late stages of training, achieving better final validation performance on CIFAR-10 and comparable final performance on enwik8. Spectral diagnostics on enwik8 show that COREM consistently increases entropy effective rank and reduces the concentration of singular energy in dominant modes, while preserving an anisotropic spectrum. For square matrix updates, COREM requires approximately 13.3% of the transformation FLOPs of Muon with five Newton-Schulz iterations.

</details>


### [184] [EmbeddGAN: A Novel GAN Framework Using an Embedding Network and Gini Distance Correlation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22508)
*MaTais Caldwell,Yixin Chen,Xin Dang,Charles Walter*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EmbeddGAN is a novel GAN framework that replaces traditional discriminator classification with an embedding network that measures statistical dependence between samples and their labels using Gini distance correlation, resulting in more stable training and competitive performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional GANs lack formal convergence guarantees, leading to practical issues like training instability, mode collapse, and hyperparameter sensitivity. The authors aim to address these limitations by developing a more theoretically sound and stable adversarial training framework.

Method: Proposes EmbeddGAN with an embedding network that projects real/fake data into a shared low-dimensional space. Uses Gini distance correlation (gCor) as objective to measure statistical dependence between embeddings and labels. Adopts minimax training where embedding network maximizes gCor (dependence) while generator minimizes it (independence).

Result: Experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CelebA show EmbeddGAN achieves competitive performance against established baselines while demonstrating notably stable training dynamics across all evaluated datasets.

Conclusion: EmbeddGAN provides a novel dependence-based adversarial training approach that offers improved training stability compared to traditional GANs while maintaining competitive generation quality, addressing key practical limitations of conventional GAN frameworks.

Abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have demonstrated strong performance in generating high-quality synthetic data. However, they are limited by no formal guarantees regarding convergence and the effectiveness of the learning process. In practice, this leads to training instability, mode collapse, and sensitivity to hyperparameters. To address this, we propose EmbeddGAN, a novel adversarial training framework based on a dependence-based objective. Instead of relying on a discriminator that classifies samples as real or fake, EmbeddGAN introduces an embedding network that learns a representation in which statistical dependence between samples and their real/fake labels is maximized, while the generator is trained to minimize this dependence. This objective is implemented using the Gini distance correlation (gCor), which equals zero if and only if the embeddings are statistically independent of the real/fake label. Minimizing this objective therefore encourages real and generated samples to become statistically indistinguishable in the learned embedding space. The embedding network projects both real and generated data into a shared low-dimensional space, where distributional discrepancies can be measured directly through pairwise distances. We adopt a minimax training strategy: the embedding network maximizes the Gini distance correlation (maximizing dependence), while the generator minimizes it (minimizing dependence). Experiments on the MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CelebA datasets demonstrate that EmbeddGAN achieves competitive performance relative to established baselines while exhibiting notably stable training dynamics on the evaluated datasets.

</details>


### [185] [The Ups and Downs of Backprop Weights](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22554)
*Giuseppe Chindemi,Benjamin F. Grewe*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Weight operators are proposed as a solution to weight entanglement in deep learning, enabling reusable functional components that can be selectively updated and recombined at inference time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses the problem of weight entanglement in deep learning, where different functions (like object recognition and motion prediction) share overlapping parameter sets, making it difficult to isolate or modify them independently. While modern architectures have dynamic selection mechanisms, they don't ensure functional components remain linked to identifiable parameter sets across samples.

Method: The paper proposes weight operators - parameterized modules that implement reusable functional components that can be composed at inference time. Learning occurs in two stages: first inferring the required operator composition for a sample, then updating only the selected operators' parameter sets. Vector Networks provide one implementation that couples operator selection to local error-driven updates within each layer.

Result: Vector Networks demonstrate that learned operators can be reused in combinations absent from training while updates remain restricted to the selected parameter sets. This provides a basis for testing functional parameter identifiability - whether an operator remains linked to the same functional component during learning.

Conclusion: Functional parameter identifiability may provide an organizing principle for models that systematically reuse and recombine learned functions while adapting only the components that need to change, addressing the limitations of standard backpropagation in managing parameter organization and selective adaptation.

Abstract: Backpropagation (BP) has driven the remarkable success of modern deep learning by enabling large hierarchical networks to learn complex functions end-to-end. Yet it does not by itself determine how parameters should be organized so that functional components can be reused and adapted selectively. For example, object recognition and motion prediction may depend on overlapping parameter sets, making them difficult to isolate or modify independently. We call this condition weight entanglement. Modern architectures dynamically select which parts of a network process each sample: nonlinearities gate units, attention selects interactions, and Mixture-of-Experts architectures route inputs to modules. Yet such selection does not ensure that the same functional component remains linked to an identifiable parameter set across samples. We propose weight operators: parameterized modules that implement reusable functional components and can be composed at inference to form the function required by each sample. Learning proceeds in two stages: the model first infers the required operator composition, then updates only the selected operators' parameter sets. Vector Networks (VNs) provide one implementation. They couple operator selection to local error-driven updates within each layer and show that learned operators can be reused in combinations absent from training while updates remain restricted to the selected parameter sets. This provides a basis for testing functional parameter identifiability: whether an operator remains linked to the same functional component during learning. We argue that functional parameter identifiability may provide an organizing principle for models that systematically reuse and recombine learned functions while adapting only the components that need to change.

</details>


### [186] [Benchmarking Hybrid Deep Learning Architectures for Predictive Maintenance in Industry 4.0](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22583)
*Zhengyang,Gu,Joseph E. Hernandez,Thomas Cook,John Burtenshaw,Sean Scott,Chris Couch*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Hybrid LSTM-Transformer models outperform pure Transformer architectures for predictive maintenance in noisy industrial environments by using LSTM as a noise filter to improve reliability and consistency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There's a "reliability gap" where predictive maintenance models that work well in lab settings fail when applied to real factory data due to noise and chaotic conditions in industrial environments.

Method: Evaluated six deep learning architectures across 700+ experimental runs, comparing Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and Transformers, with a focus on hybrid approaches combining LSTM layers with Transformer layers for noise resilience.

Result: Transformers excel at tracking stable processes but overreact to chaotic data, while hybrid LSTM-Transformer models are more resilient to factory noise. LSTM acts as a noise filter, smoothing data volatility so Transformers can focus on meaningful signals.

Conclusion: The hybrid LSTM-Transformer approach provides superior reliability and consistency for predictive maintenance in noisy industrial settings, bridging the gap between lab performance and real-world application.

Abstract: Predictive maintenance in Industry 4.0 refers to using data from sensors, machines, and production systems to estimate when equipment is likely to fail, so maintenance can be planned before a breakdown occurs [1]. However, a model that predicts maintenance may work perfectly in the lab but fail unexpectedly when applied to real factory data [2]. To solve this "reliability" gap, we evaluated six deep learning architectures across more than 700 experimental runs. We focused on the two dominant approaches in the field: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), which process data step-by-step, like reading a sentence [3], and Transformers, a recent dominant approach, which look at the entire sequence at once to spot important connections [4]. We examined whether Transformers still outperform recurrent neural networks (RNNs) when the data includes noise [5]. We found that while Transformers excelled at tracking stable, slow-moving processes, they tend to overreact to chaotic data, mistakenly taking sensor noise for meaningful signals [6]. We also found that the hybrid method that combines a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) layer with a Transformer layer is more resilient to noisy data from factory shops [7]. Functioning as a noise filter, the LSTM smooths out data volatility, allowing the Transformer to focus on the bigger picture without being distracted [8]. The hybrid model did not just improve accuracy; it proved to be significantly more consistent than complex models, delivering reliable predictions regardless of how chaotic the underlying system became.

</details>


### [187] [Augmenting PID Control with Deep Reinforcement Learning: A Hybrid Approach to the Industrial Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22584)
*Zhengyang,Gu,Joseph E. Hernandez,John Burtenshaw,Sean Scott,Thomas Cook,Chris Couch*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A hybrid PID-RL controller combines deep reinforcement learning's policy discovery with PID's reliability for complex industrial control, achieving optimal performance while maintaining stability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional PID controllers are insufficient for complex industrial processes with nonlinear, multi-input dynamics, high-dimensional state spaces, delayed effects, and conflicting multi-criterial objectives. DRL can discover optimal policies in these complex spaces but often produces unstable final policies.

Method: Developed a novel hybrid PID-RL controller that uses DRL (specifically a twin-delayed deep deterministic/TD3 agent) as a discovery tool to find optimal settings for the Industrial Benchmark's 'Gain' and 'Shift' parameters. Created a multi-objective reward function to make DRL viable, then feeds discovered parameters to a simple, tuned PID controller.

Result: The hybrid model successfully combines all three desired characteristics: achieves optimal performance and efficiency of the best DRL agent while maintaining the reliability of a classical controller.

Conclusion: Demonstrates a practical methodology for using DRL to augment rather than replace trusted industrial control systems, leveraging DRL's discovery capabilities while ensuring reliability through traditional controllers.

Abstract: As industrial processes grow in complexity, traditional Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) controllers are often insufficient for handling their non-linear, multi-input dynamics. We propose using advanced Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) to prove its advantages in these complex environments. To do this, we rely on the Industrial Benchmark (IB). The IB is a realistic simulation that tests DRL algorithms against the key challenges of industrial applications: high-dimensional state spaces, delayed effects, and conflicting multi-criterial objectives. This testbed highlights DRL's core trade-off: while its final policies can often be unstable, its unique strength is the ability to autonomously discover optimal, non-obvious policies in multi-dimensional spaces where simple controllers fail. In this paper, we propose a novel hybrid PID-RL controller that leverages DRL's discovery capability while ensuring Reliability. After developing a multi-objective reward function to make DRL viable, we use a twin-delayed deep deterministic (TD3) agent as a discovery tool to find the optimal, non-obvious settings for the IB's 'Gain' and 'Shift' parameters. By feeding these discovered parameters to a simple, tuned PID controller, our hybrid model successfully combines all three characteristics: it achieves the optimal Performance and Efficiency of the best DRL agent with the Reliability of a classical controller. This work demonstrates a practical methodology for using DRL to augment, rather than replace, trusted industrial control systems.

</details>


### [188] [TWIG: A Time-Causal Wavelet Operator for Autoregressive Forecasting on Irregular Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22585)
*Subashree Venkatasubramanian,David A. Barajas-Solano,Chuyang Liu,Daniel M. Tartakovsky,Dipankar Dwivedi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TWIG is a graph-native neural operator for autoregressive surrogate modeling on static irregular graphs that transforms node histories into causal multiscale temporal features and uses graph-wavelet operators for stable forecasting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses the challenge of autoregressive surrogate modeling for dynamical systems on irregular graphs, where existing methods need specialized handling of time causality and graph irregularity for stable closed-loop forecasting.

Method: TWIG transforms each node history into causal multiscale temporal features separating recent variation from slower memory components, then propagates these through graph-wavelet operator blocks with gated pointwise channel mixing. The architecture is inherently causal and designed for closed-loop forecasting where predictions are recursively reused.

Result: TWIG achieves lowest aggregate rollout errors on subsurface-hydrology and regional-diffusion benchmarks, ranks second on aerodynamic-flow benchmark (behind GPS Transformer), and consistently outperforms non-time-causal Graph WNO baselines across all three irregular-domain forecasting problems.

Conclusion: TWIG provides an effective and scalable approach to stable autoregressive forecasting of dynamical fields on irregular graphs, demonstrating the value of time-causal graph-native neural operators for irregular-domain surrogate modeling.

Abstract: We introduce TWIG (Time-Causal Wavelet Operator for Irregular Graphs), a graph-native neural operator for autoregressive surrogate modeling on static irregular graphs. TWIG transforms each node history into causal multiscale temporal features that separate recent variation from progressively slower memory components, then propagates these features through graph-wavelet operator blocks with gated pointwise channel mixing. The architecture is causal by construction and designed for closed-loop forecasting, where predictions are recursively reused as future inputs. We evaluate TWIG on three irregular-domain forecasting problems spanning regional diffusion, three-dimensional subsurface hydrology, and aerodynamic flow, with graphs ranging from 400 to 5,233 nodes and model capacities from approximately 70k to 10M parameters. TWIG achieves the lowest aggregate rollout errors on the subsurface-hydrology and regional-diffusion benchmarks and ranks second on the 10M-parameter aerodynamic-flow benchmark, behind the GPS Transformer. Across all three settings, TWIG consistently outperforms the corresponding non-time-causal Graph WNO baseline. These results demonstrate that TWIG provides an effective and scalable approach to stable autoregressive forecasting of dynamical fields on irregular graphs.

</details>


### [189] [User-Level Handover Decision Making Based on Machine Learning Approaches](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22593)
*João Lima,Alvaro Medeiros,Eduardo Aguiar,Vicente Angelo de Sousa Junior,Tarciana Guerra*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper compares ML methods for user-level handover decisions in adverse propagation conditions, finding SVM/MLP best for classification and LightGBM best for download time estimation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address handover decision-making challenges in wireless networks with adverse propagation conditions like buildings, coverage holes, and shadowing effects, requiring robust classification and regression methods.

Method: The study compares classical ML methods (KNN, SVM, neural networks), fuzzy logic systems, and boosting machines using ns-3 network simulator for classification and regression tasks in adverse propagation scenarios.

Result: SVM and MLP performed best for handover target classification, with fuzzy system SOFL achieving similar results with lower processing time. LightGBM provided the smallest error with short processing time for download time estimation.

Conclusion: SVM/MLP are most suitable for handover classification, while LightGBM excels at download time estimation in adverse propagation scenarios, balancing accuracy with processing efficiency.

Abstract: This letter covers a broad comparison of methods for classification and regression applications for a user-level handover decision making in scenarios with adverse propagation conditions involving buildings, coverage holes, and shadowing effects. The simulation campaigns are based on network simulator ns-3. The comparison encompasses classical machine learning approaches, such as KNN, SVM, and neural networks, but also state-of-the-art fuzzy logic systems and latter boosting machines. The results indicate that SVM and MLP are the most suitable for the classification of the best handover target, although fuzzy system SOFL can perform similarly with lower processing time. Additionally, for the download time estimation, LightGBM provides the smallest error with short processing time, even in hard propagation scenarios.

</details>


### [190] [Concurrency-Aware Process Model Forecasting with Causal Nets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22614)
*Yongbo Yu,Jari Peeperkorn,Johannes De Smedt,Jochen De Weerdt*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Process model forecasting extended to causal nets with AND/XOR semantics by predicting relation/binding counts, enabling explicit concurrency representation in future process models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing process model forecasting methods predict directly-follows graphs that cannot explicitly represent concurrency, limiting their ability to forecast process models with parallel behavior.

Method: Extends PMF to causal nets by forecasting time series of relation and binding counts, then reconstructing future process models with AND/XOR semantics from these forecasts. Introduces evaluation protocol for partial traces and workflow net construction for conformance checking.

Result: Forecasted models achieve conformance levels close to models re-mined from actual future data. They outperform static discovery baselines, especially on logs with structural changes. Filtering infrequent bindings improves conformance metrics but reduces captured concurrent behavior.

Conclusion: The approach successfully forecasts process models with explicit concurrency representation, achieving practical utility with trade-offs between conformance quality and complexity of concurrent behavior captured.

Abstract: Process model forecasting (PMF) aims to predict the process model that will characterize a future period, thereby providing a process-level view of how behavior is expected to evolve. Existing PMF methods, however, forecast directly-follows graphs, which cannot explicitly represent concurrency. We extend PMF to causal nets by forecasting time series of relation and binding counts and using these forecasts to reconstruct future process models with AND/XOR semantics. To evaluate the resulting models, we introduce a protocol that accounts for partial traces and constructs the workflow nets required for conformance checking. Experiments on four event logs show that the forecasted models achieve conformance levels close to those of models re-mined from observations in the corresponding future windows. They also outperform static discovery baselines, which retain high precision on the structurally stable log but exhibit substantial precision losses on the other three logs. Filtering infrequent bindings improves most conformance metrics, although it also removes much of the concurrent behavior captured by the models.

</details>


### [191] [Classification with Abstention Under Class-Conditional Error Constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22632)
*Mohammadreza M. Kalan,Yuyang Deng,Sanaz Hamidi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper analyzes binary classification with abstention under class-conditional error constraints, characterizing minimax rates and providing computational approaches with finite-sample guarantees.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To develop a framework for binary classification with abstention that can handle separate class-conditional error constraints while minimizing abstention rates, making it practical for complex models like neural networks.

Method: Characterizing distribution-free minimax rates of excess abstention risk, introducing surrogate-loss formulations for computational feasibility, formulating as constrained optimization, and analyzing computational complexity in convex settings.

Result: Obtained minimax rates up to logarithmic factors, derived finite-sample guarantees for surrogate formulations, characterized computational complexity, and demonstrated practical performance on datasets compared to competing methods.

Conclusion: The paper provides a comprehensive theoretical and computational framework for abstention-based classification with error constraints, balancing theoretical guarantees with practical implementability for modern machine learning models.

Abstract: We study binary classification with abstention under separate class-conditional error constraints, with the objective of minimizing abstention while keeping both errors below prescribed thresholds. We characterize the distribution-free minimax rate of excess abstention risk, up to logarithmic factors, in terms of the complexity of the hypothesis class and the sample size. To make the framework amenable to computation with models such as neural networks, we introduce surrogate-loss formulations and derive finite-sample guarantees for excess surrogate ambiguity risk. We formulate the resulting learning task as a constrained optimization problem and characterize its computational complexity in the convex setting. Finally, we evaluate our approach on various datasets and compare its performance with a competing method for this problem.

</details>


### [192] [Monotone-Constrained Diffusion Models for Long-Horizon Production Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22643)
*Temesgen Mikael Abraha,Yves Lucet*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Physics-SIMS-TS: A conditional diffusion model for oil/gas production forecasting that enforces monotonic decline constraints while maintaining accuracy, using physics-informed guidance and spatial augmentation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon forecasting from early observations is ill-posed with many possible trajectories. In oil/gas production forecasting, decisions after ~20% of well life require accurate monotonic decline forecasts.

Method: Combines conditional diffusion with: negative guidance against synthetic artifacts, decline-curve constraints, isotonic projection during sampling, spatial training augmentation, and ensembled stochastic sampling.

Result: Most accurate diffusion forecaster across 35,000+ wells in 3 jurisdictions; competitive with transformer ensembles; ensures monotonic forecasts (≤0.5% MSE cost); produces calibrated prediction intervals; leads diffusion baselines on 6 benchmarks.

Conclusion: Physics-SIMS-TS provides reliable monotonic production forecasts with diffusion models, achieving practical utility for industry decision-making while maintaining accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art methods.

Abstract: Forecasting a long horizon from only the first observations of a sequence is ill-posed: many trajectories are consistent with the same short history. We study this problem in oil and gas production forecasting, where forecasts made after roughly the first fifth of a well's producing life drive development and abandonment decisions, and where a usable forecast must describe a monotone decline. We present Physics-SIMS-TS, a conditional diffusion forecaster that combines negative guidance against synthetic artifacts, decline-curve constraints and an isotonic projection applied during sampling, spatial training augmentation, and an ensembled stochastic sampler yielding a full predictive distribution. Across three jurisdictions and more than 35,000 wells, under a shared-space, validation-frozen protocol, Physics-SIMS-TS is the most accurate diffusion forecaster in the comparison and is competitive with, but not superior to, ensembled transformer forecasters. Its forecasts are monotone by construction at a cost of at most 0.5% in mean squared error, and its trajectory ensemble yields calibrated intervals after one dispersion factor is fitted per jurisdiction. On six standard benchmarks a reversible-instance-normalization variant of the backbone is the leading diffusion baseline. We also quantify four protocol choices on which the measured ranking depends. Code and evaluation artifacts are released.

</details>


### [193] [Multi-Armed Bernoulli Bandits via Minimax Single-Arm Stopping](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22690)
*Huikang Liu,Zhengchao Wang,Daniel Kuhn,Wolfram Wiesemann*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A novel index policy for finite-horizon Bernoulli multi-armed bandits derived from minimax solutions to single-arm bandit problems, achieving order-optimal regret with improved constants.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To develop a practical index policy for finite-horizon Bernoulli multi-armed bandits that achieves minimax-optimal regret with tight constants, improving upon existing benchmark policies while maintaining computational feasibility.

Method: The approach starts by solving minimax single-arm bandit (SAB) problems using exact semi-infinite linear programming. For each unknown Bernoulli arm, a stopping policy is derived that chooses between sampling the arm or taking a known reward. These policies are then converted into indices based on cumulative continuation probabilities with monotone adjustment and reward-shortfall cap. The method extends to [0,1]-supported rewards via Bernoulli randomization and provides finite-grid implementation with quantified approximation loss.

Result: Established a distribution-free regret bound of 4.45√(KT) + 10.75K for K arms and horizon T, matching the minimax-optimal regret order. Numerical experiments show the SAB-based index policy achieves lower worst-case regret than all tested benchmark policies across various arm counts and horizons, and closely matches grid-based MAB minimax policy in two-arm setting.

Conclusion: The SAB-based index policy provides an effective, practical solution for finite-horizon Bernoulli bandits that achieves theoretical minimax-optimal regret bounds with improved constants and demonstrates superior empirical performance compared to existing benchmark policies.

Abstract: We develop an index policy for finite-horizon Bernoulli multi-armed bandits from minimax solutions to single-arm bandit (SAB) problems. Each SAB problem involves choosing between an unknown Bernoulli arm and a known reward. We show that minimizing worst-case regret of SAB problems over all non-anticipative policies admits an exact semi-infinite linear programming formulation. The resulting stopping policies offer a natural way to compare arms: the higher the known reward against which a policy continues sampling, the more promising the unknown arm. We turn this intuition into indices based on cumulative continuation probabilities, with a monotone adjustment and a reward-shortfall cap. By relating index errors to the regret of single-arm stopping policies, we establish a distribution-free regret bound of $4.45\sqrt{KT}+10.75K$ for $K$ arms and horizon $T$. This bound matches the minimax-optimal regret order established in the literature. The guarantee extends to rewards supported on $[0,1]$ through Bernoulli randomization. We also provide a finite-grid implementation with quantified approximation loss. In numerical experiments, the SAB-based index policy achieves lower worst-case regret than every tested benchmark policy across all evaluated numbers of arms and horizons, while closely matching the grid-based MAB minimax policy in the two-arm setting.

</details>


### [194] [Autonomous Model Lifecycle Management for Digital Twin-Based Manufacturing Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22701)
*Zhengyang,Gu,Thomas Cook,Fredaljohn Rohrbaugh,Joseph E. Hernandez,Chris Couch*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Autonomous manufacturing AI system that manages physics-based digital twins paired with RL controllers, using competitive retraining cycles and operator-trust scoring, deployed in automotive plants since 2023 with improved process stability and zero safety incidents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manufacturing AI must autonomously adapt to continuous distributional shifts from raw-material variability, ambient changes, and equipment aging while maintaining strict safety requirements and operator trust, since model failures risk physical damage in industrial settings.

Method: Closed-loop Cyber-Physical System with product-specialized model pairs: sequence-to-sequence physics model (LPP digital twin) and deep RL control policy (LCP). Competitive retraining cycles where multiple model variants compete across architecture families and RL algorithms. Conductor orchestrator manages plant-wide models with dependency-aware retraining and PID fallback. Human-Centric Intelligence principle embedded via operator-trust gate in LCP scoring.

Result: Operator-trust gate prevented 23% of policies from being rejected despite passing accuracy thresholds. LCP-controlled processes achieved 28-45% process stability improvements over uncontrolled baselines across multiple facilities. Zero safety incidents reported in deployment since 2023.

Conclusion: The autonomous model lifecycle management system successfully addresses manufacturing AI challenges by combining physics-based digital twins with RL controllers, competitive retraining, and human-centric trust scoring, enabling safe, stable, and trusted deployment in automotive manufacturing environments.

Abstract: Manufacturing AI systems must autonomously adapt to continuous distributional shift from raw-material variability, ambient changes, and equipment aging, under strict safeguard and operator-trust requirements where model failures risk physical damage. This paper presents a closed-loop Cyber-Physical System (CPS) for autonomous model lifecycle management in automotive manufacturing, deployed since 2023. The system manages product-specialized model pairs: a sequence-to-sequence physics model (LPP) serving as a digital twin, and a deep Reinforcement Learning (RL) control policy (LCP) trained against it. Per retraining cycle, multiple model variants spanning architecture families and RL algorithms compete; only the best-scoring candidate advances. A Conductor orchestrator autonomously manages plant-wide model inventories with dependency-aware retraining and Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) fallback. Reflecting the principle of Human-Centric Intelligence, the LCP composite score embeds an operator-trust gate penalizing policies deviating from established practice; without it, 23% of policies are rejected by operators despite passing accuracy thresholds. Across multiple facilities, LCP-controlled processes achieve process stability improvements of 28-45% over uncontrolled baselines with zero safety incidents.

</details>


### [195] [D-IMPL: A Diffusion-based Solver for Parameterized BBOs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22752)
*Yang Hu,Na Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Diffusion models are used to create an efficient solver for parameterized black-box optimization problems, learning a "minimization policy" that amortizes computation costs across instances while handling non-convex, multi-modal landscapes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Parameterized black-box optimizations (BBO) are computationally expensive when each instance requires separate optimization. Existing methods struggle with handling non-convex objectives with multi-modal landscapes and don't efficiently reuse computation across similar problems. Diffusion models' strong generative capabilities offer potential for learning optimization strategies that can be shared across BBO instances.

Method: Introduces "minimization policy" as a new solution concept - a sampling distribution over solutions concentrated around minimizers. Proposes Diffusion-based Iterative Minimization Policy Learning (D-IMPL), which uses diffusion models to learn a policy whose density is proportional to exponential of negated objective values, effectively learning to sample near optimal solutions.

Result: Theoretical analysis shows a δ-approximate minimization policy can be learned within O(log(1/δ)) iterations. Empirical evaluations demonstrate strong performance across both constrained and unconstrained BBO tasks. The approach amortizes computational costs across different BBO instances while capturing complex non-convex landscapes.

Conclusion: Diffusion models can be effectively repurposed for black-box optimization problems through the novel concept of minimization policies. D-IMPL provides an efficient, universal solver that handles complex optimization landscapes while reducing inference-time computation by learning reusable optimization strategies.

Abstract: Diffusion models have demonstrated strong power in generative modeling tasks across multiple domains, exhibiting a remarkable capability of learning complex distributions from samples. In this paper, we leverage such capability to design an efficient universal diffusion-based solver for parameterized black-box optimizations (BBO), where the optimizer has only black-box access to queries of the objective function at the learning stage, yet is able to reduce the additional computational cost at the inference stage for each BBO instance while also capturing the potential multi-modal landscape of non-convex objectives. To cast our formulation as a compatible generative modeling task, we introduce the notion of minimization policy as a new solution concept, which defines a sampling distribution over the solutions that should concentrate around the minimizer set for each BBO instance. We then propose Diffusion-based Iterative Minimization Policy Learning (D-IMPL), a practical generative-model-based solver for solving parameterized BBOs that employs diffusion models to learn a minimization policy, whose density is proportional to the exponential of the negated objective values, thereby amortizing the computational costs across different BBO instances. Furthermore, we demonstrate the performance of our D-IMPL algorithm by establishing a sample complexity guarantee showing that a $δ$-approximate minimization policy can be effectively learned within $O(\log(1/δ))$ iterations, and by extensive empirical evaluations over a range of constrained and unconstrained BBO tasks.

</details>


### [196] [Look Before You Steer: Geometry Predicts SAE Feature Steerability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22782)
*Muhammad Khan,Shlok Channawar,Akshaj Gurugubelli,Girish Gupta,Aditya Shah*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SAE feature steerability can be predicted from decoder-space geometry before any interventions, offering a way to screen features for controllability without extensive tuning sweeps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current steering methods require per-feature coefficient tuning with intervention sweeps. The authors investigate whether properties of SAEs themselves, computable before forward passes, can predict which features will be cheap or expensive to steer.

Method: Analyzed decoder-space geometry metrics (neighbor density and maximum cosine similarity to nearby decoder directions) computed from SAE weight matrices. Tested across multiple models (Gemma-2 2B/9B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B), SAE widths (16K and 65K), and different SAE training regimes (including BatchTopK SAEs).

Result: Decoder-space geometry predicts feature steerability with significant correlations (ρ up to -0.546, p<10⁻⁶, AUROC 0.610-0.822). The relationship replicates across model scales, SAE widths, and cross-architecturally, but weakens at deep layers where steering costs exceed intervention budgets. On Qwen3-8B with BatchTopK SAEs, geometry predicts steerability but not continuous ordering among responsive features.

Conclusion: Pre-steering geometry can partially inform coefficient selection, offering a path toward screening features for controllability before deployment. There are consistent depth boundaries and training regime dependencies that establish important boundary conditions for the approach.

Abstract: Steering with SAE features requires per-feature coefficient tuning, which currently demands intervention sweeps. We ask whether properties of the SAE itself, computable before any forward pass, predict which features will be cheap or expensive to steer. We show that variation in SAE feature steerability is partially predicted by decoder-space geometry: neighbor density and maximum cosine similarity to nearby decoder directions, both computable from the SAE weight matrix before any intervention, rank features by how much steering they require for a fixed behavioral effect ($ρ$ up to $-0.546$, $p < 10^{-6}$, AUROC 0.610-0.822 across conditions; the signal is rank-based, consistent with grid discreteness). This geometry-steerability relationship replicates across two Gemma-2 model scales (2B and 9B), two SAE widths (16K and 65K), and is detectable cross-architecturally on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct ($ρ= -0.266$, $n = 300$). On Qwen3-8B with BatchTopK SAEs, geometry predicts whether a feature is steerable at all but not the continuous ordering among responsive features, revealing a boundary condition tied to SAE training regime. The signal weakens at deep proportional layer depth in both models, where the cost of steering exceeds our intervention budget, a consistent depth boundary. These results provide preliminary evidence that pre-steering geometry can partially inform coefficient selection, offering a path toward screening features for controllability before deployment.

</details>


### [197] [Improved Private Sparse Covariance Estimation with Multiscale Threshold Tests](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22783)
*Zihan Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A differentially private covariance estimation method for sparse sub-Gaussian distributions that achieves optimal sample complexity by removing a √k factor from previous bounds through multiscale thresholding and better error analysis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There's a need for efficient differentially private covariance estimation for high-dimensional sparse distributions. Previous methods had suboptimal privacy-dependent sample complexity with an extra √k factor compared to known lower bounds, leaving a gap between upper and lower bounds.

Method: Developed a multiscale random-threshold algorithm that uses a multiscale allocation of threshold tests to balance reconstruction variance against query sensitivity. The key innovation is a direct operator-norm bound on centered fluctuations of ideal reconstruction that exploits conditional independence rather than accumulating entrywise errors row-wise.

Result: Achieved sample complexity of Õ(k²/α² + k√d/(αε)) for (ε,δ)-differential privacy with error ≤ ασ², improving the privacy-dependent term of previous Õ(k²/α² + k³/²√d/(αε)) bound by factor √k. This matches the lower bound of Ω̃(k²/α² + k√d/(αε)) in applicable regimes.

Conclusion: The paper provides an optimal differentially private covariance estimator for sparse distributions by eliminating the √k gap between previous upper and lower bounds through improved analysis techniques that better leverage sparsity structure and privacy-accuracy trade-offs.

Abstract: We study differentially private covariance estimation in operator norm for mean-zero sub-Gaussian distributions with unknown covariance support and at most $k$ nonzero entries per row. We develop a multiscale random-threshold algorithm with sample complexity $\ot(k^2/α^2+k\sqrt d/(α\varepsilon))$ for $(\varepsilon,δ)$-differential privacy and error at most $ασ^2$, where $d$ is the dimension and $σ$ is a known sub-Gaussian scale. The bound improves the privacy-dependent term of the existing $\ot(k^2/α^2+k^{3/2}\sqrt d/(α\varepsilon))$ \citep{kumar2026curse} upper bound by a factor of $\sqrt k$, and matches the lower bound of $\widetildeΩ(k^2/α^2 + k\sqrt{d}/(α\varepsilon))$ in its applicable parameter regime.
  Our key technical ingredient is a direct operator-norm bound on the centered fluctuations of an ideal reconstruction, exploiting conditional independence rather than accumulating entrywise errors across each row. A multiscale allocation of threshold tests balances reconstruction variance against query sensitivity. Together, these ingredients sharpen the trade-off between approximation error and privacy protection, removing the additional $\sqrt{k}$ factor from the privacy-dependent sample complexity.

</details>


### [198] [Robust Market Making with Hawkes Order Flow and Price Impact via Adversarial Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22785)
*Hao Yang,Zhenguo Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Adversarial reinforcement learning for market making is extended to include Hawkes self-exciting order arrivals and trade-induced price impact, with LSTM temporal modeling to handle regime shifts, resulting in improved left-tail performance in complex microstructure environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing adversarial RL approaches for market making rely on unrealistic Poisson order arrivals and neglect price impact, failing to capture important high-frequency market microstructure effects like clustered order flow, self-excitation, and post-trade price feedback.

Method: Extends adversarial RL to Hawkes self-exciting order arrivals and trade-induced price impact, incorporates LSTM module to handle temporal structure and non-stationarity, characterizes equilibrium through game-theoretic analysis and numerical experiments, and introduces robustness evaluation focused on left-tail returns.

Result: The method achieves improved left-tail performance in most complex microstructure environments, with pronounced gains in regimes with strong Hawkes excitation and low-to-moderate price impact. Bootstrap tests show improvements are not due to terminal directional inventory bias.

Conclusion: Combining adversarial training with temporal state representation (LSTM) can improve robustness of RL-based market-making strategies under order-flow self-excitation, price impact, and regime uncertainty.

Abstract: Market-making strategies in real limit order book markets face substantial model uncertainty and regime-shift risk. Existing adversarial reinforcement learning approaches improve robustness by formulating the Avellaneda--Stoikov market-making problem as a zero-sum game between a market maker and an environmental adversary. However, these approaches typically rely on Poisson order arrivals and neglect trade-induced price impact, limiting their ability to capture important high-frequency market microstructure effects such as clustered order flow, self-excitation, and post-trade price feedback.
  We extend adversarial reinforcement learning for market making to a more complex environment with Hawkes self-exciting order arrivals and trade-induced price impact. To mitigate the increased non-stationarity introduced by the expanded regime space, we incorporate an LSTM module that explicitly models the temporal structure of recent observations. We further characterize the equilibrium properties of the proposed framework through both game-theoretic analysis and numerical experiments, and introduce a robustness evaluation protocol focused on improvements in the left tail of the return distribution.
  Experimental results across a range of market regimes show that the proposed method achieves improved left-tail performance in most complex microstructure environments. In particular, the gains are pronounced in regimes with strong Hawkes excitation and low-to-moderate price impact. Bootstrap tests provide no evidence that these improvements are obtained through a stronger terminal directional inventory bias. These results suggest that combining adversarial training with temporal state representation can improve the robustness of reinforcement-learning-based market-making strategies under order-flow self-excitation, price impact, and regime uncertainty.

</details>


### [199] [FIRM-WM: State-factorized factual-interventional recurrent modeling for reward-free visual planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22816)
*Yilun Wu,Yunjian Zhang,Aobo Li,Mujiangshan Wang,Haitao Wu,Aqiang Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FIRM-WM is a reward-free latent world model for offline video learning that separates goal-comparable configuration from dynamic history information, enabling effective planning through factual-interventional sampling while resetting environment states for accurate predictions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses two key challenges in reward-free world models: 1) The planning state must be comparable with goal images while retaining motion history information like velocity and contact, and 2) Offline training creates a mismatch where each recorded trajectory shows only one factual future, but planning requires comparing many alternative actions not taken in the data.

Method: FIRM-WM introduces a compact pixel world model with a recurrent state that separates typed, goal-comparable configuration from a 128-dimensional dynamic fiber for prediction. It uses factual trajectories for state coverage and common-reset intervention branches to observe outcomes of alternative actions. Before executing each branch, the environment is reset with recorded values via the environment's state-setting interface.

Result: FIRM-WM achieves 99.0±1.0% on TwoRoom, 92.7±2.1% on Reacher, and 88.0±3.0% on OGBench-Cube, outperforming LeWM (89.0%, 88.0%, and 70.0%). The model uses only 2.98-3.42M parameters and records 2.13-11.60× lower planning time on these tasks.

Conclusion: FIRM-WM successfully bridges the gaps in reward-free world modeling by separating goal-comparable and history-dependent components while using factual-interventional sampling to overcome the offline training limitation, resulting in efficient planning with strong performance across diverse environments.

Abstract: Reward-free latent world models can learn from offline videos and solve new image--goal tasks by optimizing actions through predicted latent futures. This setting places two demands on the planning state: its coordinates must be comparable with a goal image. Moreover, its dynamics must retain velocity, motion trend, contact, and other history--dependent information beyond those goal coordinates. Offline training creates a second mismatch: each recorded trajectory reveals one factual future, whereas a sampling--based planner compares many actions that were not taken from the same state. We introduce FIRM-WM (Factual--Interventional Recurrent World Model), a compact pixel world model designed around these two gaps. Its recurrent state separates a typed, goal--comparable configuration from a 128-dimensional dynamic fiber used for prediction but excluded from the terminal goal cost. Broad factual trajectories provide state coverage, while common--reset intervention branches provide observed outcomes for alternative action sequences. Before executing each branch, we reset the environment and restore the same recorded values exposed by the environment's state--setting interface. Under matched CEM planning and three independent full-pipeline seeds, FIRM-WM reaches 99.0$\pm$1.0% on TwoRoom, 92.7$\pm$2.1% on Reacher, and 88.0$\pm$3.0% on OGBench-Cube, compared with 89.0%, 88.0%, and 70.0% for LeWM. The deployed model uses 2.98--3.42M parameters and records 2.13--11.60$\times$ lower planning time on these tasks.

</details>
