### [200] [Counterfactual Tool Ranking under Utility, Cost, and Privilege Constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22819)
*Jiapeng Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Counterfactual tool evaluation requires distinguishing authority, historical support, and what comparisons actually estimate; the study uses real enterprise tools and MCP transport to reveal that direct regression outperforms doubly robust evaluation in some settings but not others.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There's a need to distinguish between different aspects of counterfactual tool evaluation - authority, historical support, and what comparisons actually estimate. Current evaluation methods may produce misleading results without proper consideration of these distinctions.

Method: Used eleven executable enterprise-inspired tools with exact-propensity logs and real local Model Context Protocol transport. Conducted 45-run synthetic study, 30 realized-return control runs, and 15 experiments on 1,930 independently released Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard tasks. Evaluated two pinned local Qwen2.5 models on 200 held-out tasks.

Result: Direct regression reversed initially favorable DR results in linear settings (MAE: 0.0139 vs 0.0272). DR retained advantage under shifted environments (0.0227 vs 0.0948). On BFCL splits, selectors achieved 81.85% and 79.83% balanced accuracy. Qwen2.5 models showed strong failure to abstain under fixed prompts. Support-gap analysis showed unsupported actions cancel when shared by policies.

Conclusion: The study provides falsifiable evaluation methodology and independent public evidence rather than new DR estimators or safety claims. It demonstrates the importance of proper evaluation distinctions and shows that different methods excel in different scenarios, with no single approach universally superior.

Abstract: Counterfactual tool evaluation must distinguish authority, historical support, and what a comparison actually estimates. We study these distinctions with eleven executable enterprise-inspired tools, exact-propensity logs, and real local Model Context Protocol transport. An initial 45-run synthetic study is retained, then challenged by 30 realized-return control runs and 15 experiments on 1,930 independently released Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL) tasks. Full-return direct regression reverses an initially favorable doubly robust (DR) evaluation result in the linear setting: mean absolute errors are 0.0139 for direct regression and 0.0272 for DR. Under a shifted environment, DR retains an advantage, with errors 0.0227 versus 0.0948. On function-name-group-disjoint BFCL-derived splits, direct and DR selectors obtain balanced accuracies of 81.85% and 79.83%. Two pinned local Qwen2.5 models are evaluated on the same 200 held-out tasks, exposing a strong failure to abstain under the fixed prompt. We further characterize policy differences under missing support: unsupported actions shared by two policies cancel, allowing point identification of an incremental change when neither absolute value is identifiable. A disagreement-preserving fallback achieves this property in all five support-gap runs, but conservative sampling bounds do not certify deployment improvement. The contribution is a falsifiable evaluation method and independent public evidence, not a new DR estimator, official BFCL leaderboard score, or production-agent safety claim.

</details>


### [201] [Beyond Average Error through Oracle-Informed Stress Tests for Time-Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22820)
*Xu Lin,Runheng Zuo,Shengxuan Xu,Qitai Tan,Hongyu Lin,Xiao-Ping Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A new benchmarking framework decomposes forecasting error changes into environmental risk and forecast-oracle distance using controlled stress tests, enabling component-wise diagnosis of performance degradation across various forecasting models and scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Average squared error alone cannot distinguish whether forecasting performance degrades due to the future becoming less predictable (environmental risk) or because forecasts move farther from the conditional mean (forecast-oracle distance). Existing evaluation methods lack this decomposition capability.

Method: Introduces paired, mechanism-controlled stress tests using an origin-conditioned predictive oracle unavailable to evaluated models. Includes three end-to-end controls (null, environmental-only, and information-gap) with known attribution to verify decomposition accuracy. Applies benchmark to 24 deployable forecasters under different conditions including frequent switching and outlier-variance feedback.

Result: Under frequent switching, 14 methods show higher MSE but lower oracle distance; under outlier-variance feedback, 19 show higher MSE but lower scale-standardized MSE. Oracle distance accounts for only 0.7-3.9% of decomposed expected-risk increase in multivariate relation shifts. Several visually compelling discovery profiles fail to replicate in prespecified contrasts.

Conclusion: The benchmark successfully combines component-wise diagnosis with a held-out stability audit, complementing real-data out-of-distribution evaluation. It provides a rigorous framework for understanding whether forecasting degradation stems from environmental unpredictability or model deficiencies relative to an oracle.

Abstract: Average squared error cannot reveal whether forecasting performance degrades because the future becomes less predictable or because forecasts move farther from the conditional mean. We introduce paired, mechanism-controlled stress tests that decompose changes in expected squared error at each lead time into environmental risk and forecast-oracle distance, using an origin-conditioned predictive oracle unavailable to the evaluated models. Three end-to-end controls have known attribution. Specifically, the null, environmental-only, and information-gap controls verify that the pipeline assigns changes to the correct component. We then apply the benchmark to 24 deployable forecasters. Under frequent switching, 14 methods have higher realized MSE but lower oracle distance; under outlier-variance feedback, 19 have higher MSE but lower scale-standardized MSE. Short- and long-lead stress-response rankings have Spearman correlation 0.624, revealing substantial horizon-dependent reordering. We then study multivariate relation shifts. Across six models and three coupling severities, oracle distance accounts for only 0.7-3.9% of the decomposed expected-risk increase, and environmental-risk majority persists in an eight-channel system and a matched-difficulty audit of Ring, Block, and Hub relations. Finally, prespecified contrasts on independent data-generating process (DGP) realizations show that several visually compelling discovery profiles, including trend accumulation and the hypothesized switching reversal, do not replicate. The benchmark thus combines component-wise diagnosis with a held-out stability audit. It complements real-data out-of-distribution evaluation, which measures performance under realistic shifts when exact oracle attribution is unavailable.

</details>


### [202] [A Hybrid Attention Model Learning Unified Time-aware Patch Representation for Irregular Multivariate Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22836)
*Zhihao Lin,Li Lin,Qi Zhang,Kaiwen Xia,Shuai Wang,Jialin Qiao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A hybrid attention model for irregular multivariate time series forecasting that learns unified time-aware patch representations without imputation, using VersaTSA dataset with 30B observations for pretraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing time series foundation models fail to properly handle irregular multivariate time series (IMTS) with inconsistent inter-observation intervals and asynchronous sampling across variables, typically using imputation that injects spurious values or index-based positional encodings that ignore continuous time.

Method: 1. Time-aware patch encoding that maps variable intra-patch timestamps into fixed-size embeddings without imputation. 2. Time bias attention mechanism to calibrate inter-patch temporal misalignment and asynchronous cross-channel dependencies as auxiliary attention offset. 3. Hybrid causal mask on decoder-only Transformer that maintains bidirectional historical view while keeping forecast horizon autoregressive. 4. Curated VersaTSA archive with 30B observations for large-scale pretraining.

Result: Achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot performance on three IMTS benchmarks and remains competitive when transferred to regular MTS forecasting.

Conclusion: The proposed hybrid attention model effectively handles irregular multivariate time series forecasting by learning unified time-aware representations without resorting to imputation, bridging the gap in foundation models for irregular time series patterns.

Abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) have recently delivered impressive zero-shot performance across diverse forecasting tasks. However, real-world decision-making frequently relies on \emph{irregular multivariate time series} (IMTS), where inconsistent inter-observation intervals and asynchronous sampling across variables coexist with informative missingness. Existing TSFMs handle such inputs either through imputation that injects spurious values or through index-based positional encodings that ignore continuous time. There is still a gap in the foundation model that follows the original IMTS patterns. In this paper, we propose a hybrid attention model that learns a unified time-aware patch representation for IMTS forecasting. We first design a \emph{time-aware patch encoding} that maps a variable number of intra-patch timestamps into a fixed-size embedding, producing a uniform format for irregular patches without resorting to imputation. We then introduce a \emph{time bias attention} mechanism that calibrates inter-patch temporal misalignment and asynchronous cross-channel dependencies as auxiliary attention offset. Finally, on top of a decoder-only Transformer backbone, we adopt a \emph{hybrid causal mask} that preserves a bidirectional full view over the historical context while keeping the forecast horizon strictly autoregressive. To support large-scale pretraining under irregular settings, we also curate VersaTSA, an archive of $30$B observations that retains the native sampling sparsity of its sources. Experiments on three IMTS benchmarks and a standard regular-MTS benchmark show that our model achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot performance on IMTS and remains competitive when transferred to regular forecasting.

</details>


### [203] [Testing the Construct Validity of a Functional Valence Axis in LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22850)
*Weihan Li,Xinlei Chen,Yuhan Song,Xiaofeng Lin,Tianshi Zheng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper examines whether contrastive activation directions in LLMs represent true constructs or just correlated features, focusing on a good-bad outcome direction in maze tasks using controlled interventions to separate outcome from informational history.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Researchers want to determine what evidence is sufficient to identify the actual construct represented by contrastive activation directions, rather than just correlated features of the contrast used to extract them, particularly for good-bad outcome directions in task performance.

Method: The study uses a maze task with controlled interventions that separate realized outcomes from informational history. Tests include transfer across different explicit outcome encodings and comparing announced vs unannounced outcome histories across multiple LLM checkpoints. Also includes matched maze-RL runs comparing activation direction predictive power.

Result: Directions fitted on one explicit outcome encoding transfer well to another, indicating readouts aren't tied to surface form. However, transfer degrades substantially when same realized outcome is reached through different histories (announced vs unannounced), showing strong history dependence. In maze-RL runs, directions become more predictive of remaining return and policy becomes more dependent on them, but history dependence persists.

Conclusion: Results support a functional, value-related interpretation of the activation direction but not its identification with a history-invariant scalar valence state. The direction encodes more than just surface outcome representation and includes historical context information.

Abstract: Contrastive activation directions are often interpreted from what they decode or how strongly they steer behavior. But what evidence is sufficient to identify the construct represented by such a direction, rather than a correlated feature of the contrast used to extract it? We study this question for a good--bad outcome direction in a maze task, using controlled interventions that separate the realised outcome from the informational history through which it became known. Across multiple LLM checkpoints, directions fitted on one explicit outcome encoding transfer well to another, indicating that the readout is not tied to surface form. In contrast, when the same realised outcome is reached through announced and unannounced histories, transfer degrades substantially: even after both histories receive the same explicit outcome, the post-event readout remains strongly conditioned on the earlier announcement. In a matched maze-RL run, the post-RL direction becomes substantially more predictive of reference-MDP remaining return and the policy becomes more dependent on it at the tested sites, while this history dependence persists. These results support a functional, value-related interpretation of the direction, but not its identification with a history-invariant scalar valence state.

</details>


### [204] [CurvFlow-DTA: dual-graph discrete Ricci curvature flow for drug--target affinity prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22862)
*Jicheng Ma,Yunyan Yang,Juan Zhao,Liang Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CurvFlow-DTA improves drug-target affinity prediction by replacing static curvature with weighted Forman curvature flow on both molecular and protein graphs, achieving significant improvements in warm and cold-start settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing curvature-aware DTA approaches primarily use static curvature on drug graphs while representing proteins with sequence-derived features, leaving pair-adaptive graph geometry underexplored and limiting adaptation to unseen entities in cold-start settings relevant to practical drug screening.

Method: Uses weighted Forman curvature flow on both molecular and protein residue-residue contact graphs; precomputes label-independent flow trajectories for each entity; employs pair-conditioned selector to determine horizons read by dual-branch Flow-GINE; uses frozen ESM-2 for residue-level representations and contact scores to construct protein graphs; requires only SMILES strings and protein sequences without bound complex structure.

Result: CurvFlow-DTA improves on protocol-matched Ricci-GraphDTA baseline in every warm and cold-start setting on Davis and KIBA datasets: MSE decreases by 19.9% on Davis and 18.9% on KIBA in warm splits; across six cold-start comparisons, MSE decreases by 14.3-27.4% with higher concordance index; achieves lowest MSE on both warm benchmarks and four out of six cold-start settings among literature baselines.

Conclusion: CurvFlow-DTA successfully demonstrates the effectiveness of replacing static curvature with curvature flow for drug-target affinity prediction, particularly showing strong performance in cold-start settings where adaptation to unseen entities is crucial, using only sequence and SMILES information without requiring bound complex structures.

Abstract: Graph neural networks are widely used for drug--target affinity (DTA) prediction, and discrete Ricci curvature has recently been used to characterize molecular graph geometry. Existing curvature-aware DTA approaches mainly use static curvature on the drug graph while representing proteins primarily with sequence-derived features. This leaves pair-adaptive use of graph geometry underexplored, which may limit adaptation to unseen entities in cold-start settings relevant to practical screening.
  We present CurvFlow-DTA, which replaces a single static curvature representation with weighted Forman curvature flow on both molecular and protein residue--residue contact graphs. A label-independent flow trajectory is precomputed for each entity, and a pair-conditioned selector determines the horizons read by a dual-branch Flow-GINE. A frozen ESM-2 supplies residue-level representations and contact scores used to construct the protein graph. Inference requires only SMILES strings and protein sequences, without a bound complex structure.
  On Davis and KIBA, CurvFlow-DTA improves on the protocol-matched Ricci-GraphDTA baseline in every warm and cold-start setting. Warm-split mean squared error (MSE) decreases by $19.9\%$ on Davis and $18.9\%$ on KIBA. Across the six cold-start comparisons, MSE decreases by $14.3$--$27.4\%$, with higher concordance index (CI) throughout. Within our compiled set of literature baselines, CurvFlow-DTA achieves the lowest MSE on both warm benchmarks and across four out of six cold-start evaluation settings.

</details>


### [205] [Causilo Technical Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22866)
*Minyong Cho,Minho Jeong,Dooho Lee,Jinmo Lee,Jaemin Yoo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Causilo is a tabular foundation model that achieves state-of-the-art predictive performance with exceptionally fast inference, outperforming TabPFN-3.5-Fast while being 31.6% faster.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There's a need for tabular foundation models that combine frontier predictive performance with efficient inference, as current models often trade off one for the other.

Method: Causilo builds on TabICL's column-then-row architecture but adds a row-refinement module before row compression. It exchanges information among cell representations within each row after column encoding, then uses an additional column stage before compression into row embeddings. For efficiency, both row stages use cross-attention through fixed summary tokens to maintain linear attention cost relative to features.

Result: Causilo achieves 1785.4 Elo on TabArena with median inference time of 0.10 seconds per 1K test samples, outperforming TabPFN-3.5-Fast by 31.6% in inference time reduction. It shows strong performance across TabArena, BeyondArena, and ScoringBench benchmarks.

Conclusion: Causilo represents an advancement in tabular foundation models by achieving frontier-level predictive performance while maintaining substantially faster inference, placing it on the performance-efficiency Pareto frontier through its architectural innovations.

Abstract: We introduce Causilo, a tabular foundation model (TFM) that combines frontier predictive performance with exceptionally fast inference. On TabArena, Causilo achieves 1785.4 Elo, at a median inference time of 0.10 seconds per 1K test samples. It outperforms TabPFN-3.5-Fast with 31.6% less inference time, placing it on the performance--efficiency Pareto frontier. Causilo follows TabICL's column-then-row architecture but introduces another row-refinement module before row compression. This module exchanges information among cell representations within each row after column encoding. The refined cells then visit the context set again through an additional column stage before being compressed into row embeddings. For inference efficiency, both row stages use cross-attention through a fixed number of summary tokens, keeping their attention cost linear in the number of features. Pretrained on approximately 36M synthetic tables, Causilo delivers strong benchmark results across TabArena, BeyondArena, and ScoringBench, achieving frontier-level performance with substantially faster inference.

</details>


### [206] [Leveraging Inference-Time Compute for Diffusion Models via Global Scheduling of Denoising Trajectories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22867)
*Yuan Cao,Yifu Tang,Hangqi Li,Zeyu Zheng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper addresses computational budget allocation for diffusion model sampling, showing optimal allocation has water-filling structure, proving linear regret bounds for adaptive policies, and demonstrating 20-50% fewer function evaluations needed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: When using diffusion models with verification-based sampling (multiple candidate noise samples per step), there's a resource allocation problem: given fixed computational budget, how to best distribute search effort across the denoising trajectory steps to maximize sample quality.

Method: 1. Formulate as computational budget allocation problem. 2. Show expected gain from evaluating K candidates factorizes into step-specific sensitivity parameter times universal sample-size factor. 3. For fixed sensitivity profile, optimal allocation solves separable concave integer program with water-filling structure. 4. Prove linear regret bounds for adaptive policies. 5. Propose design anchoring allocation offline with online adaptation. 6. Extend analysis to broader family of local search operators.

Result: Theoretical analysis shows optimal allocation has water-filling structure, advantage over uniform allocation increases with sensitivity dispersion. Experiments on three families of diffusion samplers demonstrate proposed allocation achieves same quality as uniform benchmark with 20-50% fewer function evaluations.

Conclusion: Careful computational budget allocation across diffusion denoising steps significantly improves sampling efficiency. Water-filling allocation structure is optimal, and the proposed offline-anchored, online-adapted approach effectively balances worst-case guarantees with instance-specific adaptation.

Abstract: Diffusion models generate a sample by traversing a denoising trajectory, a sequence of stochastic noise-reduction steps that transforms pure noise into a draw from a target distribution. At deployment time, additional computation can improve sample quality without retraining: at each step, the sampler draws several candidate noise samples, scores the resulting predictions with a quality criterion called the verifier, and retains the best candidate at the cost of one network evaluation per candidate. This raises a resource allocation question: given a fixed budget of function evaluations, how should search effort be distributed across the steps of the denoising trajectory? We formulate this as a computational budget allocation problem. First, we show that, to leading order in the step size, the expected gain from evaluating $K$ candidates at a step factorizes into an endogenous, step-specific sensitivity parameter times a universal sample-size factor equal to the expected best of $K$ standard-normal draws. Second, for a fixed sensitivity profile, the optimal allocation solves a separable concave integer program with water-filling structure; at fixed total sensitivity, its advantage over uniform allocation increases with sensitivity dispersion in the majorization order. Third, we prove that when sensitivities vary across instances, no adaptive policy can avoid worst-case regret that grows linearly in the trajectory length, which motivates a design that anchors the allocation offline and adapts online only to recover instance-specific slack. We extend the analysis from independent random search to a broader family of local search operators, and instantiate it as an implementable algorithm. Experiments on three families of diffusion samplers show that the proposed allocation attains the quality of the uniform benchmark with 20 to 50 percent fewer function evaluations.

</details>


### [207] [Towards Full Pipeline FP8 Reinforcement Learning for LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22870)
*Fanchao Chen,Ziheng Jiang,Ziyun Wei,Zheng Zhong,Du Li,Chi Zhang,Haibin Lin,Shivaram Venkataraman*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FP8 quantization in RL pipelines causes training instability due to compounded quantization noise distorting importance ratios; proposed Calibrated Clipping method aligns FP8 bounds with BF16 distributions to eliminate entropy surges and restore performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: FP8 quantization accelerates RL training for LLMs, but maintaining stability throughout FP8 RL pipelines remains challenging. Previous work addressed train-inference mismatches, but full-pipeline FP8 RL still suffers from severe training instability (anomalous entropy surges and garbled outputs).

Method: Proposes Calibrated Clipping, a dynamic method that aligns FP8 clipping bounds with high-precision BF16 distributions by matching the lower-bound clipping quantile and rebalancing the upper bound accordingly to address compounded FP8 quantization noise.

Result: Extensive experiments across GRPO and DAPO algorithms, model scales from 8B to 32B, and multiple FP8 scaling granularities show the approach successfully eliminates entropy surges and restores performance comparable to BF16 baseline.

Conclusion: Compounded FP8 quantization noise distorts importance ratios in RL training, causing instability; Calibrated Clipping effectively addresses this by aligning quantization bounds with high-precision distributions, enabling stable FP8 RL training with performance matching BF16 baselines.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a key technique for improving the reasoning and agentic abilities of large language models (LLMs). Although FP8 quantization can accelerate RL training, maintaining stability throughout an FP8 RL pipeline remains challenging. While previous works have focused on resolving train-inference mismatches using correction techniques like TIS, we reveal that full-pipeline FP8 RL still suffers from severe training instability, manifesting as anomalous mid-training entropy surges and garbled outputs. We trace this instability to a previously overlooked cause: compounded FP8 quantization noise distorts the importance ratio, disproportionately pushing negative-advantage tokens outside the trust region and erroneously zeroing out their gradients. As a result, pathological outputs are not properly penalized and accumulate over the course of training. To address this, we propose Calibrated Clipping, a dynamic method that aligns the FP8 clipping bounds with high-precision BF16 distributions by matching the lower-bound clipping quantile and rebalancing the upper bound accordingly. Extensive experiments across GRPO and DAPO algorithms, model scales from 8B to 32B, and multiple FP8 scaling granularities demonstrate that our approach successfully eliminates entropy surges and restores performance comparable to the BF16 baseline.

</details>


### [208] [Prioritized Rollouts for Efficient World Model-based Vision-Language-Action Policy Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22879)
*Yifei Sheng,Haoxiang Ren,Zhilong Zhang,Haonan Wang,Runjie Xu,Yihao Sun,Nan Tang,Zhichao Wu,Lei Yuan,Haoxin Lin,Yang Yu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: U-GROW is a lightweight sampling method for MBRL that uses policy uncertainty to identify informative states, directing more model rollouts to states where policy improvements would be most valuable, without changing the optimization objective.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fine-tuning Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models with RL is expensive due to real-world robot interaction costs. MBRL reduces this cost but becomes computationally expensive as VLA policies scale. Current MBRL methods treat all states equally, missing that states differ in their utility for policy improvement.

Method: U-GROW (Uncertainty-Guided Rollouts) is a plug-and-play sampling layer that uses policy uncertainty to identify informative states. It directs more model rollouts to states where the policy exhibits high uncertainty (often at decision-sensitive stages). It modifies only the branched-start distribution and can be integrated into existing MBRL pipelines without changing policy optimization objectives.

Result: Experiments in simulated and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate U-GROW's efficiency and effectiveness. The method successfully identifies that policy uncertainty is concentrated in small subsets of states during decision-sensitive stages, and leveraging this for targeted rollout generation improves learning efficiency.

Conclusion: Policy uncertainty can effectively guide experience generation in MBRL. U-GROW provides a lightweight, compatible solution that improves efficiency by focusing computational resources on the most informative states for policy improvement, supporting the broader use of uncertainty-based sampling in embodied AI systems.

Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for embodied intelligence, but fine-tuning them with reinforcement learning (RL) remains constrained by the cost of real-world robot interaction. Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) reduces this cost by using a learned world model to generate rollouts for policy optimization. However, it becomes computationally expensive as VLA policies and world models scale. Existing methods typically treat states equally, overlooking substantial differences in their utility for policy improvement. In this paper, we show that policy uncertainty helps identify states with greater potential for policy improvement. The policy exhibits high uncertainty at only a small subset of states, often during decision-sensitive stages where small action differences can alter task outcomes, suggesting that policy improvements at these states could be particularly valuable. Building on these findings, we introduce U-GROW, a lightweight, plug-and-play sampling layer that directs more model rollouts to these informative states. By modifying only the branched-start distribution, U-GROW can be integrated into existing MBRL pipelines without changing the policy optimization objective. Experiments in both simulated and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of U-GROW, supporting the use of policy uncertainty to guide experience generation.

</details>


### [209] [Merge++: Universal Merge Refinement Through Data-Free Checkpoint Inversion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22886)
*Aditya Pola,Vineeth N. Balasubramanian*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Merge++ is a post-hoc model merging method that synthesizes task-representative images by inverting expert checkpoints and uses them for distillation, improving existing weight-space merging algorithms without additional data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current data-free model merging methods only operate in weight space, performing arithmetic on parameters without observing how each expert behaves during forward evaluation. This behavioral signal requires inputs, which are unavailable in data-free settings.

Method: 1) Invert expert checkpoints to synthesize task-representative images, 2) Use these synthesized images to distill expert knowledge into the merged model, 3) Apply this refinement stage universally across different merging algorithms as a complementary step.

Result: Consistent improvements across merging algorithms ranging from simple task arithmetic to state-of-the-art spectral methods, with average gains of +2 to +8 points and up to +25.9 on individual configurations.

Conclusion: Merge++ successfully addresses the limitation of weight-space methods by incorporating behavioral signals through checkpoint inversion and distillation, enabling better model merging without requiring additional data beyond the checkpoints themselves.

Abstract: Model merging consolidates fine-tuned experts into one multi-task model without retraining. All existing data-free methods approach this problem entirely in weight space. Restricted to arithmetic on parameters, these methods never observe how each expert behaves, a signal that only emerges through forward evaluation. Accessing this behavioral signal requires inputs to evaluate on, which the data-free setting prohibits. We propose Merge++, a post-hoc method that addresses this by inverting the expert checkpoints to synthesize task-representative images, then distilling expert knowledge into the merged model using those images. Merge++ requires no additional data beyond the checkpoints themselves. It applies universally across merging algorithms and operates as a complementary refinement stage independent of the underlying weight-space method. The method consistently improves merging algorithms ranging from simple task arithmetic to state-of-the-art spectral methods, with average gains of +2 to +8 points and up to +25.9 on individual configurations.

</details>


### [210] [Are Coreset Selection Methods Worth Their Cost?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22894)
*Yangze Liu,Zhongyi Han*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Coreset selection is often evaluated only by final accuracy at fixed subset sizes, ignoring selection time and training recipes. A comprehensive benchmark reveals that when accounting for wall-clock budgets, simple random sampling strategies match or beat sophisticated selection methods, and full-data training for fewer epochs often performs best.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluations of coreset selection methods focus only on downstream accuracy at fixed subset sizes, ignoring the time spent selecting the subset and the details of training recipes. This creates an incomplete picture of their practical value since selection time contributes to overall training costs.

Method: The authors create an end-to-end benchmark that standardizes downstream training and charges both selection and training to the same auditable wall-clock budget. They evaluate 11 selection methods across 4 datasets (CIFAR-10 to ImageNet-1K), 5 subset fractions, and 3 seeds, with over 1,500 released runs. They conduct budget-aware evaluations where each selector is given its most favorable operating point.

Result: Across all budget anchors on CIFAR-10 and Tiny ImageNet, no sophisticated selector wins - every winner is either class-balanced random sampling, repeated random sampling, or full-data training. On ImageNet-1K, training on all data for fewer epochs beats every selection strategy while costing less. The cost audit shows selection cost is dominated by a fixed full-dataset scan that doesn't scale well across datasets.

Conclusion: Selection time is not free preprocessing and must be included in evaluations. When properly accounting for wall-clock budgets, simple random strategies perform as well as or better than sophisticated methods, and full-data training with fewer epochs often provides the best trade-off. The paper also provides 9 correctness fixes to widely used code.

Abstract: Coreset selection picks a representative subset of the labeled training set to make training cheaper. However, it is usually evaluated by downstream accuracy at a fixed subset size, ignoring both the time spent selecting the subset and the training recipe behind each reported number. We introduce an end-to-end benchmark that standardizes downstream training and charges selection and training to the same auditable wall-clock budget, spanning 4 datasets from CIFAR-10 to ImageNet-1K, 11 selectors, 5 fractions, and 3 seeds, with over 1,500 released runs. Repeated-sampling work has shown that budget-aware evaluation already favors random strategies. Our two budget studies test whether that verdict survives when every selector is granted its most favorable operating point. Across eight wall-clock budget anchors on each of CIFAR-10 and Tiny ImageNet, no anchor is won by a sophisticated selector: every winner is class-balanced random sampling, repeated random sampling, or full-data training. In fixed-budget duels on ImageNet-1K, training on all data for fewer epochs beats every selection strategy we probe while also costing the least. A per-dataset cost audit shows that selection cost is dominated at every scale by a fixed full-dataset scan, so it cannot be amortized away by selecting a smaller fraction, and its absolute size does not extrapolate from one dataset to another. We further quantify when selection does pay back through subset reuse, and document 9 correctness fixes to a widely used codebase, one of which shifts a standard Herding baseline by nearly 6 points. Selection time is not free preprocessing, and an evaluation that ignores it measures the wrong quantity.

</details>


### [211] [Computationally efficient safe exploration in reinforcement learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22919)
*Shreeram Murali,Shankar A. Deka,Dominik Baumann*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CoLSafe-MDP is a lightweight reinforcement learning algorithm that provides safety guarantees during exploration using a constant-time Nadaraya-Watson estimator instead of computationally expensive Gaussian processes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reinforcement learning needs safety guarantees for real-life applications, but typical RL algorithms lack these guarantees. Existing safe exploration methods rely on Gaussian processes which have high computational cost (cubic scaling with data points), making them impractical for many applications.

Method: The authors propose CoLSafe-MDP algorithm based on the Nadaraya-Watson estimator, which provides bounds on estimates and scales in constant-time with the number of data points, significantly more efficient than GP-based methods.

Result: The algorithm was evaluated in a grid-based environment and on observational Martian terrain data, demonstrating its ability to safely explore and optimize constrained MDPs with much lower computational cost than GP-based approaches.

Conclusion: CoLSafe-MDP provides a computationally efficient alternative to GP-based safe reinforcement learning methods, offering safety guarantees during exploration with constant-time scaling, making it suitable for practical real-world applications where computational efficiency is crucial.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning in real-life applications requires safety guarantees during exploration. Typical reinforcement learning algorithms do not provide such guarantees, and many modifications that do rely on Gaussian processes (GPs), which have a large computational cost. We propose a computationally lightweight algorithm based on the Nadaraya-Watson estimator that safely explores and optimizes constrained Markov decision processes (MDPs). Our algorithm, \textsc{CoLSafe-MDP}, uses an estimator that scales in constant-time with bounds on the estimates, a significant improvement from its GP-based counterparts that scale cubically with the number of data points. We then evaluate its performance in a grid-based environment and on observational Martian terrain data.

</details>


### [212] [Joint Domain-Class Modeling for Federated Learning Under Feature Skew](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22932)
*Sina Najafi,Mostafa Tavassolipour,Seyed Pooya Shariatpanahi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: JDFL proposes a lightweight FL extension that handles feature skew by inferring pseudo-domains from local updates and training a joint domain-class classifier with novel supervision strategies, improving accuracy on domain-shifted benchmarks without sharing raw data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Federated learning performance degrades under feature skew where clients share labels but have different conditional input distributions due to client-specific appearance factors. Existing methods struggle with these latent domain variations without sharing private data.

Method: JDFL first infers domain clusters (pseudo-domains) from local update signals. It expands the classifier head to output M×C joint (domain-class) logits, maintaining a shared backbone. Two supervision strategies are introduced: 1) similarity-aware soft-labeling that transfers evidence between nearby domains, and 2) per-sample randomized target assignment that perturbs supervision as a low-cost regularizer. The approach is optimizer-agnostic and integrates with standard FL methods like FedAvg and SCAFFOLD.

Result: Empirical evaluations show consistent improvements in global test accuracy on standard domain-shifted image benchmarks. Ablation studies confirm gains stem from the proposed supervision and parametrization rather than mere capacity increase. The method works effectively with minimal changes to existing FL frameworks.

Conclusion: JDFL provides an effective, lightweight solution to feature skew in federated learning by making latent domain variation usable without sharing raw data. The joint domain-class parametrization with novel supervision strategies enables better representation of domain-conditioned appearance while maintaining compatibility with standard FL methods.

Abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without centralizing private data, but performance often degrades under feature skew: clients share labels while the conditional input distributions $p_i(x\!\mid\!y)$ vary due to latent, client-specific appearance factors. We propose Joint Domain-Class Federated Learning (JDFL), a lightweight, optimizer-agnostic extension that makes this latent domain variation usable without sharing raw data. JDFL first infers domain clusters called pseudo-domains from brief local update signals. It then expands the classifier head to output $M\times C$, joint (domain-class) logits. This allows the model to represent domain-conditioned appearance while keeping a shared backbone. To train the expanded head we introduce two complementary supervision strategies based on simple intuitions: a similarity-aware soft-labeling that transfers evidence between nearby inferred domains while allowing domain-specific specialization, and a per-sample randomized target assignment that perturbs supervision across the joint outputs and serves as a low-cost training-time regularizer. JDFL integrates with existing standard FL methods (e.g., FedAvg, SCAFFOLD) with minimal changes. Empirically, both supervision modes consistently improve global test accuracy on standard domain-shifted image benchmarks; ablations and sensitivity studies show the gains stem from the proposed supervision and parametrization rather than mere capacity increase.

</details>


### [213] [Token Utility Is Selection-Conditioned: Coupled Selection of Prompt Context and Response Supervision for Efficient Instruction Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22943)
*Can Wu,Xinrui Chen,Ou Wu,Yi Du*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BRIDGE is a novel method for efficient LLM instruction tuning that jointly selects prompt context and response supervision tokens using budgeted alternating selection guided by directional gradient interactions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods for LLM instruction tuning typically value prompt context and response supervision separately, which risks selection-state mismatch between how tokens are valued and what subsets are actually retained for training.

Method: BRIDGE uses directional gradient-guided token selection that captures selection-conditioned token utility through a shared validation-directed interaction surrogate. It performs budgeted alternating selection that coordinates retained subsets by aggregating precomputed interactions, and converts conditional response scores into coherent supervision spans using structure-aware projection.

Result: BRIDGE outperforms compared selection methods across three model families in mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction following tasks. The advantage over independent selection methods grows with compression in mathematical reasoning.

Conclusion: The BRIDGE framework effectively addresses the selection-state mismatch problem in LLM instruction tuning by using coordinated, interaction-aware token selection, leading to superior performance across multiple domains.

Abstract: Efficient large language model (LLM) instruction tuning requires selecting response supervision with supporting prompt context. Existing methods typically value both sides separately, risking selection-state mismatch between valuation and retained training subsets. BRIDGE (Budgeted Response-Prompt Interaction via Directional Gradient-guided Efficient Token Selection) captures selection-conditioned token utility through a shared validation-directed interaction surrogate valuing each side under the other's retained state. Budgeted alternating selection coordinates retained subsets by aggregating precomputed interactions over the current opposite-side subset to update conditional scores. Structure-aware projection converts conditional response scores into coherent supervision spans. Across three model families, BRIDGE leads compared selection methods overall in mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction following. In mathematical reasoning, its advantage over independent selection grows with compression.

</details>


### [214] [Beyond Similarity: Coverage-Aware Prompt Selection for Time Series Forecasting with LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22977)
*Daeun Ji,Minkyoung Kim,Dongkuk Kim,Yohan Lee,Beomsoo Kim,Beakcheol Jang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CASP-LLM is a coverage-aware semantic prompting framework that addresses prompt selection bias in similarity-based retrieval for LLM time series forecasting by incorporating usage-tracking and saturating-gate techniques as a coverage regularizer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current similarity-based retrieval methods in prompt-based time series forecasting concentrate on near-duplicate candidates, creating a bias toward dominant temporal patterns while overlooking rare but informative events. This prompt selection bias exists in various retrieval-conditioned pipelines but remains unexamined beyond diversity-aware retrieval approaches.

Method: The authors propose CASP-LLM, which addresses prompt selection bias by combining usage-tracking and saturating-gate techniques into a coverage regularizer that adds no learnable parameters. This framework tracks how often different prompts are used during training and encourages more balanced utilization across the prompt pool.

Result: On six long-term benchmarks and the M4 short-term benchmark, CASP-LLM matches or improves on similarity-based LLM forecasters on most dataset-horizon settings, with exceptions only on Electricity, M4-Monthly, and few-shot long-horizon settings. Controlled studies show that failure modes occur at cross-batch usage level rather than per-retrieval redundancy.

Conclusion: The research demonstrates that addressing prompt selection bias through coverage-aware regularization significantly improves time series forecasting performance. The key insight is that the problem lies in cross-batch usage imbalance rather than within-retrieval redundancy, making techniques like MMR ineffective while cross-training anchor usage regularization provides the solution.

Abstract: Similarity-based retrieval is the dominant rule for conditioning large language models (LLMs) in in-context learning, retrieval-augmented generation, and prompt-based time series forecasting. The rule concentrates on near-duplicate candidates, an issue that has motivated diversity-aware retrieval but remains unexamined in other retrieval-conditioned pipelines. We study this issue using prompt-based time series forecasting as a test bed, where a learned prompt pool is retrieved by similarity. Dominant methods in this setting retrieve top-K entries by cosine similarity without redundancy control, producing a bias toward dominant temporal patterns while overlooking rare but informative events. We propose CASP-LLM, a coverage-aware semantic prompting framework that addresses this prompt selection bias by combining usage-tracking and saturating-gate techniques into a coverage regularizer that adds no learnable parameters. On six long-term benchmarks and the M4 short-term benchmark, CASP-LLM matches or improves on similarity-based LLM forecasters on most dataset-horizon settings, with the exceptions of Electricity, M4-Monthly, and the few-shot long-horizon setting. A controlled study locates the failure mode at the cross-batch usage level rather than per-retrieval redundancy: within-retrieval diversification such as MMR does not help, whereas regularizing anchor usage across training does.

</details>


### [215] [LPINNs: First-Layer Gated Localization for Physics-Informed Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22984)
*Lakshay Chawla,Hardik Jain*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PINNs with first-layer localization functions (multiplying hidden activations by input-dependent localization) can significantly improve performance on long-domain and high-order problems, with fixed Gaussian, inverse-quadratic, and bump functions showing best results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard PINNs use one shared representation across the domain, which becomes difficult to optimize for long domains and high-order operators. The authors explore a minimal alternative approach.

Method: Multiply first hidden activation of dense PINNs by input-dependent localization functions, creating receptive fields without domain partitioning or interface losses. Tested 13 families of localization functions with various parameterizations on three problems: nonlinear harmonic oscillator, heat equation on long interval, and 4D fourth-order problem.

Result: Three configurations showed large error reductions: (1) Fixed Gaussian on harmonic oscillator reduced RMSE from 0.48369 to 0.00883; (2) Learnable inverse-quadratic on heat equation reduced from 0.2896 to 0.0306; (3) Fixed bump on 4D problem reduced from 17.5947 to 0.2260. Inverse-quadratic was the only family beating baseline on all three equations.

Conclusion: First-layer localization provides measurable improvements to baseline PINNs on long-domain and high-order problems, but careful function selection is crucial as poor choices can degrade performance significantly.

Abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) use one shared representation over the computational domain, which can become difficult to optimize on long domains and for high-order operators. We study a minimal alternative: multiply the first hidden activation of an otherwise unchanged dense PINN by input-dependent localization functions, giving first-layer units receptive fields without partitioning the domain or adding interface losses. We screen 13 families of localization functions, in up to three parameterizations each, on a nonlinear harmonic oscillator (HO), a heat equation on a long spatial interval, and a manufactured four-dimensional (4D) fourth-order problem, with ten paired seeds throughout. Three configurations give large reductions in solution error at matched budgets: (i) Fixed Gaussian localization functions on the $2π$ HO domain cut mean solution RMSE from $4.8369\times10^{-1}$ to $8.83\times10^{-3}$ at 3k epochs. (ii) The inverse-quadratic family with learnable centers and widths cuts it from $2.896\times10^{-1}$ to $3.06\times10^{-2}$ on the $8π$ heat domain at 10k epochs. (iii) Fixed bump localization functions cut it from $1.75947\times10^{1}$ to $2.260\times10^{-1}$ on the $4π$ 4D domain at 10k epochs. Every paired seed improves in these three comparisons. The screen also shows that the mechanism is not a free win: on HO only 2 of 13 families beat the baseline, and 10 of the remaining 11 are 9 to 23 times worse; on 4D four families are non-finite and five are more than three orders of magnitude worse than the baseline. The inverse-quadratic family is the only one that beats the baseline on all three equations. Overall, these results show that first-layer localization can provide measurable improvements to baseline PINNs on long-domain and high-order problems.

</details>


### [216] [On attention heads and bilinear forms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22990)
*Andrew O'Desky*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper analyzes bilinear forms in transformer attention heads, finding that trained forms cluster near rank-one profiles, with symmetric parts decomposing into hyperbolic plus zero forms for most query-key matrices.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To better understand the mathematical structure of attention mechanisms in large language models by analyzing the bilinear forms that emerge in trained attention heads.

Method: Introduce an orthogonally invariant profile map to visualize bilinear forms in a 3D simplex, analyze trained attention heads empirically, and prove theoretical results about the decomposition of symmetric parts of bilinear forms.

Result: Empirical observation shows trained bilinear forms cluster near rank-one profiles. Theoretically proved that for a Zariski-dense set of query-key matrices, the symmetric part decomposes into hyperbolic form plus zero form.

Conclusion: Attention heads in trained LLMs exhibit specific mathematical structure where bilinear forms concentrate near simple rank-one forms, and their symmetric components have a canonical decomposition, providing insights into attention mechanism geometry.

Abstract: We study the symmetric and antisymmetric parts of bilinear forms in the attention heads of trained large language models. We introduce an orthogonally invariant profile map from real bilinear forms to a three-dimensional simplex and observe that profiles of trained bilinear forms accumulate near profiles of rank-one bilinear forms. We prove that the symmetric part of a bilinear form in an attention head is the sum of a hyperbolic form and a zero form for a Zariski-dense subset of query-key matrices.

</details>


### [217] [Interpretable Multi-Hypersphere Deep Anomaly Detection for Open-set Supervised Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23008)
*Zhiji Yang,Fangyong Wang,Yue Li,Xianli Pan,Jianhua Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: IMHD-AD is a multi-class open-set anomaly detection method that constructs independent hyperspheres for each normal class with interpretable geometric decisions, achieving state-of-the-art performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods have limitations: single-hypersphere approaches can't represent class-specific locations/ranges, while multi-hypersphere methods don't fully integrate inter-class boundary constraints, learnable acceptance ranges, and interpretable decisions.

Method: Proposes IMHD-AD which constructs independent hyperspheres for each known normal class in shared feature space. Embeds class-specific hypersphere centers and radii directly into final network layer, optimizes them with shared representation using target-inside and non-target-outside constraints.

Result: Achieves highest AUC in 28 out of 30 open-set comparisons on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10. Synthetic study shows architecture must balance compactness of known classes against separability of unknown anomalies.

Conclusion: IMHD-AD effectively addresses limitations of existing methods by providing interpretable multi-hypersphere anomaly detection with explicit geometric decision boundaries and state-of-the-art performance on benchmark datasets.

Abstract: Multi-class open-set anomaly detection requires a model to characterize the normal acceptance domain formed by multiple heterogeneous subdistributions using only class-labeled samples from known normal classes, and to identify previously unseen anomalies at test time. Existing single-hypersphere methods cannot explicitly represent class-specific locations and acceptance ranges, while current multi-hypersphere or multi-class approaches do not fully integrate inter-class boundary constraints, learnable acceptance ranges, and interpretable decisions. To address these limitations, we propose Interpretable Multi-Hypersphere Deep Anomaly Detection (IMHD-AD). IMHD-AD constructs an independent hypersphere for each known normal class in a shared feature space. With target-inside and non-target-outside constraints, IMHD-AD embeds the class-specific hypersphere centers and radii directly into the final network layer and jointly optimizes them with the shared representation. The minimum signed boundary score across hyperspheres simultaneously determines open-set acceptance or rejection and provides a faithful geometric explanation of each decision. On MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10, IMHD-AD achieves the highest AUC in 28 of 30 open-set comparisons. A two-dimensional synthetic study further shows that model architecture must balance the compactness of known normal classes against the separability of unknown anomalies.

</details>


### [218] [WaveFront Decoding: Parallelized Self-Speculative Decoding for Looped Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23033)
*Hyeongju Ha,Jae-Joon Kim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Wavefront Decoding (WFD) is a training-free self-speculative decoding framework for looped language models that achieves significant speedups by co-batching drafting and verification through wavefront organization of mixed-depth states.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Looped language models increase effective depth through weight-shared recurrent blocks, but this creates high decoding latency due to T sequential recurrent-block calls per token. Traditional speculative decoding approaches don't work well with looped architectures because they require separate draft-then-verify phases.

Method: WFD exploits two key properties of looped LMs: (1) intermediate recurrence outputs can serve as effective draft predictions, and (2) weight sharing allows token states at different positions and recurrence depths to be processed in a single batched recurrent-block call. The method organizes mixed-depth states into a diagonal wavefront pattern, continuously drafting new positions at shallow depth while advancing earlier positions toward full-depth verification.

Result: WFD achieves 2.42x speedup on Ouro-2.6B and 3.54x on Huginn-3.5B over autoregressive decoding across six Spec-Bench task categories, consistently outperforming draft-then-verify approaches. With cross-recurrence KV sharing to reduce KV traffic, speedup increases to 4.81x on Huginn-3.5B.

Conclusion: Wavefront Decoding provides an effective training-free solution to reduce decoding latency in looped language models by co-batching drafting and verification within the same recurrent calls, leveraging the architectural properties of weight-shared recurrent blocks to organize computation as a wavefront rather than separate phases.

Abstract: Looped language models repeatedly apply a weight-shared block to increase effective depth without increasing parameter count, but the resulting T sequential recurrent-block calls per generated token substantially increase decoding latency. To address the issue, we introduce Wavefront Decoding (WFD), a training-free self-speculative decoding framework designed for looped language models. WFD exploits two properties of these architectures: intermediate recurrence outputs provide effective draft predictions, and weight sharing allows token states at different positions and recurrence depths to be processed in one batched recurrent-block call. WFD organizes these mixed-depth states into a diagonal wavefront, continuously drafting new positions at shallow depth while advancing earlier positions toward full-depth verification. Unlike the phase-separated draft-then-verify schedule, WFD therefore co-batches drafting and verification within the same recurrent calls, while rejected drafts are corrected using full-depth predictions. Across six Spec-Bench task categories, WFD achieves 2.42x speedup on Ouro-2.6B and 3.54x on Huginn-3.5B over autoregressive decoding, consistently outperforming draft-then-verify. Cross-recurrence KV sharing further reduces wavefront KV traffic and increases WFD's speedup to 4.81x on Huginn-3.5B.

</details>


### [219] [Optimizers for Diffusion Models: A Controlled Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23055)
*Arman Bolatov,Egor Shulgin,David Li,Abduragim Shtanchaev,Sebastian U. Stich,Maxim Panov,Eric Moulines,Peter Richtárik,Martin Takáč*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A comprehensive benchmark study comparing seven different optimizers across four discrete diffusion model formulations, showing that AdamW is not always optimal and that optimizers validated on autoregressive language model training can outperform it in diffusion tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Discrete diffusion models have shown competitive performance with autoregressive models, but optimizer selection for training them has received insufficient attention. Current practice involves inheriting optimizers from previous papers without systematic comparison, while new optimizers are typically validated only on autoregressive pretraining, which represents a different objective and loss surface.

Method: The study conducted a controlled benchmark across four diffusion formulations: masked diffusion (text8), uniform diffusion (QM9 and LM1B through Gaussian duality), and Gaussian diffusion on images (CelebA-64). Seven optimizers (AdamW, Lion, Muon, SOAP, MARS, MARS-M, Schedule-Free) were compared using the same search protocol, with winners retrained at full budget with three seeds.

Result: AdamW remains a strong default but is not always optimal - it was outperformed by a resolved margin on two of the four tasks. The best optimizer varied by diffusion formulation. Notably, methods validated on autoregressive language model pretraining transferred well: Muon, MARS-M, and SOAP each beat tuned AdamW on at least one diffusion formulation.

Conclusion: Optimizer selection deserves the same careful consideration as other components of the training recipe for diffusion models, as the optimal choice depends on the specific diffusion formulation. The study demonstrates that optimizers validated on autoregressive training can be effective for diffusion tasks, challenging the current practice of uncritically adopting AdamW.

Abstract: Discrete diffusion models now match autoregressive language models on several benchmarks, while the question of how best to train them has received far less attention: the optimizer is inherited from one paper to the next and never compared. New optimizers, meanwhile, are validated almost exclusively on autoregressive pretraining, a different objective on a different loss surface. We present a controlled optimizer benchmark across four diffusion formulations, to our knowledge the first for discrete diffusion: seven optimizers (AdamW, Lion, Muon, SOAP, MARS, MARS-M, Schedule-Free) on masked diffusion (text8), uniform diffusion (QM9, and LM1B through the Gaussian duality) and Gaussian diffusion on images (CelebA-64), each on a task with published reference values. Every optimizer receives the same search protocol, and every winner is retrained at the full budget with three seeds. AdamW is a strong default but not always the right choice: it is beaten by a resolved margin on two of the four tasks, and the winner changes with the formulation, so the optimizer deserves the same care as the rest of the training recipe. Notably, methods validated on autoregressive language model pretraining transfer well: Muon, MARS-M and SOAP each beat the tuned AdamW on at least one diffusion formulation. The benchmark, all runs and every figure are reproducible end to end from the released code at https://github.com/armanbolatov/diffusion-baselines.

</details>


### [220] [MolSC: Leveraging Substituent Contributions to Enhance Fine-grained Molecular Understanding in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23073)
*Hyuntae Park,Sooyeon Kim,Jiwon Park,SangKeun Lee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces MolSC, a dataset of substituent contributions (property changes from attaching specific substituents to molecular scaffolds), and shows that training on it improves molecular LLMs' ability to capture fine-grained structure-property relationships where existing models fail.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current molecular Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle to capture fine-grained structure-property relationships, particularly how small, localized modifications (substituents) alter a molecule's behavior. There's a need to address this limitation in molecular understanding.

Method: 1) Introduced MolSC dataset containing 181K substituent-level examples of property changes from attaching specific substituents to molecular scaffolds, curated from manually annotated bioactivity records. 2) Created MolSC-Bench evaluation benchmark of 1,541 examples disjoint at scaffold, substituent, and molecule levels. 3) Trained models on MolSC and evaluated their performance on substituent contribution prediction and downstream molecular tasks.

Result: Existing molecular LLMs and strong proprietary models (GPT-5.2, Gemini-3-Flash) show limited reliability in substituent contribution prediction. In contrast, training on MolSC substantially improves this ability and achieves strong performance across diverse downstream molecular tasks.

Conclusion: Substituent contribution learning is a key component of fine-grained molecular understanding, and the MolSC dataset enables significant improvements in molecular LLMs' ability to capture localized structure-property relationships.

Abstract: Recent advances in natural language processing have led to molecular Large Language Models (LLMs) with strong performance across diverse chemistry tasks. However, they still struggle to capture fine-grained structure-property relationships, particularly how small, localized modifications alter a molecule's behavior. To address this limitation, we introduce MolSC, a dataset of substituent contributions, defined as property changes induced by attaching specific substituents to molecular scaffolds. Curated from manually annotated bioactivity records, MolSC spans structural-alert liability, target-specific bioactivity, and physicochemical descriptors, and contains 181K substituent-level examples for training. We further propose MolSC-Bench, a held-out evaluation benchmark of 1,541 examples disjoint from MolSC at the scaffold, substituent, and molecule levels. Our experiments show that existing molecular LLMs and strong proprietary models such as GPT-5.2 and Gemini-3-Flash show limited reliability in substituent contribution prediction. In contrast, training on MolSC substantially improves this ability and achieves strong performance across diverse downstream molecular tasks. These results highlight substituent contribution learning as a key component of fine-grained molecular understanding.

</details>


### [221] [AirGC-CD: Gaussian-Circulant Precoding for Exactly Debiasable PAPR Reduction in Over-the-Air Federated Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23084)
*Jonggyu Jang,Hyeonsu Lyu,Hyun Jong Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AirGC-CD is an over-the-air federated learning scheme that uses partial Gaussian circulant precoding before clipping to enable unbiased aggregation, reduce transmission overhead, and handle the PAPR-SNR trade-off in communication-limited environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Over-the-air FL suffers from high PAPR requiring either clipping (causes bias) or power back-off (reduces SNR), and transmits uncompressed data (one channel use per parameter), making large-model training impractical.

Method: Uses partial Gaussian circulant matrix precoding before clipping, ensuring Gaussian distribution regardless of update sparsity. This allows clipping to be inverted on average using a Bussgang gain, providing unbiased aggregation. The linear precoder also acts as a compressor, reducing transmission from d to m dimensions using O(d log d) FFT operations.

Result: AirGC-CD achieves exactly unbiased aggregation with clipping adding only variance. It provides closed-form solutions for clipping ratio trade-off and reduces transmission costs. Experiments on five image datasets show superior performance to baseline over-the-air FL, especially at low SNR, with fewer channel uses.

Conclusion: AirGC-CD effectively addresses the PAPR-SNR trade-off in over-the-air FL by enabling unbiased clipping via Gaussian precoding while simultaneously compressing transmissions, making large-model FL more practical in communication-limited scenarios.

Abstract: Over-the-air federated learning lets edge devices transmit their local updates simultaneously, reducing the communication overhead. The resulting waveform, however, has a peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR) that grows with the model dimension, and keeping the amplifier in its linear range leaves two remedies: clipping the peaks or backing off the transmit power. Neither remedy is without cost: i) the clipping distortion appears at the receiver as a bias that cannot be removed, and ii) back-off keeps the signal intact but degrades the average signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Independent of this trade-off, the transmission remains uncompressed, spending one channel use per model parameter, which keeps large-model training out of reach. To address these challenges, we propose AirGC-CD, an over-the-air scheme that precodes each local update with a partial Gaussian circulant matrix before clipping. In AirGC-CD, the precoder's output is exactly Gaussian regardless of the update's sparsity, so the clipping function is designed for a known distribution instead of inheriting it from the data. This enables the clipping to be inverted on average by a single scalar Bussgang gain in closed form, and we prove that the resulting aggregate is exactly unbiased, with clipping adding only variance. The clipping ratio is then the only free parameter left, trading the variance of the clipping against the SNR loss from back-off, and we derive its near-optimum in closed form. Since the precoder is linear, it also acts as a compressor, reducing the transmission from the model dimension d to the sketch dimension m at a cost of only O(dlog d) via two fast Fourier transforms, whereas a Gaussian sketch costs O(md). Experiments on five image datasets show that AirGC-CD outperforms baseline over-the-air FL schemes in most settings, particularly at low SNR, while using fewer channel uses per round.

</details>


### [222] [Neural Spectral Capacity: Measuring and Designing Architectures from Network Specification Alone](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23087)
*Chenyu Zhu,Ruoyu Zhao,Zhichao Lu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Neural Spectral Capacity (NSC) is a novel architecture scoring metric based on weight matrix singular-value spectra that outperforms traditional metrics (#Params, #FLOPs) and enables efficient architecture search through dynamic programming.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional architecture metrics like #Params and #FLOPs fail to capture architectural structure differences - two architectures with identical parameter budgets but different depth-width ratios or layer allocations score identically but behave differently. There's a need for a better, structure-aware metric for architecture design and compression.

Method: Propose Neural Spectral Capacity (NSC), a closed-form scalar based on the singular-value spectrum of each weight matrix. Under random initialization, NSC can be computed from architectural specs alone (no data, gradients, or model instantiation) using the Marchenko-Pastur law. Introduce NSC-DP, an exact dynamic-programming solver that finds the architecture globally maximizing NSC under resource constraints in seconds on CPU.

Result: NSC outperforms #Params, #FLOPs, and training-free proxies in ranking across 7 Transformer and CNN families. NSC-DP discovers a Transformer-XL architecture on WikiText-103 that beats human-designed baseline in 2 seconds. Prunes LLaMA-7B to best 5.7B model across 8 commonsense reasoning tasks without calibration data, ~5900x faster than strongest training-free proxy baseline.

Conclusion: NSC provides a theoretically-grounded, structure-aware alternative to traditional architecture metrics, enabling efficient, optimal architecture search and compression without requiring training or data, with significant practical advantages over existing approaches.

Abstract: Modern Transformer design and compression both reduce to allocating capacity under a budget. The standard scalars for these decisions, #Params and #FLOPs, capture size and compute but not architectural structure: two architectures with identical parameter budgets but different depth-width, head, or FFN allocations receive identical scores yet behave differently. We propose Neural Spectral Capacity (NSC), a closed-form scalar grounded in the singular-value spectrum of each weight matrix. Under standard random initialization, the Marchenko-Pastur law renders NSC computable from the architectural specification alone, with no model instantiation, data, or gradients. Its layer-wise additive structure admits NSC-DP, an exact dynamic-programming solver returning the architecture globally maximizing NSC under resource constraints in seconds on a CPU -- a guarantee that black-box search over existing training-free proxies cannot provide. Empirically, NSC outperforms #Params, #FLOPs, and representative training-free proxies in ranking across seven Transformer and CNN families (on FlexiBERT, $τ= 0.505$ on pairs differing in #Params by less than 10%, where #Params collapses to 0.082); NSC-DP discovers a Transformer-XL architecture on WikiText-103 that beats the human-designed baseline in 2 seconds; and prunes LLaMA-7B to the best 5.7B model across eight commonsense reasoning tasks without any calibration data, about 5900x faster than the strongest training-free proxy baseline.

</details>


### [223] [The Role of Coordinates in Pareto Regret for Adversarial Multi-Objective Bandits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23092)
*Changkun Guan,Mengfan Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper analyzes adversarial multi-objective bandits where reward loss patterns affect Pareto regret. While easier coordinates with smaller cumulative loss might help in theory, unknown easy coordinates don't improve worst-case Pareto regret bounds. The paper establishes matching lower and upper bounds on Pareto regret and develops adaptive algorithms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing work suggests that easier coordinates (those with smaller cumulative loss) might reduce Pareto regret in multi-objective bandits, but in practice, one may not know which coordinate is easier. The authors want to understand whether this lack of information affects the theoretical guarantees and worst-case performance bounds.

Method: 1) Theoretical analysis showing that unknown easy coordinates don't improve worst-case Pareto regret order, 2) Lower bound proof for minimax expected Pareto regret, 3) Application of Poly-INF algorithm to fixed coordinate when easy coordinate is known, 4) Development of reward-doubling version of Poly-INF that adapts to unknown easy coordinates.

Result: 1) Proved minimax expected Pareto regret is Ω(min{T-L₀,√[K(T-L₀)]}) for K≥4 arms, T≥6 rounds, and ≥2 coordinates, which decreases with L₀ even when known, 2) Showed known easy coordinate allows matching upper bound using Poly-INF, 3) Developed adaptive algorithm without knowledge of easy coordinate that still achieves matching minimax rate, 4) Results have no extra log T factor and are independent of number of coordinates.

Conclusion: Unknown easy coordinates don't improve worst-case Pareto regret bounds in adversarial multi-objective bandits, but the optimal rate can still be achieved through adaptive algorithms. The work provides complete characterization with matching lower and upper bounds, and the developed adaptive algorithm maintains optimal performance without requiring knowledge of which coordinate is easier.

Abstract: Adversarial multi-objective bandits hold the potential to help us optimize choices (arms) whose reward is a multidimensional vector chosen by an adversary and whose performance is measured by Pareto regret. We define loss as one minus reward and measure the easiness of a coordinate by the smallest cumulative loss of the arms on it, and call the coordinate easier when this quantity is smaller. Existing work suggests that in theory an easier coordinate may reduce Pareto regret. However, in practice, one may not know which coordinate is easier. On the negative side, we show that this lack of information eliminates the possibility: a smaller cumulative loss does not improve the worst-case order of Pareto regret. Precisely, let \(L_d\) be the smallest cumulative loss along coordinate $d$ over $T$ rounds. For \(K\ge4\) arms, \(T\ge6\) rounds, and at least 2 coordinates, we prove that the minimax expected Pareto regret is \(Ω(\min\{T-L_0,\sqrt{K(T-L_0)}\})\). It is monotonically decreasing in \(L_0\), even when \(L_0=\min_d L_d\) itself is known. On the positive side, this result motivates the possibility that other coordinates, not just the easy one, may suffice to attain the optimal rate of Pareto regret. When $L_0$ is known, we apply Poly-INF to a fixed coordinate and obtain an upper bound on Pareto regret that exhibits the same order and thus matches the lower bound. Without such knowledge, we develop a reward-doubling version of Poly-INF that adapts to this unknown quantity while still attaining the matching minimax rate. Another implication is that it has no extra \(\log T\) factor and is independent of the number of coordinates.

</details>


### [224] [When Does Adversarial Refinement Help? A Negative Result and Open Problem in Adapting R3GAN to Time Series Imputation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23102)
*Yufeng He*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Stable GANs (R3GAN) adapted for time series imputation show minimal improvement over linear baselines, underperforming diffusion models despite addressing GAN instability issues.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate whether modern GANs with provable convergence (R3GAN) can revive adversarial imputation for time series, given that diffusion models have largely replaced GANs due to training instability concerns.

Method: Adapted R3GAN to 1D temporal data using coarse-to-fine refinement framework with frequency-domain discriminator. Audited 14 saved configurations across 3 datasets, examining both mean/zero-start and linear-start configurations.

Result: Negative results: Mean/zero-start configurations improved 48.4-70.2% but linear-start configurations showed mean change of -0.7% (range -3.0% to +1.1%). R3GAN-1D underperformed BRITS by 5.8x on Weather dataset. Adversarial signal appears inert or harmful compared to diffusion methods.

Conclusion: Adversarial refinement with stable GANs doesn't significantly improve time series imputation over linear baselines, unlike diffusion models. The paper identifies open problem of why learned discriminators fail to provide useful refinement gradients while diffusion denoisers succeed, and calls for matched discriminator-removed ablation as key next experiment.

Abstract: Diffusion models and transformers have supplanted GANs for multivariate time series imputation, largely on grounds of GAN training instability.
