Conclusion: RLVR² provides a verifiable ranking paradigm that effectively addresses the limitations of linear score aggregation in rubric-based RL, enabling more principled handling of heterogeneous criteria and better performance across diverse tasks.

Abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) is expanding from tasks with well-defined correctness signals, such as mathematics and code, toward multifaceted quality requirements specified by multi-dimensional rubrics. Since policy optimization consumes one scalar per rollout, rubric-based pipelines must map multiple criterion scores into a scalar reward. This aggregation is often treated as score scaling, but it implicitly determines how quality dimensions trade off during training. The prevailing practice, normalizing each criterion and taking a linear combination, assumes that cardinal score differences are comparable across criteria and that gains on one criterion compensate for failures on another; both assumptions are unreliable when criteria are semantically heterogeneous. We propose Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rubric-based Ranking (RLVR$^2$), a verifiable ranking paradigm for rubric-based RLVR. For each criterion, RLVR$^2$ converts rubric scores into criterion-specific within-group ordinal outcomes, recovers a latent utility from the resulting comparison matrix, and merges these utilities into one training signal. By retaining only within-group ordering and discarding raw score magnitudes, RLVR$^2$ avoids calibrating heterogeneous rubric scales. It further supports objective-preserving attribute adjustment: auxiliary attributes that correlate with observed rankings but are not training objectives can enter the estimation without expanding the rubric or rewarding them directly. Across three model scales and 16 benchmarks, RLVR$^2$ consistently outperforms representative rubric-based baselines, achieving the best overall performance on most benchmarks at every scale. Analysis shows it controls systematic effects tied to reasoning efficiency and response formatting while preserving the quality objective.

</details>


### [249] [TRACE: Tractable Routing Autoencoder for Clinical ECG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23460)
*Shunbo Jia,Runze Ma,Haonan Lyu,Haijin Zhang,Qiang Yang,Caizhi Liao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TRACE is a tractable ECG autoencoder with a 32D clinical latent space pre-specified into perfusion, structure, and conduction subspaces, enabling decision-pathway auditable diagnoses with no performance penalty compared to uninterpretable models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep learning models for ECG diagnosis, including foundation models pretrained on millions of recordings, lack decision-pathway auditability - clinicians cannot trace diagnoses to physiological pathways or intervene on them, limiting clinical utility and interpretability.

Method: TRACE uses a 32-dimensional clinical latent space specified in advance from domain knowledge, partitioned into perfusion, structure, and conduction subspaces. Each subspace routes to its own diagnostic head by design, with orthogonality penalty regularization, and reconstructs ECG through a decoder that permits latent perturbation.

Result: TRACE outperforms unconstrained classifiers and matches/beats an ECG foundation model pretrained on 10M recordings (with only ~1/8 parameters) on PTB-XL and Georgia datasets. It transfers effectively to CPSC2018 cohort by re-specifying routing table. Routing contract is verified through joint probe, erasure, and perturbation analyses. Removing the specified partition costs significant performance (1.70-2.76 AUC points).

Conclusion: The pre-specified clinical ontology provides decision-pathway auditability at no macro-F1 cost compared to arbitrary assignments, enabling clinicians to trace ECG diagnoses to specific physiological pathways while maintaining state-of-the-art diagnostic performance.

Abstract: Deep learning has advanced automated electrocardiogram (ECG) diagnosis, but the field's most accurate models, foundation models pretrained on millions of recordings, are not decision-pathway auditable: a clinician cannot trace a diagnosis to a physiological pathway or intervene on one. We propose TRACE, a Tractable Routing Autoencoder for Clinical ECG, whose 32-dimensional clinical latent space is specified in advance from domain knowledge rather than discovered by optimization. TRACE partitions this space into perfusion, structure, and conduction subspaces, routes each to its own diagnostic head by design, regularizes the partition with an orthogonality penalty, and reconstructs the ECG through a decoder that permits latent perturbation. On PTB-XL and Georgia, TRACE exceeds unconstrained classifiers and stays ahead of an ECG foundation model pretrained on ten million recordings, evaluated by linear probe on frozen features, at roughly an eighth of the parameter count. On the nine-label CPSC2018 cohort, which carries no structural class, the framework transfers with only the routing table re-specified to a perfusion/rhythm/conduction partition. Joint probe, erasure, and perturbation analyses verify the routing contract, and perturbing the depolarization and repolarization pathways modulates the reconstructed waveform. Removing the specified partition and its orthogonality penalty costs 1.70 AUC and 11.30 macro-F1 points on PTB-XL, and 2.76 AUC and 16.92 macro-F1 points on Georgia. A capacity-matched permutation control places arbitrary assignments within 0.34 AUC points of the ontology routing and leaves macro-F1 statistically level (p=0.619): the ontology supplies decision-pathway auditability at no macro-F1 cost.

</details>


### [250] [ITSY: Causal Discovery From Irregular Time-Series Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23516)
*Wenbo Xu,Yue He,Yunhai Wang,Yueguo Chen,Kun Kuang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ITSY: A new continuous-optimization method for causal discovery from irregular time series with missing data, jointly learning causal graphs while imputing missing values under linear model assumptions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most structural causal model methods for time series require complete observation windows and become misspecified when samples are missing, creating a gap in methods for irregular time series data.

Method: ITSY reformulates the structural equation to use nearest available history instead of potentially missing current slices, jointly imputes missing values while learning causal graphs, and uses a weighted reconstruction objective to correct noise transformations.

Result: ITSY consistently improves graph recovery over representative SCM-based baselines across synthetic regimes varying missingness, scale, graph density, and noise, and on a real-world benchmark.

Conclusion: ITSY establishes a focused solution for irregular linear first-order dynamics and clarifies the assumptions required for nonlinear or higher-order extensions, demonstrating effectiveness for causal discovery from irregular time series.

Abstract: Structural causal models for time series recover contemporaneous and lagged effects, but most methods require complete observation windows and become misspecified when samples are missing. We introduce ITSY, the first continuous-optimization method for causal discovery from irregular time series under a linear model. ITSY reformulates the structural equation so that prediction uses the nearest available history rather than the possibly missing current slice, and jointly imputes missing values while learning both graphs. A weighted reconstruction objective corrects the noise transformation induced by this reformulation. Across synthetic regimes varying missingness, scale, graph density, and noise, and on a real world benchmark, ITSY consistently improves graph recovery over representative SCM-based baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results establish a focused solution for irregular linear first-order dynamics and clarify the assumptions required for nonlinear or higher-order extensions.

</details>


### [251] [Feature Suppression and Differential Privacy for Residential Traffic Classification: A Two-Home Federated Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23521)
*Márton Pál Lipcsey-Magyar,Adrian Pekar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper compares feature suppression versus differential privacy for residential traffic classification in federated learning, finding feature suppression achieves better accuracy than DP-SGD but doesn't provide formal privacy guarantees.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Residential traffic classification supports service management but faces challenges: heterogeneous traffic across homes, privacy constraints, and privacy-aware training imposing uneven costs across traffic categories.

Method: The study uses simulated two-client federated learning with 1.62 million preprocessed gateway-collected flows across six categories. It compares three approaches: full-feature baseline, feature suppression (FS-mild excludes four timing features), and DP-SGD under fixed record-level privacy. Evaluation uses stratified and temporal splits across five seeds.

Result: FS-mild achieves higher combined macro-F1 and worst-group F1 than DP-SGD across all seeds and both model capacities. DP-SGD incurs pronounced minority-category losses, especially in smaller homes. Privacy probes show near-chance discrimination but inconsistent rankings, failing to establish equivalent privacy to formal methods.

Conclusion: Feature suppression serves as a useful input-minimization baseline but is not a substitute for formal privacy mechanisms like differential privacy, as it doesn't provide equivalent privacy guarantees despite better performance on classification metrics.

Abstract: Residential traffic classification supports service management, but learning across homes must account for heterogeneous traffic and privacy constraints. Privacy-aware training may impose uneven costs across traffic categories. We study this tradeoff in simulated two-client federated learning using 1.62 million preprocessed gateway-collected flows across six categories. We compare a full-feature baseline, feature suppression (FS), and differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) under one fixed record-level privacy setting. FS-mild excludes four timing features from 16 model inputs; it provides no formal privacy guarantee. With size-proportional aggregation, FS-mild achieves higher combined macro-F1 and worst-group F1 (the minimum per-class F1 across homes) than DP-SGD in all five seeds at both model capacities under stratified and temporal splits. The tested DP-SGD configuration incurs pronounced minority-category losses, especially in the smaller home, but FS-mild does not uniformly improve on the full-feature baseline. On stratified-split models, loss-based and shadow-model membership probes show near-chance aggregate discrimination without a consistent ranking across probes; this does not establish equivalent privacy. These findings support FS as an input-minimization baseline, not a substitute for formal privacy.

</details>


### [252] [Predicting Out-of-Distribution Generalization of Neural Operators via Observable Spectral Error Decomposition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23529)
*Hang-Cheng Dong,Pengcheng Cheng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Neural operators for PDEs lack reliable OOD generalization. The paper proposes a spectral filter parameterization that decomposes errors into observable components, enabling predictable OOD diagnostics without ground truth.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current neural operator approaches to out-of-distribution generalization in PDE solving are empirical and black-box, reporting aggregate error metrics without explaining why errors arise or when they will grow. This lack of predictability and auditability presents a critical barrier to deployment.

Method: Parameterizes the learned solution operator as a spectral filter h_θ(λ) acting on eigenvalues of the underlying elliptic operator, implemented via Chebyshev polynomial expansions and trained with a weak-form objective. This allows exact decomposition of energy-norm error into spectral approximation and distribution-dependent spectral weighting terms.

Result: Derives three diagnostics: conservative in-band supremum ε_sup, global RMS proxy ε_rms, and sample-dependent effective metric ε_eff(f). These can be computed without ground-truth solutions. Experiments show ε_eff(f) consistently predicts energy error under various distribution shifts while global metrics can be misleading.

Conclusion: The framework shifts OOD assessment of neural operators from black-box benchmarking to operator-structure diagnostics, providing a practical route to auditable scientific machine learning with predictable and explainable error behavior under distribution shifts.

Abstract: Neural operators have emerged as powerful surrogates for solving partial differential equations (PDEs), yet their reliability under distribution shift remains a critical barrier to deployment. Existing approaches to out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization in operator learning are largely empirical and black-box: they report aggregate error metrics without explaining why errors arise or when they will grow. We propose a structure-preserving framework that makes OOD generalization predictable and auditable. Our key idea is to parameterize the learned solution operator as a spectral filter $h_θ(λ)$ acting on the eigenvalues of the underlying elliptic operator, implemented via Chebyshev polynomial expansions and trained with a weak-form objective. This parameterization admits an exact decomposition of the energy-norm error into two observable components: a model-dependent spectral approximation term and a distribution-dependent spectral weighting term induced by the input. From this decomposition we derive three diagnostics: a conservative in-band supremum $\vareps_{\mathrm{sup}}$, a global RMS proxy $\vareps_{\mathrm{rms}}$, and a sample-dependent effective metric $\vareps_{\mathrm{eff}}(f)$. These diagnostics can be computed without access to ground-truth solutions. Through four controlled experiments, we show that $\vareps_{\mathrm{eff}}(f)\|f\|$ consistently predicts energy error under in-distribution, in-band spectral shift, out-of-band tail, and compound shifts, whereas global metrics can be systematically misleading. Our framework shifts OOD assessment of neural operators from black-box benchmarking to operator-structure diagnostics, providing a practical route to auditable scientific machine learning.

</details>


### [253] [Decoupled Causal Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23535)
*Zhengkang Guan,Fei Wu,Kun Kuang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DCD is a novel causal discovery method that decouples non-target variables using weighting functions to directly identify Markov boundaries, then iteratively constructs CPDAGs by exploiting structural asymmetries in MBs, achieving strong performance especially in challenging noise regimes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Causal discovery from observational data is fundamental but challenging. Existing approaches rely on conditional independence tests, structure scores, or restrictive functional assumptions, which have limitations. The authors aim to develop a new perspective that avoids these limitations.

Method: DCD directly identifies Markov boundaries by decoupling non-target variables via weighting functions, such that only variables within the MB preserve dependence with the target under the decoupled distribution. Then, it iteratively constructs CPDAG by exploiting structural asymmetries within the Markov boundaries.

Result: The authors establish theoretical identifiability, soundness, and completeness of DCD. Empirical evaluations demonstrate strong performance, with particular excellence in challenging noise regimes.

Conclusion: DCD provides a novel decoupling-based approach to causal discovery that doesn't rely on traditional conditional independence tests, structure scores, or restrictive functional assumptions, offering a promising alternative with strong theoretical guarantees and empirical performance.

Abstract: Causal discovery from observational data is a fundamental yet challenging task in scientific research. While existing approaches are primarily based on conditional independence tests, structure scores, or restrictive functional assumptions, we propose Decoupled Causal Discovery (DCD), a novel decoupling-based perspective that does not rely on these methodologies. DCD directly identifies the Markov boundary (MB) by decoupling non-target variables via weighting functions, such that only variables within the MB preserve dependence with the target under the decoupled distribution. Building on this, DCD iteratively constructs the Completed Partially Directed Acyclic Graph (CPDAG) by exploiting structural asymmetries within the MBs. We establish the theoretical identifiability, soundness, and completeness of DCD. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that DCD achieves strong performance, particularly excelling in challenging noise regimes.

</details>


### [254] [Preserving Geometric Integrity in Graph Prompting via Measure-Constrained Optimal Transport](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23547)
*Xiangyu Wang,Shuo Wang,Ruiyi Fang,Zhao Kang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MINT is an optimal transport framework for graph prompt learning that prevents prompt concentration by globally controlling prompt utilization through transport constraints while maintaining local compatibility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current graph prompt learning approaches suffer from node-adaptive routing that can concentrate assignment mass on a small subset of prompts, even when individual node-prompt matches are locally meaningful, leading to suboptimal prompt utilization.

Method: Proposes MINT (Measure-INtegrity Transport), an entropically regularized optimal transport framework that formulates node-to-prompt adaptation as a globally coupled allocation problem with transport costs for local geometric compatibility and explicit control over graph-wide prompt utilization through prescribed prompt-side marginals.

Result: MINT remains competitive in few-shot adaptation across standard citation networks and heterophilic graphs. Controlled experiments show fixed-marginal routing controls prompt utilization with measurable end-to-end effects, while topology augmentation addresses structural mismatch.

Conclusion: MINT provides an optimal transport solution to prevent prompt concentration in graph prompt learning, with routing and topology playing complementary roles in addressing utilization and structural mismatch issues.

Abstract: Graph prompt learning enables parameter-efficient adaptation of frozen Graph Neural Networks to downstream tasks through lightweight prompt parameters. As routing becomes increasingly node-adaptive, however, independently optimized local decisions can collectively concentrate assignment mass on a small subset of a finite shared prompt bank, even when individual node--prompt matches remain locally meaningful. We propose MINT (Measure-INtegrity Transport), an entropically regularized optimal transport framework that formulates node-to-prompt adaptation as a globally coupled allocation problem. The transport cost favors local geometric compatibility, while a prescribed prompt-side marginal explicitly controls graph-wide prompt utilization. We further derive an exact variance decomposition that separates prompt-side geometric variance into retained prompt-update variation and within-node barycentric dispersion, together with a conditional stability bound for the frozen-encoder forward map. Across standard citation networks and additional heterophilic graphs, MINT remains competitive in few-shot adaptation. Controlled and end-to-end experiments further distinguish the roles of routing and topology: fixed-marginal routing controls graph-wide prompt utilization and has measurable end-to-end effects on citation networks, while topology augmentation provides a complementary, graph-dependent mechanism for addressing structural mismatch. Code is available at https://github.com/Ga1axy0051/MINT.

</details>


### [255] [Physics-residual machine learning predicts oxygen-evolution catalyst activity beyond the training range from sparse polarization measurements](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23549)
*Yong-Woon Kim,Jihyeok Lee,Sungtae Park,Sooseok Choi,Yung-Cheol Byun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Physics-residual machine learning combines Tafel equation extrapolation with learned corrections to predict oxygen-evolution catalyst activities beyond measured ranges, reducing errors by 29-52% and enabling efficient screening with shorter measurements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Screening oxygen-evolution catalysts requires predicting activities beyond measured potential windows, where current methods struggle because the deciding activity often lies above all recorded measurements during fitting.

Method: Physics-residual machine learning: 1) Tafel equation extrapolates candidate's measured current and slope, 2) learned residual (attenuated with feature-space distance) corrects magnitude, 3) applicability-domain score identifies predictions above training range before measurement.

Result: On a 322-candidate library (282 above training maximum), method achieved mean absolute error of 0.203 mA cm⁻² vs. 1.330 for data-driven ML. Only 35 labelled catalysts needed for fitting. In independent datasets, reduced overpotential error by 29-52%.

Conclusion: The approach enables efficient catalyst screening by allowing shorter measurements per candidate while still accurately ranking most active compositions, significantly outperforming purely data-driven methods for extrapolation beyond training data.

Abstract: Screening oxygen-evolution catalysts on combinatorial libraries requires deciding which candidates receive the remaining measurements. The deciding activity lies beyond each candidate's measured potential window and often above every activity recorded during fitting. We predict it by physics-residual machine learning: the Tafel equation extrapolates the candidate's own measured current and slope, a learned residual attenuated with feature-space distance corrects the magnitude, and an applicability-domain score identifies predictions above the training range before measurement. In a separately fabricated 322-candidate library, 282 above the training maximum, two measurements per candidate gave a mean absolute error of 0.203 mA cm$^{-2}$ against 1.330 for the selected data-driven machine-learning model. Errors inside the training range remained comparable, and 35 labelled catalysts were enough to fit it. In two independent datasets the same construction lowered the overpotential error by 29 to 52%. Campaigns can therefore shorten each measurement and still rank the most active compositions.

</details>


### [256] [Global Ranks Survive, Selected Heads Shift: BOS-Sink Topology under 4-bit Weight-Only Quantization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23585)
*Kuanlin Chen,Chen-Wei Kuo,Cheng-En Ou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Sink-aware deployment shortcuts may not be safe for 4-bit quantization - global rankings transfer well but specific head sets and layer policies need revalidation after quantization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To test whether sink-aware deployment shortcuts are safe for 4-bit weight-only post-training quantization, as sink-aware methods identify important attention heads before quantization for reuse at the edge.

Method: Developed Sink Topology Consistency (STC) metrics to analyze rank preservation, top-k overlap, and layerwise sink-mass shift. Tested on Qwen2.5-0.5B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, and Llama-3.2-1B models with 4-bit NF4 quantization, examining cross-domain shifts and calibration transfer stability.

Result: Global bf16-to-4-bit rank correlation remains high (ρ_s ≥ 0.980) but top-k overlap is only moderate (0.619-0.793). Significant layerwise variations observed: Qwen terminal layers shift 6.2-7.9x more than model means, while Llama-3.2-1B shows uniform drift. Cross-domain overlap degrades more for Qwen models. Matched-domain recalibration reaches stability at small sample sizes, but partial layer updates insufficient for Qwen models.

Conclusion: Global rankings often transfer in 4-bit quantization, but discrete head sets, layer-local policies, and cross-domain calibration should be revalidated after quantization. The deployment shortcut is not fully safe without careful verification.

Abstract: Sink-aware deployment may identify important first-token attention heads before a model is quantized, then reuse that map at the edge. We test when this shortcut is safe for 4-bit NF4 weight-only post-training quantization (PTQ). Our Sink Topology Consistency (STC) metrics separate global rank preservation, top-$k$ set overlap, and layerwise sink-mass shift, and distinguish per-input sensitivity from calibration-map transfer. Across Qwen2.5-0.5B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, and Llama-3.2-1B, global bf16-to-4-bit ranks remain high at 4,096 tokens ($ρ_s \geq 0.980$), yet top-$k$ Jaccard overlap is only 0.619-0.793, corresponding to 76.5-88.5% membership retention. The global statistic also masks local failures: terminal Qwen layers shift by 6.2-7.9x their model means, whereas Llama-3.2-1B shows low, nearly uniform drift. Under a C4-to-LongBench shift, cross-domain overlap degrades more than the within-domain precision comparison for both Qwen models, but not for Llama-3.2-1B. Matched-domain 4-bit recalibration reaches 90% of a split-half stability plateau at the smallest tested $n=8$ for both Qwen models and $n=32$ for Llama-3.2-1B, though not as a sharp threshold; for the two Qwen models, updating only selected layers does not reach the full-map stability criterion. On Jetson Orin NX, the 16-sample workload takes seconds for the two models with valid on-device sink measurements. The practical message is precise: global rankings often transfer, but discrete head sets, layer-local policies, and cross-domain calibration should be revalidated after quantization.

</details>


### [257] [Cost-Aware Reinforcement Learning with Action Masking and Projection for Battery Energy Storage Dispatch under Suppressed-Spread Market Shifts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23590)
*Kuanlin Chen,Chen-Wei Kuo,Cheng-En Ou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PPO-based BESS controller uses physical action masks and emergency projections for feasibility, with economic advisory from forecasts. It achieves 30.59-36.77 USD profit in T1 and 18.04-22.94 USD in T2 periods, remaining below MPC benchmark but stable across forecast types.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: BESS dispatch must maintain operational feasibility while declining price spreads reduce profit margins for cycling. There's a need to separate economic optimization from physical feasibility enforcement in battery control systems.

Method: Uses proximal policy optimization (PPO) controller with pre-selection physical action masks and emergency projections separated from causal, forecast-informed economic advisory. Compares across five PPO seeds, uses 24-step forecasts, and conducts M0-M6 ablation study to analyze effects of mask and projection removal.

Result: PPO achieved 30.59 USD profit in T1 and 18.04 USD in T2 windows versus 36.77 and 22.94 USD for proxy-cost MPC. Economic advisory raised T2 profit from 16.45 to 18.04 USD. Controller stable under daily/weekly/seasonal forecasts, weakens under persistence, and remains below MPC. Mask removal causes thousands of infeasible requests, while removing both physical layers exposes ramp violations.

Conclusion: Successfully separates economic screening from feasibility enforcement but doesn't claim formal safety, lifecycle-optimal aging, or RL dominance over MPC. The approach demonstrates practical feasibility constraints handling while maintaining economic performance.

Abstract: Battery energy storage system (BESS) dispatch must preserve operational feasibility while declining price spreads reduce the margin available to pay for cycling. We study a proximal policy optimization (PPO) controller whose pre-selection physical action mask and emergency projection are separated from a causal, forecast-informed economic advisory. All forecast-dependent methods receive the same causal 24-step forecast and grid-side settlement. Across five PPO seeds, advice-on net profit is 30.59 and 18.04 USD per 336-hour T1 and T2 window, versus 36.77 and 22.94 USD for proxy-cost MPC; PPO remains below this reference in both periods. Advice raises T2 profit from 16.45 to 18.04 USD while reducing throughput, but is immaterial in T1. On disjoint weekly blocks, PPO is stable under daily, weekly, and blended seasonal forecasts, weakens under persistence, and remains below proxy-cost MPC. Paired diagnostics localize changes to the observed 5-10 USD/MWh regime with mixed SoC-dependent effects. An M0-M6 ablation shows that mask removal sends thousands of infeasible requests to projection, while removing both physical layers exposes ramp violations. The evidence separates economic screening from feasibility enforcement without claiming formal safety, lifecycle-optimal aging, or RL dominance.

</details>


### [258] [Bilinear Optimization Divergence: Diagnosing Factor-Constrained LoRA Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23594)
*YongShun Wang,JianLin Su,Yong Ma*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Analyzes how orthogonality in LoRA factors affects update protection, introducing diagnostic BOD and methods (SFOR, WRP) for shared/fresh adapters with controlled experiments showing improved backward transfer and accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand when orthogonality in LoRA factors actually protects composed updates against interference, as orthogonality alone is insufficient - protection depends on task-start state, parameterization, and optimizer displacement.

Method: Introduces Bilinear Optimization Divergence (BOD) as an anchor-relative diagnostic. Develops finite-step analysis distinguishing shared vs fresh adapters. Proposes Semi-Frozen Orthogonal Routing (SFOR) for shared adapters and Weight Residual Projection (WRP) for enforcing displacement. Tests on Qwen3-8B with controlled two-task and four-task experiments.

Result: Controlled experiments reduced normalized historical response from 19.12% to 0.005% in shared adapters and from 7.72% to 0.002% in cumulative O-LoRA. Four-task experiments show SFOR improves backward transfer from -2.47 to -0.86, while O-LoRA hard protection improves three-order mean AA from 80.27% to 81.30% and forgetting measure from 2.20 to 0.43.

Conclusion: The analysis provides architecture-conditioned guidance on which constraints to enforce, how to enforce them (SFOR/WRP), and how to interpret empirical value. Shows stricter feasibility doesn't always improve final performance, emphasizing need for context-aware constraint selection.

Abstract: Orthogonality in a LoRA factor does not by itself specify what the composed update protects: the answer depends on the task-start state, the parameterization, and the realized optimizer displacement. We formalize this question through Bilinear Optimization Divergence (BOD), an anchor-relative diagnostic of effective-update response on selected historical features. The finite-step analysis distinguishes two cases. In a shared adapter, protecting the routing displacement leaves a learned-anchor residual through the changing companion factor. In a fresh zero-output block, a feasible routing state can protect the composed update while both current factors remain trainable. These conditions yield Semi-Frozen Orthogonal Routing (SFOR) for shared adapters and current-block hard protection for cumulative O-LoRA; Weight Residual Projection (WRP) enforces the required displacement after the optimizer step. Controlled two-task traces verify the predicted residual paths, reducing normalized historical response from 19.12% to 0.005% in the shared family and from 7.72% to 0.002% in the cumulative family. Four-task experiments on Qwen3-8B characterize the resulting trade-offs: SFOR improves backward transfer (BWT) from -2.47 to -0.86 with nearly unchanged average accuracy (AA), while O-LoRA hard protection improves three-order mean AA from 80.27% to 81.30% and forgetting measure (FM) from 2.20 to 0.43. Component controls also show that stricter feasibility need not improve final task performance. Together, the analysis and evidence provide an architecture-conditioned account of which constraint to enforce, how to enforce it, and how to interpret its empirical value.

</details>


### [259] [ETH-TraceBench: A Large-Scale Event-Stream Benchmark for Ethereum DeFi under Temporal, Protocol, and Contract Shift](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23659)
*Kemal Kirtac,Carsten Maple*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ETH-TraceBench is a benchmark for evaluating Ethereum DeFi transaction representations under various shift conditions (temporal, protocol, pool/infrastructure, symbolic), showing that while simple models achieve high aggregate performance, they struggle with protocol novelty and chronological modeling isn't as important as expected.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While Ethereum DeFi provides public, time-stamped transaction data, the public symbols can create strong machine-learning shortcuts. There's a need to evaluate representations under realistic shift conditions rather than just aggregate performance.

Method: Created ETH-TraceBench with 1.35 billion transactions spanning Jan 2021-Dec 2025. Used fixed 911,267-instance supervised sample with temporal splits: train on 2021-2024, model selection on 2025H1, test on 2025H2. Evaluated multiple models (TraceStats-GB, TopicEmitterHashMLP, TopicEmitterTrace-SGD) under protocol novelty, unseen-pool conditions, and symbolic masking.

Result: Simple models achieve high aggregate performance (0.953-0.959 macro-F1 on DEX test set), but drop sharply under protocol novelty (0.743-0.794). Unseen protocols like Uniswap v4 and Ekubo v1 are materially harder. Chronological modeling provides no consistent advantage over random shuffling. Protocol novelty and transfer conditions are the main evaluation challenges.

Conclusion: ETH-TraceBench emphasizes evaluating Ethereum DeFi representations under difficult transfer and controlled-input conditions rather than focusing on single aggregate scores. Protocol novelty poses significant challenges, and chronological structure may be less important than assumed for achieving high aggregate performance.

Abstract: Ethereum decentralized finance (DeFi) provides a public, time-stamped record of transaction-level event streams, but the same public symbols can create strong machine-learning shortcuts. We introduce ETH-TraceBench, a benchmark for evaluating Ethereum DeFi representations under temporal, protocol, pool/infrastructure, and symbolic shift. The raw event universe covers January 2021-December 2025 and contains 1.35 billion transactions with logs and 5.01 billion raw log rows. Model evaluation uses a fixed 911,267-instance supervised sample, training on 2021-2024, selecting models on 2025H1, and testing on 2025H2. Simple models perform strongly on the aggregate temporal test: TraceStats-GB reaches 0.953 macro-F1 and TopicEmitterHashMLP 0.959 on the canonical DEX test set. Performance drops sharply under protocol novelty, with macro-F1 of 0.794, 0.743, and 0.766 for TraceStats-GB, TopicEmitterTrace-SGD, and TopicEmitterHashMLP, while strict unseen-pool scores remain 0.927, 0.897, and 0.935. Uniswap v4 and Ekubo v1, both absent from supervised training, are materially harder than the full test. Jointly masking emitter and topic identity reduces DEX macro-F1 to 0.916 and liquidation macro-F1 to 0.774 for TopicEmitterTrace-SGD. A standard Transformer over log-index-ordered events provides no consistent advantage over a deterministic shuffle of the same events, indicating that high aggregate scores can arise without sophisticated chronological modeling. A natural-prevalence audit estimates 2025H2 DEX prevalence among logged Ethereum transactions at about 22.5%, and a deterministic 400-transaction audit finds complete agreement with task label sources and independently re-queried raw-log counts. ETH-TraceBench therefore treats difficult transfer and controlled-input conditions, rather than a single aggregate score, as the main evaluation target.

</details>


### [260] [One Patch, Three Roles: What Is Actually Coupled in Autoregressive Time-Series Forecasting?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23686)
*Ziang Li,Yue Huang,Guoxu Zhou,Na Han,Jie Wen,Lunke Fei,Xiaozhao Fang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A framework called Autoregressive Trajectory Distillation (ATD) enables flexible patch length selection for faster autoregressive forecasting while maintaining quality, with Spectrum Tangent correction further improving accuracy without added parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current patch-based autoregressive time-series forecasting ties input representation, learned transitions, and recursive execution to a single patch length, limiting flexibility. The authors seek to understand which of these roles can be adjusted separately for better efficiency and performance.

Method: 1) Atomic-encoding study to understand sensitivity to model width vs. atom grouping; 2) Autoregressive Trajectory Distillation (ATD) which fits frozen parent models' recursive trajectories with lightweight parallel exits, enabling selectable execution speeds (ATD-1/2/4/8); 3) Spectrum Tangent correction that applies residual projection along train-selected periodic history direction without adding neural parameters or Transformer calls.

Result: ATD-8 achieves 5.54× end-to-end speedup with stable quality across widths. ATD improves trajectory fidelity in all 21 seed runs but forecast accuracy in 15/21 runs. Spectrum Tangent reduces MSE by 2.54% and MAE by 2.33% at horizon 720 across seven datasets while remaining 3.24× faster than recursive inference. Findings recur across three public AR parents.

Conclusion: The work successfully separates representation, transition, and execution as independent design axes in autoregressive forecasting. ATD enables flexible speed-quality tradeoffs, while Spectrum Tangent provides accuracy improvements without computational cost, demonstrating that autoregressive components can be optimized independently.

Abstract: Patch-based autoregressive time-series forecasting often ties input representation, learned transitions, and recursive execution to one patch length. We ask which of these roles can be adjusted separately. A supporting atomic-encoding study finds greater sensitivity to model width than to atom grouping on the evaluated grid. Our main finding is that a frozen parent's recursive trajectory is easier to fit than the observed future with lightweight parallel exits. Autoregressive Trajectory Distillation (ATD) turns this into selectable ATD-1/2/4/8 execution, with ATD-1 exactly recovering the parent. On a paired four-data-set comparison, ATD-8 reaches $5.54\times$ end-to-end speedup with stable quality across widths. Fewer calls do not automatically remove the parent's existing forecast error: ATD improves trajectory fidelity in all 21 seed runs but forecast accuracy in only 15 against matched clean-future supervision. We further find a correctable residual projection along a train-selected periodic history direction. Spectrum Tangent applies this correction without adding neural parameters or Transformer calls. At horizon 720, it reduces mean squared error (MSE) and mean absolute error (MAE) by 2.54% and 2.33% over seven data sets and two output widths, while remaining $3.24\times$ faster than recursive inference. Level and shape projections sometimes disagree. Trajectory compressibility, the fidelity-accuracy mismatch, and the correction recur across three public AR parents. Together these results separate representation, transition, and execution as AR design axes. Code is available at https://github.com/RowanFFF/ATD-Spectrum-Tangent.

</details>


### [261] [A multi-temporal dataset for mapping burned areas in the Brazilian Cerrado using time series of remote sensing imagery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23687)
*Alisson Cleiton de Oliveira,Thales Sehn Körting*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Multi-temporal satellite dataset for mapping burned areas in Brazilian national park (2020-2022) using Random Forest classifier, showing best results when distinguishing between totally burned, partially burned, and non-burned classes then reclassifying.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To create and evaluate a multi-temporal tabular dataset for mapping burned areas using satellite imagery from WFI sensors, addressing the need for accurate burned area mapping without complex inter-satellite calibration requirements.

Method: Created dataset from CBERS-4A, CBERS-4, and AMAZONIA-1 satellites with spectral bands and indices. Applied Random Forest classifier with two approaches: binary classification (burned/non-burned) and three-class classification (totally burned, partially burned, non-burned). Used seven validation approaches with accuracy, precision, recall, and IoU metrics.

Result: Best results achieved when using three individual classes then reclassifying totally burned as burned area and grouping partially burned with non-burned. When compared to MCD64A1 product, omission errors for burned area were 22% (2020), 28% (2021), 59% (2022) and commission errors were 46%, 43%, 46% respectively.

Conclusion: The WFI sensor is effective for burned area mapping without inter-satellite spectral calibration. The multi-class approach with reclassification performs best, and further exploration with other machine learning algorithms is recommended to assess dataset potential and limitations.

Abstract: This paper introduces a multi-temporal tabular dataset derived from satellite images to map burned areas in the Chapada dos Veadeiros National Park, in Goiás, Brazil, covering the years 2020 to 2022. The dataset contains blue, green, red, and near-infrared bands, as well as the BAI, EVI, GEMI, NDVI, and NDWI spectral indices from the WFI sensor on the CBERS-4A, CBERS-4, and AMAZONIA-1 satellites, organized into a regular grid. We applied the Random Forest classifier to develop and validate models based on samples labeled as totally burned, partially burned, and non-burned. Two classification approaches were tested: one combining burned and non-burned areas into binary classes and another distinguishing between totally burned (TB), partially burned (PB), and non-burned (NB) classes. Seven validation approaches assessed different post-classification combinations, focusing on accuracy, precision, recall, and intersection over union (IoU) metrics. Results showed higher IoU when TB, PB, and NB were used as individual classes and TB was reclassified as burned area (BA) while PB and NB were grouped as non-burned. Comparing the annual results of this approach to the MCD64A1 product, the errors of omission for the BA class were 22% in 2020, 28% in 2021 and 59% in 2022, while the errors of commission were 46%, 43% and 46%, respectively. The study highlights the utility of the WFI sensor for burned area mapping without inter-satellite spectral calibration and suggests further exploration with other machine learning algorithms to evaluate the dataset potential and limitations.

</details>


### [262] [Tail-Weight Control and Localized Generalization in Nearly Low-Rank Adversarial Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23688)
*Kunyu Wang,Dehan Wang,Wenjun Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper studies norm-constrained linear classification with adversarial perturbations in a Gaussian model featuring a low-dimensional informative subspace plus independent noise tail. It provides theoretical guarantees for principal-space learning and shows experimentally that excess risk decreases with sample size.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to understand and guarantee robust linear classification in high-dimensional settings where data has a low-dimensional informative structure (principal subspace) plus independent noise components, particularly under Euclidean adversarial perturbations.

Method: The method uses theoretical analysis of norm-constrained linear classification with bounded ramp loss in Gaussian models. Key techniques include: principal-space witness analysis, path-specific density bounds for constants, boundary normalization to remove common attack penalties, and establishing joint local growth under isotropic principal covariance assumptions.

Result: Main results: 1) A principal-space witness with risk below one half forces near-optimal predictors to have small tail weight. 2) Under isotropic principal covariance, unique population minimizer exists with joint local growth. 3) Boundary normalization removes common attack penalty from centered margins. 4) Finite-sample guarantees governed by principal dimension and total tail energy. 5) Experiments show decreasing excess risk and tail use with sample size, and stable behavior when tail dimension grows at fixed total energy.

Conclusion: The paper establishes theoretical foundations for robust linear classification in structured high-dimensional settings, showing that principal-space learning can be effective even with adversarial perturbations. The analysis provides localized guarantees and demonstrates that excess risk decreases with sample size while being largely unaffected by tail dimension when total tail energy is fixed.

Abstract: We study norm-constrained linear classification under Eu clidean adversarial perturbations in a Gaussian model with a low-dimen sional informative subspace and an independent noise tail. For bounded ramp loss, we prove that a principal-space witness with risk below one half forces every near-optimal predictor to have small tail weight. A path-specific density bound yields constants without requiring positive tail variance. Under isotropic principal covariance, we establish a unique population minimizer and joint local growth. Boundary normalization then removes the common attack penalty from centered margins, giving localized finite-sample guarantees governed by principal dimension and total tail energy. Globalized growth removes the entrance condition at weaker constants; a model-aware comparison retains local guarantees. Experiments with twenty paired repetitions show decreasing excess risk and tail use with sample size, and nearly unchanged behavior when tail dimension grows at fixed total energy. Pure-noise controls and optimizer diagnostics clarify the scope and limitations of these conclusions.

</details>


### [263] [GenVoid: Uncertainty-Aware Learning of Subsurface Material Defects with an Experimentally Validated Physics-Informed Generative Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23761)
*Trishit Mondal,Prajwal Bharadwaj,Nikhil Karanjgaokar,Ameya D. Jagtap*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GenVoid is a physics-informed generative model framework that identifies internal voids in 2D/3D solids from surface displacement measurements alone, handling uncertainty and various material behaviors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Internal voids are common defects in manufactured structures but challenging to characterize because they're hidden; current methods struggle with indirect inference from surface measurements, uncertainty handling, and diverse material behaviors.

Method: A physics-informed generative model framework that incorporates governing mechanics equations into generative inference, enabling probabilistic void reconstruction from noisy displacement measurements across linear elastic, hyperelastic, and plastic materials in complex geometries.

Result: The method successfully infers hidden voids from both synthetic datasets and experimental measurements, introduces an observability measure quantifying sensitivity of boundary measurements to interior stiffness perturbations, and establishes systematic relationships between defect location, sensor configuration, and reconstruction fidelity.

Conclusion: GenVoid provides a physics-informed, uncertainty-aware approach for non-invasive defect characterization and offers quantitative design principles for measurement strategies in solid mechanics inverse problems.

Abstract: Internal voids are ubiquitous defects in manufactured structures, yet their characterization remains challenging because their geometry is hidden and can only be inferred indirectly from accessible measurements. Here we introduce \textit{GenVoid}, a physics-informed generative model-based framework for identifying internal voids in complex two- and three-dimensional solids from surface displacement measurements alone. By incorporating the governing mechanics into a generative inference framework, \textit{GenVoid} enables void identification across linear elastic, hyperelastic and plastic material behaviours and accommodates complex two- and three-dimensional structural geometries. Importantly, the framework explicitly accounts for uncertainty and noise in displacement measurements, producing probabilistic reconstructions of internal void geometry rather than a single deterministic estimate. We demonstrate the approach using high-fidelity synthetic datasets and experimentally measured displacement fields obtained from in-situ mechanical experiments, establishing its ability to infer hidden voids from realistic displacement measurements. To quantify the fundamental limits of such inference, we further introduce an observability measure that characterizes the sensitivity of boundary measurements to localized stiffness perturbations within the interior under an ensemble of applied loads. This framework provides a direct connection between defect location, sensor configuration and reconstruction fidelity, enabling systematic assessment of how the number and spatial distribution of boundary measurements govern void-identification accuracy. To this end, these results establish a physics-informed and uncertainty-aware approach for non-invasive characterization of hidden defects and provide a quantitative basis for designing measurement strategies for inverse problems in solid mechanics.

</details>


### [264] [Statistical Convergence of Transformer Encoder-Accelerated Robust Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23775)
*Suman Banerjee,Hiroyasu Tsukamoto*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Transformer-warm-started robust RL with conformal prediction provides certified convergence bounds without requiring knowledge of true transition dynamics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional reinforcement learning algorithms struggle computationally in large state-action spaces, and obtaining optimal action-value functions is intensive. There's a need for methods that can provide statistical convergence guarantees while handling uncertainty in transition dynamics.

Method: Proposes a robust RL framework with: 1) Transformer-based action-value function warm-start using natural language prompts for task specifications; 2) R-contamination model to characterize uncertainty in state transition kernels; 3) Conformal prediction using trajectory-level nonconformity scores from contracting Bellman residuals to certify convergence.

Result: Transformer warm-start reduces initial error and accelerates convergence. Conformal bounds track true error trajectory more tightly than existing guarantees. The method yields pre-certified stopping rules requiring little knowledge of true transition kernel.

Conclusion: The integration of transformer-based warm-start with conformal prediction for robust RL provides statistically rigorous convergence guarantees, handles transition uncertainty effectively, and outperforms existing methods in tracking error and convergence speed.

Abstract: Obtaining the optimal action-value function in Markov decision processes is computationally intensive in large state--action spaces. In this study, we present statistically rigorous convergence results for a robust reinforcement learning algorithm warm-started by a transformer-based action-value function prediction, where natural language prompts encode task specifications. Our framework adopts the R-contamination model to characterize uncertainty in the state transition kernel, and employs conformal prediction to certify convergence via trajectory-level nonconformity scores constructed from the contracting Bellman residual. The resulting conformal quantile bounds the gap between the running and optimal action-value functions simultaneously over all iterations, thereby yielding a pre-certified stopping rule that requires little knowledge of the true transition kernel. Numerical case studies on perturbed maze environments of varying size and contamination level confirm that the transformer-based warm start measurably reduces the initial error and accelerates convergence, while the proposed conformal bounds track the true error trajectory more tightly than existing guarantees.

</details>


### [265] [Falling Trees: A Model Class for Interpretable Risk Prioritization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23780)
*Varun Babbar,Zachery Boner,Margo Seltzer,Cynthia Rudin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Falling trees introduce a new interpretable model family that maintains monotonic risk constraints like falling rule lists but allows tree-structured branching, offering better balance between interpretability, expressiveness, and risk prioritization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many real-world decisions require prioritizing high-risk cases, but existing interpretable models like falling rule lists (FRLs) have restricted single-path structures that limit their expressiveness.

Method: Introduce falling trees with monotonic risk constraints and tree-structured branching. Present GRAVITree, a dynamic-programming-with-bounds algorithm for learning the Rashomon set of falling trees under depth and branching constraints.

Result: Falling trees match or outperform falling rule lists and other interpretable baselines in clinical datasets and public classification benchmarks, often producing more sparse decisions for high-risk instances.

Conclusion: Falling trees strike a practical balance between interpretability, expressiveness, and risk prioritization for high-stakes settings, enabling user-desired model expressivity between rule lists and full decision trees.

Abstract: Many real-world decisions require prioritizing high-risk cases, such as clinicians prioritizing high-risk patients before lower-risk ones. Falling rule lists (FRLs), which are ordered if--then rules with monotonically decreasing risks, provide an interpretable framework for such tasks; however, their single-path structure yields a highly restricted model class. We introduce falling trees, a new family of interpretable models that enforces the same monotonic risk constraint while permitting tree-structured branching. We present GRAVITree, a novel dynamic-programming-with-bounds algorithm for learning the Rashomon set of falling trees under depth and branching constraints. Our formulation can interpolate between rule lists and full decision trees, enabling user-desired model expressivity. In a new clinical dataset and in many public classification benchmarks, falling trees match or outperform FRLs and other interpretable baselines, often producing more sparse decisions for high-risk instances. Our results show that falling trees strike a practical balance between interpretability, expressiveness, and risk prioritization for high-stakes settings.

</details>


### [266] [Belted Engression: Sufficient Dimension Reduction for Generative Distributional Regression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23789)
*Wenxi Tan,Bing Li,Lingzhou Xue*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Belted Engression is a new compress-then-generate framework that uses sufficient dimension reduction to efficiently model complex covariate dependencies for conditional generation, achieving better performance with fewer parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional sufficient dimension reduction (SDR) frameworks weren't designed for conditional generation, and modern generative models struggle with complex covariate dependencies. There's a need to bridge SDR principles with conditional generative modeling.

Method: Proposes Belted Engression framework that embeds a structural bottleneck (belt) into generative architecture, creating a compress-then-generate paradigm driven by sufficient representation learning. Theoretically proves equivalence between SDR condition and law-preserving generative factorization.

Result: Theoretically: proves equivalence between SDR condition and generative factorization, establishes finite-sample convergence rates sharper than existing results, shows belted architecture has asymptotically vanishing parameter count. Empirically: achieves superior distributional prediction and SDR recovery with fewer trainable parameters in simulations and real-world applications.

Conclusion: Belted Engression provides a unified, parameter-efficient framework for generative distributional regression that successfully bridges sufficient dimension reduction with conditional generation, offering both theoretical guarantees and practical performance improvements.

Abstract: Modern conditional generative models face significant challenges when learning complex covariate dependencies. While sufficient dimension reduction (SDR) provides a principled approach to compress these dependencies, traditional SDR frameworks were not formulated for conditional generation. To bridge this gap, we propose Belted Engression, a unified and architecturally parameter-efficient framework for generative distributional regression. Our approach establishes an end-to-end compress-then-generate paradigm driven by sufficient representation learning, embedding a structural bottleneck into the generative architecture. Theoretically, we prove that the standard SDR condition is equivalent to a law-preserving generative factorization, which is achieved at the global optimum of the population Belted Engression objective. Furthermore, by uncovering a localized Bernstein-type control for the energy-score loss, we establish finite-sample convergence rates that are sharper than those of existing results. We also prove that this belted architecture is strictly smaller, operating with an asymptotically vanishing parameter count relative to the unstructured baseline. Extensive simulations and real-world applications demonstrate that Belted Engression achieves superior distributional prediction and SDR recovery with fewer trainable parameters.

</details>


### [267] [Iterative Atom Refinement: A Monotonicity Principle for Dictionary Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23812)
*Alexander Christie,Miguel Moscoso,Alexei Novikov,George Papanicolaou,Chrysoula Tsogka*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces Iterative Atom Refinement (IAR), a simple algorithm for recovering individual dictionary atoms from sparse observations, with rigorous convergence theory showing it can identify generating atoms in just three refinement steps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dictionary learning aims to recover unknown dictionaries from observations with sparse coefficient vectors. The challenge is developing efficient algorithms that can reliably recover individual dictionary atoms from such observations.

Method: Introduces the Iterative Atom Refinement (IAR) algorithm: starts from random direction, repeatedly selects observations most strongly correlated with current iterate, and updates direction by averaging selected data.

Result: Develops rigorous convergence theory using high-dimensional probabilistic estimates and novel monotonicity principle for atom-selection probabilities. Shows that small initial advantage of one atom is amplified until that atom is isolated. Under model assumptions, IAR identifies generating atom after only three refinement steps.

Conclusion: IAR provides a simple yet effective approach to dictionary atom recovery with strong theoretical guarantees. Numerical experiments support the theory and show the dynamics accurately capture dictionary refinement behavior observed in practice.

Abstract: Dictionary learning seeks to recover an unknown dictionary $A$ from observations ${\bf y}_i = A{\bf x}_i$ with sparse coefficient vectors ${\bf x}_i$. We introduce the \emph{Iterative Atom Refinement} (IAR) algorithm, a simple procedure for recovering individual dictionary atoms. Starting from a random direction, IAR repeatedly selects the observations most strongly correlated with the current iterate and updates the direction by averaging the selected data. Our main contribution is a rigorous convergence theory of IAR. Using high-dimensional probabilistic estimates and a novel monotonicity principle for atom-selection probabilities, we show that a small initial advantage of one atom is amplified until that atom is isolated. Under our model assumptions, IAR identifies a generating atom after only three refinement steps. Numerical experiments support the theory and show that the resulting dynamics accurately capture the behavior observed in dictionary refinement.

</details>


### [268] [Real-time Generalizable Heart Valve Mechanics for Clinical Disease Assessment via a Physics-Conditioned Neural Operator](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23826)
*Shawn Koohy,Wensi Wu,Matthew A Jolley,Paris Perdikaris*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PCNO is a transformer-based neural operator that achieves 15,260x speedup over finite element simulations for predicting mitral valve mechanics, enabling rapid clinical assessment of valve pathologies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mitral regurgitation affects over 2% globally and causes significant mortality, but few patients with severe disease get corrective surgery. Traditional finite element simulations are too slow for clinical use and parameter exploration.

Method: Physics-Conditioned Neural Operator (PCNO) - a transformer-based surrogate model that predicts leaflet displacement, strain, and stress fields. It's conditioned on systolic blood pressure and tissue properties, trained on functional, regurgitated, and pathological valves including various pathologies.

Result: Achieves up to 15,260x speedup over fine mesh finite element simulations with comparable accuracy. Can identify pathology class and resolves diagnostic metrics within 3.5% error even under out-of-distribution extrapolation.

Conclusion: PCNO enables rapid assessment of valve mechanics for earlier, more precise clinical intervention by overcoming the speed limitations of traditional simulations while maintaining accuracy for pathological cases.

Abstract: Mitral regurgitation is the most common heart valve disorder worldwide, affecting over 2% of the global population, rising to at least 10% in adults over 75, and causing approximately 15% of valvular heart disease-related deaths. Yet only a minority of patients with severe disease undergo corrective surgery. Rapid assessment of valve mechanics could enable earlier, more precise intervention, but traditional finite element simulations remain too slow for clinical timelines and parameter sweeps. We introduce the Physics-Conditioned Neural Operator (PCNO), a transformer-based surrogate that predicts leaflet displacement, strain, and stress fields across mitral and tricuspid geometries, conditioned on systolic blood pressure and tissue properties. Trained on functional, regurgitated, and pathological valves, including tethering, P2 prolapse, and annular dilation, PCNO achieves up to a 15,260x speedup over fine mesh finite element simulations with comparable accuracy, identifies pathology class, and resolves diagnostic metrics within 3.5% error under out-of-distribution extrapolation.

</details>


### [269] [GLR-MM: Graph-Based Global-Local Reconstruction for Robust Multimodal Chest X-ray and EHR Representation Learning under Missing Modalities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23876)
*Surbhi Sharma,Nikhil Manali,Devesh Maheshwari*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GLR-MM is a graph-based framework that uses both within-patient and inter-patient information to handle missing multimodal data in early ICU mortality prediction, outperforming existing methods when data is severely incomplete.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clinical multimodal models often need to make predictions before all CXR and EHR data are available. Existing methods don't effectively combine within-patient evidence with clinically similar inter-patient information to handle missing data.

Method: Proposes GLR-MM: Graph-Based Global-Local Reconstruction framework that maps 5 CXR-EHR modalities to shared space, reconstructs missing embeddings through local cross-modal and global graph-attention branches, adaptively fuses estimates, and optimizes class-balanced prediction, reconstruction, and contrastive objectives.

Result: On 9,620 MIMIC-derived ICU stays with 10%, 30%, and 50% random modality missingness: MUSE performs better under mild/moderate missingness, but GLR-MM achieves higher AUROC (+0.0088) and AUPRC (+0.0249) at 50% missingness.

Conclusion: Graph-guided reconstruction is most beneficial when clinical multimodal inputs are severely incomplete, demonstrating the value of leveraging both local and global (inter-patient) evidence for handling missing data in ICU mortality prediction.

Abstract: Clinical multimodal models must often predict before all chest X-ray (CXR) and electronic health record (EHR) inputs are available. Existing approaches align observed representations, model missingness, or reconstruct across modalities, but do not jointly exploit within-patient and clinically similar inter-patient evidence. We propose GLR-MM, a Graph-Based Global-Local Reconstruction framework for early ICU mortality prediction. It maps five CXR-EHR modalities to a shared space, reconstructs missing embeddings through complementary local cross-modal and global graph-attention branches, adaptively fuses their estimates, and optimizes class-balanced prediction, reconstruction, and contrastive objectives. On 9,620 MIMIC-derived ICU stays, we evaluate 10%, 30%, and 50% random modality missingness with shared deterministic masks. MUSE performs better under mild and moderate missingness, whereas GLR-MM achieves higher AUROC and AUPRC at 50% by 0.0088 and 0.0249, respectively. These results indicate that graph-guided reconstruction is most useful when inputs are severely incomplete.

</details>


### [270] [Actionable Insights from Observational Data: The Case of Advanced Classes in K-12 Education](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23836)
*Nabit Bajwa,Seth B. Hunter,Sanmay Das*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Advanced English courses have modest positive effects on achievement, but enrollment patterns show mismatches - students who would benefit most (middle achievers, Black students, lower SES) are less likely to enroll, revealing equity issues in course selection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understanding causal effects of advanced classes in K-12 education is challenging due to selection bias - students choose whether to enroll, so it's difficult to separate effects of coursework from underlying student characteristics like ability and motivation.

Method: Leveraged a novel observational dataset from a US public school system with student course enrollment decisions, academic histories, demographics, and outcomes around a district-wide policy change introducing optional open-enrollment advanced middle-school courses. Used careful data analysis to address identification challenges caused by non-random enrollment.

Result: Advanced English courses have net positive but modest effects on student achievement. However, benefits are unevenly distributed: students with largest predicted gains (middle achievers) are less likely to enroll, and Black students and those with lower socio-economic status show significantly lower enrollment rates despite potential benefits.

Conclusion: Careful analysis of observational data can identify actionable insights, particularly mismatches between predicted benefits and actual enrollment patterns, highlighting equity issues in advanced course selection and opportunities for targeted outreach to underrepresented groups.

Abstract: A fundamentally challenging question in K-12 education is about the effects of taking more advanced or challenging classes. It is particularly complex because students (and/or their parents) choose whether to enroll in these classes, making causal analysis challenging. In this paper, we begin to tackle this question by taking advantage of a novel dataset from a public school system in the US. This dataset records students' course enrollment decisions, prior academic histories, demographics, and subsequent outcomes around the time of a district-wide change that introduced optional open-enrollment advanced middle-school courses in subject areas. This is a rich observational dataset, but enrollment in advanced classes is driven by student characteristics and choices rather than random assignment. This creates a core identification challenge: the same factors that influence enrollment in advanced courses are also predictive of academic outcomes. As a result, simple comparisons between enrolled and non-enrolled students are confounded, and naive estimates may reflect underlying differences in student ability, motivation, or support rather than the impact of coursework itself. Our analysis shows that enrolling in advanced English courses has a net positive but modest effect on student achievement outcomes. However, these benefits are unevenly distributed: some students with relatively large predicted gains ("middle achievers" in prior years) are less likely to enroll than others. Some other groups (e.g. Black students and those with lower socio-economic status) also demonstrate significantly lower propensity to enroll. This gap between predicted benefit and observed enrollment illustrates how careful data analysis can extract actionable insights from large observational datasets, including identifying students who appear well-positioned to benefit but do not select into advanced options.

</details>


### [271] [Circuit-Diff: Factual Edit-based Intervention Method for Localizing Knowledge in Attribution Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23892)
*Edward G. Friedman,Xiangchen Song*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Circuit-Diff is a method that uses low-rank factual edits on neural networks to identify knowledge-related features in attribution graphs, making Cross-Layer Transcoders (CLTs) more interpretable for circuit discovery.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While CLTs generate attribution graphs for circuit discovery, the nodes in these graphs are unlabeled features, requiring manual interpretation through pruning and hand-labeling. This makes CLTs difficult to use effectively for understanding neural network circuits.

Method: Circuit-Diff intervenes on the neural network model with low-rank factual edits and observes which features in the CLT's attribution graph change under these edits. The features whose roles change are flagged as related to the edited knowledge. The approach includes multi-prompt aggregation and rule-based supernode labeling tools.

Result: On examined edits, flagged nodes include not just object token detectors but also features for the history, geography, and associations surrounding old and new objects. The method shows reliability of frozen CLTs after factual edits, causal testing by patching on up to 24 CounterFact edits, and includes a case study demonstrating effectiveness.

Conclusion: Circuit-Diff provides a practical method to automatically label and identify knowledge-related features in CLT attribution graphs, making circuit discovery more accessible and interpretable through factual interventions and open-source tooling.

Abstract: Mechanistic interpretability defines features as the fundamental units of a neural network and circuits as the weighted subgraphs that carry out its computation. Because individual neurons are polysemantic, Cross-Layer Transcoders (CLTs) were introduced as a way to approximate a model's circuits by generating an attribution graph. The nodes of that graph, however, are unlabeled features: reading a graph means pruning it and then working out by hand what each surviving node means. To make CLTs easier to use for circuit discovery, we introduce Circuit-Diff, which intervenes on the model itself with a low-rank factual edit and takes the features whose role in the attribution graph changes under that edit as related to the edited knowledge. On the edits we examine, the flagged nodes are not only detectors of the object token: read off the CLT's released feature dashboards, they include features for the history, geography and associations surrounding the old and new objects. We formalize the method, measure how reliable a frozen CLT remains after a factual edit, test the selected nodes causally by patching them on up to 24 CounterFact edits, give a case study, and release an open-source implementation built on the circuit-tracer package, together with two further tools (multi-prompt aggregation and rule-based supernode labeling).

</details>


### [272] [From Regional to Global: Transfer Learning for Atmospheric Transport Emulators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23838)
*Jeff Clark,Elena Fillola,Nawid Keshtmand,Raul Santos-Rodriguez,Matthew Rigby*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper evaluates spatial transferability of atmospheric transport emulators across four world regions to enable efficient global greenhouse gas emissions estimation using satellite data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional physics-driven Lagrangian Particle Dispersion Models (LPDMs) are too computationally expensive and don't scale well to modern satellites' high-resolution data for global greenhouse gas emissions estimation. While previous work developed a fast emulator for South America, expanding to global coverage requires understanding spatial transferability across heterogeneous regions.

Method: The paper evaluates spatial transferability capabilities across four world regions (South America, East Asia, South Asia, North Africa) using both region-specific and multi-region models, and conducts leave-one-region-out experiments. It characterizes regional differences by analyzing input variable and output footprint distributions.

Result: Not explicitly stated in the abstract, but the evaluation provides insights into cross-region generalization and transfer learning capabilities, comparing regional versus multi-regional modeling approaches for atmospheric transport emulation.

Conclusion: This work builds intuition for cross-region generalization and transfer learning, aiding progress toward efficient global greenhouse gas emissions estimates by understanding how to scale regional atmospheric transport emulators to global coverage while maintaining computational efficiency.

Abstract: Greenhouse gas emissions estimates can be derived using inverse methods by combining atmospheric concentration observations with chemical transport models. The latter traditionally use physics-driven simulators such as Lagrangian Particle Dispersion Models (LPDMs), which are expensive to run and do not scale well to modern satellites' high resolution data. Previously we developed a performant atmospheric transport emulator that approximates LPDM outputs ("footprints") over South America ~1,000X faster than the UK Met Office's LPDM. Expanding towards global emulation is not straightforward, as atmospheric transport is regionally heterogeneous. This paper evaluates spatial transferability capabilities of models across four world regions: South America, East Asia, South Asia, North Africa using both region-specific and multi-region models, and leave-one-region-out experiments. Regional differences are characterised in the context of input variable and output footprint distributions. This work builds intuition in cross-region generalisation and transfer learning, aiding regional performance towards efficient global emissions estimates.

</details>


### [273] [Misaligned Clinical Risk Classification and Cost Asymmetry in Open-Weight Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23999)
*Star S. D. Liu,Xiyu Ding,Robert B. Barrett,Alberto Santamaria-Pang,Nic Dobbins,Harold P. Lehmann*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LLMs encode patient risk and cost information but fail to reliably integrate them into cost-correct clinical decisions, with only larger models showing representational tracking of output changes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how LLMs integrate patient risk assessment with clinical cost tradeoffs, since this integration remains poorly understood despite LLMs' potential clinical applications.

Method: Used four open-weight LLMs (Qwen-2.5-7B/32B and Llama-3.1-8B/70B) with a public diabetes dataset. Varied 11 FN to FP cost ratios across three phrasings to examine internal representations and behavioral outputs. Analyzed risk recovery, cost direction recovery, and representational shifts.

Result: Patient risk was linearly recoverable (AUC ≈ 0.83), and cost direction was recoverable in every model. However, representational shifts only tracked output changes in larger models. Responses to cost magnitude were direction-agnostic. Only 2 of 12 model-phrasings showed both opposing responses to FN vs FP costs and cost-correct ordering. Cost direction representations didn't invert as expected under mirror-symmetric encoding.

Conclusion: LLMs encode risk and cost information but don't reliably integrate them into cost-correct decisions. Clinical evaluations should include tradeoff tests, phrasing sensitivity analysis, and default operating point assessments alongside predictive performance.

Abstract: How large language models (LLMs) integrate patient risk with clinical cost tradeoffs remains poorly understood. We investigated how four open-weight LLMs (Qwen-2.5-7B/32B and Llama-3.1-8B/70B) internally represent cost tradeoffs, how these representations relate to clinical predictions, and whether decisions shift as predicted by the specified cost direction and magnitude. Using a public diabetes dataset, we varied 11 false-negative (FN) to false-positive (FP) cost ratios across three phrasings and examined representations and behavioral outputs. Patient risk was linearly recoverable on par with conventional classifiers (AUC $\approx 0.83$), and cost direction was recoverable in every model. However, representational shifts in cost direction tracked output changes only in the two larger models, and responses to cost magnitude were predominantly direction-agnostic. Only 2 of 12 model-phrasings showed both opposing responses to increasing FN versus FP costs and cost-correct ordering.
