Representationally, a direction fitted on one cost side did not invert when transferred to the other, as expected under mirror-symmetric encoding. These findings suggest that LLMs encode risk and cost information but do not reliably integrate them into cost-correct decisions. Clinical evaluations should therefore include tradeoff tests, phrasing sensitivity, and default operating points alongside predictive performance.

</details>


### [274] [Adaptive Determinantal Client Scheduling in Federated Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23843)
*Wen Xu,Ben Liang,Gary Boudreau,Hamza Sokun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ADCS introduces determinantal point processes for diverse client scheduling in federated learning, balancing quality and diversity to improve performance for worst-off clients.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current federated learning client scheduling focuses on quality metrics (convergence speed, average performance) but neglects client diversity, which is crucial for handling data/system heterogeneity and improving worst-case client performance.

Method: Uses determinantal point processes (DPPs) with gradient-based kernel matrices to model client diversity, develops Adaptive Determinantal Client Scheduling (ADCS) with fast MAP inference, and provides theoretical analysis of gradient approximation error and convergence for non-convex losses.

Result: ADCS outperforms state-of-the-art client scheduling algorithms (both quality-based and diversity-based) in comparative numerical experiments, showing better overall performance.

Conclusion: Diversity-aware client scheduling using DPPs effectively addresses federated learning heterogeneity challenges, balancing quality and diversity to enhance performance, particularly for worst-off clients.

Abstract: Scheduling clients for model training is critical in federated learning due to both data and system heterogeneity. Most previous works focus on the quality of the scheduled clients to achieve faster convergence, shorter wall-clock convergence time, or better average model performance. They rarely consider the diversity of clients, which is important to counter heterogeneity and improve performance for the worst-off clients. In this work, we advocate the use of determinantal point processes (DPPs) to model and enhance the diversity in client scheduling. We first design the kernel matrices of DPPs using gradient information and quality scores, which inherently enables a flexible quality-diversity trade-off. Applying fast MAP inference over DPPs, we propose Adaptive Determinantal Client Scheduling (ADCS) in FL. We further quantify the gradient approximation error of ADCS and develop convergence analysis for general biased client selection in FL with non-convex loss functions. We conduct comparative numerical experiments showing that ADCS outperforms state-of-the-art client scheduling algorithms, including both quality-based and diversity-based ones.

</details>


### [275] [FlashBoB: I/O-Efficient Exact Backward-over-Backward for Softmax Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24089)
*Anthony Givans,Michael Crawshaw,Mingrui Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FlashBoB is an I/O-efficient algorithm for backward-over-backward (BoB) in softmax attention that enables exact second-order differentiation for long-context workloads without materializing large intermediate tensors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Softmax attention is a major bottleneck for long-context workloads. While FlashAttention optimizes forward and first backward passes, it doesn't support backward-over-backward (BoB), which is essential for second-order optimization, meta-learning, and other applications. Existing BoB implementations either materialize large intermediate tensors or exhaust GPU memory at long sequence lengths.

Method: FlashBoB uses a hierarchical affine structure in softmax double backward, where two row-wise scalars determine all outputs through affine transformations. This enables a two-pass schedule with bounded on-chip SRAM usage and minimal off-chip HBM traffic. The algorithm keeps computation within on-chip tiles and avoids all N×N intermediate tensors.

Result: FlashBoB achieves Θ(N²d²/M) HBM traffic and matches the inherited large-cache lower bound for exact forward attention. It scales exact attention BoB to N=262K on a single A100 80GB GPU, where prior PyTorch baselines fail at N=16K, and is up to 6.3× faster than FlashBack.

Conclusion: FlashBoB makes exact second-order attention practical at long-context sequence lengths where prior implementations cannot run efficiently, enabling applications like second-order optimization, meta-learning, and gradient-based memory for transformer models.

Abstract: Transformer models built on the attention mechanism have become a central building block in modern deep learning, yet softmax attention remains a major bottleneck for long-context workloads. While FlashAttention makes the forward and first backward passes I/O-efficient, it does not support backward-over-backward (BoB), which enables exact differentiation through the backward pass for applications such as second-order optimization, test-time training, gradient-based memory, and meta-learning. Existing BoB implementations either materialize large intermediate tensors or exhaust GPU memory at long sequence lengths. We present FlashBoB, an exact, I/O-efficient algorithm for BoB in softmax attention that keeps computation within on-chip tiles and avoids all $N \times N$ intermediate tensors, where $N$ is the sequence length. The key insight is a hierarchical affine structure in the softmax double backward: two row-wise scalars determine all outputs through affine transformations. This yields a two-pass schedule with bounded on-chip static random-access memory (SRAM) usage and minimal off-chip high-bandwidth memory (HBM) traffic. FlashBoB achieves $Θ(N^2 d^2/M)$ HBM traffic ($d$ is the head dimension and $M$ is the memory size) and, within the standard FlashAttention-style score-recomputation model, matches the inherited large-cache lower bound for exact forward attention. Empirically, it scales exact attention BoB to $N=262\text{K}$ on a single A100 80GB GPU, where prior PyTorch exact baselines fail by $N=16\text{K}$, and is up to $6.3\times$ faster than FlashBack. These results make exact second-order attention practical at long-context sequence lengths where prior implementations cannot run efficiently.

</details>


### [276] [PROSE: A Theory of Optimal Stopping with Perishable Evidence for Peer Selection in Intermittently Connected Decentralised Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23845)
*Christos Anagnostopoulos*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Decentralized federated learning requires optimal peer selection using perishable evidence, solved via Markov optimal stopping with reservation values, with theoretical guarantees and instantiation as PROSE policy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Decentralized federated learning eliminates central servers but faces challenges with transient peer availability in mobile systems. Evaluating peers consumes contact time, and evidence about peers decays due to link expiration and model drift, creating a perishable-evidence problem for peer selection.

Method: Develops self-contained optimal stopping theory for peer selection: formalizes decision as finite-horizon Markov optimal-stopping with costly information acquisition and outside options. Uses reservation value (Snell-envelope structure), provides stage-uniform drift-aware concentration bounds, mobility-aware stopping rules, closed-form solutions for Poisson arrivals, and myopic-optimality theorems for volatile regimes.

Result: Proves optimal policy existence with reservation values, provides concentration bounds and certification rules, characterizes comparative statics showing link hazard effects, derives closed-form waiting values for Poisson contacts, establishes myopic optimality conditions, and instantiates as PROSE - a lightweight local policy recovering classical limits.

Conclusion: Developed comprehensive optimal stopping theory for decentralized federated learning peer selection with perishable evidence, providing analytical framework with theoretical guarantees and practical PROSE implementation that addresses mobility challenges while recovering classical sequential decision limits.

Abstract: Decentralised federated learning removes the aggregation server but makes collaboration dependent on transient peer availability. In mobile and intermittently connected systems, evaluating a promising peer consumes contact time and may cause the exchange opportunity itself to vanish, so that the evidence a learner gathers about a peer is perishable: it decays because links expire and because peer models drift while old measurements age. This paper develops a self-contained theory of optimal stopping for the resulting peer-selection problem. We formalise a receiver's within-contact decision as a finite-horizon Markov optimal-stopping problem with costly information acquisition and a future-arrival outside option, and prove that it admits an optimal policy characterised by a reservation value (Snell-envelope structure). Around this formulation we prove: (i) stage-uniform, drift-aware concentration and a maximin certification rule that is correct with high probability together with a finite-sample identification bound; (ii) a mobility-aware value of-information stopping rule and comparative statics showing that higher link hazard lowers the value of continued probing and enlarges the stopping region; (iii) a closed-form value of waiting under marked-Poisson contact arrivals, together with a search-theoretic reservation value whose comparative statics we characterise; and (iv) a myopic-optimality theorem establishing that, in sufficiently volatile (monotone) mobility regimes, the one-step confidence-safe rule is a sound surrogate for the optimal policy and never stops prematurely. We instantiate the theory as PROSE (Perishable-evidence Reservation-value Optimal Stopping for Exchange), a lightweight, fully local policy, and delineate the static contact and drift-free limits in which classical sequential decision problems are recovered. The development is entirely analytical.

</details>


### [277] [Reinforcement Learning under State and Outcome Uncertainty: A Foundational Distributional Perspective](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24103)
*Larry Preuett,Qiuyi Zhang,Muhammad Aurangzeb Ahmad*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Extends Distributional RL to partially observable domains (POMDPs), introducing new distributional Bellman operators and psi-vectors for tracking return distributions of conditional plans.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world planning tasks involve uncertainty about environment states and variability in policy outcomes. The paper aims to develop safer algorithms for partially observable settings by addressing both forms of uncertainty simultaneously.

Method: Extends Distributional RL to POMDPs by introducing new distributional Bellman operators for partial observability. Proposes finite representation of return distributions via psi-vectors (generalizing classical alpha-vectors). Develops Distributional Point-Based Value Iteration (DPBVI) integrating psi-vectors into standard point-based backup procedures.

Result: Proves convergence of distributional Bellman operators under supremum p-Wasserstein metric. Provides source code for further research. DPBVI enables tracking of return distributions for each conditional plan, laying foundation for risk-sensitive control.

Conclusion: The work bridges Distributional RL and POMDP planning, providing a framework for future risk-sensitive control in domains with rare, high-impact events that require careful management under partial observability.

Abstract: In many real-world planning tasks, agents must tackle uncertainty about the environment's state and variability in the outcomes of any chosen policy. We address both forms of uncertainty as a first step toward safer algorithms in partially observable settings. Specifically, we extend Distributional Reinforcement Learning (DistRL)-which models the entire return distribution for fully observable domains-to Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs), allowing an agent to learn the distribution of returns for each conditional plan. Concretely, we introduce new distributional Bellman operators for partial observability and prove their convergence under the supremum p-Wasserstein metric. We also propose a finite representation of these return distributions via psi-vectors, generalizing the classical alpha-vectors in POMDP solvers. Building on this, we develop Distributional Point-Based Value Iteration (DPBVI), which integrates psi-vectors into a standard point-based backup procedure-bridging DistRL and POMDP planning. By tracking return distributions, DPBVI lays the foundation for future risk-sensitive control in domains where rare, high-impact events must be carefully managed. We provide source code to foster further research in robust decision-making under partial observability.

</details>


### [278] [Opinion Leader Dynamics: How Sparse Attention Shapes Token Clustering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24202)
*Jingkun Liu,Yue Song*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Sparse attention creates token clusters that converge internally while maintaining separation, explained through opinion leader dynamics as Wasserstein gradient flows with exponential convergence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sparse attention reduces quadratic cost while maintaining performance, but theoretical understanding of how restricted token interactions shape representation evolution remains limited.

Method: Model tokens as particles on unit sphere using opinion leader dynamics framework: explicit model with fixed representatives creating attraction potentials, and implicit model with disconnected interaction groups evolving toward consensus directions. Both formulated as reverse Wasserstein gradient flows.

Result: Established exponential convergence under suitable conditions; empirical analysis shows sparse-attention LLMs (Kimi-K3, MiniMax-M3, DeepSeek-V4-Flash) exhibit clearer cluster separation and higher clustering scores than dense-attention GLM-4.7-Flash across four benchmarks.

Conclusion: Sparse attention supports alignment within token groups while preserving separation between them through distinct group-level attractors, providing dynamical account of how restricted interactions shape representation evolution in LLMs.

Abstract: Sparse attention reduces the quadratic cost of global self-attention while retaining strong empirical performance, but how its restricted interactions shape the evolution of token representations remains theoretically underexplored. Modeling tokens as particles on the unit sphere, we introduce opinion leader dynamics, a framework that identifies two mechanisms through which token groups converge internally while maintaining distinct limiting directions. In the explicit model, fixed representatives induce a potential that attracts tokens toward distinct local maxima. In the implicit model, disconnected interaction groups evolve toward separate consensus directions. We formulate both models as reverse Wasserstein gradient flows and establish exponential convergence under suitable conditions. We further connect these theoretical predictions to token evolution in frontier sparse-attention LLMs that motivate our framework. Across four benchmarks, Kimi-K3, MiniMax-M3, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash consistently exhibit clearer cluster separation and higher clustering scores than the dense-attention model GLM-4.7-Flash in projected token representations. These observations support the relevance of the predicted multiple-group structure to trained frontier LLMs, while finite-particle simulations illustrate the theoretical convergence behavior. Together, our results connect restricted token interactions to distinct group-level attractors, providing a dynamical account of how sparse attention can support alignment within groups while preserving separation between them.

</details>


### [279] [Hessian Rank Constraint for Learning Structure of Nonlinear Latent Variable Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24241)
*Zijian Li,Ruichu Cai,Feng Xie,Xinshuai Dong,Haoyue Dai,Yuewen Sun,Yujia Zheng,Guangyi Chen,Yingyao Hu,Kun Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a cross-Hessian Rank Constraint (HRC) method for nonlinear latent causal discovery that generalizes traditional Tetrad constraints to handle general nonlinear mixing functions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods for uncovering latent variables and their causal relations often rely on restrictive assumptions like linear relations or invertible mixing functions, limiting their applicability to real-world nonlinear scenarios.

Method: Proposes the cross-Hessian Rank Constraint (HRC) which leverages rank properties of the cross-Hessian of observed-data log-density. When two groups of observed variables are d-separated by lower-dimensional latent variables, the rank equals the latent dimension under mild affine derivative assumptions.

Result: HRC reduces to Tetrad constraints in linear Gaussian cases and provides a rank-based tool for nonlinear latent discovery. The method was instantiated for one-factor measurement settings to locate latent variables and recover causal structure up to Markov equivalence, with experimental validation on synthetic and real datasets.

Conclusion: HRC offers a promising approach for nonlinear latent causal discovery that works under more general conditions than existing methods, bridging linear and nonlinear cases while providing practical tools for structure recovery.

Abstract: Uncovering latent variables and their causal relations from observed data is a fundamental yet challenging problem. Existing methods often rely on restrictive assumptions, such as linear relations or invertible mixing functions. To better address this problem under general nonlinear mixing procedures, we propose a condition called the cross-Hessian Rank Constraint (HRC), which serves as a primitive rank-based tool for nonlinear latent causal discovery. In particular, we show that a rank-based property arises from the cross-Hessian of the observed-data log-density in the nonlinear case, revealing information about the latent variables, and reduces to the Tetrad constraints in the linear Gaussian case. More specifically, when two groups of observed variables are d-separated by a set of lower-dimensional latent variables, the rank of this cross-Hessian is equal to the dimension of the latent variables, under a mild affine derivative assumption on the conditional log-density derivatives. This assumption can be naturally satisfied when the noise level is low or the relevant nonlinearity is moderate. As a downstream application, we instantiate HRC in the pure one-factor measurement setting for locating latent variables and recovering their causal structure up to Markov equivalence. Experimental results on synthetic and real-world datasets support the theoretical claims.

</details>


### [280] [Collaborative Streaming Anomaly Detection with Interactive Explanations and Ensemble Consensus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23883)
*Diogo Risca,Afonso Lourenço,Ricardo Martins,Goreti Marreiros*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A collaborative streaming anomaly detection system that integrates human analysts into the detection loop through ensemble methods and interpretable surrogate models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The need for robust anomaly detection in high-speed data streams that incorporates human expertise for better decision-making and interpretability.

Method: Combines heterogeneous detectors with normalization-based weighted consensus, uses artifact-aware rules to stabilize anomaly scoring, creates interpretable surrogate models, and enables human analysts to intervene by adjusting consensus behavior and refining rules.

Result: Evaluation on industrial stream with 260,000 events and 3 anomalous episodes shows robust detection and actionable human-AI interaction.

Conclusion: The system successfully integrates human analysts into anomaly detection workflows, creating a collaborative human-AI approach that improves detection robustness and interpretability.

Abstract: We present a collaborative streaming anomaly detection system for high-speed data streams that explicitly integrates human analysts into the decision loop. The system combines heterogeneous detectors and aggregates their outputs through a normalization-based weighted consensus, complemented by artifact-aware rules to stabilize anomaly scoring under deployment. To improve interpretability, it derives surrogate models that approximate the ensemble consensus and expose human-readable sensor conditions associated with anomalous behavior. Analysts can actively intervene by reviewing anomaly episodes, adjusting consensus behavior, and refining surrogate rules used for anomaly prediction, producing a human-adjusted ensemble. We evaluate the approach on an industrial stream with 260\,000 events and 3 anomalous episodes, showing robust detection and actionable human-AI interaction.

</details>


### [281] [MemCalib: Benchmarking and Optimizing Memory Use in LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24259)
*Ruike Cao,Fanyu Zhao,Fugen Yao,Liang Dong,Jian Xu,Guanjun Jiang,Yifei Zhao,Han Zhang,Li Xiao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MemCalib-RL: A novel bidirectional credit assignment algorithm that improves LLMs' ability to appropriately calibrate memory influence in responses, addressing systematic over-use and under-use problems that current models exhibit.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLMs struggle with appropriate memory calibration - they frequently over-use or under-use memory rather than matching each proposition's influence to its target level, leading to biased, low-quality responses. This critical capability for agent memory systems has been largely overlooked.

Method: The authors introduce MemCalib benchmark for evaluating memory use and propose MemCalib-RL, an ordered bidirectional counterfactual credit-assignment algorithm that separates over- and under-use signals and localizes their credit to response tokens through exact atom ablation.

Result: Results on Qwen3-8B, Ministral-3-8B-Instruct, and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B show MemCalib-RL achieves best overall performance while better balancing over-use and under-use, with gains generalizing beyond MemCalib. Common post-training algorithms (GRPO, on-policy self-distillation) show directional skew, improving in one direction while deteriorating in the other.

Conclusion: Memory calibration is a critical but overlooked capability in LLMs. The proposed MemCalib-RL algorithm effectively addresses systematic memory calibration problems by separating and localizing over-use and under-use signals, leading to more balanced and appropriate memory influence in responses across different model scales and families.

Abstract: The effectiveness of agent memory ultimately depends on whether the underlying LLM gives each memory in context an appropriate degree of influence over its response. Yet this capability has remained largely overlooked. To assess this capability, we introduce MemCalib, a benchmark grounded in realistic memory-system scenarios for evaluating memory use and advancing optimization algorithms. Results on the MemCalib test set reveal that frontier open- and closed-source models struggle to use memory appropriately. They frequently over-use or under-use memory rather than matching each proposition's actual use to its target level, leading to biased, low-quality responses. Experiments with common post-training algorithms, including group relative policy optimization and on-policy self-distillation, further reveal a clear directional skew: trained models improve in one direction while deteriorating in the other. We therefore propose MemCalib-RL, an ordered bidirectional counterfactual credit-assignment algorithm that separates over- and under-use signals and localizes their credit to response tokens through exact atom ablation. Results across model families and scales (Qwen3-8B, Ministral-3-8B-Instruct, and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B) show that MemCalib-RL achieves the best overall performance while better balancing over-use and under-use, with gains generalizing beyond MemCalib in external benchmark evaluation. Further experiments support its design choices and robustness and provide insight into its training dynamics.

</details>


### [282] [TTSE: A Two-Track Online Self-Evolution Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24289)
*Ruimin Pei,Yongkang Wu,Shangyi Zheng,Yaqing Zhang,Deyang Li,Jianjun Tao,Xinyu Zhang,Xiang Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TTSE is a dual-track self-evolution framework for LLM agents that separates environmental facts (FACT) from task implementation procedures (TIP) to enable continuous online adaptation and long-term autonomy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM agent approaches treat environmental knowledge as fixed external input rather than part of ongoing evolution, and reinforcement learning methods typically adapt only to fixed task distributions or single environments, limiting long-term autonomy in continuously interactive environments.

Method: Proposes TTSE (Two-Track Self-Evolution) framework with dual-track online evolution: FACT (environmental facts verified through interaction evidence) and TIP (task-conditioned implementation procedures). Uses decision-theoretic analysis to decompose agent risk into environment-representation regret and conditional-execution regret, bounding downstream risk.

Result: TTSE shows advantages on GDPevo (ablation experiments), superior task adaptation on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld benchmarks, compatibility with existing skill self-evolution methods, improved aggregate scores on SOPBench's five major domains when combined with Bayesian-Agent, and stable outperformance on real end-to-end PinchBench task benchmark across three independent runs.

Conclusion: TTSE provides an effective dual-track self-evolution framework for LLM agents that enables continuous adaptation in interactive environments, addressing limitations of current approaches by separating environmental knowledge evolution from task implementation procedures.

Abstract: As Large Language Model (LLM) agents are applied in continuously interactive environments, driving the evolution of their own capabilities becomes a core problem for achieving long-term autonomy. Currently, environmental knowledge is typically treated as an external fixed input rather than as part of the agent's ongoing evolution. Reinforcement learning methods usually optimize policies through environmental interaction but tend to adapt only to fixed task distributions or single environments. This paper proposes TTSE (Two-Track Self-Evolution), a dual-track online self-evolution framework that separates evolving knowledge into FACT (environmental facts, whose reliability is continuously verified through interaction evidence) and TIP (task-conditioned implementation procedures). From a decision-theoretic perspective, we decompose the agent's excess risk into environment-representation regret and conditional-execution regret, characterize the conditions under which environment-conditioned policies strictly outperform condition-agnostic policies, and bound the downstream risk in terms of FACT identification error and cross-condition mismatch cost. In practice, TTSE's ablation experiments on GDPevo validate the advantage of dual-track evolution. On the classic agent task benchmarks ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, TTSE further demonstrates superior task adaptation. Moreover, TTSE is broadly compatible with existing skill self-evolution methods; combined with the Bayesian-Agent algorithm, a single-track ablation validates the dual-track advantage, substantially improving the aggregate score across the five major domains of SOPBench over three independent repetitions. Finally, on the real end-to-end task benchmark PinchBench, TTSE is integrated into a general agent framework via retrieval-based injection and stably outperforms the baseline across three independent runs.

</details>


### [283] [GDN Tree-Scan: Served Tree Verification for Recurrent-Hybrid Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23900)
*Zhiyuan Ma*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Tree speculative decoding for recurrent-hybrid language models requires careful handling of recurrent states; GDN Tree-Scan achieves 27% throughput gain by efficiently verifying multiple candidates while maintaining recurrent state consistency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard tree speculative decoding assumes attention-only transformers, but recurrent-hybrid models break this assumption because they require carrying recurrent states along candidate paths. Without proper recurrent state management, verifiers can use correct attention masks while still conditioning on impossible recurrent histories, leading to incorrect verification.

Method: GDN Tree-Scan system integrates into vLLM with: 1) FlashAttention-2 tree-bias attention, 2) branch-local GDN scan/replay for recurrent state management, 3) device-side multidraft commitment, and 4) accepted-chain-only state publication. It specifically handles Gated-DeltaNet hybrid language models.

Result: On Qwen3.6-27B-FP8 checkpoint with temperature 0.6, a six-node root-branch tree increases committed tokens/event by 17.2% with near-native verify-forward time. Achieves 23.88 token-weighted decode tokens/s vs 18.80 for native five-step MTP (27.0% throughput gain). Per-request latency increased by 4.0%, with end-to-end wall time remaining prefill-heavy.

Conclusion: Tree speculative decoding for recurrent-hybrid models requires careful recurrent state tracking; GDN Tree-Scan successfully addresses this challenge and demonstrates significant throughput improvements while maintaining empirical equivalence within observed native probability variations.

Abstract: Tree speculative decoding verifies multiple candidate continuations in one target forward pass. For attention-only transformers, the verifier mainly needs an ancestry mask. Recurrent-hybrid language models break this assumption: a candidate row must also carry the recurrent state that native sequential decode would have produced along its root-to-node path. Otherwise, a verifier can use a correct attention mask while still conditioning on an impossible recurrent history.
  We present GDN Tree-Scan, a served verifier for Gated-DeltaNet hybrid language models integrated into vLLM. The system combines FlashAttention-2 tree-bias attention, branch-local GDN scan/replay, device-side multidraft commitment, and accepted-chain-only state publication. On the public Qwen3.6-27B-FP8 checkpoint, in a clean batch-one (B=1) SWE/Codex decode gate at temperature 0.6, a six-node root-branch tree increases committed tokens/event by 17.2% at near-native verify-forward time and reaches 23.88 token-weighted decode tokens/s versus 18.80 for native five-step MTP (E5), a 27.0% token-weighted decode-throughput gain. The per-request-equal latency view is +4.0%, and end-to-end task wall time remains prefill-heavy. Empirical equivalence evidence is scoped to recurrent-oracle probability-rescore (p-rescore) closure within the observed native flip floor, not a full distribution-distance proof.

</details>


### [284] [KV-COBRA: KV Cache Compression via Co-Optimized Bit-Rank Allocation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24298)
*Sihyeon Ha,Jaeho Lee,Yo-Seb Jeon*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: KV-COBRA is a KV-cache compression method that co-optimizes rank and bit-width allocation per attention head, achieving superior compression at low bit-rates by balancing truncation and quantization losses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current KV-cache compression methods fail at extreme bit-rates because they apply uniform rank and bit-width allocation across all attention heads, ignoring that different heads have different optimal trade-offs between rank truncation and quantization.

Method: KV-COBRA formalizes compression as a resource-allocation problem: 1) balances rank-truncation loss against quantization loss within each head, 2) redistributes budget across heads to minimize total distortion, 3) uses fused Hadamard rotation to equalize per-channel variance, and 4) reorders SVD basis by attention-KL importance for query-awareness. The allocator also extends to joint K+V compression.

Result: On perplexity, zero-shot, and long-context benchmarks from 0.5 to 4 bits per dimension (bpd), KV-COBRA shows the smallest accuracy degradation among evaluated methods at low bpd, with no per-token overhead.

Conclusion: The key limitation of KV-cache compression at extreme bit-rates is not the compression scheme itself, but how the budget is allocated across attention heads. By co-optimizing rank and bit-width per head, standard low-rank projection and scalar quantization can achieve significantly better compression performance, especially at low bit-rates.

Abstract: What limits KV-cache compression at extreme bit-rates? We argue that it is not the choice of compression scheme, but how its budget is allocated across attention heads. Existing methods apply rank and bit-width uniformly, ignoring that each head has a different optimal mix of rank truncation and quantization. We show that co-optimizing rank and bit-width per head, using only standard low-rank projection and scalar quantization, dominates uniform allocation, with the largest gains at low bit-rates. Our method, KV-COBRA (Co-Optimized Bit-Rank Allocation), formalizes this as a resource-allocation problem: it balances rank-truncation loss against quantization loss within each head, then redistributes budget across heads to minimize total distortion. A fused Hadamard rotation equalizes per-channel variance, and reordering the SVD basis by attention-KL importance makes the solver query-aware. The same allocator extends to joint $K{+}V$ compression. On perplexity, zero-shot, and long-context benchmarks from $0.5$ to $4$ bits per dimension (bpd), KV-COBRA shows the smallest accuracy degradation among evaluated methods at low bpd, with no per-token overhead.

</details>


### [285] [Multivariate quantile regression via Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23906)
*Andrew Polar,Michael Poluektov*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Novel algorithm for predicting conditional joint distributions in stochastic systems using KAN ensembles, with a new GoF test.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses the challenge of predicting conditional joint distributions of vector-valued targets in stochastic systems where randomness is intrinsic (not from observation errors or additive noise). Existing methods like multivariate quantile regression are less challenging as they deal with predefined regions or probability levels.

Method: Uses ensembles of Kolmogorov-Arnold networks (KANs) as flexible function approximators for identification. Also introduces a new discrepancy measure for joint distributions and a goodness-of-fit test based on this measure for validation and calibration.

Result: Proposes a novel identification technique for conditional joint distributions that is particularly well-suited to KAN ensembles, though theoretically not restricted to them. Develops a new GoF test that can be used more broadly beyond this specific application.

Conclusion: The method provides an effective approach for predicting conditional joint distributions in stochastic systems with intrinsic randomness, using KAN ensembles as a practical implementation choice, along with a novel GoF test for validation that has broader applicability.

Abstract: This paper introduces a novel algorithm for predicting conditional joint distributions of vector-valued targets in stochastic systems whose randomness is intrinsic rather than arising from observation errors or additive noise. Multivariate quantile regression also involves modeling conditional joint distributions but represents a less challenging task. It predicts the probability that vector-valued targets fall within predefined regions, identifies regions corresponding to predefined probability levels, or performs both tasks simultaneously. The proposed identification technique employs ensembles of Kolmogorov--Arnold networks (KANs) as flexible function approximators. Although the suggested technique is not theoretically restricted to KANs, KANs are particularly well suited to the proposed construction and are therefore used throughout this study. In addition to the training procedure, this work introduces a new discrepancy measure for joint distributions and a goodness-of-fit (GoF) test based on it. This GoF test was initially developed to validate and calibrate the proposed identification technique and is used here in an ad hoc manner. Although the test could be tabulated for broader use, such a tabulation is not pursued in this work. The test is also applicable more generally.

</details>


### [286] [The Undetected Damage of Quantization on Retrieval and How to Fix It](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24322)
*Luca Zhou,Alessandro Zirilli,Daniele Solombrino,Roberto Dessì,Emanuele Rodolà*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Quantization affects retrieval tasks more than classification; a scoring gap between top predictions determines quantization reliability and guides adaptive precision strategies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand why quantization hurts retrieval more than classification, and to develop methods for determining when quantized models can be trusted and where to allocate precision resources efficiently.

Method: Analyze the gap between top scores in quantized models, use this gap to predict quantization reliability, and propose task-specific strategies: for retrieval, allocate extra bits to critical layers; for classification, route low-gap inputs to full precision.

Result: Quantization changes 14-46% of top-1 retrieval results; the gap between top scores predicts model robustness; retrieval has few queries with sufficient gap; adaptive strategies recover most benefits at reduced cost.

Conclusion: The scoring gap is a key factor in quantization reliability; task-aware adaptive precision allocation can significantly reduce quantization costs while maintaining performance.

Abstract: We show that a quantized model that keeps its classification accuracy still changes $14$ to $46\%$ of its top-1 retrieval results, and that aggregate ranking metrics reveal only part of this damage. We tie this failure to the gap between the two highest scores and use that gap to decide when a quantized answer can be trusted and where additional precision should be spent. We show that the top-1 result is guaranteed to survive quantization only when this gap exceeds twice the largest rounding error. In classification, scores are the logits, and the loss function pushes the correct class away from other classes, encouraging this gap. In retrieval, scores are query-document scores, and nothing separates the top-1 item from the second. This gap can be measured without labels. Before deployment, it predicts which models will break under quantization, and at deployment time it tells, per input, whether the quantized answer still matches the full-precision answer. Most classification inputs have a gap wide enough to trust the quantized answer, but few retrieval queries do. That gap motivates a different fix in each task. In retrieval, spending extra bit-width on the layers whose quantization moves the gap most recovers up to three-quarters of an extra bit's benefit for half its cost. In classification, routing the few low-gap inputs to full precision recovers most of the lost accuracy at a fraction of the cost.

</details>


### [287] [A discrete generative model of neuronal spiking activity on microelectrode arrays](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23907)
*Md Sayed Tanveer,Mohammed A. Mostajo-Radji,Ge Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A discrete generative model using spatiotemporal motifs learns a reusable representation for array-wide neural spiking activity without assay-specific parameters, outperforming baseline methods on reconstruction and generation tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generative models of neural activity are valuable for characterizing dynamics and simulating experiments, but existing approaches assume fixed neurons. High-density microelectrode arrays produce sparse, array-wide binary spike volumes where observed electrodes vary across assays.

Method: Uses a discrete generative model with shared vocabulary of spatiotemporal motifs. A residual vector-quantized autoencoder learns the motif vocabulary, while a factorized masked transformer predicts where activity occurs and which motif appears at each active location.

Result: Achieves 5.2× voxel-level reconstruction average precision compared to matched flat tokenizer, and 1.4-2.6× site-level average precision for masked completion and free generation. Motifs are broadly reused across assays with only 9% of motif use entropy explained by assay identity.

Conclusion: Establishes a compact, reusable representation for array-wide spiking activity without learned assay-specific parameters, providing a scalable foundation for generative modeling across diverse neural preparations.

Abstract: Generative models of neural activity could help characterize tissue dynamics, compare experimental conditions, and simulate population activity for applications ranging from disease and drug-response studies to closed-loop experimentation. Existing approaches, however, typically assume a fixed set of sorted neurons, whereas high-density microelectrode arrays produce extremely sparse, array-wide binary spike volumes in which the observed subset of electrodes varies across assays. We introduce a discrete generative model that represents this activity using a shared vocabulary of spatiotemporal motifs. A residual vector-quantized autoencoder learns the motif vocabulary, while a factorized masked transformer predicts where activity occurs and which motif appears at each active location. We evaluate the model on 31 assays spanning human brain organoids and acute \emph{ex vivo} human hippocampal tissue. The learned motifs are broadly reused: assay identity explains only $9%$ of the entropy in motif use, and motif overlap across tissue types is comparable to overlap within them. When representation quality is evaluated independently of the generative prior, our approach achieves $5.2\times$ the voxel-level reconstruction average precision of a matched flat tokenizer. For masked completion and free generation, the full model achieves $1.4$--$2.6\times$ the site-level average precision of the matched generative baseline and outperforms it across all four families of generation metrics. These results establish a compact, reusable representation for array-wide spiking activity without learned assay-specific parameters, providing a scalable foundation for generative modeling across diverse neural preparations.

</details>


### [288] [Information-Time Proximal Policy Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24380)
*Yongcheng Zeng,Xinyu Cui,Yan Song,Guoqing Liu,Hongsheng Xin,Kaike Zhang,Cheng Deng,Kun Zhan,Jian Ying,Jian Zhao,Haifeng Zhang,Jun Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: InfoPPO reparameterizes PPO training for LLMs using information density instead of token count for temporal progression, enabling better long-horizon reasoning through state-dependent update constraints and adaptive clipping.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RLVR methods parameterize temporal progression by token-by-token generation in Markov Decision Processes, but this ignores the highly non-uniform information flow along autoregressive trajectories. Token-count-based progression fails to handle long-horizon reasoning effectively due to issues with discounting and supervision attenuation.

Method: InfoPPO reparameterizes temporal progression using information density rather than raw token count. This creates a common state-dependent structure for temporal credit propagation and policy updates. The method includes adaptive clipping that adjusts the clipping threshold at each token position based on the information density of its corresponding state, enabling more targeted policy updates while preserving proximal control.

Result: Experiments on Qwen3 models show consistent gains over competitive baselines across five challenging competition-style mathematical reasoning benchmarks. InfoPPO maintains stable accuracy and response length across non-trivial discount settings where token-time PPO deteriorates.

Conclusion: InfoPPO successfully addresses limitations of token-time PPO for LLM reasoning by introducing information-time parameterization, providing theoretical grounding for state-dependent update constraints through adaptive clipping, and demonstrating practical improvements in challenging reasoning tasks.

Abstract: RLVR has substantially improved the reasoning capabilities of LLMs. However, existing methods typically parameterize temporal progression in the Markov Decision Process by token-by-token generation, despite the highly non-uniform information flow along autoregressive trajectories. In this paper, we propose InfoPPO, which reparameterizes temporal progression using information density rather than raw token count. This reparameterization induces a common state-dependent structure for both temporal credit propagation and policy updates. InfoPPO restores the effectiveness of non-trivial discounting in long-horizon reasoning, retaining effective-horizon contraction while avoiding excessive attenuation of terminal supervision over long token sequences. Moreover, the information-time policy-improvement analysis naturally leads to a state-dependent update constraint, which we implement through adaptive clipping. By adapting the clipping threshold at each token position to the information density of its corresponding state, this mechanism enables more targeted policy updates while preserving proximal control. Theoretically, we extend performance-difference and policy-improvement analyses to the information-time MDP, deriving a policy-improvement lower bound when policy changes are regulated by information density. We further connect the general information-time analysis to practical LLM policy optimization by relating state-wise information density to local policy movement, while also providing theoretical grounding for the adaptive update mechanism. Experiments on Qwen3 models demonstrate consistent gains over competitive baselines across five challenging competition-style mathematical reasoning benchmarks. InfoPPO also maintains stable accuracy and response length across non-trivial discount settings under which token-time PPO deteriorates.

</details>


### [289] [Matched-Input Estimates Differ in Sign Across Architectures: Auditing EEG Foundation Models on Motor Imagery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23924)
*Kevin Zhou,Sparsh Roy*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Recent benchmarks disagree on EEG foundation model transfer capabilities; this study audits LaBraM and CBraMod on motor imagery tasks, finding supervised methods outperform foundation models even with optimal fine-tuning, and showing input pipeline differences create inconsistent results across architectures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is disagreement in recent benchmarks about when pretrained EEG foundation models transfer effectively to downstream brain-computer interface tasks, creating uncertainty about their practical utility compared to task-specific supervised methods.

Method: Conducted validation-locked protocol audits of LaBraM and CBraMod foundation models on motor imagery tasks, controlling for preprocessing, architecture, optimization, freeze depth, checkpoint selection, temperature scaling, and method selection using only training-session data. Compared against supervised comparators and investigated input pipeline confounds by retraining supervised architectures on broadband arrays.

Result: On four-class BCI Competition IV-2a, all supervised comparators outperformed every foundation-model configuration, even with validation-selected fine-tuning. Input pipeline differences produced opposite accuracy effects across architectures: broadband improved ATCNet by 0.078 accuracy while reducing EEG Conformer accuracy by 0.088. The four-class deficit didn't reproduce uniformly - on two-class BNCI2014-004, no separation was detected between fine-tuned CBraMod and supervised comparators.

Conclusion: EEG foundation models show inconsistent performance compared to supervised methods, with results depending on dataset characteristics and input pipelines. A single comparator may not provide architecture-invariant decomposition of pretrained-versus-supervised performance gaps, suggesting careful benchmarking design is needed for fair comparisons.

Abstract: Pretrained EEG foundation models are increasingly proposed as general-purpose encoders for brain-computer interfaces, yet recent benchmarks disagree about when their representations transfer to downstream tasks. We audit LaBraM and CBraMod on motor imagery under a validation-locked protocol in which preprocessing, architecture, optimization, freeze depth, checkpoint, temperature, and method selection are determined using training-session data only. On four-class BCI Competition IV-2a, every supervised comparator evaluated here outperforms every foundation-model configuration, including validation-selected fine-tuning. We then examine a key confound: foundation models and task-specific decoders are normally evaluated using different input pipelines. Retraining three supervised architectures on the broadband arrays consumed by the foundation models produces matched-input accuracy differences of opposite sign across architectures: broadband input improves ATCNet by 0.078 accuracy while reducing EEG Conformer accuracy by 0.088. None of the three individual matched-input terms is significant after multiple-comparison correction at n = 9, so we treat the sign variation descriptively rather than as a formal architecture-by-pipeline interaction. These observed sign differences suggest that a single comparator may not provide an architecture-invariant decomposition of a pretrained-versus-supervised performance gap. The four-class deficit also does not reproduce uniformly across motor-imagery datasets: on two-class BNCI2014-004 we cannot detect the same separation between fine-tuned CBraMod and the supervised comparators. Finally, validation-fitted temperature scaling returns foundation-model calibration error to the supervised range despite substantially lower four-class accuracy.

</details>


### [290] [Artificial Structure Function Search: Preserving Artificial Functional Connectivity for Structured Pruning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24401)
*Mindula Illeperuma,Rafael Pina,Charuka Herath,Sharmarke A. Gabayre,Varuna De Silva*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ASF-S is a structured pruning framework using Principle Gradient Importance (PGI) for prune-candidate selection, inspired by brain structure-function relationships, achieving 70% parameter reduction without retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current structured pruning methods rely on opaque heuristics or weight-based criteria that don't consider structural dependencies in neural networks, limiting their effectiveness.

Method: Proposes Artificial Structure Function Search (ASF-S) framework using Principle Gradient Importance (PGI) selection criteria inspired by brain structure-function relationships, ensuring pruned structure respects topographical organization of output layers.

Result: Achieves 70% parameter reduction with models that can recover baseline accuracy without retraining pruned layers, outperforming recent benchmarks with PGI as selection criterion and ASF-S as pruning framework.

Conclusion: Careful prune candidate selection criteria like PGI can find accurate smaller networks, and Artificial Functional Connectivity (AFC) provides evidence that structured pruning can be more effective when considering structural relationships in neural networks.

Abstract: Structured pruning is a model compression technique that is used to reduce the computational cost of deploying deep neural networks on resource-constrained devices. Popular methods of pruning rely on opaque heuristics or weight-based criteria that give no indication as to the structural dependencies in the network. To address these limitations we present Artificial Structure Function Search (ASF-S): a novel structured pruning framework. ASF-S utilizes Principle Gradient Importance (PGI): a novel prune-candidate selection criteria that is inspired by structure-function relationships in the brain. By ensuring the pruned structure of the model respects topographical organization of the output layer, we define Artificial Functional Connectivity (AFC) for artificial neural networks. AFC provides evidence to demonstrate that accurate smaller networks can be found using careful prune candidate selection criteria. We present results for PGI as a selection criterion and for ASF-S as a pruning framework against recent benchmarks, demonstrating that our method yields model variants with 70\% parameter reduction, that can recover baseline accuracy without re-training the pruned layers.

</details>


### [291] [The Neural Forcing for Three-Dimensional Incompressible Navier-Stokes finite time blowup](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23934)
*Beibei Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A neural framework for forced 3D Navier-Stokes flow with two parts: computational forcing system (Part I) and mathematical certification layer (Part II) that together aim to establish finite-time blowup.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the long-standing open problem of finite-time blowup in 3D incompressible Navier-Stokes equations by developing a combined computational and mathematical approach that separates neural candidate discovery from rigorous continuum analysis.

Method: Two-part framework: Part I uses physics-informed neural networks to generate structured external-force trajectories, optimized through differentiable PDE rollouts or PPO-Clip, with validation via independent fixed-force replay. Part II provides mathematical certification through integrated reciprocal-vorticity criteria, Riccati-type growth analysis, validated computational-to-continuum transfer strategy, and conditional positive-probability closure.

Result: Develops a complete framework where the computational forcing system generates candidate force fields, and the mathematical certification layer provides rigorous analysis showing that selected forcings imply finite-time loss of smooth continuation. The proof is established at the continuum level.

Conclusion: The paper presents a novel two-stage neural-mathematical framework that separates computational discovery from rigorous certification, offering a potential pathway to establishing finite-time blowup in forced 3D Navier-Stokes equations through a combination of machine learning and mathematical analysis techniques.

Abstract: We present a two-part neural framework for forced three-dimensional incompressible Navier--Stokes flow. Part~I develops the computational forcing system. A physics-informed neural model generates structured external-force trajectories, candidates are optimized through differentiable PDE rollouts or PPO-Clip, and selected forcings are frozen and checked by independent fixed-force replay. Part~II provides the mathematical certification layer. It separates neural candidate discovery from continuum analysis, derives integrated reciprocal-vorticity criteria that imply Riccati-type growth and finite-time loss of smooth continuation, develops a validated computational-to-continuum transfer strategy, and establishes a conditional positive-probability closure for a nondegenerate neural output law. The proof is complete at the continuum level.

</details>


### [292] [ARM: Attention with Routed-Memory for Learnable Sparse Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24417)
*Qiuhao Zeng,Jerry Huang,Peng Lu,Ruiyi Fang,Gezheng Xu,Zihao Jing,Yufei Cui,Charles Ling,Gang Niu,Boyu Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ARM introduces a differentiable, fixed-size memory system with hierarchical routing for KV caching that learns to select and update memory slots, avoiding hard eviction and improving long-context reasoning efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite advances in long-context inference, LLMs remain fundamentally limited by traditional KV caching mechanisms that require eviction/pruning strategies, which often discard core information to manage growing cache sizes, leading to information loss.

Method: Proposes Attention with Routed Memory (ARM) - a novel KV caching structure featuring: 1) fully differentiable, fixed-size memory system with hierarchical router, 2) Gumbel-Softmax for memory slot selection, 3) sigmoid-gated updates that softly combine new and stored information, and 4) training a policy to dynamically select varying memory amounts at inference.

Result: ARM achieves superior performance and efficiency compared to fixed KV-caching approaches on standard commonsense and long-context reasoning benchmarks, while maintaining efficiency in both memory usage and generation latency.

Conclusion: ARM provides a scalable and effective solution for long-context reasoning by introducing a learnable, adaptive memory management system that reduces information loss compared to hard eviction approaches, enabling better retrieval across both short and long contexts.

Abstract: Despite advances in long-context inference, large language models (LLMs) remain fundamentally limited by the key-value (KV) caching mechanisms that are necessary for stable computation. Techniques such as selective token eviction and pruning have vastly mitigated these issues, but often discard core information to manage the growing cache. In this paper, we propose Attention with Routed Memory (ARM) a novel KV caching structure that introduces a fully differentiable, fixed-size memory system organized as a hierarchical router. Via a Gumbel-Softmax, ARM learns to select memory slots and perform sigmoid-gated updates that softly combine new and stored information, avoiding hard eviction and reducing information loss. By further training a policy to dynamically select varying amounts of memory at inference, ARM adapts its accesses for both simple contexts and inputs that require deeper reasoning, enabling more scalable and effective retrieval on both short- and long-contexts. Experimental results on standard commonsense and long-context reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that ARM achieves superior performance and efficiency compared to fixed KV-caching approaches, while remaining efficient and scalable in terms of both memory and generation latency.

</details>


### [293] [MGRD: Compact morphology-gated residual diffusion for variance-aware cross-domain neurite forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23990)
*Tsung Yeh Hsieh,Cosmin Anitescu,Chunghwan Kim,Victoria A. Webster-Wood,Yongjie Jessica Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MGRD is a compact stochastic model that forecasts future neurite morphology from observed frames, reducing computational burden while providing uncertainty estimates for case prioritization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-term time-lapse imaging of neurite morphology is resource-intensive. Existing deterministic models like gSTA cannot represent variability among plausible futures, limiting their utility for uncertainty-aware forecasting.

Method: Proposes Morphology-Gated Residual Diffusion (MGRD), a stochastic surrogate model that forecasts 20 future frames from 10 observed frames, conditioning on morphology features from the latest observation. Uses diffusion modeling with parameter-efficient architecture.

Result: MGRD reduces trajectory-wise mean MAE by 39.6% vs gSTA on iPSC data, improves skeleton F1 by 45.3%, uses only 1.01% of gSTA's parameters, trains 10x faster. Without retraining, improves performance on mouse data. Variance scores enable case prioritization, reducing MAE by ~17% when filtering lowest-variance cases.

Conclusion: MGRD establishes a compact stochastic framework for neurite morphology forecasting with uncertainty estimation, enabling efficient resource allocation through case prioritization across simulation and microscopy datasets.

Abstract: Tracking neurite morphology over time helps characterize structural changes during neuronal development and deterioration, but long-term time-lapse imaging is resource-intensive and difficult to scale. Forecasting future morphology could reduce this burden. Existing neurite digital-twin models such as gated spatiotemporal attention (gSTA) produce a single deterministic forecast without representing variability among plausible futures. We introduce Morphology-Gated Residual Diffusion (MGRD), a compact stochastic surrogate that jointly forecasts twenty future neurite-morphology frames from ten observed frames while conditioning on morphology features derived from the latest observation. On controlled phase-field trajectories, MGRD reduces trajectory-wise mean MAE by 9.7% relative to a matched control while updating 4.46 times fewer parameters. On human iPSC-derived neuron microscopy, MGRD improves all four reported metrics over gSTA, including a 39.6% reduction in trajectory-wise mean MAE and a 45.3% increase in skeleton F1. Without mouse-domain retraining or fine-tuning, MGRD also improves MAE and skeleton F1 on mouse cortical-neurosphere microscopy across 10-40-min sampling intervals and forecast horizons beyond 13 hours. Repeated sampling provides a case-level variance score for ranking forecast difficulty. Retaining approximately 60% of the lowest-variance cases reduces mean MAE by 17.6% on iPSC microscopy and 16.8% on simulation data. MGRD uses 1.01% of gSTA's parameters, requires less than one tenth of its training-update time, and generates a 50-step DDIM trajectory 7.9% faster when morphology features are cached. These results establish MGRD as a compact stochastic surrogate for neurite-morphology forecasting and case prioritization across simulation and microscopy datasets.

</details>


### [294] [WPBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Wind Power Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24444)
*Yuhan Zhu,Jilin Hu,Xinying Cai,Yingshan Li,Li Ma,Xiangfei Qiu Linsen Li,Kai Zhang,Yao Fu,Weihao Jiang,Bin Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: WPBench is a comprehensive benchmark for wind power forecasting that addresses limitations in existing benchmarks through extensive dataset coverage, diverse model evaluation, and structure-aware diagnostics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing wind power forecasting benchmarks have significant limitations: limited coverage of wind scenarios (turbine scale, variable composition, spatial structure), incomplete model family coverage, misaligned evaluation metrics, and limited structure-aware diagnostics beyond temporal patterns.

Method: WPBench integrates 26 public datasets organized by turbine scale and variable composition (single-turbine, multi-turbine, univariate, multivariate). It benchmarks 19 representative models across traditional methods, deep temporal models, spatio-temporal models, and foundation models under unified processing, training, and evaluation protocols.

Result: WPBench enables systematic model comparison by assessing not only point-wise errors but also forecast-curve fidelity and computational efficiency. It provides structure-aware diagnostics across temporal, variable-dependency, and spatial-dependency perspectives.

Conclusion: WPBench offers a comprehensive, fair, and extensible benchmark that supports systematic evaluation of wind power forecasting methods across diverse scenarios, providing a reusable platform for future research in renewable energy integration and power system operations.

Abstract: Accurate, reliable, and deployable wind power forecasting is critical for power system dispatch, renewable energy integration, and electricity market operations. Progress in this field hinges on the ability to empirically and comprehensively benchmark forecasting methods. Yet existing benchmarks fall short of supporting systematic evaluation in four key aspects: 1) limited coverage of wind power scenarios across turbine scale, variable composition, and spatial structure; 2) incomplete coverage of forecasting model families; 3) evaluation metrics misaligned with wind power requirements; and 4) limited structure-aware diagnostics beyond individual temporal patterns. To address these limitations, we propose WPBench, a comprehensive, fair, and extensible benchmark for wind power forecasting. WPBench integrates 26 public datasets organized by turbine scale and variable composition, spanning single-turbine, multi-turbine, univariate, and multivariate settings. Under unified processing, training, and evaluation protocols, it benchmarks 19 representative models covering traditional methods, deep temporal models, spatio-temporal models, and foundation models. Beyond point-wise errors, WPBench assesses forecast-curve fidelity and computational efficiency, and delivers structure-aware diagnostics across temporal, variable-dependency, and spatial-dependency perspectives. Together, these capabilities enable systematic model comparison across diverse wind scenarios and provide a reusable platform for future research.

</details>


### [295] [Simpler Methods Work Better for L1 Penalized Logistic Models and Large Datasets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23995)
*Edward Raff,James Holt*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Older L1-penalized linear model solvers outperform newer "state-of-the-art" methods, and a simple LBFGS baseline with minor tweaks is surprisingly effective for production-scale ML pipelines despite theoretical limitations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: L1-penalized linear models remain state-of-the-art for high-dimensional tasks but many solvers are inefficient, slow, difficult to parallelize, and hard to integrate into MLOps pipelines for large-scale industry applications.

Method: The authors empirically test several proposed state-of-the-art L1 solvers from literature against older methods and introduce a simple baseline using LBFGS on sub-gradients with minor tweaks.

Result: Older methods outperform newer "state-of-the-art" solutions, and the simple LBFGS baseline proves highly effective, easy to support, and scalable for production use despite being theoretically non-convergent.

Conclusion: Practical considerations for production deployment often trump theoretical perfection; researchers should avoid overconfident claims that hinder production adoption, and simple, scalable solutions can be more valuable than theoretically optimal but impractical methods.

Abstract: Linear models with an $L_1$-norm penalty remain state-of-the-art for high-dimensional ($d > 1,000,000$) tasks, offering a straightforward method for solving real-world industry problems. Despite their widespread use in industry and utility, many $L_1$ solvers are not effective for general use, are prohibitively slow, and are ineffective in parallelization. This makes them difficult to train in an MLOps pipeline on large industry-scale corpora. In this work, we test several proposed ``state-of-the-art'' solutions from the literature and find that older methods are currently far superior for general use. We also identify several recommendations for academics to perform research that avoids erroneously overconfident results, which can prevent the transition to production use. Equally surprising, we find that a new and simple baseline, using LBFGS on a sub-gradient, is highly effective with minor tweaks, despite being dismissed in the literature for theoretical non-convergence. In practice, we find it is an easier-to-support and easier-to-scale method for production use.

</details>


### [296] [Lifted Bellman Linear Programming for Offline Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24489)
*Hyukjun Yang,Jongchan Park,Narim Jeong,Donghwan Lee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ALBUM is a novel offline RL method that replaces regression losses with inequality constraints imposing Bellman optimality, eliminating need for target networks, EMA updates, and off-policy corrections while maintaining competitive performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard offline RL methods use regression losses with bootstrapped value targets requiring target networks and EMA updates for stability. Multi-step targets need off-policy correction, adding complexity. The authors seek a simpler, more stable approach that avoids these issues.

Method: Proposes Lifted Bellman Linear Program (LBLP) that lifts Bellman optimality constraints to joint (Q,V) space using only dataset state-action pairs. Relaxes constraints into hinge penalties, creating ALBUM with detached K-step rollout targets. No squared regression losses, target networks, or EMA updates needed.

Result: ALBUM matches average performance of FQL and compares to recent action-chunking methods on OGBench while using single critic with Gaussian policy, fewest parameters, and least peak GPU memory among compared methods.

Conclusion: ALBUM provides a simpler, more efficient offline RL framework that eliminates key complexities of traditional methods (target networks, EMA updates, off-policy corrections) while achieving competitive performance with reduced computational resources.

Abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) typically trains a critic by minimizing a regression loss against bootstrapped value targets stabilized by target networks with exponential moving average (EMA) updates. Multi-step targets incorporate behavior-policy actions and therefore require off-policy correction. We instead impose in-sample Bellman optimality on the critic through inequality constraints. We formulate the Lifted Bellman Linear Program (LBLP), which lifts the linear programming characterization of Bellman optimality to the joint $(Q,V)$ space so that every constraint involves only state-action pairs in the dataset. Its unique minimizer is the in-sample optimal pair, and constraints along $K$-step segments of dataset trajectories leave this minimizer unchanged for any rollout policy and horizon. Under deterministic dynamics, this minimizer lies between the best dataset return and the optimal value. Relaxing the constraints into hinge penalties recovers the same solution above a finite penalty coefficient in the tabular case. Approximate Lifted Bellman Unconstrained Minimization (ALBUM) implements this relaxation with neural networks and detaches the $K$-step rollout targets by stop gradient. Its objective contains no squared regression onto bootstrapped targets, so it can be trained without target networks or EMA updates. Under deterministic dynamics, the LBLP solution is a stationary point of the detached update under a coefficient condition independent of $γ$ and $K$, and the inequality constraints allow discounted returns along dataset trajectories to serve as lower bounds without off-policy correction or action chunking. On OGBench, ALBUM uses a single critic with a Gaussian policy, matches the average performance of FQL, and is comparable to recent action-chunking methods, while using the fewest parameters and the least peak GPU memory among all compared methods.

</details>


### [297] [On Emergent Capabilities and Model Merging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24504)
*Luca Zhou,Emanuele Rodolà*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Model merging preserves emergent capabilities shared by both parents, cannot create superadditive emergent capabilities, and dilutes emergent capabilities from single parents faster than trained capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: With fine-tuned checkpoints and adapters filling public repositories, model merging has become a common operation. The paper investigates what happens to emergent capabilities (behaviors not explicitly trained for) when models are merged, as emergent behaviors may not compose the same way as trained capabilities.

Method: Studied two independent testbeds (activation oracles and emergent-misaligned models) across three model families. Analyzed how model merging affects emergent capabilities through systematic weight arithmetic experiments on merged models.

Result: Three key findings: 1) Merging preserves emergent capabilities when both parents carry them (e.g., merging misaligned checkpoints retains misalignment). 2) Merging cannot create superadditive emergent capabilities (weighted merges of single-task oracles don't match jointly-trained oracles). 3) When only one parent carries an emergent capability, merging dilutes it faster than the accompanying trained capability.

Conclusion: Emergent behaviors in model artifacts do not compose the same way as trained capabilities during model merging, with implications for safety and capability composition in open-source model repositories.

Abstract: Fine-tuned checkpoints and adapters now fill public repositories, and the most common operation applied to these artifacts is model merging: arithmetic on their weights that assembles capabilities cheaply. We ask what this operation does to emergent capabilities: behaviors an artifact carries that were never an explicit training target. Studying two independent testbeds (activation oracles and emergent-misaligned models) across three model families, we find that the answer is threefold. First, merging preserves an emergent capability that both parents carry: merging two misaligned checkpoints retains most of their broad misalignment across the whole mixing range. Second, merging cannot create an emergent capability that is superadditive in its parents: no weighted merge of two single-task oracles reaches the jointly-trained oracle's auditing ability. Third, when only one parent carries the capability, merging dilutes it faster than the trained capability that accompanies it: the gap is significant in most settings. In short, emergent behaviors of an artifact do not compose the way its trained capability does.

</details>


### [298] [ShapeLex: Decoupling Local Shape Symbolization and Global Scale Modeling for Text-Controlled Time Series Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24003)
*Subo Wei,Jianqi Gao,Mingyan Fan,Shaorong Xie,Xinzhi Wang,Yongpeng Dong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ShapeLex decouples text-to-time-series generation into discrete shape vocabulary and continuous attribute modeling for more accurate and interpretable sequence generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing text-controlled time series generation methods couple semantic understanding and sequence modeling in a single continuous latent space, which lacks explicit local semantic anchors and proper separation between global continuous attributes and local discrete shapes. This leads to key local structures being smoothed, missed, or misplaced.

Method: ShapeLex introduces a three-stage approach: 1) Induces a reusable vocabulary of discrete shape units (like rises, spikes, drops) from training data to form an interpretable symbolic space, 2) Uses an autoregressive generator to select shapes based on text descriptions, adjust attributes (position, duration), and compose them into shape skeletons, 3) Applies a mixture-density scale head to model overall level and volatility for realistic global scale restoration.

Result: Experiments on twelve public datasets with real user-written text and downstream forecasting tasks show ShapeLex generates time series that better match real data distributions than existing methods. The method also enables automatic synthesis of paired supervision from the learned vocabulary, avoiding annotation costs that scale with dataset size.

Conclusion: ShapeLex successfully addresses the limitations of existing text-to-time-series generation methods by decoupling discrete shape modeling from continuous attribute modeling, resulting in more accurate and interpretable generation while improving scalability through automatic supervision synthesis.

Abstract: Text-controlled time series generation aims to synthesize sequences that follow natural-language descriptions while remaining faithful to real data distributions. Existing paradigms often couple semantic understanding and sequence modeling in a single continuous latent space, lacking explicit local semantic anchors and separation between global continuous attributes and local discrete shapes. As a result, key local structures may be smoothed, missed, or misplaced. We propose Shape Lexicon (ShapeLex), which decouples text-to-sequence generation into discrete symbolization of local shapes and continuous modeling of global attributes. ShapeLex first induces a reusable vocabulary of discrete shape units, such as rises, spikes, and sharp drops, from training data, forming an interpretable symbolic space. An autoregressive generator then selects shapes according to the textual description, adjusts attributes such as position and duration, and composes them in temporal order into a shape skeleton. Finally, a mixture-density scale head models and samples the overall level and volatility to restore realistic global scale. Experiments on twelve public datasets, real user-written text, and downstream forecasting tasks show that ShapeLex generates series that better match real data distributions than existing methods. In addition, paired supervision is automatically synthesized from the learned vocabulary, avoiding annotation costs that grow with dataset size and improving scalability.

</details>


### [299] [$t_0$: A Time-Series Foundation Model for Forecasting with Context](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24559)
*Lucas Meyer,Claudio Sole,Huikan Xiang,Nicolas Li,Lucas Franceschino,Arnau Quera-Bofarull,Maarten P. Scholl,Joachim Fainberg,Geoffrey Négiar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: t0 is a family of open-weights foundation models for multivariate time series forecasting that achieves competitive zero-shot performance without task-specific retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To develop foundation models for time series forecasting that can handle multivariate contexts with target history, past covariates, and known-future covariates in a zero-shot manner without requiring task-specific retraining.

Method: Transformer-based architecture alternating attention along time and across variates, producing probabilistic forecasts through quantile predictions. Pretrained on curated public data combined with synthetic generator families containing covariate-to-target dependencies.

Result: t0-alpha (102M params) achieves CRPS of 0.4941 on GIFT-Eval, t0-beta (256M params) achieves CRPS of 0.4738 and MASE of 0.6865 (3rd place, within 4.0% of best zero-shot model).
