On fev-bench: 42.2 and 46.7 skill scores. Known-future covariates improve skill by 6.3 percentage points. On Victoria electricity-demand, among most accurate with year-long context. On ERCOT prices, reduces MAE of baseline by 38%.

Conclusion: The t0 family demonstrates strong zero-shot forecasting capabilities across diverse time series tasks, showing the effectiveness of foundation models for multivariate time series forecasting with proper architectural design and pretraining strategy.

Abstract: We present $t_0$, a family of open-weights foundation models for forecasting with multivariate context. We release its first two members: $\texttt{t0-alpha}$ and $\texttt{t0-beta}$, respectively 102M and 256M parameters. Both condition their forecasts on target history, past covariates, and known-future covariates, without task-specific retraining. Their transformer layers alternate attention along time and across variates. They produce probabilistic forecasts through quantile predictions. Pretraining combines curated public data with synthetic generator families constructed to contain covariate-to-target dependencies. On GIFT-Eval, $\texttt{t0-alpha}$ reaches an aggregate CRPS of 0.4941, and $\texttt{t0-beta}$ a CRPS of 0.4738 and a MASE of 0.6865, third on both and within 4.0% of the best zero-shot TSFM. On fev-bench they score 42.2 and 46.7 in skill, the latter third again and 2.0 points behind the leader. We analyze $\texttt{t0-alpha}$ in depth. Known-future covariates raise its skill by 6.3 percentage points across 30 tasks. The report also examines its calibration, its rollout strategy on long horizons, and its robustness to missing data. On the Victoria electricity-demand benchmark, $\texttt{t0-beta}$ is among the most accurate models with a context of nearly a year. In an independent Macrocosm evaluation of hourly ERCOT prices over 29 months, both cut the MAE of the lagged-price baseline by 38%.

</details>


### [300] [Graph-to-Grid (G2G): Continuous-Coordinate Feature Painting for Soccer Pass Surfaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24040)
*Kaan Günay,Orhun Gun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Painting player features onto a grid via bilinear interpolation improves pass prediction models over raster-based methods, showing consistent gains across different datasets and model architectures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing dense pass surface models use rasterized per-cell counts that lose precise player positional information. There's a need to understand how different spatial representation methods (rasterization vs. interpolation) affect model performance for pass prediction in soccer.

Method: Proposes "painting" - bilinearly interpolating player features onto a grid based on measured coordinates, allowing end-to-end training of per-player encoders. Evaluated on 53,628 passes from 2022 World Cup data using cross-validation, tested across different datasets, and compared against various baselines including raster-based methods, offset channels, finer rasters, attention mechanisms, and raster-free decoders.

Result: Painting improves pass selection likelihood by about 0.25 nats over raster-only methods. The gain comes mostly (75%) from simply painting raw player features without learned encoders. Gains persist across different model architectures (SoccerMap, U-Net) but disappear when frozen across data providers. Gains are robust to cross-validation and dataset changes but compress with injected tracking error.

Conclusion: Bilinear interpolation of player features onto grids ("painting") provides measurable improvements over rasterization for pass prediction tasks, with most benefits coming from the spatial representation itself rather than learned feature encoders. The method shows consistent advantages but is sensitive to data distribution shifts between providers.

Abstract: Dense pass surfaces give, for every pitch cell, whether a pass played there would arrive, whether the carrier would choose it, and what the possession would then be worth. The networks that draw them read the state as a raster of per-cell counts, losing where inside a cell each player stands. LiDAR detectors, bird's-eye-view perception and graph weather models move entity features onto a grid, binning each entity to a cell or learning the transfer. We evaluate the interpolated form: each player's features are scattered bilinearly onto the grid at the player's measured coordinates, so the surface loss trains the per-player encoder end to end. Those systems adopt an interface; this paper measures one. On 53,628 passes from the 2022 World Cup, painting improves selection likelihood over the same core fed rasters alone by about a quarter of a nat: in every match of an eight-fold cross-validation, with every arm tuned over five seeds, and after retraining on seven Bundesliga and 2. Bundesliga matches from another provider. Thirteen pre-specified studies locate the gain: painting the nine raw player features with no encoder carries three quarters of it, and the learned encoder and message passing add a smaller, resolved increment. Painting also helps the original SoccerMap and a canonical U-Net, whereas offset channels, a finer raster, an attention painter and a raster-free decoder do not. Frozen across the provider boundary the likelihood advantage is lost; injected tracking error compresses it. These results concern observed-endpoint prediction, not calibrated evaluation of hypothetical passes.

</details>


### [301] [Overlay\_dx - Automating forecasting evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24586)
*Long Ngo,Mohammed Amine Chamli,Jonathan Rivalan,Thomas Jaillon*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Overlay_dx is a novel visual-numerical evaluation metric for time series prediction that measures the percentage of predictions within confidence intervals and computes the area under the overlay curve for quantitative performance assessment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional evaluation metrics for time series prediction provide numerical values but lack comprehensibility, making it difficult to effectively differentiate model performances and hindering clear model comparison.

Method: Proposes overlay_dx, a visual metric that plots the percentage of predictions falling within confidence intervals around actual values. Once plotted, it computes the area under the overlay curve to provide a quantitative measure of alignment between predicted and actual values across different thresholds and predictions.

Result: Through extensive experiments, the approach demonstrates a unified evaluation framework combining both visual and numerical assessments, enabling improved model comparison and providing valuable insights for research and optimization in time series prediction.

Conclusion: Overlay_dx successfully addresses the limitations of traditional metrics by offering a comprehensive evaluation approach that combines visual comprehensibility with quantitative rigor for better model performance differentiation and comparison in time series prediction.

Abstract: Traditional evaluation metrics provides numerical values but often lack comprehensibility, hindering effective differentiation of model performances. Our work addresses this challenge by introducing overlay\_dx, a novel evaluation metric measuring the performance of time series prediction models. Overlay\_dx is a visual metric that represents the percentage of predictions falling within a confidence interval around actual values. Additionally, once evaluation results are plotted, overlay\_dx computes the area under the overlay curve, providing a quantitative measure of alignment between predicted and actual values across different thresholds and predictions. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that our approach offers a unified evaluation framework that combines both visual and numerical assessments, enabling improved model comparison and providing valuable insights for further research and optimization efforts in time series prediction.

</details>


### [302] [Q-DEQ: Discrete Solving and Quantization for Deep Equilibrium Models in Time Series Forecasting under Edge Deployment Coding Constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24042)
*Ruotong Yang,Hongdong Zhu,Qi Gao,Yin Ma,Hai Wei,Kai Wen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Q-DEQ: A deep equilibrium model for time series forecasting that uses discrete optimization with binary encoding to solve local updates, achieving parameter compression and low-bit representations suitable for edge deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Edge deployment requires forecasting models with compact parameter storage and low-bit representations. While deep equilibrium models (DEQs) reduce parameter costs through implicit depth, their usual Anderson solver operates in continuous real domain, which may not be optimal for resource-constrained edge devices.

Method: Proposes Q-DEQ which formulates local updates in DEQ forward solving as discrete optimization problems. Constructs candidate directions from current state and iteration history, uses local quadratic residual model to evaluate combinations. Binary encoding yields QUBO problems solvable by simulated annealing or coherent Ising machines. After fixed-point solving, applies W8A8 fake quantization to shared layer's weights and activations.

Result: Evaluated with iTransformer backbone on five multivariate time series forecasting datasets. Relative MSE differences from explicit multi-layer baseline range from -1.16% to +2.90%, achieving lower MSE on two datasets. DEQ parameter sharing reduces parameter counts by 1.8x-3.82x; combined with W8A8 quantization, static weight storage reduced by 4.3x-12.8x. CPU-based SA and Kaiwu CIM produce closely matching forecasts.

Conclusion: Establishes local discrete solving as a viable component of DEQ time series forecasting and provides a route for executing fixed-point updates through different combinatorial optimization backends, enabling efficient edge deployment with significant parameter compression.

Abstract: Edge deployment motivates forecasting models with compact parameter storage and low-bit representations. Deep equilibrium models (DEQs) obtain implicit depth by repeatedly applying a shared layer, reducing the parameter cost of explicit layer stacking. Their usual Anderson solver, however, searches for update coefficients in the continuous real domain. We propose Q-DEQ, which formulates local updates in DEQ forward solving as discrete optimization problems. Candidate directions are constructed from the current state and iteration history, and a local quadratic residual model is used to evaluate their combinations. Binary encoding of the direction coefficients yields a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem that can be solved by simulated annealing (SA) or a coherent Ising machine (CIM). After fixed-point solving, a re-forward pass applies W8A8 fake quantization to the shared layer's weights and activations. We evaluate Q-DEQ with an iTransformer backbone on five multivariate time series forecasting datasets. Relative MSE differences from the explicit multi-layer baseline range from $-1.16\%$ to $+2.90\%$, with lower MSE on two datasets. DEQ parameter sharing reduces parameter counts by factors of $1.80\times$--$3.82\times$; combined with W8A8, static weight storage is reduced by factors of $4.3\times$--$12.8\times$. Local QUBO problems solved using CPU-based SA and the Kaiwu CIM physical backend produce closely matching downstream forecasts. These results establish local discrete solving as a viable component of DEQ time series forecasting and provide a route for executing fixed-point updates through different combinatorial optimization backends.

</details>


### [303] [GraphToolbox: A Configurable Python Framework for Graph Neural Network Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24609)
*Eloi Campagne,Yvenn Amara-Ouali,Yannig Goude,Argyris Kalogeratos*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GraphToolbox is an open-source Python framework that unifies all stages of GNN-based electricity forecasting experiments into one configuration-driven pipeline, addressing the fragmentation of current tools.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Electricity forecasting involves spatially related signals that GNNs can naturally represent, but building complete GNN forecasting experiments is laborious because graph construction, model selection, training, aggregation, and interpretation use incompatible tools.

Method: GraphToolbox provides a unified pipeline with data-driven graph construction, adapter for instantiating/training 51 PyTorch Geometric convolutions with recurrent cells, online expert aggregation, forecasting interpretability, and significance testing on cached forecasts.

Result: On French regional load, 48 convolutions achieved 1.14% to 1.60% error, reduced to 0.98% with online aggregation, outperforming classical baselines. On net-load, direct graph models were less accurate than classical models, though component-wise forecasting improved them.

Conclusion: GraphToolbox enables systematic architectural evaluation of GNN models for electricity forecasting through a unified experimental interface, demonstrating practical value in organizing and comparing forecasting approaches.

Abstract: Electricity forecasting often involves spatially related signals observed over regions, substations, and feeders, and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) provide a natural way to represent these relations. Building a complete GNN forecasting experiment is nonetheless laborious, because graph construction, model selection, training, aggregation, and interpretation sit in incompatible tools. We present GraphToolbox, an open-source Python framework that unifies these stages in one configurationdriven pipeline built on PyTorch Geometric. It offers data-driven graph construction, an adapter that instantiates and trains 51 of the 65 PyTorch Geometric convolutions together with the recurrent cells of PyTorch Geometric Temporal, online expert aggregation, forecasting interpretability, and significance testing on cached forecasts. We evaluate the pipeline in two case studies. On French regional load, the 48 convolutions included in the complete forecasting sweep fall in a band from 1.14% to 1.60% error, online aggregation lowers this to 0.98%, and the graph models improve on classical additive and boosting baselines. On net-load, direct graph models are less accurate than a classical additive model, while forecasting each physical component separately improves them without closing that gap. Both comparisons use the same experimental interface, illustrating the role of GraphToolbox in systematic architectural evaluation.

</details>


### [304] [Augmented Hypothesis Testing with Persona-Based LLM Simulations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24629)
*Ziyad Benomar,Aymen Al Marjani,Paul Missault,Saab Mansour*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A framework for learning-augmented A/B testing that uses predictions from ML models (with unknown quality) to reduce sample sizes while maintaining statistical validity, with methods for both population-level directional predictions and individual-level predictions, validated using persona-based LLM simulations on real-world datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: A/B testing is expensive (large sample sizes, long timelines, high costs) and while ML predictions of experimental outcomes exist, their uncertain quality prevents replacing human experiments entirely. However, these predictions still contain useful signal that could reduce experimental costs.

Method: Two complementary methods: (1) For population-level directional predictions (binary treatment effect sign), uses asymmetric testing with consistency and robustness bounds within learning-augmented algorithms paradigm; (2) For individual-level predictions, introduces Generalized PPI++ (GPPI) that extends Prediction-Powered Inference to handle nonlinear prediction errors through higher-dimensional transformations.

Result: Validated framework using persona-based LLM simulations (AI agents with user personas predicting behavior) spanning both granularity levels. Experiments on four real-world datasets show substantial reduction in experimental costs while preserving rigorous statistical validity.

Conclusion: The proposed learning-augmented hypothesis testing framework effectively leverages predictions of unknown quality to reduce A/B testing costs, maintaining statistical robustness against inaccurate predictions while benefiting from accurate ones, with applications validated through persona-based LLM simulations.

Abstract: A/B testing requires large sample sizes, long timelines, and significant costs. When auxiliary predictions of experimental outcomes are available from machine learning models, uncertain prediction quality precludes replacing human experiments entirely, yet these predictions may still contain useful signal. We propose a principled framework for learning-augmented hypothesis testing that leverages predictions of unknown quality to reduce sample sizes while maintaining statistical validity. Predictions naturally vary in granularity, from coarse aggregate signals to fine-grained individual-level estimates, and our framework addresses both ends of this spectrum: (1) for population-level directional predictions, where only a binary signal on the treatment effect sign is available, we use an asymmetric test and prove consistency and robustness bounds within the learning-augmented algorithms paradigm; (2) for individual-level predictions, we introduce Generalized PPI++ (GPPI), extending Prediction-Powered Inference to handle nonlinear prediction errors through higher-dimensional transformations. Both methods benefit from accurate predictions while remaining robust to inaccurate or adversarial ones. We validate our framework using persona-based LLM simulations, where AI agents equipped with user personas predict individual behavior, as a natural prediction source spanning both granularity levels. Experiments on four real-world datasets demonstrate that our methods, combined with persona-based predictions, substantially reduce experimental costs while preserving rigorous statistical validity.

</details>


### [305] [iSDFT: Information-Proximal Self-Distillation for Continual Learning in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24646)
*Ahmed Khaled Khamis,Xiaotong Ji,Hassan Jaber,Rasul Tutunov,Matthieu Zimmer,Jun Wang,Haitham Bou-Ammar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: iSDFT improves on-policy self-distillation by controlling how much teacher information is transferred at each prediction state, rather than always distilling toward the full demonstration-conditioned teacher.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current SDFT always distills toward the full demonstration-conditioned teacher, fixing teacher influence at the full-teacher endpoint without control over how much demonstration information should be transferred at each prediction state.

Method: Introduces Information-Proximal SDFT (iSDFT) that treats teacher as a budgeted information source. At each token, selects distribution closest to current student that satisfies prescribed teacher-information constraint, yielding closed-form exponential target with locally determined tilt. Also anchors student to frozen base policy to control cumulative drift.

Result: Across 4 LLM backbones and 2 specialization tasks, iSDFT improves vanilla SDFT in 7/8 model-task settings, matches in remaining one. Provides tighter retention on original SDFT benchmark suite (73% evaluations within 0.5 points of base model vs 52% for strongest baseline), and achieves largest mean improvement on 10 additional math/coding/competition-math benchmarks.

Conclusion: Controlling how much and when teacher information is introduced improves specialization while preserving broader capability.

Abstract: On-policy self-distillation fine-tuning (SDFT) learns new skills from demonstrations while reducing forgetting, but it always distils toward the full demonstration-conditioned teacher. This fixes teacher influence at the full-teacher endpoint, providing no control over how much demonstration information should be transferred at each prediction state. We introduce Information-Proximal SDFT (iSDFT), which instead treats the teacher as a budgeted source of information. At each token, iSDFT selects the distribution closest to the current student that satisfies a prescribed teacher-information constraint, yielding a closed-form exponential target with a locally determined tilt. To control cumulative drift, we further anchor the student to its frozen base policy. Across four heterogeneous LLM backbones and two specialisation tasks, iSDFT improves vanilla SDFT in 7 of 8 model-task settings and matches it in the remaining one. It also provides tighter retention on the original SDFT benchmark suite, with 73% of evaluations remaining within 0.5 points of the base model versus 52% for the strongest baseline, while achieving the largest mean improvement on all ten additional mathematics, coding, and competition-mathematics benchmarks. These results show that controlling how much and when teacher information is introduced improves specialisation while preserving broader capability.

</details>


### [306] [SPeaR: Test-Time Adaptation with Steering Primitives for Realigning Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24111)
*Muhammad Sudipto Siam Dip,Ali Etemad*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SPeaR is a test-time adaptation method that steers frozen pretrained models' intermediate representations using lightweight learnable modules instead of updating model parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing test-time adaptation methods adapt pretrained models by updating their parameters, which limits what can be adapted and where adaptation can occur within the network. The authors want a more flexible approach that keeps the pretrained network frozen while enabling adaptation.

Method: SPeaR inserts lightweight learnable modules at stage boundaries in frozen pretrained networks. These primitives are optimized directly from the test stream without source data or supervised warm-up. Optimization uses a gated objective that reduces uncertainty only when beneficial, a diversity regularizer to prevent collapse, and a multi-depth anchor for stability.

Result: SPeaR consistently matches or outperforms methods that adapt orders of magnitude more parameters across CIFAR-10-C, CIFAR-100-C, and ImageNet-C. It remains robust across wide batch sizes, preserves source-domain performance during continual adaptation, and the same primitive transfers across convolutional and Transformer architectures.

Conclusion: Steering early representations is the most effective test-time adaptation strategy, and lightweight modules that steer intermediate representations can achieve comparable or better performance than full parameter adaptation while maintaining the integrity of the pretrained model.

Abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) addresses distribution shift using only unlabeled test data. Existing methods typically adapt pretrained models by updating their parameters, limiting both what is adapted and where adaptation can occur within the network. We instead keep the pretrained network frozen and steer its intermediate representations. We introduce SPeaR (Steering Primitive for Realigning Representations), which inserts lightweight learnable modules at stage boundaries and optimizes them directly from the test stream, requiring neither source data nor supervised warm-up. Each primitive is optimized using a gated objective that reduces uncertainty only when adaptation is beneficial, along with a diversity regularizer to prevent collapse, and a multi-depth anchor to stabilize adaptation. We show that steering early representations is the most effective strategy, and that the same primitive transfers across convolutional and Transformer architectures. Across CIFAR-10-C, CIFAR-100-C, and ImageNet-C, SPeaR consistently matches or outperforms methods that adapt orders of magnitude more parameters, remains robust across a wide range of batch sizes, and preserves source-domain performance during continual adaptation.

</details>


### [307] [Corrective Forcing: Unified Post-Training for Diffusions and Flows in Generative Speech Enhancement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24651)
*Qing Yao,Lijian Gao,Qirong Mao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Corrective Forcing (CoF) is a post-training paradigm that addresses training-inference mismatch in diffusion and flow models for speech enhancement by forcing models to learn from self-generated rollouts and correct their predictions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion and flow models for speech enhancement suffer from a training-inference mismatch: during training they use analytical path states, but during inference they use self-generated rollout states along sampling trajectories, causing prediction and discretization errors to accumulate.

Method: CoF corrects clean-speech predictions on rollout states toward ground truth under dynamic sampling schedules, exposing models to varying inference conditions. It regularizes local evolution using locally corrected counterfactual transitions as references for factual transitions, using a shared clean-speech prediction parameterization applicable across diffusion and flow formulations.

Result: Experiments with SB-VE and OT-CFM models demonstrate improvements in perceptual quality and reconstruction fidelity, together with robust performance across different numbers of sampling steps.

Conclusion: Corrective Forcing provides an effective post-training paradigm to address training-inference mismatch in diffusion and flow models for speech enhancement, improving performance and robustness across various inference conditions.

Abstract: Diffusion and flow models, as promising generative paradigms for speech enhancement, face a training--inference mismatch: training uses analytical path states, whereas inference recursively evaluates models on self-generated rollout states along discretized sampling trajectories. This mismatch causes prediction and discretization errors to accumulate. To address it, we introduce Corrective Forcing (CoF), a post-training paradigm that forces diffusion and flow models to learn from self-generated rollouts and correct their predictions. CoF corrects clean-speech predictions on rollout states toward the ground truth under dynamic sampling schedules, exposing the model to varying inference conditions. It further regularizes local evolution using locally corrected counterfactual transitions as references for factual transitions. By expressing model outputs through a shared clean-speech prediction parameterization, CoF applies the same post-training objective across diffusion and flow formulations. Experiments with SB-VE and OT-CFM demonstrate improvements in perceptual quality and reconstruction fidelity, together with robust performance across different numbers of sampling steps.

</details>


### [308] [PAC-Bayesian Meta-Learning for Few-Shot Identification of Linear Dynamical Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24117)
*Chenfeng Huang,George Michailidis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A PAC-Bayesian meta-learning framework (PBML-LTI) for few-shot linear time-invariant system identification that handles temporal dependence and provides uncertainty quantification with theoretical guarantees.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional LTI system identification faces challenges with short, noisy, or high-dimensional trajectories and cannot exploit shared structure across related systems. Most meta-learning methods assume i.i.d. data, which doesn't hold for sequential LTI trajectories.

Method: Proposed PBML-LTI framework learns a transferable prior over task-specific LTI dynamics while preserving task heterogeneity. Uses Bayesian adaptation for new systems with limited data. Addresses temporal dependence with martingale PAC-Bayes analysis and derives support-query predictive-risk bound, leading to fit-KL meta-training objective.

Result: Provides accurate system estimates with principled uncertainty quantification for new LTI systems using limited data. Theoretical results include finite-sample guarantees for dependent dynamical data, transition-matrix recovery, and multi-step trajectory prediction.

Conclusion: PBML-LTI enables effective few-shot LTI system identification by leveraging shared structure across systems while handling temporal dependence, with theoretical guarantees connecting uncertainty-aware meta-identification to finite-sample analysis of dependent data.

Abstract: Identifying linear time-invariant (LTI) dynamical systems is challenging when trajectories are short, noisy, or high-dimensional. Traditional system identification typically treats each system independently and cannot exploit shared structure across related systems. We propose PBML-LTI, a PAC-Bayesian meta-learning framework for few-shot LTI system identification that learns a transferable prior over task-specific dynamics while preserving task heterogeneity. Each task corresponds to an unknown LTI system, and the meta-learner uses training trajectories to learn a data-dependent prior over transition matrices. For a new system with limited data, PBML-LTI performs Bayesian adaptation under this prior to obtain a task-specific posterior, providing accurate estimates and principled uncertainty quantification.
  A key challenge is temporal dependence, since LTI trajectories violate the i.i.d. assumptions underlying most PAC-Bayes meta-learning analyses. We address this with a martingale PAC-Bayes analysis for dependent trajectory losses and derive a support-query predictive-risk bound that motivates a fit-KL meta-training objective. The bound clarifies the roles of empirical fit, posterior complexity, and prior quality in few-shot adaptation under sequential dependence. We further derive corollaries for transition-matrix recovery and multi-step trajectory prediction, connecting uncertainty-aware meta-identification with finite-sample guarantees for dependent dynamical data.

</details>


### [309] [Enhancing Transformer Representations of Symbolic ODE Expressions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24746)
*Xiyue Fan,Adam Prugel-Bennett,Stuart E. Middleton*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces tree positional embeddings and contrastive learning to improve transformer models' ability to learn structured symbolic representations of differential equations that preserve commutative properties, showing consistent performance advantages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current approaches to solving differential equations focus on numerical approximations or blind symbolic search through fitting to numerical data, but lack structured representations that preserve commutative properties and support mathematical reasoning in symbolic forms. Standard transformer positional embeddings are designed for sequences and may not efficiently capture the hierarchical tree structures of symbolic differential equations.

Method: The authors investigate tree positional embeddings for symbolic ODE tasks, systematically studying their effectiveness across different settings. They apply contrastive learning to support commutative properties in mathematics based on learned structural representations, and conduct ablation studies to understand how these methods interact in modeling symbolic mathematical structures.

Result: Tree positional embeddings aid learning in early epochs and continue to improve performance throughout training, yielding consistent advantages across various data sizes and tasks. The learned structural representations enable better preservation of commutative properties through contrastive learning.

Conclusion: Tree positional embeddings significantly enhance transformer models' ability to learn structured symbolic representations of differential equations, supporting mathematical reasoning and commutative properties that are often overlooked in traditional numerical approximation approaches.

Abstract: Existing approaches to solving differential equations, such as symbolic regression, physics informed neural networks, and neural operators, typically focus on numerical approximations or blind symbolic search via fitting to numerical data. Less attention has been paid to learning structured representations of mathematical expressions that preserve commutative properties and could support mathematical reasoning in symbolic forms. Transformer models have shown strong capabilities in solving symbolic differential equations. However, standard positional embeddings in transformers are designed for sequence data. Symbolic differential equations are naturally represented by expression trees, so these positional embeddings may not efficiently capture their hierarchical structures. We investigate existing tree positional embeddings in symbolic ordinary differential equation (ODE) tasks. We systematically study their effectiveness under different settings. Our results show that tree positional embeddings aid learning in early epochs and continue to improve performance throughout, ultimately yielding consistent advantages across various data sizes and tasks. Based on learned structural representations, we apply contrastive learning to support the commutative property in mathematics. Ablation studies provide insight into how these methods interact in modelling symbolic mathematical structures.

</details>


### [310] [CLOOPD: Closing the Learner Loop in On-Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24141)
*Keye Zheng,Hanyu Li,Zhan Cheng,Yuan Gao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CLOOPD introduces a closed-loop framework for on-policy distillation that separates teacher-signal acquisition from student-side realization, enabling better allocation of actor work under token budgets and improving sample efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing on-policy distillation methods consume teacher-scored trajectories with just one actor update, potentially wasting valuable teacher signals. There's a need to better utilize scored batches by allowing multiple passes and measuring realization quality.

Method: CLOOPD separates teacher-signal acquisition from realization: selects adaptive α waypoints within KL envelope, freezes scored batches and advantages, re-forwards student after each actor pass, measures realization, and allocates actor work under token budgets. Includes deterministic 2-/3-pass policies and token-priced variants.

Result: Across six 300-step runs, all CLOOPD policies improved over one-pass TOP-D: macro accuracy increased from 15.41 to 17.78 (CLOOPD-Fixed2) and 19.36 (CLOOPD-Fixed3). CLOOPD-Fixed3 reached 15.35 accuracy at step 100, nearly matching TOP-D's step-300 performance while using 67.2% fewer teacher-scored tokens and 28.0% fewer GPU-hours.

Conclusion: CLOOPD provides an effective framework for budgeting how fully students learn from teacher-scored tokens, demonstrating significant efficiency gains and positioning as a valuable approach for on-policy distillation with constrained resources.

Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) pays twice for each fresh batch: the student generates trajectories and a stronger teacher scores them. Existing methods improve which trajectories are scored and how the teacher signal is constructed, but usually consume it with one actor update. We introduce CLOOPD, a closed-loop framework separating teacher-signal acquisition from student-side realization. CLOOPD selects an adaptive $α$ waypoint inside a KL envelope, freezes the scored batch and its advantages, re-forwards the student after each actor pass, measures realization, and allocates actor work under a separate token budget. The framework includes deterministic two- and three-pass policies, token-priced CLOOPD-TPMR, and a budget-matched control. Across six 300-step runs on an 8-H20 node, every CLOOPD policy improves the one-pass TOP-D anchor at comparable teacher-token scale: macro accuracy rises from 15.41 to 17.78 with CLOOPD-Fixed2 and 19.36 with CLOOPD-Fixed3. At step 100, CLOOPD-Fixed3 reaches 15.35, nearly matching TOP-D at step 300 while using 67.2% fewer teacher-scored tokens and 28.0% fewer GPU-hours. Earlier 8-A100 ablations show adaptive $α$ eliminates observed trust-envelope violations; a third pass adds headroom. These results position CLOOPD as a framework for budgeting how fully students learn from teacher-scored tokens.

</details>


### [311] [When Tomorrow Becomes Today: Self-Evolving Policies for Agentic Time-Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24862)
*Yifan Hu,Xilin Dai,Zhiyuan Qu,Yiding Liu,Zewei Dong,Jiang-ming Yang,Qiang Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TimEvolve is a time series agent that systematically converts realized outcomes into persistent joint updates of expert trust, path selection, and intervention strength, achieving state-of-the-art performance across multiple domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current time series agents don't systematically convert realized outcomes into persistent updates to the joint orchestration policy. They primarily use prior experience through forecast refinement, reflection, or retrieval, but lack systematic conversion of delayed feedback from deployment into policy updates for later forecasting.

Method: TimEvolve uses a frozen-backbone architecture that converts each realized outcome into persistent joint updates of expert trust, agent path selection, and intervention strength. It follows a temporally ordered predict, reveal, and update protocol that applies feedback to subsequent forecasts. The system commits all numerical expert forecasts and candidate agent paths before target observation, allowing each realized outcome to evaluate the entire alternative set.

Result: Experiments across eight Time-MMD domains show TimEvolve achieves the best average MSE and MAE ranks among fifteen methods and the lowest errors on both metrics in seven domains. It demonstrates superior performance in agentic time series forecasting through systematic learning from deployment feedback.

Conclusion: The results demonstrate the value of learning forecasting policies from the futures encountered during deployment. Systematic conversion of delayed feedback into persistent joint policy updates enables superior adaptation in evolving time series environments.

Abstract: Agentic time series forecasting concerns systems whose underlying mechanisms evolve, making the relative effectiveness of numerical models, reasoning strategies, and intervention rules inherently time-varying. Consequently, a time series agent must adapt the forecasts it produces and the orchestration policy that determines which components to trust and how to coordinate them. The deployment process naturally provides supervision for this adaptation as forecast horizons elapse and realized targets reveal the effectiveness of earlier decisions. Committing all numerical expert forecasts and candidate agent paths before target observation allows each realized outcome to evaluate the entire alternative set, providing delayed feedback without additional annotation. However, existing time series agents primarily incorporate prior experience through forecast refinement, reflection, or retrieval, without systematically converting realized outcomes into persistent updates to the joint orchestration policy governing later origins. To exploit this delayed feedback systematically, we introduce TimEvolve, a frozen-backbone time series agent that converts each realized outcome into persistent joint updates of expert trust, agent path selection, and intervention strength. A temporally ordered predict, reveal, and update protocol applies this feedback to subsequent forecasts. Experiments across eight Time-MMD domains show that TimEvolve achieves the best average MSE and MAE ranks among fifteen methods and the lowest errors on both metrics in seven domains. These results demonstrate the value of learning forecasting policies from the futures encountered during deployment.

</details>


### [312] [Luck Is Not Skill: When Do Paired Rollouts Help Group-Relative RL of LLM Agents?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24144)
*Nazmus Sakib*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Pairing rollouts with shared noise schedules reduces reward-contrast variance but doesn't always reduce gradient variance, showing the distinction between improving reward comparisons and actual learning benefits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Independent environment noise in group-relative reinforcement learning obscures comparisons between rollouts of the same prompt, making it hard to distinguish signal from noise when evaluating reward contrasts.

Method: Introduces paired rollouts that share an event-keyed noise schedule within each group while preserving each rollout's marginal distribution. Studies the method theoretically and empirically with a controlled study training a 2B tool-use agent under tool faults and grader flips.

Result: Under tool faults, pairing improves final noisy-test success by +5.1 percentage points on average with all three seeds showing positive differences, though misses the registered learning-curve criterion. Gradient probe shows lower mean-centered covariance traces: 21-30% for grader flips and 40-63% for tool faults.

Conclusion: Pairing reduces between-schedule variance in reward contrasts but doesn't guarantee reduced gradient variance or learning speed benefits, highlighting the distinction between improving reward comparisons and actual learning improvements.

Abstract: Group-relative reinforcement learning compares rollouts of the same prompt, but independent environment noise can obscure these comparisons. We study paired rollouts, which share an event-keyed noise schedule within each group while preserving each rollout's marginal distribution. Pairing removes the between-schedule component of reward-contrast variance, but need not reduce gradient variance. For one-sided grader noise, we derive an exact condition for reduction and give a counterexample in which reward contrasts improve while gradient variance increases. A controlled study trains a 2B tool-use agent under tool faults and grader flips, with three seeds per design. The protocol was registered with a disclosed, previously completed pilot. Under tool faults, pairing improves final noisy-test success by +5.1 percentage points on average, with all three seed differences positive, but misses the registered learning-curve criterion. The criterion is also missed under grader flips: the validation-AUC difference is +0.003 (95% interval [-0.029, +0.033]). A gradient probe on eight distinct checkpoints from two fault-trained trajectories finds lower mean-centered covariance traces under both noise types: 21 to 30% for grader flips and 40 to 63% for tool faults. These finite-sample measurements support the variance mechanism without establishing a general learning-speed benefit. The results distinguish improving reward comparisons, reducing estimator variance, and improving learning.

</details>


### [313] [Exactness at Inference: A Representational Criterion for Out-of-Distribution Generalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24942)
*Filipe Marinho Rocha,Inês Dutra,Vítor Santos Costa,Luís Paulo Reis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper argues that models only generalize out-of-distribution when they compute representations structurally equivalent to the generating mechanism, not approximations. This exactness enables extrapolation and constrains inference, with tensor logic at zero temperature providing an example that passes this criterion.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to understand why models fail to generalize outside their training distribution. Current approaches often fit approximations rather than discovering structurally equivalent representations, leading to poor extrapolation and inability to handle novel entities or distant queries.

Method: The paper uses Tensor Logic as a framework to analyze generalization. At zero temperature, tensor contraction becomes equivalent to discrete logic with orthonormal embeddings and Boolean tensors. The approach establishes a criterion for exact representability and applies it to analyze different architectures including Logic Tensor Networks, differentiable ILP, and hybrid models.

Result: Results show that exact representations (not approximations) are necessary for out-of-distribution generalization. Tensor Logic at T=0 and differentiable ILP pass the exactness criterion, while Logic Tensor Networks fail. The paper identifies piecewise-affine extrapolation divergence and inability to bind novel entities as manifestations of this shortfall. On law-derived partitions, exact representations can answer 56.3% of distant queries that ensembles handle with false confidence.

Conclusion: The conclusion advocates for inducing exact representations rather than fitting approximations, as only exact hypothesis classes can certify what training data leave underdetermined. Common inductive biases reach exactness only through human injection, supporting the argument for discovering structurally equivalent mechanisms rather than surrogates whose residuals diverge outside training data and compound under composition.

Abstract: A model generalizes outside its training distribution only when it computes a representation structurally equivalent to the generating mechanism, not an approximation fitted to it. Such equivalence is necessary for exactness in and out of distribution, and extrapolation is governed by this exactness at inference, whatever its realization. Tensor Logic shows this: a zero-temperature contraction is equivalent to discrete logic, deducing in place with no artefact extracted, its tensors Boolean, its embeddings orthonormal, only its arithmetic continuous. Lacking infinite recursion it reaches Datalog, not Prolog, and though exact over closed domains it needs external memory to bind a novel entity. The criterion needs neither a discrete representation nor an extracted expression, and constrains inference, not training: an exact marginal in $[0,1]$ passes, a Neural Network thresholded to a hard label does not. Logic Tensor Networks fail it, while differentiable ILP and Tensor Logic at $T=0$ pass. Piecewise-affine extrapolation divergence and an inability to bind novel entities are two faces of a shortfall in exact representability. For hybrid architectures, a propagation rule follows: the output inherits the bounds of every fitted estimator on its path, explaining which axes fail in equivariant models and the ARC-AGI induction/transduction split. Only an exact hypothesis class certifies what the training data leave underdetermined: on a law-derived partition it finds the $56.3\%$ of distant queries that are answerable, which ensembles meet with false confidence and distance metrics rank backwards. Common inductive biases, from symmetries to memory, reach exactness only because humans inject them, an argument for inducing exact representations rather than fitting surrogates whose residuals, even at the arithmetic floor in training, diverge outside the data and compound under composition.

</details>


### [314] [Mind or Message? Auditing Theory of Mind in Multi-Agent Social Simulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24146)
*Cong Li,Cheng Chen,Thomas Fung,Alex Rossi,Yi Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Language model agents in social simulations appear socially fluent but economically poor - they negotiate successfully (96.2% agreement) but miss optimal deals, leaving 20.5% value unclaimed, because they track conversation surface rather than inferring partner's actual mental states.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate whether language model agents in social simulations genuinely understand partners' minds or merely respond to surface conversation features. The authors aim to determine if agents engage in true mental state inference or just surface-level processing.

Method: Created 40 multi-issue negotiations with known hidden preference weights and Pareto frontiers. Two model families negotiated across 160 dyads, with transcripts frozen before analysis. Conducted 2880 counterfactual probes manipulating single factors: reader's stake, partner's tone, identity label, and recursion order while keeping evidence identical.

Result: Agents reached agreement in 96.2% of dyads but only 0.7% of deals were Pareto optimal, leaving 20.5% joint value unclaimed. They missed perfectly aligned issues in 76.6% of deals. Probes showed agents engage in egocentric projection (15.0% priority shift when own payoff changed) rather than true inference. Agents predicted partner's beliefs about them 72.5% correctly, but those partner beliefs were only 51.2% correct.

Conclusion: Language model agents in social simulations are socially fluent but economically inefficient negotiators because they track surface conversation features rather than inferring actual mental states. They engage in egocentric projection and lack true theory of mind despite appearing to understand partners.

Abstract: Language model agents are increasingly used to simulate social interaction, and the resulting transcripts read as though the agents understand one another. We ask whether that appearance rests on a model of the partner's mind or on the surface record of what the partner said. We build a social simulation in which both questions have exact answers: 40 multi-issue negotiations whose hidden preference weights and whose full Pareto frontier are known by construction. Two model families negotiate across 160 dyads, every transcript is frozen before any measurement, and 2880 counterfactual probes then hold the evidence byte identical while moving one factor at a time: the reader's own stake, the partner's tone, an identity label, and the order of recursion. The agents are socially fluent and economically poor. They reach agreement in 96.2% of dyads with 0 protocol failures, yet only 0.7% of deals land on the Pareto frontier, they leave 20.5% of the available joint value unclaimed, and they miss the one issue on which their interests are perfectly aligned in 76.6% of deals; on the frontier and on that aligned issue, a package drawn at random from the set both sides would accept does as well. The probes locate the failure. Swapping only the reader's own payoff sheet, while the partner's words and offers stay identical, moves the inferred top priority by 15.0 percentage points, which is egocentric projection rather than inference, while a tone rewrite moves it by 5.3 percentage points and an identity label by 0.0. Most tellingly, an agent predicts what its partner believes about it 72.5% of the time while that partner's belief is itself correct only 51.2% of the time: the agents track the conversation far better than they track the mind behind it.

</details>


### [315] [Rare Event Estimation via Iterative Unalignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24969)
*Hanming Yang,Daksh Mittal,Jing Dong,Hongseok Namkoong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Novel importance sampling method using differentiably parameterized language models to efficiently estimate extremely rare event probabilities in stochastic agent trajectories, achieving 800× computational efficiency gains over naive Monte Carlo for events with probabilities below 10⁻⁷.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As autonomous agents become more prevalent, extremely rare catastrophic events along their stochastic trajectories can occur. Safe deployment requires understanding how often these rare events might happen, not just whether they can occur. Estimating such probabilities is computationally challenging due to the combinatorial explosion of possible trajectories.

Method: Develops a new importance sampling method that perturbs the original model's weights to construct a proposal distribution. The proposal is itself a differentiably parameterized language model, enabling gradient-based search over weight space. Combines a differentiable surrogate for event amplification with adaptive regularization that dynamically balances amplification against estimator stability.

Result: Evaluated on ~120M and ~2.6B models across three event families spanning 300+ rare events as rare as 10⁻⁹. Achieved over 800× compute-weighted efficiency gains over naive Monte Carlo for events with probabilities lower than 10⁻⁷, with reference probabilities computed with <10% relative standard error.

Conclusion: The proposed gradient-based importance sampling approach enables efficient estimation of extremely rare event probabilities in large language models, addressing a critical safety need for autonomous agent deployment by providing reliable risk quantification without prohibitive computational costs.

Abstract: As agents are deployed with increased autonomy, even extremely rare events along their stochastic output trajectories can occur and prove catastrophic. Safe deployment therefore does not depend on whether these events can occur, but on how often they might. We study the problem of estimating the probability of rare events that arise from stochastic variation in the agent's own actions. Estimating this type of risk requires searching over the combinatorially vast space of trajectories. Naive Monte Carlo is computationally prohibitive in this regime, and constructing effective importance sampling (IS) proposals requires coordinated changes to a context-dependent chain of conditional distributions. We develop a new IS method that perturbs the original model's weights to construct the proposal. The proposal is itself a differentiably parameterized language model, enabling gradient-based search over weight space. We formulate an objective that combines a differentiable surrogate for event amplification and an adaptive regularization scheme that dynamically balances amplification against estimator stability. We evaluate our approach on $\sim$120M and $\sim$2.6B models across three event families spanning 300+ rare events as rare as $10^{-9}$, with reference probabilities computed with $<10\%$ relative standard error. In our most verifiable settings, we observe that our IS estimator achieves over $800\times$ compute-weighted efficiency gains over naive Monte Carlo for events with probabilities lower than $10^{-7}$. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/namkoong-lab/iterative-unalignment.

</details>


### [316] [Acceptance-Aware Draft Model Training for Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24150)
*Tianhua Xia,Mugilan Ganesan,Yifei Feng,Haiyu Wang,Maximilian Egger,Sai Qian Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes new training losses that directly optimize acceptance length in speculative decoding, rather than using distribution-matching proxies like KL divergence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current draft-model training methods optimize cross-entropy or KL divergence as proxies, but these don't directly optimize acceptance length - the key determinant of speculative decoding speedup. Additionally, acceptance mechanisms differ between greedy and sampling-based decoding, requiring tailored approaches.

Method: 1. For greedy verification: Expected Accepted Length (EAL) loss that explicitly maximizes expected acceptance length.
2. For sampling-based decoding: Window Total Variation (WTV) loss that optimizes overlap between temperature-scaled draft and target distributions while accounting for sequential acceptance dependencies.
3. Both can be combined with Group-Relative Reinforcement Learning (GRPO) using simulated acceptance length as reward.

Result: Experiments across different target/draft models, tasks, and decoding settings show consistent improvement in acceptance length over KL-based training. WTV provides strong gains under sampling-based decoding, while EAL better matches greedy verification.

Conclusion: Directly optimizing the acceptance objective with losses tailored to the decoding mode is more effective than conventional distribution-matching objectives for speculative decoding.

Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) inference by using a lightweight draft model to generate multiple candidate tokens that are verified by the target model in a single forward pass. Its speedup is largely determined by the acceptance length, yet existing draft-model training methods mainly optimize cross-entropy or Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence as proxies. These objectives encourage distribution matching but do not directly optimize acceptance length, and the acceptance mechanism also differs between greedy and sampling-based decoding.
  In this work, we propose acceptance-length-aware training losses that directly optimize the expected number of accepted tokens within a speculative window. For greedy verification, we derive an expected accepted length (EAL) loss that explicitly maximizes expected acceptance length. For sampling-based decoding, we introduce a window total variation (WTV) loss that optimizes the overlap between temperature-scaled draft and target distributions while accounting for sequential acceptance dependencies. Both objectives can be further combined with a group-relative reinforcement learning stage (GRPO) using simulated acceptance length as the reward.
  Experiments across different target and draft models, tasks, and decoding settings show that our losses consistently improve acceptance length over KL-based training. WTV provides particularly strong gains under sampling-based decoding, while EAL better matches greedy verification. These results show that directly optimizing the acceptance objective, with losses tailored to the decoding mode, is more effective than conventional distribution-matching objectives.

</details>


### [317] [RRSI: Regularized Recursive Self-Improvement of Agent Harnesses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24972)
*Peng Xia,Rujun Han,Zifeng Wang,Yanfei Chen,Yufan Zhang,Yoonho Lee,Chengsong Huang,Han Yu,Zhongying CuiZhu,Yifei Ming,Huaxiu Yao,Burak Gokturk,Tomas Pfister,Chen-Yu Lee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RRSI introduces regularization techniques into recursive self-improvement of LLM agent harnesses to prevent overfitting to training tasks and improve generalization to out-of-distribution benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current recursive self-improvement methods for LLM agent harnesses tend to overfit to training tasks, showing large in-distribution performance gains that don't generalize well to out-of-distribution benchmarks, limiting the practical utility of automated harness evolution.

Method: RRSI incorporates regularization principles through a constrained proposal and selection framework: (1) proposer with temporally annealed budget limiting edit bundles and encouraging unexplored trajectories, (2) selector with critic screening benchmark-specific proposals and pruner removing small, expensive, or useless changes.

Result: Across eight benchmarks (coding, agentic workspace, engineering design), RRSI achieves up to 14.1 points improvement on evolved splits and up to 4.7 points on five out-of-distribution benchmarks, while producing harnesses that run on 30% fewer policy tokens than unregularized evolution.

Conclusion: Regularizing harness self-improvement with constrained proposal and selection mechanisms effectively prevents overfitting, improves generalization to unseen tasks, and produces more efficient agent systems compared to unregularized evolution approaches.

Abstract: An LLM agent's capability is largely magnified by its harness, namely the prompts, control flow, tooling, memory, and context management surrounding the frozen backbone model. Recent methods increasingly automate this process by iteratively proposing and selecting component-wise edits of an agent harness, practically establishing a form of recursive self-improvement (RSI) at the agent-system level. However, such recursive evolution may overfit by memorizing the training tasks, showing large in-distribution gains that shrink or even vanish on out-of-distribution benchmarks. We introduce Regularized Recursive Self-Improvement of Agent Harnesses (RRSI), which incorporates the principles of regularizations into harness self-improvement by constraining the evolution candidate proposal and selection. The proposer operates with a temporally annealed budget, limiting how many edits a candidate can bundle, and it encourages unexplored trajectories based on evolution history. The selector is equipped with a critic and a pruner: the critic screens benchmark-specific proposals, while the pruner, removes changes that are too small, too expensive, or no longer useful. Together these constraints favor reusable agent mechanisms over benchmark-specific ones or even noises. Across eight benchmarks spanning coding, agentic workspace and engineering design tasks, RRSI gains up to 14.1 points on the split it evolves against and up to 4.7 points on the five out-of-distribution benchmarks, while producing a harness that runs on 30% fewer policy tokens than the unregularized evolution. Code is available at https://github.com/google-research/rrsi and project page is https://regularized-rsi.com/.

</details>


### [318] [H-Spec: Parallel Speculative Decoding Without a Drafter-Side KV Cache](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24197)
*Weifan Jiang,Krishna Teja Chitty-Venkata,Megan Flynn,Reed Meyerson,Zhenting Qi,Tianyu Wu,Eldar Kurtic,Minlan Yu,Alexandre Marques*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: H-Spec is a hybrid Mamba-attention parallel drafter for speculative decoding that combines target-context injection methods to eliminate separate drafter KV cache overhead while maintaining draft quality throughout blocks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current block diffusion drafters for speculative decoding suffer from overhead: they require separate drafter-side KV caches that grow with concurrency (increasing memory and KV-write costs), or using direct target KV reuse fails to maintain draft quality through entire blocks.

Method: Proposes hybrid target-context injection: complements direct target KV reuse with target hidden states only at the last input position, requiring no separate drafter KV cache. H-Spec implements this with hybrid Mamba-attention parallel drafter: Mamba modules initialized with projected last-token hidden states, while attention modules reuse target KVs in place. Mamba's parallel scan preserves block-parallel drafting despite its recurrent formulation.

Result: Across three target models and diverse tasks: improves 5.0-13.3% in mean accepted length and 5.3-12.6% in batch-size-1 inter-token latency speedup. Under concurrent serving: consistently achieves higher throughput with lower KV cache utilization than baselines across evaluated concurrency levels.

Conclusion: H-Spec successfully addresses the trade-off between draft quality and KV cache overhead in speculative decoding by combining hybrid target-context injection with Mamba-attention architecture, achieving significant improvements in both decoding efficiency and serving performance.

Abstract: Speculative decoding losslessly accelerates large language model inference by having a lightweight draft model predict future tokens for verification by the target model. Recent block diffusion drafters further reduce drafting latency by predicting multiple tokens in parallel. However, existing block drafters project target hidden states at every input position into a separate drafter-side KV cache, incurring per-request memory and KV-write overhead that grow with concurrency; directly reusing target KVs in place removes this cache but fails to sustain draft quality throughout the block. We propose a hybrid target-context injection method that complements direct target KV reuse with target hidden states only at the last input position, requiring no separate drafter-side KV cache. Building on this design, we propose H-Spec, a hybrid Mamba-attention parallel drafter that consumes the two target-context sources through complementary modules. Mamba modules are initialized with projected last-token target hidden states, while attention modules reuse target KVs in place. Despite its recurrent formulation, Mamba's parallel scan allows H-Spec to preserve block-parallel drafting. Across three target models and diverse tasks, H-Spec improves over the best baseline by 5.0--13.3% in mean accepted length and 5.3--12.6% in batch-size-1 inter-token latency speedup. Under concurrent serving, H-Spec consistently achieves higher throughput while maintaining lower KV cache utilization than baselines across evaluated concurrency levels.

</details>


### [319] [Displacement Geometry Captures Platonic Shared Reality Across Models and Modalities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24209)
*Chenming Shang,Yujin Tang,Jun Jie Ou Yang,Ruize Xu,Adam Breuer,Nikhil Singh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Models share semantic geometry (directions between concepts) not absolute positions; capabilities can be transferred between models via linear alignment without fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To reconcile the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (which claims models converge on shared reality models) with recent findings of weak pointwise similarity between models, investigating what is actually shared across independently trained models.

Method: Analyze 44 independently trained vision and language encoders across modalities and capability pairs; use orthogonal alignment to examine preservation of displacement vectors; decompose representations into shared semantic vs private capability components.

Result: Displacement vectors (directions between samples) are substantially preserved across models after orthogonal alignment, while absolute positions are not; representations split into linearly aligned semantic components and non-aligned capability components; concept-level analysis shows parent concepts orthogonal to child variations.

Conclusion: Semantics align linearly but capabilities do not, enabling capability transfer between models using a single forward pass (Shadow Casting). This allows capabilities to be downloaded and imported across models without fine-tuning, as demonstrated by SHADOWCLIP outperforming fine-tuned baselines with far less compute.

Abstract: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) claims that independently trained models converge on a shared statistical model of reality, yet recent work finds only weak pointwise similarity between models. In this paper, we show that what models share is not the location of samples in representation space, but the directions (displacement vectors) between them. Under a single orthogonal alignment--rotation and reflection only--these displacement vectors are substantially preserved across 44 independently trained vision and language encoders spanning modalities and asymmetric capability pairs, consistent with the PRH evidence. The samples' absolute positions are not, consistent with recent counter-evidence. Both arise from a single decomposition: representations split into a shared semantic component that is linearly aligned across models, and a private capability component that is not. We trace this geometry to concept-level structure: within a model, parent concepts are orthogonal to their child variation vectors; across models, concept displacements are parallel. Our theory falsifiably predicts (and experiments confirm) that fine-tuning preserves pointwise similarity but collapses displacement, and that relational distillation does the opposite.
  A major implication is that, because semantics align linearly but capabilities do not, capabilities can be imported from one model to another using a single cached forward pass through the source. We call this Shadow Casting. As a proof of concept, our SHADOWCLIP instantiation outperforms strong fine-tuned baselines at orders of magnitude less compute. A cache can be released alongside open model weights, letting one model's capabilities be downloaded and imported into any number of other models without fine-tuning.

</details>


### [320] [Adaptive Forgetting for Nonstationary Optimization: Towards Robust EEG Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24233)
*Hongyu Zhu,Lin Chen,Jing Chen,Yuting Zhou,Mingsheng Shang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AFOR is a tensor-wise adaptive optimizer with dynamic second-moment decay coefficients that improves cross-subject EEG decoding by adapting to noisy, variable EEG signals through local gradient state analysis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cross-subject EEG decoding faces challenges due to low signal-to-noise ratios, subject variability, and gradient nonstationarity. Traditional Adam/AdamW optimizers use fixed second-moment decay coefficients that assume homogeneous gradient statistics across layers and time, which limits adaptability to cross-subject EEG signals and degrades generalization performance.

Method: AFOR converts fixed second-moment decay coefficient into dynamic coefficient estimated online from local gradient state. It combines two components: 1) Residual-Alignment Signal Scorer (RASS) that summarizes local gradient residuals and directional agreement into a signal-quality score, and 2) Adaptive Forgetting Controller (AFC) that maps this score through self-referential normalization to bounded per-step decay coefficient, with cumulative-product initialization correction maintaining consistency under time-varying decay.

Result: Under strict cross-subject protocol on three EEG benchmarks covering emotion recognition, motor imagery, and sleep staging, AFOR achieves best average performance among compared optimizers. It improves mean test accuracy over Adam by 3.00%, 2.07%, and 4.38% respectively on the three benchmarks.

Conclusion: AFOR successfully addresses limitations of fixed-coefficient optimizers for cross-subject EEG decoding by adaptively adjusting forgetting rates based on local gradient state, leading to improved generalization across subjects in practical EEG applications.

Abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) provides non-invasive monitoring of brain activity and is widely used in emotion recognition, motor imagery and sleep staging. Although within-subject decoding has achieved considerable progress, cross-subject generalization remains a central challenge in practical applications. EEG decoders are typically trained with Adam/AdamW under a fixed second-moment decay coefficient, even though cross-subject learning involves low signal-to-noise ratios, subject variability, and gradient nonstationarity. A fixed coefficient implicitly assumes that gradient statistics are homogeneous across layers and time, which can limit model's adaptability to cross-subject EEG signals and degrade generalization. To address these issues, we propose AFOR, a tensor-wise adaptive optimizer that converts the fixed second-moment decay coefficient into a dynamic coefficient estimated online from local gradient state. AFOR combines a Residual-Alignment Signal Scorer (RASS) and an Adaptive Forgetting Controller (AFC). RASS summarizes local gradient residuals and directional agreement into a signal-quality score, and AFC maps this score through self-referential normalization to a bounded per-step decay coefficient, with cumulative-product initialization correction maintaining consistency under time-varying decay.
  Under a strict cross-subject protocol on three EEG benchmarks that cover three representative fields, AFOR achieves the best average performance among the compared optimizers, improving the mean test accuracy over Adam by 3.00%, 2.07%, and 4.38%, respectively.

</details>


### [321] [Reinforcement Learning Inspired Black-box Adversarial Attacks for Computer Vision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24249)
*Florian Krone,Elena Hoemann,Sven Hallerbach*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A reinforcement learning inspired black-box adversarial attack (RIBA) that generates perturbations with fewer queries than state-of-the-art methods, matching white-box performance on adversarially trained models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neural networks in computer vision are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, but most attacks use unrealistic white-box threat models requiring full model access. There's a need for more practical black-box attacks that work with limited query access to target models.

Method: Proposes RIBA (Reinforcement Learning Inspired Black-box Adversarial attack), which leverages reinforcement learning concepts to optimize perturbations against non-differentiable target models in black-box settings. RL algorithms are inherently query-efficient, making them suitable for black-box attack scenarios.

Result: RIBA achieves significant query reductions: 25.4% fewer median queries against ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 and 22.5% fewer median queries against ViT-B/16 on ImageNet compared to state-of-the-art attacks. RIBA can also match white-box attack performance on adversarially trained models.

Conclusion: RIBA demonstrates that reinforcement learning principles can effectively optimize black-box adversarial attacks with high query efficiency, addressing practical limitations of existing attacks and making adversarial threats more realistic for safety-critical applications.

Abstract: Neural networks, both convolution or transformer based, are essential for modern computer vision systems. However, they are vulnerable to small perturbations, almost imperceptible to humans, which significantly alter the model's prediction. These adversarial attacks are often considered to be a significant threat to the implementation of neural networks in safety-critical applications. Most attacks utilize the white-box threat model and therefore require full access to the target model, making them unrealistic to use in practice. We propose a novel approach under the more realistic black-box threat model that utilizes concepts from reinforcement learning to optimize perturbations with a non-differentiable target model. Reinforcement learning algorithms have already been optimized to be query efficient, making them an ideal starting point when designing black-box adversarial attacks. We show the success of our reinforcement learning inspired black-box adversarial attack (RIBA) in generating adversarial perturbations using only a small number of queries to the target model, by comparing it to state of the art attacks on different models on the Cifar10 and ImageNet data sets. RIBA takes $25.4\%$ fewer median queries to generate attacked images against a ResNet-18 on Cifar10 and $22.5\%$ fewer median queries to fool a Vit-B/16 model on ImageNet. Additionally, we demonstrate that RIBA can match the performance of white-box attacks on an adversarially trained model.

</details>


### [322] [Explainable Predictive Condition-based Maintenance of Naval-Propulsion Systems using Fuzzy Logic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24250)
*Dionisis Kalogeropoulos,Georgia Sovatzidi,Panagiotis G. Kalozoumis,Dimitris K. Iakovidis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A novel explainable predictive maintenance framework using fuzzy decision trees and deep residual neural networks for naval vessels, achieving 99.24% accuracy with interpretable results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The shipping industry requires effective maintenance for operational availability and safety. While predictive maintenance offers advantages over conventional systems, existing methods lack explainability - they don't help users understand why failures occur, limiting trust and practical adoption.

Method: The paper proposes a novel framework combining a fuzzy decision tree with a deep residual neural network. The framework generates fuzzy local rules from datasets and provides explainable outcomes using cause-and-effect relationships that users can understand.

Result: Experiments on a publicly available dataset show the framework achieves 99.24% accuracy, demonstrating high effectiveness in predictive maintenance while providing interpretable explanations of its predictions.

Conclusion: The proposed explainable predictive maintenance framework successfully addresses the interpretability gap in existing systems, providing both high accuracy and understandable explanations, which builds user trust and enables better decision-making for naval vessel maintenance.

Abstract: The shipping industry has a significant impact on the global economy, emphasizing the need for operational availability and safety through the use of effective maintenance techniques. During the last decades, predictive maintenance (PdM) has emerged as a promising solution compared to the existing conventional maintenance systems. This is because it offers several advantageous functions, such as damage predictions for vessel components, reduced downtime, improved and extended life of machinery, as well as higher safety during voyages. However, existing methodologies developed for performing PdM do not provide explanations of their results to users, so that they can understand the failures that may occur. To address this limitation, this paper proposes a novel framework based on a fuzzy decision tree and a deep residual neural network, aiming to perform explainable PdM on naval vessels. The proposed framework is able to generate fuzzy local rules based on the dataset used, and can provide explanations of its outcomes, using cause-and-effect relationships, in a way that are understandable to users, thereby gaining their trust. Experiments using a publicly available dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, as it achieves an accuracy of 99.24%.

</details>


### [323] [High-Dimensional Online Change Point Detection with Adaptive Thresholding and Interpretability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24278)
*Sven Jacob,Bardh Prenkaj,Weijia Shao,Gjergji Kasneci*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A novel change point detection framework using Sliced Wasserstein distance for improved scalability and interpretability, reducing false positives by 48% while maintaining competitive detection performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional CPD methods face computational challenges in high-dimensional settings and provide limited explanations for detected changes, restricting practical usability in applications like activity recognition, finance, cybersecurity, manufacturing, and autonomous systems.

Method: Four key contributions: (1) Transform multivariate sequential data into 1D scores using SW distance, (2) Analyze distributional behavior showing random slices approximate Gamma distribution for threshold calibration, (3) Propose self-adapting online CPD algorithm with adaptive quantile-based threshold, (4) Introduce model-specific framework for contrastive explanations.

Result: Empirically reduces false positives by at least 48% on average compared to popular online and offline CPD baselines, while maintaining competitive or superior detection performance, with interpretable change-point annotations.
