Conclusion: The SW-based CPD framework offers practical improvements in scalability and interpretability, making it suitable for deployment in high-stakes applications where both accurate detection and explainability are crucial.

Abstract: Change point detection (CPD) identifies abrupt and significant changes in sequential data, with applications in human activity recognition, financial markets, cybersecurity, manufacturing, and autonomous systems. Traditional CPD methods often face computational challenges in high-dimensional settings and typically provide limited explanations for detected changes, which can restrict their practical usability. This paper introduces a CPD framework that improves scalability and interpretability by leveraging the Sliced Wasserstein (SW) distance. Our contributions are fourfold: (1) we transform multivariate sequential data into one-dimensional scores using the SW distance, making the resulting representation compatible with existing CPD methods; (2) we analyze the distributional behavior of random slices of the SW distance and show that, under suitable assumptions, they can be approximated by a Gamma distribution, providing a principled basis for threshold calibration; (3) we propose a self-adapting online CPD algorithm that combines this SW-based score with an adaptive quantile-based threshold; (4) we introduce a model-specific framework for generating contrastive explanations for annotated change points. Empirically, our method reduces false positives by at least $48\%$ on average compared with popular online and offline CPD baselines, while maintaining competitive or superior detection performance. Code is available at https://github.com/jsve96/SWCPD_Code. At the same time, it produces interpretable change-point annotations, making it practical for deployment in high-stakes applications.

</details>


### [324] [SupportCal: Label-Free Calibration of Post-Trained LLMs via Reference Support and Corroboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24303)
*Linhan Luo,Lequan Lin,Dai Shi,Feng Chen,José Miguel Hernández-Lobato,Junbin Gao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Post-trained language models often become overconfident. SupportCal introduces a label-free calibration method that weights disagreement examples based on PLM reference support, improving calibration over agreement-only approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Post-training improves task performance but degrades confidence calibration, making models overconfident. Since labeled calibration data is costly/unavailable, pretrained language models provide natural label-free references for calibration. Prior methods only use examples where post-trained and pretrained models agree, excluding disagreements, but this may not be optimal.

Method: SupportCal: a label-free post-hoc calibration method that retains agreement examples at unit weight and assigns continuous weights to disagreement examples based on the PLM's relative support and corroboration from pretrained references selected from a size-compatible candidate pool.

Result: SupportCal yields lower Expected Calibration Error (ECE) than agreement-only baseline for nearly all evaluated target-model configurations on MedMCQA and MathQA. Same pattern observed on TweetEval Sentiment classification task.

Conclusion: Reintroducing disagreement examples with continuous weighting based on PLM support improves calibration over binary agreement-only approaches. SupportCal provides effective label-free calibration by leveraging multiple pretrained references to assess disagreement examples.

Abstract: Post-training often improves task performance but can degrade confidence calibration, leaving post-trained language models (PoLMs) more overconfident than their corresponding pretrained language models (PLMs). Because task-specific labeled calibration data can be costly or unavailable, the corresponding pretrained PLM provides a natural label-free reference for post-hoc calibration. Prior agreement-gated PLM-referenced calibration fits a scalar temperature using only examples on which the PoLM and its PLM reference agree, excluding disagreement examples because direct alignment can drive the fitted temperature excessively high and induce under-confidence. We revisit this binary treatment. A controlled reintroduction diagnostic reveals a non-monotonic aggregate effect: admitting a moderate fraction of disagreement examples can improve calibration, whereas the benefit diminishes as unit-weight inclusion approaches the full disagreement set. We introduce SupportCal, a label-free post-hoc method that retains agreement examples at unit weight and assigns disagreement examples continuous weights based on the own-base PLM's relative support and corroboration from pretrained references selected from a size-compatible candidate pool. We further characterize when the resulting weighted objective admits a finite optimal temperature. Across MedMCQA and MathQA, SupportCal yields lower ECE than the agreement-only baseline for nearly all evaluated target-model configurations; supplementary TweetEval Sentiment results show the same pattern on a fixed-label classification task.

</details>


### [325] [A Distributional Optimisation Perspective on Combining Models in Deep Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24328)
*Congye Wang,Yan Lin,Zheyang Shen,Matthew A. Fisher,Chris. J. Oates*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a principled approach to joint training of model combinations using distributional optimization, analyzing ensembles and adapter averaging as entropy-regularized optimization problems, developing algorithms including functional variational gradient descent, and empirically validating on synthetic tasks and LLM fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current methods for combining predictions from different models use separate, ad hoc training of individual models and combination rules. Distributional optimization offers an opportunity for principled joint training by treating model collections as discrete distributions to be optimized, but this potential is not well-understood.

Method: The authors: (1) cast ensembles and low-rank adapter averaging as entropy-regularized distributional optimization, analyzing convexity properties; (2) develop algorithms including a functional variant of variational gradient descent; (3) conduct empirical study on synthetic classification tasks and fine-tuning large language models on commonsense reasoning benchmarks.

Result: The paper identifies that ensemble optimization yields a convex objective while adapter-averaging does not, meaning existing convergence guarantees for mean field Langevin dynamics only apply to ensembles. The authors assess existing and novel algorithms and report empirical performance across different tasks.

Conclusion: Distributional optimization provides a principled framework for joint training of model combinations, with different algorithmic implications for ensembles vs. adapter averaging, and the proposed methods show practical value across synthetic and real-world tasks including LLM fine-tuning.

Abstract: Combining predictions from different models can improve performance at machine learning tasks, but the training of the individual models and the rule used to combine them are typically chosen separately, and by ad hoc means. Recent advances in distributional optimisation (i.e. where the optimisation occurs over the set of probability distributions) offer an opportunity for principled joint training, viewing the collection of models as a discrete distribution whose support points are to be optimised, but the potential of these methods is not well-understood. In this paper we (1) cast two standard combination strategies - ensembles and low-rank adapter averaging - as entropy-regularised distributional optimisation, observing that the resulting objective is convex in the ensemble case but not in the adapter-averaging case, so that existing convergence guarantees for mean field Langevin dynamics transfer only to the former; (2) assess existing and novel algorithms for this task, including a functional variant of variational gradient descent; and (3) report an empirical study spanning synthetic classification tasks and fine-tuning of large language models on a commonsense reasoning benchmark.

</details>


### [326] [Pharmacokinetic State Space Models for Unbiased Prediction of Haemodynamic Collapse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24338)
*Rithin Nagaraj,Sudiksha Chindula,Bhaskarjyoti Das*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A Mamba-based model that uses drug infusion history to predict intraoperative hypotension achieves better performance than existing methods while maintaining constant memory usage, enabling practical clinical deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing IOH prediction models ignore valuable drug infusion history despite its direct pharmacological relevance, leading to reactive rather than predictive clinical management of this serious complication.

Method: A Mamba-based architecture that incorporates drug infusion history (propofol and remifentanil effect-site concentrations) with lead-gap filtering to prevent learning ongoing hypotension patterns rather than predicting future events.

Result: The model achieves AUROC of 0.7360 and AUPRC of 0.1794 (2.73x over random baseline), with drug features contributing 13.9% performance gain and lead-gap filtering preventing 16.7% AUROC degradation.

Conclusion: Drug infusion history encodes predictive hemodynamic information, and Mamba-based architectures offer practical advantages over Transformers for continuous intraoperative prediction due to constant memory footprint.

Abstract: An Intraoperative Hypotension (IOH) event is a frequent complication during administration of general anaesthesia with serious downstream consequences, yet clinical management remains reactive and not predictive. Existing predictive models, however, ignore drug infusion history as a valuable signal for prediction despite its direct pharmacological relevance. Our model achieves an Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.7360 and an Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve (AUPRC) of 0.1794, representing a 2.73-fold lift over the random guessing AUPRC baseline (0.0657), with the removal of propofol and remifentanil effect-site concentrations resulting in a 13.9% AUPRC drop compared to the full model. This is consistent with the hypothesis that pharmacokinetic trajectories encode impending haemodynamic changes before they manifest in the Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP). Additionally, this paper shows that training without lead-gap filtering degraded AUROC by 16.7%, empirically confirming that unfiltered models learn to detect ongoing hypotension rather than predict future events. Finally, a Mamba-based architecture achieves the aforementioned high prediction performance while maintaining a constant memory footprint across a range of sequence lengths, unlike the quadratic VRAM overhead typical of vanilla Transformers, making it the more practical choice for continuous intraoperative deployment.

</details>


### [327] [Explainable Neuro-Fuzzy Prediction for Trustworthy Decision-Making in Maritime](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24358)
*Dionisis Kalogeropoulos,Georgia Sovatzidi,Dimitris K. Iakovidis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A neuro-fuzzy explainable decision-making framework for maritime maintenance prediction that combines deep learning with two-stage explainability (feature attribution and local rules) for trustworthy AI.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Predicting when maritime systems require maintenance is critical to avoid hazards and costly consequences. There's a need for trustworthy AI systems in safety-critical maritime applications where users need to understand machine inferences.

Method: Proposes an explainable decision-making framework integrating a neuro-fuzzy prediction model with a two-stage explainable component: 1) feature-attribution explanations using gradient-based saliency maps, and 2) local rule extraction using a fuzzy decision tree. The framework is generic and can integrate with any deep learning approach.

Result: The framework demonstrates superior performance with average AUC-ROC values reaching up to 99% on public benchmark datasets, outperforming state-of-the-art approaches. Successfully applied to early fault detection in a naval propulsion system dataset.

Conclusion: This represents the first fuzzy logic-based framework enabling both feature-level and local rule-based explanations of black box models, providing trustworthy predictions with explainability for maritime maintenance applications.

Abstract: Predicting when maritime systems require maintenance can be critical, avoiding hazards and costly consequences. To address this problem, this paper proposes an explainable decision-making framework that integrates a neuro-fuzzy prediction model with a two-stage explainable component. The first stage of this component produces feature-attribution explanations, using gradient-based saliency maps, and the second stage extracts local rules using a fuzzy decision tree. The proposed framework is generic and can be integrated into any deep learning-based approach, rendering it explainable. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first fuzzy logic-based framework enabling both feature-level and local rule-based explanations of black box models. This approach aims to foster trustworthiness in decision making through user-understandable machine inferences. The performance of the proposed framework using a deep residual-based neural backbone is evaluated on various general-purpose public benchmark datasets, and its utility in maritime is demonstrated in the context of early fault detection in a naval propulsion system dataset. The results indicate that it can provide predictions outperforming relevant state-of-the-art approaches, with an average AUC-ROC (Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve) value, reaching up to 99%, while offering the advantage of explainability.

</details>


### [328] [Prescriptive SVD-Inspired Attention via Spectral Energy Retention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24370)
*Vasileios Arampatzakis,Vasileios Sevetlidis,George Pavlidis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SVDA introduces a learned diagonal spectrum into self-attention, enabling diagnostic interpretation and operational intervention like spectral energy retention to reduce dimensions while maintaining accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard self-attention's dense dot-product formulation makes it difficult to identify structurally important internal directions and modify them without disrupting model performance.

Method: SVD-Inspired Attention (SVDA) with learned diagonal spectrum, enabling diagnostic interpretation through spectral entropy, effective rank, sparsity, alignment, selectivity, and perturbation response. A diagnosis-intervention-verification framework is proposed, with spectral energy retention intervention evaluated.

Result: Across FashionMNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Food-101, ρ=0.90 prescription removes 24.5-53.7% of score directions, reduces parameters by 2.6-4.3%, reduces estimated MACs by 2.8-5.4%, with minimal accuracy changes (-0.03 to +0.05 percentage points).

Conclusion: SVDA serves as an intrinsically interpretable attention mechanism whose learned spectrum exposes an operational coordinate system for deterministic and verifiable modification of attention-score formation.

Abstract: Self-attention is central to modern Transformer architectures, but its dense dot-product formulation makes it difficult to identify which internal directions are structurally important and which can be modified without disrupting the model. SVD-Inspired Attention (SVDA) addresses part of this problem by introducing a learned diagonal spectrum into the query-key score interaction, making latent attention directions explicitly inspectable through indicators such as spectral entropy, effective rank, sparsity, alignment, selectivity, and perturbation response. This paper examines the transition from diagnostic interpretation to operational intervention. A diagnosis--intervention--verification framework is proposed, and one intervention is evaluated: spectral energy retention in the attention-score pathway. Across FashionMNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Food-101, the $ρ=0.90$ prescription removes 24.5--53.7\% of score directions, reduces parameters by 2.6--4.3\%, and reduces estimated MACs by 2.8--5.4\%. The paired mean accuracy change of the dimension-reduced model ranges from $-0.03$ to $+0.05$ percentage points over three seeds. These results support SVDA as an intrinsically interpretable attention mechanism whose learned spectrum exposes an operational coordinate system for deterministic and verifiable modification of attention-score formation.

</details>


### [329] [Credit Access is Associated with Improved Food Security in the Horn of Africa](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24382)
*Jordi Cerdà-Bautista,Vasileios Sitokonstantinou,José Manuel Veiga López-Peña,Duccio Piovani,José María Tárraga,Gustau Camps-Valls*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Credit access reduces acute food insecurity by 2% in Somalia and Horn of Africa, with meaningful impact on vulnerable populations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Climate change threatens food security, especially in vulnerable communities, creating need to understand how financial access affects food security in crisis-affected settings where randomized evaluations are difficult.

Method: Observational machine-learning framework estimating causal association between credit access and food insecurity using harmonized dataset (2015-2022) of environmental, socioeconomic, and conflict factors. Includes identification assumptions, robustness tests, and refutation tests.

Result: Greater credit access associated with 2% reduction in acute food insecurity at population level. Given 16% of population typically in crisis, this represents meaningful shift within at-risk group.

Conclusion: Provides context-specific evidence on financial access-food security correlation in data-scarce, crisis-affected settings, and offers transparent framework for integrating heterogeneous data when randomized evaluations are infeasible.

Abstract: The intensification of climate change poses a growing threat to food security, especially in vulnerable communities. This study employs an observational machine-learning framework to estimate the causal association between access to credit and acute food insecurity in Somalia and across the Horn of Africa, drawing on a harmonized dataset spanning key environmental, socioeconomic, and conflict-related factors from 2015 to 2022. Results indicate that greater credit access is associated with a 2% reduction in acute food insecurity at the population level over the study period. Given that, on average, 16% of the population is in crisis, this effect represents a meaningful shift within the at-risk group. We interpret these estimates under explicit identification assumptions and complement them with robustness and refutation tests. The results provide context-specific evidence on how financial access correlates with food security outcomes in data-scarce, crisis-affected settings, and offer a transparent framework for integrating heterogeneous data sources when randomized evaluations are infeasible.

</details>


### [330] [Machine Learning-Based Prediction of Childhood Stunting in Bangladesh: Fairness and Temporal Robustness Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24386)
*Md Ahshanul Haque,Muhammad Ashad Kabir*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Machine learning models were developed for predicting childhood stunting in Bangladesh using national survey data, with TabPFN showing best performance but varying results across time periods and subgroups.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Childhood stunting remains a major public health concern in Bangladesh, influenced by multiple factors. There's a need for accurate prediction models that consider temporal robustness and fairness across different population subgroups.

Method: Used nationally representative Bangladesh Demographic and Health Survey data (2007-2022). Included children 0-59 months with complete anthropometric data. Used 2007, 2011, 2014 for model development and 2018, 2022 for temporal testing. Evaluated 12 feature-selection approaches and 11 ML models including TabPFN and conventional algorithms. Assessed performance with multiple metrics and examined subgroup fairness by sex, residence, and socioeconomic status.

Result: TabPFN showed highest balanced accuracy (67.58%) in development test, while Gradient Boosting performed best in 2018 and XGBoost in 2022 temporal testing. Model performance varied across survey rounds and subgroups, with 35.05% stunting prevalence in the analytic sample of 18,844 children.

Conclusion: The study highlights the importance of temporal validation, subgroup fairness assessment, and transparent interpretation in public health prediction modeling. Model performance varies across time and population groups, emphasizing the need for careful validation practices in public health applications.

Abstract: Childhood stunting remains a major public health concern in Bangladesh and reflects long-term growth failure influenced by child, maternal, household, socioeconomic, and health-service factors. This study used nationally representative Bangladesh Demographic and Health Survey data from 2007 to 2022 to develop machine learning models for population-level prediction of childhood stunting and to assess temporal robustness and subgroup fairness. Children aged 0-59 months with complete anthropometric and predictor data were included. Data from the 2007, 2011, and 2014 survey rounds were used for model development, while the 2018 and 2022 rounds were retained as temporal test datasets. Twelve feature-selection approaches were assessed, and the KNN permutation importance-selected predictor set was used for final model evaluation. Eleven machine learning models were evaluated: ten conventional algorithms and one pretrained tabular foundation model, TabPFN. Performance was assessed using balanced accuracy, AUROC, F1-score, Brier score, and expected calibration error. Subgroup fairness was examined by child sex, place of residence, and socioeconomic status. The final analytic sample included 18,844 children, of whom 35.05% were stunted. In the development hold-out test dataset, TabPFN showed the highest observed balanced accuracy overall at 67.58%, while AdaBoost showed the highest observed balanced accuracy among conventional models at 67.51%. In temporal testing, the highest observed balanced accuracy was found for Gradient Boosting in BDHS 2018 and XGBoost in BDHS 2022. Model performance varied across survey rounds and subgroups, highlighting the importance of temporal validation, subgroup fairness assessment, and transparent interpretation in public health prediction modeling.

</details>


### [331] [NAVIR: Neuromorphic Audio-Visual Speech Recognition for Robust Human-Robot Interaction on Edge Hardware](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24391)
*Leonidas Delimpasis,Panagiota Moraiti,Antonis Porichis,Panos Chatzakos,Michail Karamousadakis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: NAVIR is an audio-visual speech recognition system designed for neuromorphic hardware that combines lip motion and audio cues to overcome industrial noise, achieving low energy consumption while maintaining accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Voice control in industrial settings faces acoustic noise that degrades audio-only speech recognition. Existing AVSR systems are too computationally expensive for edge devices, needing a solution that can operate efficiently on resource-constrained neuromorphic processors like BrainChip Akida.

Method: End-to-end AVSR system with separate spatial and temporal encoding modules: per-frame visual encoder, temporal video encoder, and spectrogram audio encoder, all based on AkidaNet architecture. Features are fused by lightweight predictor head and decoded with constrained beam search. Training uses connectionist temporal classification with noise-augmented audio followed by quantization-aware training fine-tuning.

Result: Quantized model achieves 14.0% WER under noise and 3.3% WER on speaker splits on GRID benchmark, outperforming audio-only baselines. Achieves 98.6% command accuracy on industrial corpus. Energy analysis shows 13-fold advantage over ANN counterparts, with 5-100x lower energy than conventional hardware while sustaining 14.5 inferences per second.

Conclusion: NAVIR successfully demonstrates a complete multimodal AVSR pipeline on neuromorphic hardware, achieving both improved accuracy over audio-only systems and significant energy efficiency advantages, making it suitable for edge deployment in noisy industrial environments.

Abstract: Voice-controlled interaction in industrial settings is hampered by acoustic noise, which severely degrades audio-only speech recognition. Audio-visual speech recognition (AVSR) addresses this by fusing lip-motion cues with the audio stream, but state-of-the-art pipelines rely on three-dimensional convolutions, recurrent units, and attention modules that exceed the budget of typical edge devices. We present NAVIR, an end-to-end AVSR system targeting the BrainChip Akida neuromorphic processor, which natively supports only sequential two-dimensional convolutional inference. The pipeline factorises spatial and temporal encoding into separate AkidaNet-based modules: a per-frame visual encoder, a temporal video encoder, and a spectrogram audio encoder, fused by a lightweight predictor head and decoded by constrained beam search. Models are trained with connectionist temporal classification on noise-augmented audio and then fine-tuned with quantization-aware training. On the GRID benchmark, the quantized audio-visual model reaches 14.0% word error rate (WER) under noise on the unseen-speaker split and 3.3% WER on the overlapped-speaker split, against 22.5% and 11.8% for audio-only baselines, and it attains 98.6% command accuracy at 1.5% WER on a task-specific industrial-command corpus. Operation-count analysis indicates a 13-fold energy advantage of the spiking formulation over its artificial neural network counterpart at 27.6% mean firing rate. On-board measurements show roughly 5-fold lower energy per inference than a Raspberry Pi central processing unit on the lip-reading model, and over 100-fold lower than a laptop graphics processing unit, while sustaining 14.5 inferences per second. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first complete multimodal AVSR pipeline running on neuromorphic hardware of this class.

</details>


### [332] [Climate Variability Modulates the Impact of Price Spikes on Food Insecurity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24394)
*Jordi Cerdà-Bautista,Vasileios Sitokonstantinou,Homer Durand,Gherardo Varando,Michele Ronco,Gustau Camps-Valls*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces "sensitivity regimes" - regions stratified by their vegetation response to El Niño - and shows how combining this climate context with price spikes can improve food security early warning and anticipatory action in sub-Saharan Africa.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite climate patterns like El Niño being predictable months in advance, they are not incorporated as an early-warning component in food-security responses, creating a gap in anticipating and preventing food crises.

Method: The study introduces "sensitivity regimes" to stratify regions by direction and strength of vegetation response to El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO). It integrates remote sensing, socioeconomic data, and causal machine learning to estimate how food price spikes affect acute food insecurity across different sensitivity regimes in sub-Saharan Africa.

Result: In regions where ENSO systematically suppresses vegetation, a price spike raises the share of population at acute risk by 5.4 percentage points in the following month. In regions where vegetation is unaffected by or positively linked to ENSO, the estimated effect is smaller (~2 percentage points) and statistically insignificant.

Conclusion: Climate context is critical for understanding food security vulnerabilities. Sensitivity regimes can be combined with price-spike triggers to stage anticipatory action: ENSO state flags vulnerable regions months ahead, enabling pre-positioned responses that avert the largest jumps in acute food insecurity.

Abstract: Climate variability influences whether a market disruption escalates into a food crisis, yet broad climate patterns like El Niño, tracked months before they alter hydro-climatic conditions, are still not incorporated as an early-warning component in food-security responses. We address this gap by introducing sensitivity regimes, a stratification of regions by the direction and strength of their vegetation response to the El Niño Southern Oscillation, and using them to estimate how food price spikes affect acute food insecurity across sub-Saharan Africa. Integrating remote sensing, socioeconomic data, and causal machine learning, we find that in regions where ENSO systematically suppresses vegetation, a price spike raises the share of the population at acute risk by 5.4 percentage points in the following month. In regions where vegetation is unaffected by or positively linked to ENSO, the estimated effect is smaller (around 2 percentage points) and statistically insignificant. These results demonstrate that climate context is critical for understanding food security vulnerabilities. Sensitivity regimes can be combined with operational price-spike triggers to stage anticipatory action: the ENSO state flags vulnerable regions months ahead, and a pre-positioned response in those regions to a price spike would avert the largest jump in acute food insecurity.

</details>


### [333] [Probabilistic Modelling of Operational Design Domains, A New Approach for Testing AI Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24397)
*Hans-Werner Wiesbrock*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A framework using probabilistically extended ontologies (PEONs) to create representative test sets for ML-based systems with statistical test evaluation methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional testing fails for ML-based systems because failures can't be fixed like traditional bugs, test results must be interpreted statistically, and comprehensive test sets covering the operational design domain (ODD) with representativeness are needed.

Method: Introduce Probabilistically Extended Ontologies (PEONs): ontologies describing the ODD augmented with probability distributions over the partitioning they induce, using marginal distributions and functionally described dependencies rather than conditional probability tables. Algorithms based on couplings and optimal transport complete this to a Bayesian network.

Result: From PEONs derive: representative test case sampling, rigorous end-of-test criteria for quality targets and significance levels, methods for re-evaluating existing test results, and assessing training data balance. Demonstrated practical modeling of complex ODD using automatic train operation example.

Conclusion: PEONs provide a principled approach to statistical testing of ML-based systems by creating representative test sets from ODD descriptions with probability distributions, enabling proper statistical interpretation of test results and systematic quality assessment.

Abstract: The conventional testing process quickly fails when applied to ML-based systems such as obstacle detection in vehicles: if an obstacle is not detected in a test, classical bug fixing is impossible and an AI system will always retain shortcomings. Test results can therefore only be interpreted statistically, which in turn requires test sets that are not only complete with respect to the operational design domain (ODD) of the system, but also representative of it. To this end, we introduce probabilistically extended ontologies (PEONs): ontologies describing the ODD, augmented with a probability distribution over the partitioning they induce. Instead of unmaintainable conditional probability tables, only marginal distributions and functionally described dependencies need to be specified; algorithms based on couplings and optimal transport complete this specification to a Bayesian network. From a PEON we derive the sampling of representative test cases, rigorous end-of-test criteria for given quality targets and significance levels, and methods for re-evaluating existing test results and for assessing the balance of training data. We demonstrate the practical modelling of a complex ODD using the example of automatic train operation.

</details>


### [334] [Prior-Amortized In-Context Bayesian Inference for Generalized Linear Mixed-Effects Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24422)
*Alex Kipnis,Marcel Binz,Eric Schulz*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MetaBeta is a pretrained neural network for fast, prior-amortized Bayesian inference over GLMMs that can generalize to new priors and datasets without retraining, achieving speedups of 2-3 orders of magnitude compared to NUTS.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bayesian inference for GLMMs using MCMC/NUTS is accurate but computationally expensive and must restart from scratch for every new dataset, model, and prior, limiting practical application.

Method: Uses a neural network architecture with two set transformers and conditional normalizing flows to capture the two-level posterior structure of GLMMs. Trained on millions of simulated datasets across continuous, binary, and count outcomes. Accepts prior families and hyperparameters as inputs for zero-shot generalization.

Result: MetaBeta matches NUTS in parameter recovery, calibration, and out-of-sample prediction on benchmarks. Provides inference 2-3 orders of magnitude faster than NUTS, works as a stand-alone sampler or to warm-start NUTS, and maintains fidelity across various challenging scenarios including misspecification and data-poor regimes.

Conclusion: MetaBeta enables fast, prior-amortized Bayesian inference over GLMMs with neural networks while maintaining the statistical guarantees of traditional MCMC methods, offering a practical solution for hierarchical data analysis.

Abstract: Hierarchical data is ubiquitous in the empirical sciences and is most commonly analyzed with generalized linear mixed-effects models (GLMMs). Bayesian inference for GLMMs yields calibrated uncertainty but requires MCMC; the No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS) is the gold standard but is slow and must restart from scratch for every new dataset, model and prior. We introduce metabeta, a pretrained neural network for prior-amortized in-context Bayesian inference over GLMMs. Unlike previous neural posterior estimators that fix the prior at training time, metabeta accepts prior families and hyperparameters as inputs at test time, enabling zero-shot generalization. Two set transformers and conditional normalizing flows mirror the posterior's two-level structure (global parameters shared across groups, local parameters per group). The model is trained on millions of realistic simulated datasets spanning continuous, binary, and count outcomes. By default, the flow posterior is refined by Independence Metropolis-Hastings against the unnormalized posterior, so its correctness rests on the sampler rather than the network; this yields tuning-free inference two to three orders of magnitude faster than NUTS. Alternatively, the flow can warm-start NUTS, giving nearly identical inference with substantially increased speed and stability. On controlled benchmarks with ground-truth parameters, metabeta matches NUTS in parameter recovery, calibration and out-of-sample prediction. On out-of-distribution real datasets, its posteriors closely match those of NUTS across all parameter types, and they remain faithful under misspecified likelihoods and priors, out-of-distribution predictors, collinear designs, and data-poor regimes. The model is open-source and open-weights and thus immediately deployable.

</details>


### [335] [1% of Tokens Can Be Enough: On Gradient Estimation in On-Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24432)
*Huanxin Sheng,Zhiling Ye,Haonan Wang,Jian Wang,Jinjie Gu,Jian Kang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces an Information-Efficiency Ratio (IER) to improve sparse on-policy distillation by considering both usefulness of teacher guidance and gradient estimation reliability, enabling better token selection with small token budgets (0.1%-1%).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses a limitation in sparse on-policy distillation (OPD) where useful teacher guidance can yield noisy updates when its gradient is estimated from sampled next tokens. This noise problem in gradient estimation motivates the development of a better token selection method.

Method: The authors study the gradient estimation problem in information geometry at a fixed prefix and propose an Information-Efficiency Ratio (IER) based on a signal-to-noise decomposition. They use a candidate-set approximation to enable token selection based on IER and combine it with existing usefulness scores while maintaining the sampled reverse-KL training objective.

Result: On mathematical and medical reasoning tasks, adding IER improves existing token selectors in multiple settings. Sparse configurations with IER match or exceed full OPD (without token selection) even at small token budgets of 0.1%-1%.

Conclusion: The results demonstrate that accounting for both usefulness and gradient-estimation reliability when allocating sparse supervision leads to better performance. The proposed IER method effectively addresses the noise problem in sparse OPD, enabling efficient token selection for knowledge distillation.

Abstract: Sparse on-policy distillation (OPD) allocates teacher supervision to a small subset of tokens in student-generated trajectories. However, useful teacher guidance can yield a noisy update when its gradient is estimated from a sampled next token. We study this estimation problem at a fixed prefix in information geometry and propose an information-efficiency ratio (IER) based on a signal-to-noise decomposition. IER characterizes relative gradient estimation error under an optimal scalar baseline. A candidate-set approximation enables token selection based on IER and its combination with existing usefulness scores, while retaining the sampled reverse-KL training objective. On mathematical and medical reasoning tasks, adding IER improves existing selectors in multiple settings, with sparse configurations matching or exceeding full OPD without token selection at small token budgets of 0.1\%--1\%. These results support accounting for both usefulness and gradient-estimation reliability when allocating sparse supervision. Our code is available at https://github.com/BruceSheng1202/IER-OPD.

</details>


### [336] [Comparing Latent Concept Formation in State Space Models and Transformers via Sparse Autoencoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24440)
*Rithin Nagaraj,Rupa Laalasa Oruganti,Prerna Subhashchandra Kunder,Ashwini M Joshi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SSMs like Mamba and Transformers don't show systematic representational divergence - 99.98% of their learned features align, supporting architectural universality for semantic understanding, with only 0.02% diverging features related to rigid syntax compression.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to investigate whether Selective State Space Models (SSMs like Mamba) and Transformers learn fundamentally different latent representations due to Mamba's recurrent bottleneck that compresses past context into a fixed-size state, raising questions about architectural representational divergence for mechanistic interpretability.

Method: The researchers use Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to conduct large-scale feature-level correspondence analysis between Mamba-130m and Pythia-70m models over a 10-million token corpus, examining feature alignment and divergence patterns.

Result: Contrary to expectations of widespread architectural divergence, 99.98% of Mamba features cluster toward the upper alignment boundary with Pythia features, showing no systematic representational divergence. Only 0.02% of features diverge, specifically related to rigid syntax parsing where Mamba compresses unrelated syntactical anomalies into polysemantic "junk drawer" neurons due to its state capacity limitations, while Pythia's attention mechanism can handle distinct formatting edge-cases separately.

Conclusion: Architectural routing mechanisms may have negligible impact on core semantic understanding, with representational divergence confined to extreme structural margins. The findings provide preliminary feature-level support for the Universality Hypothesis, suggesting that different architectures learn similar semantic representations despite their different computational mechanisms.

Abstract: The quadratic scaling of Transformer self-attention has driven the adoption of sub-quadratic Selective State Space Models (SSMs) like Mamba, which compress past context into a fixed-size recurrent hidden state. This strict informational bottleneck raises a foundational question for mechanistic interpretability: do SSMs and Transformers learn fundamentally distinct latent representations? In this work, we employ Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to conduct a large-scale, feature-level correspondence analysis between Mamba-130m and Pythia-70m over a 10-million token corpus. Contrary to hypotheses predicting widespread architectural divergence, we find no evidence of systematic representational divergence between architectures: across the observed Jaccard distribution, 99.98% of Mamba features cluster toward the upper alignment boundary, providing preliminary feature-level support for the Universality Hypothesis. We further identify and qualitatively characterize this microscopic fraction (0.02%) of diverging features, finding patterns consistent with the hypothesis that the recurrent bottleneck selectively limits the parsing of rigid syntax rather than broad semantic ontology. We demonstrate that while Pythia's unconstrained attention permits the monosemantic decomposition of distinct formatting edge-cases, Mamba is forced to compress unrelated syntactical anomalies into polysemantic "junk drawer" neurons to preserve state capacity. Collectively, these results suggest that architectural routing mechanisms may have negligible impact on core semantic understanding, with representational divergence confined to extreme structural margins.

</details>


### [337] [MUSE: Dependency-Aware Adaptation of a Frozen Vision Backbone for Multivariate Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24441)
*Xinying Cai,Junkai Lu,Yuhan Zhu,Xiaoyun Yu,Xiangfei Qiu,Jilin Hu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MUSE is a dependency-aware adaptation framework that uses frozen pretrained MAE for multivariate time-series forecasting by balancing independent visual representation spaces with cross-variable dependency modeling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large vision models (LVMs) offer promising cross-domain transfer to time-series forecasting, but face two key challenges: 1) balancing independent visual representation spaces with cross-variable dependency modeling, and 2) adapting vision backbones pretrained on natural images to the distinct temporal semantics of time-series images.

Method: Proposes MUSE with two main modules: Variable Context Refinement Module (VCR) aggregates shared temporal information within each variable and models cross-variable contextual dependencies while preserving independent visual spaces. Temporal-Periodic Refinement Module (TPR) performs lightweight refinement at different encoder depths and models across-period temporal dependencies and within-period periodic dependencies. Both modules independently produce forecasts fused through a learnable prediction-level gate.

Result: Experiments on 10 real-world datasets demonstrate that MUSE achieves state-of-the-art performance in multivariate time-series forecasting.

Conclusion: MUSE effectively addresses the challenges of adapting pretrained vision models to time-series forecasting through dependency-aware adaptation while keeping the pretrained backbone frozen, achieving superior forecasting performance.

Abstract: Multivariate time-series forecasting is essential to many real-world applications. Recent large vision models (LVMs) offer a promising paradigm by transferring cross-domain visual priors to time-series forecasting. However, existing LVM-based methods face two key challenges: balancing independent visual representation spaces with cross-variable dependency modeling, and adapting vision backbones pretrained on natural images to the distinct temporal semantics of time-series images. To address these challenges, we propose MUSE, a dependency-aware adaptation framework built on a fully frozen pretrained MAE. First, the Variable Context Refinement Module (VCR) aggregates shared temporal information within each variable and models cross-variable contextual dependencies while preserving independent visual spaces. Second, the Temporal-Periodic Refinement Module (TPR) performs lightweight refinement at different encoder depths and explicitly models across-period temporal dependencies and within-period periodic dependencies. The two modules independently produce forecasts, which are fused through a learnable prediction-level gate. Experiments on 10 real-world datasets demonstrate that MUSE achieves state-of-the-art performance.

</details>


### [338] [RAILS: Retrieval-Augmented Incremental LLM Clustering at Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24464)
*Armin Oliya,Aleksandra Sawczuk,Radosław Białobrzeski*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RAILS is a retrieval-augmented incremental LLM clustering system that scales document clustering through batching and incremental label pool management, outperforming previous LLM-clustering methods on multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Using LLMs for production-scale document clustering faces challenges: prompts can't hold entire label spaces, and serial per-document processing lacks necessary throughput for real workloads.

Method: RAILS converts clustering into a loop over a growing label pool, scales through document batching with bounded concurrency, and uses a retrieval-augmented incremental approach to manage the label space efficiently.

Result: On six public benchmarks, RAILS outperforms the strongest prior LLM-clustering method, improving accuracy from 51.2% to 59.3%, NMI from 67.2% to 74.8%, and ARI from 45.4% to 54.7%. In a SaaS ticket-topic-discovery pipeline, it replaced HDBSCAN with higher quality and transparent prompt-driven control.

Conclusion: RAILS provides a scalable, high-performance LLM-based clustering solution suitable for production deployment, addressing throughput limitations while maintaining quality and offering transparent control through prompts.

Abstract: Using a Large Language Model (LLM) as the clusterer at production scale is hard: prompts cannot hold the entire label space, and per-document serial processing does not deliver the throughput real workloads require. We present RAILS, a retrieval-augmented incremental LLM clusterer that turns clustering into a simple loop over a growing label pool and scales through document batching with bounded concurrency. On six public benchmarks RAILS exceeds the strongest prior LLM-clustering method on average, lifting accuracy from 51.2% to 59.3%, NMI from 67.2% to 74.8%, and ARI from 45.4% to 54.7%. We further report production-deployment evidence from a SaaS ticket-topic-discovery pipeline, where RAILS has replaced a traditional HDBSCAN stage with higher clustering quality, transparent prompt-driven control, and stateful incremental operation.

</details>


### [339] [A Temporal Knowledge Graph for Music Festival Lineup Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24467)
*Julia Gastinger,Thilo Dieing,Christian Meilicke,Heiner Stuckenschmidt*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Music festival lineup prediction using temporal knowledge graphs, with new dataset and evaluation of TKG models vs LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Music festival lineups result from complex temporal relationships among artists, genres, releases, labels, and past performances, making this a natural application for temporal knowledge graph forecasting that complements existing benchmarks.

Method: Created a temporal knowledge graph covering 380 festivals over 55 years with 90K festival performance quadruples, formalized lineup forecasting as temporal link prediction, and evaluated six TKG forecasting models against zero-shot Large Language Models.

Result: The paper presents a new TKG dataset as a resource for forecasting evaluation, assesses capabilities and limitations of six TKG models on festival lineup prediction, and compares them against LLMs applied zero-shot.

Conclusion: The resource grounds TKG evaluation in a concrete real-world application domain, complementing existing benchmarks while enabling future research in music festival lineup forecasting and temporal knowledge graph applications.

Abstract: Music festival lineups emerge from complex relationships among artists, genres, releases, labels, and past performances, making the prediction of future lineups a natural fit for temporal knowledge graph (TKG) forecasting. In this work, we present a TKG covering 380 festivals over 55 years, comprising more than 90K festival performance quadruples along with information on festivals, artist tours, and artist metadata, and release it as a resource for TKG forecasting evaluation. We formalize festival lineup forecasting as temporal link prediction between artists and festivals at future timestamps. We evaluate six TKG forecasting models on this task, analyze their capabilities and limitations, and compare them against Large Language Models applied zero-shot. Our resource complements existing TKG benchmarks by grounding evaluation in a concrete, real-world application domain.

</details>


### [340] [Universal Multi-Modal Traceformer: Integrating Heterogeneous Context for Process Event Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24579)
*Fabian Spaeh,Jingxing Fang,Shandian Zhe,Bin Shen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: UMT is a Transformer-based framework that incorporates heterogeneous multi-modal context (numerical, categorical, textual, metadata) into event sequence prediction, improving next-event activity and time forecasting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing event-sequence models focus only on event activities and timestamps, overlooking the rich heterogeneous contextual information (numerical measurements, categorical attributes, textual descriptions, metadata) that accompanies real-world event logs, limiting their predictive capabilities.

Method: UMT uses a Transformer backbone with: 1) Universal feature encoder to map diverse feature types into shared representation space, handling context at event and trace levels; 2) Per-event Perceiver module to dynamically weight and integrate contextual features; 3) Multi-scale interval representation for heavy-tailed inter-arrival times with joint scale-specific predictions.

Result: Experiments on 13 real-world event logs demonstrate that UMT improves both next-event activity and time prediction over existing approaches.

Conclusion: UMT provides a unified framework for incorporating heterogeneous multi-modal context into event sequence prediction, significantly enhancing predictive performance by effectively modeling diverse contextual information and complex temporal distributions.

Abstract: Event logs arise in a wide range of real-world processes, capturing not only event activities and timestamps but also multi-modal contextual information. Existing event-sequence models, including many temporal point process approaches, primarily model event activities and timestamps while overlooking heterogeneous context, such as numerical measurements, categorical attributes, textual descriptions, and metadata associated with individual events and entire traces. In this paper, we propose Universal Multi-Modal Traceformer (UMT), a unified framework for incorporating heterogeneous process context into next-event prediction. Built on a Transformer backbone, UMT introduces a universal feature encoder that maps diverse feature types into a shared representation space and handles contextual information at both the event and trace levels. UMT further develops a per-event Perceiver module that dynamically weights contextual features and adaptively integrates them into event-token representations. To accommodate the heavy-tailed and potentially multi-modal distribution of inter-arrival times, UMT represents each interval at multiple temporal scales and jointly predicts the corresponding scale-specific quantities. Experiments on 13 real-world event logs show that UMT improves both next-event activity and time prediction over existing approaches.

</details>


### [341] [Taking a Second Look: Correcting Sea Ice Forecasts with Sparse Observations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24591)
*Tianshuo Zhang,Xianglei Xing,Aowen Yang,Jia Gao,Wenzhe Zhai,ShanShan Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ECHO introduces state-dependent error propagation for sea ice forecasting, outperforming fixed propagation methods across diverse conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sea ice forecasts suffer from accumulating errors over time, while new SIC observations are sparse. Fixed propagation methods don't account for the spatial variability of errors, which concentrate near high-gradient ice edges while homogeneous interiors need minimal propagation.

Method: Introduces ECHO (Evidence-guided Correction with Heterogeneous prOpagation) with two variants: ECHO-Scale adapts propagation distance while preserving correction geometry, and ECHO-Delta learns a bounded residual around fixed propagation. Both methods make propagation distance state-dependent rather than fixed.

Result: Both ECHO variants outperform fixed propagation across all 96 standard evaluation settings spanning diverse priors, observation times, sparsity levels, geometries, and noise conditions. ECHO-Delta achieves the best average accuracy, while ECHO-Scale is more robust to geometry shifts.

Conclusion: State-dependent error propagation (ECHO) significantly improves sea ice forecasting accuracy compared to fixed propagation methods. Different ECHO variants offer trade-offs between accuracy and robustness, making them suitable for different operational scenarios.

Abstract: Sea ice forecasts are issued several days ahead, allowing errors to accumulate while new, often sparse sea ice concentration (SIC) observations become available. We find that fixed-propagation errors concentrate near structured, high-gradient ice edges, whereas homogeneous interiors require limited propagation, suggesting that propagation distance should be state dependent. We therefore introduce ECHO (Evidence-guided Correction with Heterogeneous prOpagation), where ECHO-Scale adapts propagation distance while preserving correction geometry, and ECHO-Delta learns a bounded residual around fixed propagation. Across all 96 standard evaluation settings spanning diverse priors, observation times, sparsity levels, geometries, and noise conditions, both outperform fixed propagation. ECHO-Delta achieves the best average accuracy, while ECHO-Scale is more robust to geometry shifts. Code is available at https://github.com/yingtian22/TAKING-A-SECOND-LOOK.

</details>


### [342] [Muon Can Outperform Dedicated Continual Learning Methods](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24678)
*Sebastian George Sincari,Bogdan Alexandru Gheorghe,Antonio Barbalau*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: IncLoRA with Muon optimizer matches specialized CL methods on Standard CL Benchmark and outperforms AdamW on TRACE by using orthogonal updates that spread energy across more singular directions rather than constraining update directions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current continual learning with LoRA methods mitigate forgetting by penalizing overlap between new updates and past weights, which restricts update directions without controlling how update energy is distributed. The authors question whether such task-aware restrictions are necessary or if a generic orthogonalization mechanism from the optimizer is sufficient.

Method: Train plain incremental LoRA (IncLoRA) with Muon optimizer, which orthogonalizes each update, and compare against O-LoRA and ELLA methods. Evaluate across five seeds and three task orders on Standard CL Benchmark, and three seeds on TRACE. Analyze update geometry differences between Muon and AdamW optimizers.

Result: IncLoRA+Muon reaches the accuracy band of dedicated CL methods on Standard CL Benchmark and improves on every AdamW configuration on TRACE. Muon spreads updates over 7.0 effective singular directions while AdamW confines updates to 1.4-1.8 directions, with no overlap in tracked runs. A second update-constraining mechanism doesn't help and can cost 8.4 points of accuracy and plasticity.

Conclusion: One update-constraining mechanism (either from loss or optimizer) is sufficient for continual learning. The advantage of dedicated CL methods may be partly explained by the geometry of optimizer updates rather than specialized task-aware mechanisms. Orthogonalization through the optimizer (Muon) can achieve comparable performance to dedicated CL methods.

Abstract: Continual learning with Low-Rank Adapters (LoRA) typically mitigates forgetting by penalizing the overlap between a new update and the accumulated past weights, which discourages certain update directions without controlling how an update distributes its energy over the ones that remain. We ask whether that restriction has to be task-aware, or whether a generic one supplied by the optimizer is enough. We train a plain incremental LoRA (IncLoRA) with Muon, which orthogonalizes each update, and compare it against O-LoRA and ELLA over five seeds and three task orders on the Standard CL Benchmark and three seeds on TRACE. IncLoRA+Muon reaches the accuracy band of the dedicated methods on Standard CL and improves on every AdamW configuration on TRACE. One update-constraining mechanism is enough, whether it comes from the loss or from the optimizer; on Standard CL a second one does not help, and for the most restrictive method it costs 8.4 points of accuracy and the plasticity to fit each task. What separates the two optimizers is not the size of the update, which under Muon is 0.91 to 2.06 times that under AdamW, but how it is distributed. AdamW confines it to between 1.4 and 1.8 effective singular directions, Muon spreads it over 7.0, and the two do not overlap in any tracked run. Part of the advantage usually attributed to dedicated CL methods may therefore be explained by the geometry of the optimizer's updates.

</details>


### [343] [Guaranteed Low-Rank Tensor Recovery from Modewise Measurements via Normalized Block-Weighted Riemannian Gradient Descent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24679)
*Yushi Zhou,Feng Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes an adaptive block-weighted modewise Riemannian gradient descent method for efficient recovery of low-rank tensors from linear measurements, achieving faster convergence with memory-efficient operations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To develop an efficient method for recovering low-multilinear-rank tensors from linear measurements that addresses challenges of convergence speed, computational efficiency, and recovery reliability near recovery thresholds.

Method: An adaptive block-weighted modewise Riemannian gradient descent method that combines memory-efficient modewise measurements with normalized adaptive weighting for core and factor components. The weighting strategy improves convergence without increasing multilinear-rank bounds or retraction core size.

Result: Establishes local linear convergence under tensor restricted isometry property with suitable initialization, derives sampling guarantees for sub-Gaussian and SORS measurements. Numerical experiments show reduced iteration counts and computational time while maintaining reliable recovery performance.

Conclusion: The proposed adaptive block-weighted method provides an efficient solution for low-rank tensor recovery with improved convergence speed and computational efficiency, particularly effective near recovery thresholds and for structured SORS measurements.

Abstract: We consider the recovery of low-multilinear-rank tensors from linear measurements and propose an adaptive block-weighted modewise Riemannian gradient descent method. The method combines memory-efficient modewise measurements with a normalized adaptive weighting strategy for the core and factor components of the Riemannian gradient. The weighting improves convergence without increasing the multilinear-rank bound of the search direction or the size of the reduced core used for retraction. Under the tensor restricted isometry property and a suitable initialization, we establish local linear convergence and derive sampling guarantees for sub-Gaussian and subsampled orthogonal with random sign (SORS) measurements. Numerical experiments on synthetic low-Tucker-rank tensors show that the proposed method reduces iteration counts and computational time while maintaining reliable recovery performance, especially near the recovery threshold and for structured SORS measurements.

</details>


### [344] [A Federated Artificial Intelligence Framework for Optimizing Pancreatic Cancer Treatment - Strategy Update](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24718)
*Anne-Christin Hauschild,Amirreza Aleyasin,Nils H. Beyer,Lisa Fricke,Jonas Hügel,Maryam Moradpour,Anh-Tien Nguyen,Youngjun Park,Sophia Rheinländer,Tim Beissbarth,Elisabeth Hessmann,Martin Middeke,Matthias Lauth,Maximilian Reichert,Ulrich Sax*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Federated Learning enables GDPR-compliant AI development for pancreatic cancer analysis across distributed sites using Docker containers and novel algorithms that handle partially overlapping features, though scaling to more sites remains challenging.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Centralized data collection for AI in healthcare faces GDPR compliance challenges. Federated Learning offers a practical alternative to access distributed disease-related resources while maintaining data privacy for applications like pancreatic cancer subtype identification and treatment assessment.

Method: Using Docker containers as local FL hubs with centrally developed FL scripts that generate local models. Applying a novel FL algorithm that handles partially overlapping features specific to local sites, leveraging data extracted and annotated using the German oncology core data set (oBDS).

Result: Successfully addressed major roadblocks including infrastructure operational concepts, ethics approval for novel architectures, and site support. Preliminary results show FL algorithms work robustly with partially overlapping features (demonstrated on public datasets). FL architecture allows GDPR-compliant collaboration across sites.

Conclusion: The federated learning approach shows promise for GDPR-compliant healthcare AI development, but scaling to more sites presents significant challenges despite successful initial implementation and overcoming major administrative/technical hurdles.

Abstract: While a centralized approach involving patient consent to collect and analyze data centrally would theoretically offer the best data quality and predictive performance, it is not always feasible in practice. Federated Learning (FL) architectures have shown to be a very promising approach to use and access distributed disease related resources within the GDPR boundaries. In a previous case report, we described the preconditions at the participating sites and necessary administrative and process related steps to prepare data, people and infrastructure for improving subtype identification and assessing treatment options in pancreatic cancer. We update this report sharing our experience in tackling the challenges and show preliminary results of the actual federated learning AI pipelines. At the participating sites, we have to identify and annotate the data being accessible after extraction and transformation in a local FL hub - in our case a centrally developed and distributively deployed Docker container. This container comprises the FL scripts generating local models. We apply a newly developed FL algorithm considering all local features, including partial overlapping features specific to the local sites. Theoretically, an annotation in a cancer setting should succeed using the German oncology core data set (oBDS), which is already utilized for mandatory reporting to cancer registries, and can be sustained in the FL setting. The FL algorithms deal robustly with partially overlapping features as we showed with public data sets. Major roadblocks including straightening operational concepts for the infrastructures, ethics approval for such novel architectures and support for every site have been addressed. However, scaling up this approach in the future faces hurdles; while including broader multi-modal data sets should be feasible, large-scale deployment to more sites remains challenging.

</details>


### [345] [An Exact Junction-Tree Extended Formulation for Optimal Classification Trees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24741)
*Jiancheng TU,WenqiFan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Exact linear programming formulation for optimal classification trees using junction-tree representation, with significant performance improvements over existing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Need for optimal classification trees with exact solutions, as existing methods face scalability issues and difficulty certifying optimality within computational limits.

Method: Develops integral LP formulation using junction-tree representation, applies exact reductions to shrink model size, and implements two solution methods: column generation and message passing that exploit parallelizable subtree optimization.

Result: Exact reductions significantly reduce formulation size; LP formulation certifies instances where MIP fails; column generation and message passing certify more instances and achieve order-of-magnitude speedup over state-of-the-art exact methods.

Conclusion: The junction-tree LP formulation with exact reductions and specialized solution methods provides a scalable, certifiably optimal approach for bounded-depth classification trees that outperforms existing exact methods.

Abstract: We develop an exact linear programming (LP) formulation for bounded-depth classification trees with binary features, using a junction-tree representation. The formulation is integral and supports recursive subtree optimization. Exact reductions make the model smaller while preserving the optimal value and recovery of an optimal tree. The reduced model supports two solution methods: column generation and message passing. Column generation solves integral restricted LPs and uses bounds over the full feasible domain to certify optimality. Message passing recursively combines optimal subtree costs. Both methods solve common subtree problems that, once the preceding tree decisions are fixed, can be evaluated independently and in parallel. Computational experiments show that the exact reductions substantially reduce the size of the junction-tree formulation. The resulting linear programming formulation certifies instances for which the tested mixed-integer formulation does not establish optimality within the same computational budget, while the column-generation and message-passing methods certify more instances and achieve an order-of-magnitude reduction in geometric-mean runtime relative to an existing state-of-the-art exact method for optimal classification trees.

</details>


### [346] [Inference of Unknown Dynamical Components Using Next Generation Reservoir Computing: From Chaotic Systems to Climate Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24754)
*Jule Budnick,Andrew Keane,Serhiy Yanchuk*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: NGRC outperforms traditional RC for inferring unseen system components, requiring less data and computation while maintaining accuracy, with applications validated on both simulated and real-world climate data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses the need for efficient data-driven methods to infer unseen components of dynamical systems from limited observable variables, which is important for understanding complex systems where full state measurements may not be available.

Method: The study compares Next Generation Reservoir Computing (NGRC) with traditional Reservoir Computing (RC) using two benchmark systems (Lorenz and Rössler) where two unknown components are inferred from one given component. The approach involves analyzing the relationship between time-delayed steps and temporal resolution, and extends the method to real-world ENSO climate data to infer one observable from remaining variables.

Result: NGRC achieves accurate inference results while requiring fewer training data and less computational time than RC. An inverse proportional relationship was identified between needed time-delayed steps and temporal resolution. Despite noise and complexity in real-world ENSO data, NGRC shows promising inference capabilities.

Conclusion: The findings demonstrate NGRC's potential for efficient inference of unseen components in both controlled dynamical systems and real-world applications, with practical implications for climate science and other complex system analysis domains.

Abstract: We investigate next generation reservoir computing (NGRC) as a data-driven approach for inferring unseen components of dynamical systems. We compare NGRC with traditional reservoir computing (RC) using the Lorenz and Rössler system, where two unknown components are inferred from one given component. For both systems, NGRC achieves accurate results while requiring fewer training data and less computational time than RC. We identified an inverse proportional behavior between the number of time-delayed steps needed for NGRC and the temporal resolution, indicating that the physical time span covered by the delay interval is an important factor in determining the required number of delayed steps. Finally, we apply NGRC to the observational climate data of ENSO (El Niño--Southern Oscillation) and infer one observable from the remaining variables. Despite the noise and complexity of the real-world data, the NGRC shows promising results. Our findings demonstrate the potential of NGRC for efficient inference of unseen components in both controlled dynamical systems and real-world data.

</details>


### [347] [Complex KDA: Understanding and Enhancing the Expressivity of Kimi Delta Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24797)
*Julien Siems,Riccardo Grazzi,Korbinian Pöppel,Jaisidh Singh,Arber Zela,Timur Carstensen,Jenia Jitsev,Frank Hutter,Volkan Cevher,Antonio Orvieto,Aaron Klein*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Complex KDA (CKDA) extends Kimi Delta Attention to realize 2D rotations by combining delta-rule transformations with reflection gates, achieving better expressivity while maintaining efficiency and stability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Linear RNNs based on delta-rule have limited expressivity due to linear updates with low-rank correction. While composing two delta-rule transitions can model 2D rotations, this increases rank and computational cost. The authors aim to achieve similar expressivity more efficiently.

Method: Extend KDA by combining two range extensions: allowing gates in [-1,1] and delta-rule coefficient β in [0,2]. This creates Complex KDA (CKDA) which combines a single delta-rule transformation with channel-wise reflection gates, preserving diagonal-plus-rank-one structure and non-expansiveness.

Result: CKDA achieves the state-tracking expressivity of DeltaProduct₂ with one fewer layer, can track every finite group isomorphic to SO(3) subgroups, and shows strongest length extrapolation on S₃, S₄, and periodic audio tasks. In language modeling, it outperforms Transformers and other linear RNNs while matching KDA baseline performance.

Conclusion: CKDA successfully combines efficiency and expressivity by extending parameter ranges of KDA, enabling 2D rotations while maintaining stability and diagonal-plus-rank-one structure, making it a promising approach for sequence modeling with good scaling behavior.

Abstract: Linear RNNs based on the delta-rule enable efficient sequence modeling, but their linear updates with a low-rank correction constrain their expressivity. Prior work has shown that composing two delta-rule transitions in a single recurrent update can model a 2D rotation, but this increases the rank and the cost of the updates compared to a single transition. We show that Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) can realize 2D rotations by combining a single delta-rule transformation with a second reflection supplied by its channel-wise gate. This requires extending the parameter ranges of KDA by combining two existing range extensions: allowing gates in $[-1,1]$ and the delta-rule coefficient $β$ in $[0,2]$. We call the resulting model Complex KDA (CKDA). It preserves KDA's stability and efficiency, with transitions that remain diagonal-plus-rank-one and non-expansive, while reaching the state-tracking expressivity of DeltaProduct$_2$. We characterize the expressivity of CKDA and prove that every orthogonal diagonal-plus-rank-one matrix is exactly a CKDA transition matrix. A single CKDA layer can track every finite group isomorphic to a subgroup of $\mathrm{SO}(3)$, and many state-tracking results use one fewer layer for CKDA compared to other diagonal-plus-rank-one Linear RNNs. Empirically, combining both extensions yields the strongest length extrapolation among tested KDA range settings on $S_3$, $S_4$, and periodic audio continuation. In language modeling, CKDA outperforms Transformers and other linear RNNs, obtains similar results to a KDA baseline, and shows promising scaling behavior. Our code is open source at https://github.com/OpenEuroLLM/ComplexKDA and our models are available at https://huggingface.co/collections/openeurollm/complexkda.

</details>


### [348] [G-NAC: Graph Neural Automata Clustering via Emergent Domain Formation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24823)
*Keith Miller,Tristan Crawford*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: G-NAC is an unsupervised graph clustering method that uses recurrent graph-neural cellular rules on fixed neighborhood graphs to evolve latent states, then converts them into spectral affinity for partitioning, achieving state-of-the-art performance on 73 clustering tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper introduces a novel approach to unsupervised clustering that leverages graph-structured data and cellular automata concepts, aiming to develop a method that can handle large-scale graph data with good scalability while maintaining competitive clustering performance.

Method: G-NAC treats observations as cells on a fixed neighborhood graph. It uses a shared recurrent graph-neural cellular rule to evolve latent domain states through local interactions between cells. These evolved states are then converted into a rank-based spectral affinity matrix for final partitioning.

Result: Across 73 clustering tasks from 57 benchmark datasets, G-NAC achieved mean ARI of 0.7951, comparable to Genie (0.7941) and higher than other baselines. The method showed linear scaling in training time and GPU memory from 5,000 to 100,000 nodes, and learned rules successfully transferred to independent 100,000-node samples.

Conclusion: The work demonstrates a successful recurrent graph-clustering formulation that achieves competitive performance with good scalability. However, the method's effectiveness depends on graph quality, readout design, and similarity between source and target graphs for successful transfer learning.

Abstract: We introduce Graph Neural Automata Clustering (G-NAC), an unsupervised clustering method in which observations interact as cells on a fixed neighborhood graph. A shared recurrent graph-neural cellular rule evolves latent domain states through local interactions, which are converted into a rank-based spectral affinity for partitioning. Across 73 clustering tasks from 57 benchmark datasets, G-NAC achieved a mean adjusted Rand index (ARI) of 0.7951, comparable to Genie at 0.7941 and higher than the other evaluated baselines. Empirical training time and GPU memory scaled approximately linearly from 5,000 to 100,000 nodes. Learned transition rules also transferred from smaller source graphs to independent 100,000-node samples generated under matched conditions. These results demonstrate a recurrent graph-clustering formulation while identifying dependencies on graph quality, readout design, and source-target similarity.

</details>


### [349] [Learning Prognostic Variables for AI Convective Parameterizations via Symbolic Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24882)
*Jurij Schönfeld,Tom Beucler,Julien Savre,Steven Sherwood,Veronika Eyring*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces a memory-enhanced prognostic parameterization approach for climate modeling that learns prognostic memory variables to carry past information, improving climate statistics and temporal structure compared to local-in-time diagnostic parameterizations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current hybrid AI-physics climate models use local-in-time diagnostic parameterizations that lack memory of previous states, which is unrealistic for processes like convection that have intrinsic persistence. This limitation reduces model accuracy for temporally-dependent processes.

Method: 1) Compress past information into low-dimensional latent space using autoencoder. 2) Train neural network to parameterize subgrid processes using latent representations. 3) Replace autoencoder with symbolic equations governing latent variable evolution, creating additional prognostic memory variables integrated alongside resolved atmospheric state.

Result: The memory-informed approach improves climate statistics and temporal structure compared to diagnostic parameterizations without memory. A forced multivariate linear ordinary differential equation recovers most of the added value achieved by autoencoder-based approach. Method demonstrates realistic diurnal cycle of tropical land precipitation.

Conclusion: Prognostic memory variables can effectively enhance hybrid AI-physics climate models by carrying important past information, leading to improved representation of temporally-dependent processes like convection and precipitation cycles, with symbolic equations providing efficient implementation.
